title: G6 cannot see a Django .update() on an immutable model - it matches TABLE names, and the ORM says Invoice
surface: gate
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: G6 forbids raw UPDATE/DELETE naming invoices/invoice_lines/payments/journal_entries/journal_lines. Django code says Invoice.objects.filter(...).update(...) - SINGULAR model name, no table name on the line - so hard rule 4's commonest real-world violation shape is invisible to the gate that exists to catch it. Found while red-proving a NARROWING of G6 for trigger definitions: the probe asserted a queryset .update() would still be caught, and it was not, and never had been. Nothing in the codebase currently does this - the hole is latent, not exploited.
prevention: Fix: match the singular model attribute forms too (.objects...update(/.delete() where the line names an immutable MODEL), then re-run the whole backend for false positives before trusting it. Deliberately NOT done in the same commit as a billing schema: widening a hard-rule gate needs its own change and its own red-proof over every existing call site. ── **FIXED 2026-08-15 (with DEF-056, one change, one red-proof).** G6 gained rule 2b: `\.(update|delete)\s*\(` on a line naming an immutable MODEL (Invoice, InvoiceLine, Payment, JournalEntry, JournalLine, whole-word so PaymentMethod/BillRun do not collide). PROVED RED on the real tree before being trusted: a file containing `models.Invoice.objects.filter(tenant_id=tenant_id, pk=invoice_id).update(total=0)` made G6 FAIL naming that line, where the pre-change rule returned False on the identical text. RE-RUN OVER THE WHOLE BACKEND FIRST as this column requires: **3 hits, not the 1 DEF-056 measured four days earlier** — the tree gained two while the hole stayed open, which is the argument for closing it rather than re-measuring it. All three are legitimate and each is an allow entry with a reason AND a revisit condition: assemble_document.py deletes DRAFT lines (BR-BIL-023/004); corrections.py stamps `corrects_invoice_id` on a rebill while it is still a draft (OQ-120); corrections.py moves the original to `corrected`, `status` being the one column the immutability trigger permits after issue. The allow-list keys on (path, exact statement text) and NEVER on a path or a line number, so a DIFFERENT `.delete()` in an allowlisted file still fails — that shape is pinned in the gate's self-test — and an entry whose statement changes goes stale and fails until it is re-justified.

title: Three of NFR-24's five mandatory monthly-partition tables ship UNPARTITIONED ('No exceptions')
surface: backend
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: NFR-24 names both tables in a mandatory monthly-partition set and says 'No exceptions'. invoice_lines shipped unpartitioned in W3 and journal_lines in W5, and NOTHING CAUGHT EITHER: no gate reads NFR-24, and the partition guard (test_us_aud_001_partition_rls) checks that EXISTING partitions are RLS-guarded, not that a table which SHOULD be partitioned IS. So a performance/retention rule with real consequences at 3,000 connections has no machine reading it at all. Found by the W5 ledger lane reporting its own deviation rather than taking it quietly; the W3 one had gone unreported. AMENDED 2026-08-11: a third table is in the same shape and this row named only two. outbound_messages (W3, notifications) is in NFR-24's mandatory set and also shipped flat -- there under OQ-108, where monthly RANGE would force created_at into every unique constraint and switch CLAUDE.md hard rule 6 (idempotency) OFF, letting a re-released bill send twice. Found by the G16 lane, which had to enumerate the set to build the gate; nobody had counted the five against the migrations before.
prevention: Fix has two halves and the second is the durable one: (1) decide the partition key -- OQ-107, because entry_date is the book date every trial-balance groups by while created_at prunes nothing for that query; (2) ADD A GATE that reads NFR-24's table list and fails when a listed table is not partitioned. Half (1) without half (2) leaves the next table in the set free to ship flat again. HALF (2) DONE 2026-08-11: G16 partition-cov (10-scripts/gates/g16_partition_coverage.py), registered in run_gates.py and merge-blocking. It has no table list in it -- it parses NFR-24's own sentence, so a sixth table added there is enforced with no edit to the gate -- and it ties out core/partitioning.py's REGISTRY and ACTIVE_TABLES claims against the migrations, which is how meter_reads' missing ACTIVE_TABLES entry (the quiet half of DEF-027) would now be caught. Proved RED on seven shapes including this defect's own. The three tables genuinely blocked are excused only via 10-scripts/gates/partition_exceptions.txt, which FAILS when its cited OQ closes -- the exception cannot outlive the question. HALF (1), the partition key, is still OQ-107/OQ-108 and unresolved: the gate chose nothing. FIXED - VERIFIED 2026-08-15 ON A LIVE POSTGRES CLUSTER AND BY THE GATE, both halves now done. Half (1), the partition KEY, was ruled by the PO on 2026-08-12 closing OQ-107: BOTH TABLES PARTITIONED BY YEAR, and NFR-24 own monthly" wording is SUPERSEDED by that ruling. Half (2), the durable one, was G16 partition-cov, built 2026-08-11 - it parses NFR-24 own sentence rather than carrying a table list, so a sixth table added there is enforced with no edit to the gate. THE RULING IS NOW BUILT: migrations billing/0016_partition_invoice_lines_by_year.py and ledger/0005_partition_journal_lines_by_year.py. MEASURED, not read: on a freshly migrated database (sbh_e2e_batchA_lane, sbh_j24_lane) pg_class reports relkind=p with 2 child partitions for BOTH invoice_lines and journal_lines, where an unpartitioned table reports relkind=r with 0. G16 own line now reads: NFR-24 5 mandatory tables; 4 partitioned (audit_log, invoice_lines, journal_lines, meter_reads); 1 unpartitioned under live open questions: outbound_messages->PO-RULED. That last one is a RATIFIED exemption, not a gap: monthly RANGE would force created_at into every unique constraint, so a bill released 30 Sept and re-run 2 Oct would land in a different partition, pass the duplicate check and send the customer a SECOND COPY - the no-duplicate guarantee wins (hard rule 6). ONE OBSERVATION WORTH CARRYING, and it is a gate blind spot rather than this defect: G16 reads the CODE registry against NFR-24, never a database, so it cannot see a table declared partitioned and never migrated. The developer database smartbillhub is in exactly that state today - both tables still relkind=r on it - because it predates the migrations. Harmless for a dev box, and precisely the shape the deploy dry-run exists to catch."

STILL OPEN: BR-RAT-028's plan-level minimum floor is the other genuinely per-bill computation and has no input on the seam (GT-13 PROPOSED); price_bill is where it goes when the input exists.

title: The move-out guard against issued bills had NEVER run - its seam resolved a module that does not publish the read
surface: backend
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: apps/customers/services._check_move_out_against_issued_bills enforces US-CUS-005 TC-6 (a move-out may not be dated behind the last issued bill; BR-BIL-004 makes corrections new rows). It was written before invoices existed and is correct. But apps/customers/seams.last_issued_invoice_period_end resolved apps.billing.SERVICES -- the resolver's default kind -- and billing's services module publishes only assess_late_fee. So the lookup returned None on EVERY call, the guard recorded move_out_date_not_checked_against_issued_bills, and the move-out went through. Every move-out, since the day the guard was written. NOTHING CAUGHT IT AND THE TESTS ARE THE REASON: test_us_cus_004_005_move_in_out.py monkeypatches the seam, so it supplies the answer the seam could not fetch. A test that provides the answer cannot discover that nobody was asking the question. G13 catches an unpassed PROP on a component; it does not look at seam resolution, so this whole class of cross-module wiring is unguarded. Found by the plan-assignment lane, which needed the same read and looked at how the existing one was wired.
prevention: Two parts. (1) billing publishes last_issued_invoice_period_end(account_id) in apps/billing/selectors.py and the seam resolves with kind='selectors'. The refusal itself needed no change -- it was always correct. (2) tests/test_def_035_move_out_guard_wired.py drives the REAL seam against a REAL issued bill, which is the assertion the monkeypatched tests structurally could not make; red-proved by restoring the default kind, and tc1 failed with the seam answering None against a real issued bill. It also pins that a DRAFT does not constrain a move-out -- getting that backwards would be worse than the defect, since a run that drafted 500 bills would freeze 500 accounts out of moving out. DURABLE HALF NOT YET BUILT: a gate that resolves every seams.py lookup at import and fails when the target does not exist would catch this whole class. Named rather than deferred silently -- G13 proved that the built-not-wired family needs a machine, and seams are the half it does not watch. DURABLE HALF BUILT 2026-08-11 — G20 (10-scripts/gates/g20_seam_implementers.py, registered in run_gates.py, merge-blocking). It harvests all 90 documented cross-module seam contracts across 14 seam modules — from the PROSE in each seam's docstring AND from the late-bound resolver calls — and fails when a named callable is absent from the owning module (NO IMPLEMENTER) or lives at another kind (WRONG KIND). Red-proved on this exact tree, twice: removing the financial_records_exist re-export from apps/billing/services.py takes run_gates from PASS to MERGE BLOCKED naming the file and the line, and removing kind="selectors" from apps/customers/seams.py:219 does the same for the wrong-kind shape. Both mutations were restored and the restoration verified by hash. 13 legitimate gaps are PARKED with a written reason and an expiry guard that fails the moment the missing symbol appears — the rot mechanism that let this defect live. G20 does NOT check signatures, types or exception hierarchies, and says so in its own docstring, so DEF-047's family stays uncovered.

title: A backend refusal can ship a raw message key to the screen and G15 cannot see it
surface: backend
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: Backend refusals carry a message_key that the frontend renders from 07-frontend/src/i18n/locales/*.json. [], props.collapsed ?? internalCollapsed, props.accessibleModules passed straight to a helper). Each survivor either gets a caller or an ALLOW entry with a reason and a revisit condition, which is the record the ALLOW list is meant to be. title: The seeded holiday calendar covers ONE year and nothing renews it - in January it silently reverts to weekends-only
surface: backend
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: Provisioning seeds the US federal holidays for the year the tenant signs up (PO ruling 2026-08-11). Nothing renews it. A tenant provisioned in 2026 has no 2027 dates, so on 1 January every business-day grace calculation quietly reverts to skipping weekends only - no error, no log line, no failing test. THE PO'S OWN WORKED CASE DEMONSTRATES IT: a bill due Thu 24 Dec 2026 with 5 business days' grace must charge on Tue 5 Jan 2027 (their figure). That answer requires 1 Jan 2027 to be in the calendar. With only the provisioned year seeded the fee lands Mon 4 Jan - a day early, ON A PUBLIC HOLIDAY, for every customer of that tenant. Nothing caught it because there is nothing to catch: the calendar is data, not code, and no gate reads whether a tenant's data covers the period being billed. It is the same shape as the partition window in DEF-027 - a create-ahead resource that stops being created.
prevention: ASSERTED, NOT JUST NOTED: tests/test_us_ten_011_us_holidays.py tc6 asserts BOTH outcomes - the wrong one with a single year seeded and the PO's correct figure with two - so the gap is visible in the suite rather than passing silently. A test that proved only the good case would have hidden it. Two candidate fixes, neither chosen here: (a) a create-ahead job on the core.partitioning model, renewing every tenant's calendar for the following year - the precedent exists and its failure mode is understood; (b) seed on first use, so a grace calculation reaching an unseeded year mints it. (b) is simpler and self-healing; (a) is visible and schedulable. A THIRD option is worth naming and rejecting: making the grace clock compute US holidays directly. That would hardcode one country into the money math and silently override any tenant that edited its own calendar, which is the opposite of the PO's 'for time being' framing. The durable half also wants a guard - a check that no tenant's calendar ends before the period any open bill run covers. FIXED 2026-08-16. THE CHOICE, since the row named two candidates and left both open: option (b), seed-forward, NOT (a) a create-ahead job - and the reason is specific rather than stylistic. THIS PRODUCT HAS NO SCHEDULER WIRED (the collections ladder endpoint records no_scheduled_caller), so a renewal job would be a comment claiming a guarantee in the one place whose failure is invisible until January. BUILT: (1) provisioning seeds the sign-up year AND the next; (2) services.ensure_us_holidays_through is idempotent, so any caller that knows a horizon can assert it and a scheduler can call it later with no change; (3) G24 holiday-horizon, merge-blocking, two clauses. ONE DESIGN DECISION THAT WOULD HAVE DONE DAMAGE IF TAKEN THE OBVIOUS WAY: a literal reading of seed-on-first-use puts the write in the grace clock, which is a SELECTOR - a read that writes can fail on a replica, inside another module transaction, or under a role with no INSERT. Writes stayed in services, and the gap that leaves is STATED in the docstring rather than implied. Second: the top-up EXTENDS and never RE-SEEDS. An empty calendar means the tenant deleted the dates (BR-TEN-039 makes the calendar theirs, and a utility outside the US does exactly that); empty and brand-new look identical in the data, so only provisioning may seed from empty. A top-up treating empty as needs-seeding would silently re-impose US federal holidays on a tenant that removed them, on every call. RED-PROVED, FOUR BRANCHES, each run and quoted: (a) provisioning reverted to one year - provisioning seeds ONE year: apps/tenancy/services.py calls _seed_us_holidays once and never for a following year; (b) a live tenant whose calendar stops short - tenant ... calendar ends 2026-12-25, short of 2027, business-day grace in 2027 would skip weekends only; (c) a tenant who deleted every holiday - PASSES, their choice respected; (d) topped up - PASSES reporting 1 tenant calendar(s) checked, all reach it. Clause (a) was proved in an ISOLATED GIT WORKTREE, not the shared tree. THE FIX CONFIRMED ITSELF: the two existing tests that asserted the DEFECT went RED on the fix (tc5 and tc6), which is the strongest evidence available that the behaviour actually moved. Both rewritten rather than deleted so the reversal stays readable; tc6 now takes the PO Christmas figure off what a provisioned tenant ACTUALLY holds instead of a set the test assembles for itself - the old shape could prove the arithmetic while the product still shipped Mon 4 Jan. 7 passed on live Postgres. THREE FLAWS IN MY OWN WORK, FOUND AND FIXED BEFORE COMMIT, all three the same species as defects already in this register: (i) the gate first reported every-non-empty-calendar-covers-it while running against a database holding ZERO calendars - a vacuous truth dressed as a positive finding, exactly the skipped-test-reads-green shape; it now prints what it actually checked and zero says zero. (ii) tc7 first counted a year holidays by calendar year, off by one because 1 Jan 2028 is a Saturday observed Fri 31 Dec 2027 - tc3 had ALREADY written that trap down and the mistake was made anyway, which is the argument for tc3 existing. (iii) writing THIS row, the first attempt embedded raw double quotes inside the quoted field and produced a malformed record - the very corruption shape that destroyed DEF-105 and DEF-107 earlier the same evening. Caught by checking the column count before committing rather than after. NOTE ON THIS FILE, and it cost two attempts: it now carries MIXED line endings - the header block is CRLF and newer rows are bare LF - so a byte patcher that splits on CRLF silently matches nothing and reports success. Patch by RECORD boundary, escape every embedded quote as a doubled quote, and confirm with both git diff --numstat and a column-count check that exactly one well-formed record moved.

title: The reads list came back OLDEST-FIRST and the sort direction was parsed then dropped

NOTHING CAUGHT IT BECAUSE EVERY TEST OF THE PROPERTY USED A GATHER FAILURE: tc2 (planless unit), tc3 (missing read). Both are billing's own exception types, so the loop looked robust while it was robust to only half of what can fail. Found by tc6 of the decisions lane, where 'bill without the service' on a single-service account leaves nothing to price and rating refuses - the test asserted one break and got a dead run. A comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee (hard-won law 1), and here the comment was the loop's own docstring.
prevention: Fixed at the SEAM, not the call site: apps/billing/rating_seam.py now publishes PricingRefused(BillingRuleError) and wraps both price_period and price_bill, resolving rating's RatingError base class BY NAME through the same late binding it already uses for rating's callables - so billing does not import rating and rating still does not import billing. The seam already adapted the owner's RESULT (_as_rated_bill); it now adapts the owner's REFUSAL, in the same place and for the same reason. Only RatingError is caught: an AttributeError inside the engine is an engine bug and must not reach a clerk as 'this account cannot be priced'. calculate_run catches PricingRefused BEFORE its base class so the break names price-usage rather than assemble-document (BR-BIL-040), with retryable=False - the fix is in Plans & Rates, and a retry button here would always fail. RED-PROVED TWICE, both executed: (A) with the seam's _refusal_types() returning () - the defect as it was - tc8 dies on 'apps.rating.pricing.errors.UomMismatch: service 'electric': read unit 'kWh' is not the billed unit 'gal'' and tc6 on 'RatingInputError: price_bill received no services'; (B) with the seam translating but the loop's PricingRefused clause removed, the run survives and tc8 fails 'assert 'rule_refused' == 'rating_refused_to_price'' - the mislabel half. tests/test_us_bil_004_run_loop.py tc8 is the permanent guard and uses a REAL mis-configuration (a plan billing in gallons against a kWh meter), not a mock, with two good accounts either side; the count is the proof, the same way tc2's is. Every seam in rating_seam.py has the same shape - metering's consumption_from_registers, payments' allocate_payment - and each owner has its own error hierarchy. A gate that reads each apps/*/errors.py base class and asks whether the callers of that module's seams name it would catch the rest before they cost a run.

title: Commit 68a7ba2 ships db/rls_billing_w3.sql with NO policy on invoices - a parallel lane committed another lane's working tree mid red-proof

escape_reason: The bills-read lane was executing the law-7 RED proof for its isolation suite, which required TEMPORARILY removing the invoices policy from 06-backend/db/rls_billing_w3.sql to watch the isolation tests fail. During that window a DIFFERENT lane ran a commit over the shared working tree ('git commit -A' shape) and captured the mutilated file. Commit 68a7ba2 therefore creates the invoices table with RLS never applied - CLAUDE.md hard rule 1. It is CLOSED in current HEAD (72fac16 picked up the restored file; git show HEAD:06-backend/db/rls_billing_w3.sql contains CREATE POLICY invoices_tenant_isolation) and the working tree is correct, so no deployed environment is affected today. But anyone who bisects, deploys or runs migrations FROM 68a7ba2 gets cross-tenant-readable invoices. Nothing caught it because every gate ran on the tree AFTER restoration and reported green; no check reads a commit's contents in isolation, and the tests that would have failed are the very ones the lane was deliberately making fail. THE GENERAL LAW: nothing in a red-proof window is safe while lanes commit the shared tree. Law 7 (prove a guard RED first) and parallel lanes on one working tree are directly in tension, and nobody had noticed.
prevention: IMMEDIATE: 68a7ba2 must not be deployed or bisected from; the file is correct at HEAD and no fix commit is needed for the tree. 'git add -A' over a shared tree is the mechanism, and it will do this again - a red-proof window is exactly when the tree is deliberately broken, and it is also when a parallel lane is most likely to be finishing. Three candidate rules for the PO: (a) commit explicit paths only, never -A/-a; (b) run red-proofs in a git worktree so the shared tree is never mutilated; (c) a pre-commit check that refuses a commit touching db/*.sql or 10-scripts/gates/** unless the lane declares it. (b) is the strongest - it makes the tension structurally impossible rather than remembered - and it costs one command. A gate CANNOT catch this class after the fact: by the time gates run, the tree is restored and green. VERIFIED CLOSED 2026-08-15 ON A LIVE POSTGRES CLUSTER, not by reading the file. Reading the .sql file would have proved only that the TEXT was restored; the cluster proves the policy is actually APPLIED. THE PROCESS HALF REMAINS THE POINT and is now a standing lane-briefing rule: every lane brief carries NEVER git add -A / git commit -a / git add . over the shared tree, add explicit authored paths only. That is a briefing CONVENTION, not a gate - nothing mechanically refuses a broad add, so this prevention is enforced by instruction alone and would not survive a lane that ignores it.

title: Concurrent pytest runs share ONE Postgres test database, and the resulting `assert not self._finalizers` errors look exactly like a defect in whichever file is running

title: G6's immutability rule cannot see an ORM write, and the gate's own comment claimed for months that it could
surface: gate
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: G6's hard-rule-4 check fires when a line contains the word UPDATE or DELETE **and** an immutable TABLE name from IMMUTABLE_TABLES ('invoices', 'invoice_lines', 'payments', 'journal_entries', 'journal_lines' - lowercase, plural, the DB names). Django ORM code does not contain those strings: it names MODELS. `Invoice.objects.filter(pk=1).update(total=0)` lowercases to '...invoice.objects...' and 'invoices' is not in it, so the single most likely way a developer actually mutates an issued invoice from Python has never been visible to this gate. Raw SQL is caught; the ORM is not. WHAT MAKES THIS A LAW-1 DEFECT RATHER THAN JUST A GAP: the gate's own docstring listed the covered forms as '`UPDATE invoices SET ...`, `DELETE FROM invoices`, `.update(` and `.delete()` all still fail, and that was PROVED before this line was trusted.' The last two were never true. A reader deciding whether to add another guard would have read that sentence and concluded the ORM was already covered. The false claim lived inside the guard itself. Found while red-proving two false-positive fixes to the same gate: the proof harness asserted the four forms the comment named, two came back MISSED, and re-running them against the ORIGINAL pre-change logic showed they had always been missed - so the fix had broken nothing and the comment had been wrong all along.
prevention: The false CLAIM is corrected in this change; the HOLE is deliberately left open, because widening a gate is its own change with its own red-proof and its own review - the precedent DEF-030 set and DEF-041's prevention column restates. THE MEASUREMENT IS DONE so the widening is a decision and not an investigation: adding an ORM shape (`\.(update|delete)\s*\(` beside an immutable MODEL name) over the whole backend today yields exactly ONE hit, 06-backend/apps/billing/stages/assemble_document.py:208, `models.InvoiceLine.objects.filter(invoice__in=existing).delete()` - and that line is LEGITIMATE: it discards the lines of a DRAFT being replaced, which BR-BIL-023/BR-BIL-004 expressly permit. So the widening costs one allowlist entry with a reason, not a triage backlog. The hard part is that no static check can tell a draft from an issued row, so the exception must be scoped and reasoned rather than path-wide - a path-wide pass would silently cover every future ORM write in billing's write stage, which is the money path this rule most exists to protect. Worth pairing with the DB-level guarantee: the immutability TRIGGERS already refuse an issued-row UPDATE regardless of how it is issued, so the true exposure is a draft-shaped mistake and a missing test, not an unprotected database. That is why this is major and not critical. ── **FIXED 2026-08-15.** The hole this row deliberately left open is closed as its own change with its own red-proof — see DEF-030's prevention column for the widening, the 3-hit measurement and the verbatim red-proof. The docstring is now true in both directions: it describes rule 2b, states plainly that no static check can tell a DRAFT row from an ISSUED one (which is why the exceptions are per-STATEMENT and never path-wide), and the self-test's 'the ORM forms are ABSENT from this list on purpose' note is replaced rather than left to become the next false claim.

title: The E2E CI job tests for a path that does not exist, so it prints 'Passing by design' on every PR and would keep doing so if fifty journey specs were written
surface: gate
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: `.github/workflows/qa.yml` gates its E2E step on `[ -f 08-qa/01-e2e/package.json ] && ls 08-qa/01-e2e/tests/*.spec.ts`. NEITHER PATH EXISTS AND NEITHER IS WHERE THE SPECS LIVE: there is no package.json under 08-qa/01-e2e, that tests/ directory holds `money-journey.spec.md` (a markdown SPECIFICATION, not a runnable spec), and the one real Playwright spec is at `07-frontend/e2e/W0-smoke.spec.ts` with its config at `07-frontend/playwright.config.ts`. So the condition is unsatisfiable by construction and the job takes its else-branch on every pull request, printing "QA E2E suites pending app bring-up ... Passing by design". The sentence is TRUE today, which is what makes it dangerous: it will keep printing after someone writes fifty journey specs in the frontend folder, because the job is not looking there. A reader checking whether journeys run sees a green qa job and a reassuring notice. COMPOUNDING IT, the browser spec that does exist calls `skipUnlessAppServer` and SKIPS when nothing answers on E2E_BASE_URL — deliberately, so CI stays green before the compose stack exists — and nothing in CI starts an app server. So even a correctly-pointed job would report a pass over zero executed browser assertions. Found by the PO asking a direct question — whether E2E runs front-end to back-end to front-end or back-end to back-end. The answer is neither: 1,651 backend tests drive the real cross-module chain, 875 frontend tests run against MOCKED responses, and NOTHING exercises a browser against a live server. 304 journey documents describe flows that no code executes; gate G12 reports itself SKIP and is honest about it. The qa job is the one surface that reports a pass.
prevention: Two fixes, and the small one is not the important one. (1) Point the job at `07-frontend/playwright.config.ts` and `07-frontend/e2e/*.spec.ts` so it can find what exists. (2) THE ONE THAT MATTERS: make a skipped browser suite REPORT ITSELF rather than pass silently. A job whose only possible outcomes are 'passed' and 'passed' is not a check. It should print the count it executed and fail — or at minimum warn loudly — when a suite it was asked to run executed zero assertions, which is the same discipline the golden harness already applies with its 8/8 self-test guards and G19 applies with its 3/3 shapes. Then the real work, which is a story and not a fix: nothing starts an app server in CI, so no journey can run anywhere. G12 is a wave-close gate waiting on exactly that. title: A bill renders its consumption as '684.000000 kWh' to a utility clerk - the money column trims its trailing zeros and the quantity column does not

title: A brand-new billing migration cannot be applied to any Postgres at all: a lone % in a RAISE aborts it, and payments/0002 documents that exact trap
surface: backend
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: apps/billing/migrations/0013_rls_budget_billing.py line 59 raises 'account_budget_events is APPEND-ONLY - the budget variance balance DERIVES from these rows, so % is refused.' schema_editor.execute() passes params=() to psycopg, which then treats the whole string as a format template, so a single % is an incomplete placeholder and `manage.py migrate` dies with ProgrammingError before ANY later migration runs. Found by this lane while bringing up a live database for its own trigger proofs - not by a test, because the default test database is SQLite and every RunPython in that migration returns early on a non-postgresql vendor. payments/0002, billing/0002 and ledger/0002 each carry a NOTE ON %% explaining the trap; this one did not follow it. || CONFIRMED AND MEASURED 2026-08-11 by Eng-Lead on a live cluster, not inferred: a fresh database plus `python manage.py migrate` dies with `psycopg.ProgrammingError: incomplete placeholder: '%'; if you want to use '%' as an operator you can double it up, i.e. use '%%'`. The PL/pgSQL is CORRECT — `%` is a RAISE format placeholder substituted by `lower(TG_OP)`. The break is one layer up: Django's `schema_editor.execute()` defaults `params` to an empty TUPLE, not None, so the driver attempts interpolation on the way past and a lone `%` is an incomplete placeholder. SCOPE, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: a sweep of every migration found six more lone `%` characters, and ALL SIX are prose inside a docstring quoting the 0002 trigger — 0010 executes no SQL of its own. So exactly one real instance existed. WHY NO GATE SAW IT, AND THIS IS THE ACTUAL DEFECT: the entire backend suite runs on SQLite, where the string is never interpolated, so 1,772 tests and 19 gates passed over a product that COULD NOT MIGRATE A REAL DATABASE AT ALL. `.github/workflows/ci-backend.yml` starts no Postgres service and never runs `migrate`; `migration-guard.yml` only blocks EDITS to committed migrations and never executes one.
prevention: Fixed by escaping to `%%`, and verified in BOTH directions on a live cluster: the full migration set now applies clean end to end, and `pg_proc.prosrc` shows the function reached Postgres carrying a single live `%`, so the trigger still substitutes the operation name at raise time. Escaping it wrongly would have silenced the message instead of the error. The 26 budget tests pass. THE DURABLE FIX ALREADY LANDED TODAY, WHICH IS WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE IT WAS NOT BUILT FOR THIS: the ONLY workflow in this repo that boots Postgres and runs `migrate` is `qa.yml` — the end-to-end stack built this afternoon under the PO's ruling *"we ahve to prove against human clicking"*. That work was justified as proving the RENDERED figure; it also happens to be the only thing standing between this class of defect and a deployment, because it is the only CI path that touches a real database. Two things still worth doing: (a) add a Postgres service and a `migrate` step to `ci-backend.yml` so a migration defect fails the BACKEND job rather than waiting for the browser job; (b) a grep gate for a lone `%` in executed migration SQL is possible but is the weaker guard — it must distinguish executed SQL from docstring prose, and this sweep showed the prose outnumbers the code six to one. Running the migration is the check; grepping for one spelling of one failure mode is a proxy for it.

A signed sum over mixed conventions reads $272.30 on a run where the customer owes $222.30 — the credit ADDED instead of subtracted. The panel works today only because it sums MAGNITUDES per row (Sum(Abs(...)), never abs(Sum(...))) and applies the direction once, which is a defensive workaround in the reader rather than a fix at the column.

The convention is on the MODEL as the row asked: `credit_notes.amount <= 0` (`ck_credit_notes_amount_not_positive`, migration billing/0020), so the DATABASE refuses a positive amount from every path -- an import, a console, the callers this product does not have yet. title: The stub gate punishes the exact hygiene it exists to enforce — honest past-tense prose about a REMOVED stub re-trips it

title: Money renders with 4 decimals on screen where the ruling says 2
surface: frontend
found_in: review

reported_by: AP documentation lane, while choosing free OQ numbers
title: Open questions have been live in shipped code with no registry row — EIGHT of them across five modules, and two gates that should catch it both miss
surface: backend
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: The registry ended at OQ-194, so OQ-195 looked free. It is not. **OQ-195** is raised by name in `apps/payments/credit.py` (a refund against a credit balance built from several payments needs a B2 schema change), and **OQ-196/OQ-197** are cited about twenty times across `apps/notifications/{catalogs,rendering,models,dispatch_config}.py` and a migration (the email/SMS token catalogs, and the payment-plan notice class that a rule creates and no spec gives a body to). **None of the three had a row in `12-governance/01-open-questions.md`.** **BOTH GATES THAT LOOK LIKE THEY COVER THIS MISS IT, for different reasons — that is the finding.** **G17** compares registry rows to registry rows only, so an OQ minted in CODE and never registered is invisible to it by construction. **G8** would catch a stub citing an unregistered OQ, but its regex is **LINE-SCOPED**, and `credit.py` puts `raise NotImplementedError(` on one line and `"OQ-195: …"` on the next — so a perfectly ordinary multi-line raise walks straight past it. Same class as DEF-053. The cost is not hypothetical: the next lane needing an OQ number reads the registry, sees 194, and mints a DUPLICATE that two lanes then use to mean two different things. ── **2026-08-15, LATER THE SAME DAY: the ledger lane's repo-wide sweep found FIVE MORE, and they are a contiguous block.** **OQ-127** (may one idempotency column serve two sources — a path checking the wrong one lets money in twice), **OQ-128** (which allocation class a `minimum_adjustment` line belongs to — it decides how much of a customer's tax counts as collected, and therefore what is owed to a tax authority), **OQ-129** (does a partial payment meet tax lines pro-rata, last or first — **19 citations** across ledger reporting, the ledger API and the payments models, and no row anywhere), **OQ-130** (does a counter payment debit cash or undeposited funds) and **OQ-185** (a plan-deletion guard that deliberately over-counts). Eight orphans in total across payments, ledger, billing and notifications. **The block shape is the tell:** 127-128-129-130 are consecutive, which means they were minted together in one conversation and the batch was never written down — not four independent oversights but one missing step, repeated. All eight are now registered with their code citations.
prevention: **MITIGATED 2026-08-15, not fixed:** the three questions are now retrospectively registered with their code citations and their origin stated, and the AP lane took OQ-200..204 rather than 195..199 — leaving 198/199 free rather than splitting a block, so no lane is ever handed an ambiguous number. THE ACTUAL FIX, and it is two small changes to existing gates: (1) make G8's OQ-citation regex MULTI-LINE so a normal `raise NotImplementedError(\n "OQ-###…")` is read; (2) add a check that every OQ-### appearing anywhere in `06-backend/`, `07-frontend/` or `04-docs/` resolves to a registry row — the reverse direction of what G17 does today, which is the direction that catches minting. Prove both RED against `credit.py` and `catalogs.py` as they stand before trusting them green (hard-won law 7). The general law: a gate that checks a registry is internally consistent has not checked that the registry is COMPLETE. ── **AND A SECOND FAILURE MODE, LEARNED BY CAUSING IT.** The morning fix — registering orphans retrospectively — created a DUPLICATE when it was applied to a lane that was still running: the lane minted its own IDs for the same two questions and repointed every citation, so one question ended up with two IDs. The five found later were therefore registered ONLY after every lane owning that code had finished. **The rule that follows and is now practice: register an orphan only when no live lane owns the code that cites it, or tell that lane the moment you do.** The mechanical fix is unchanged and still owed: make the stub gate's citation regex MULTI-LINE (an ordinary two-line `raise` walks past it today), and add a check that every OQ-### appearing anywhere in the backend, frontend or docs resolves to a registry row — the reverse of what the duplicate-ID gate does, and the direction that catches minting. **Nine ID collisions or orphans in one session is not a discipline problem; it is a missing gate.** ── **FIXED 2026-08-15: both changes made, both proved RED.** (1) G8's citation reader is MULTI-LINE, bounded by the raise's own PARENTHESES rather than a line count — the first version used a fixed window, ran off the end of a one-line raise and charged a stub with an unrelated OQ from the next comment block, so the window now closes when the parens balance and comment lines are skipped the way G6 skips them. RED-PROVED on the DEF-096 shape verbatim: a wrapped `raise NotImplementedError(` with the id on the next line was invisible to the line-scoped rule and FAILS now. **It immediately found a real one the old gate could never see** — `apps/customers/services.py` cites OQ-133/136/137, all CLOSED 2026-08-12 — filed as its own row and PARKED in the gate (the file is owned by a live lane; this row's own rule says report, do not edit). (2) Clause B added: every OQ-### anywhere in 06-backend/, 07-frontend/ or 04-docs/ must resolve to a registry row — 1,125 files, 193 ids, all resolving. RED-PROVED against a minted-and-unregistered id: **G17 reported PASS on it and G8 FAILED**, which is this row's finding demonstrated rather than asserted. One orphan exists today, OQ-217, cited by `billing/issue.py` and `payments_seam.py` in the working tree and not in HEAD — PARKED, not registered, because this row's hardest-learned rule is that registering an orphan under a LIVE lane is what produced a duplicate id. The park EXPIRES: the moment OQ-217 gains a registry row the gate fails until the park is deleted in that diff.

reported_by: metering lane (self-reported); diagnosis corrected by the orchestrating session
title: The BILLED lock on a meter read is unreachable — the read's identity is published by metering and DROPPED at billing's contract boundary
surface: backend
found_in: review
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: `apps/metering/services.mark_read_billed` is published for billing to call at issue time and **nothing calls it**, so a read that HAS been billed still reads as `committed`. A clerk correcting it therefore takes the plain supersede path and **no correction linkage is recorded** — precisely the failure US-MET-016 exists to prevent. **THE METERING LANE REPORTED THIS AS "one call in the issue path" AND THAT IS NOT RIGHT; the correct diagnosis is worse and is why this has a row of its own.** Measured, file by file: (1) `apps/metering/selectors.billing_reads_for_unit` DOES publish `read_id` on every row — the identity exists and crosses the seam; (2) `apps/billing/runs._readings_for_unit` builds `ServiceReading` from those rows and **does not copy it**; (3) `ServiceReading` has no `read_id` field at all; (4) the string `read_id` appears **nowhere** in `apps/billing/`; and (5) `issue_invoice(invoice, *, issued_at, template_id, …)` receives only the Invoice — by issue time the readings are gone entirely. So the identity is thrown away at billing's own contract boundary and cannot be recovered where the lock must be applied. **This is a multi-file contract change on the money path, not a one-line call**, and calling it one line is how it would get attempted at the end of a session by somebody with no room left. Nothing caught it because no gate reads a PUBLISHED function for callers — G20 proves a declared seam RESOLVES, never that anyone invokes it, which is the backend twin of the unwired-prop hole G13 covers on the frontend.
prevention: FIX, in order: add `read_id` to `apps/billing/contracts.ServiceReading`; copy it in `runs._readings_for_unit` (the row already carries it); carry the set of priced read ids to issue — either on the account's billing data or as a run-scoped map — and call `mark_read_billed` through billing's seam pattern for each, inside the issue transaction. `mark_read_billed` is already idempotent and refuses a SUPERSEDED row, so a re-issue is safe. **Red-prove it by correcting a billed read and asserting the correction linkage is written** — the plain supersede path succeeding is the defect. THE GENERAL GAP WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX: G20 proves a seam resolves and nothing proves a published cross-module function has a CALLER. Every other built-not-wired defect in this register is the same shape seen from a different side.

title: A migration's RAISE uses %% where the SQL is executed with params=None, so PL/pgSQL sees two format specifiers and refuses to compile the function — apps/billing/migrations/0019_rls_bill_templates.py blocks EVERY migrate and EVERY test run in the repo, on BOTH tiers
surface: backend

introduced_in: the same commit that added the bill-template append-only trigger
escape_reason: CLAUDE.md says 'escape literal % as %%' and that is right for RunSQL WITH params; with params=None Django performs no %-substitution, so %% reaches Postgres literally and RAISE reads it as two specifiers with no arguments. No gate distinguishes the two cases, and the failure is invisible until a migration actually runs — `makemigrations --check` does not execute SQL. The second half is the same file's POLICY block: it uses plain migrations.RunSQL rather than core.migrationtools.PostgresOnlySQL, so 'ALTER TABLE bill_templates ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY' is sent to sqlite too and the whole developer test tier dies with 'near ENABLE: syntax error'

Durable prevention: a gate rule that any migrations.RunSQL whose SQL contains ALTER TABLE ... title: Finance Written-off YTD renders the literal text null USD to a user in PRODUCTION
surface: frontend
found_in: deployed
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: Seen by the PO on the live deployment at smartbillhub.bynry.com/silver-creek-water/finance: the Revenue and AR strip shows BILLED $0.00, COLLECTED $0.00, STILL OWED $0.00, COLLECTION % Not available with its reason, DAYS SALES OUTSTANDING Not available with its reason - and WRITTEN OFF YTD reading the literal string "null USD". Five tiles handle absence correctly and the sixth prints the word null beside a currency. RevenueArPage builds it as money(kpis.written_off_ytd), and money() is a one-line pass-through: it wraps whatever it is handed in an amount/currency pair with no null branch, so a null amount reaches MoneyCell and is rendered. THE CLASS IS THE ONE THIS RELEASE KEPT HITTING, in its most literal form: a figure that cannot be answered is shown as a value rather than as an absence. Everywhere else on this very page the pattern is right - Not available, plus a sentence explaining why - which is what makes the exception a slip rather than a design choice. ESCAPE ROUTE: no gate compares a money renderer against a nullable field, and the page carried tests that pass because their fixtures always supply a figure. It reached production because the ONE state nobody seeded was the empty one - a brand-new tenant with no write-offs, which is every tenant on day one.
prevention: FIXED 188be75. What a user reads now, verbatim from the running app on a tenant provisioned through the real signup: WRITTEN OFF YTD - Not available - "Year-to-date needs the first day of this utility's financial year, and this page reads one accounting period rather than a year. This screen will not work that date out for itself, so the total is left unsaid - a zero here would say 'nothing has been written off', which is a different statement." Three changes: (1) endpoints.ts types written_off_ytd string OR null, which is what wire.py has always served - the narrow type is why tsc never asked S36 to branch; (2) the tile branches to AbsentFigure, whose reason prop is required, keyed on the server's own gap code; (3) MoneyCell/formatMoney now RAISE MoneyAmountAbsent on a nullish amount - a money renderer cannot render an absence because an absence needs a reason and it has none to give, and a silent dash would be a second path around AbsentFigure's required prop. A malformed amount keeps its verbatim rendering (12.3.4 USD beats NaN) and a real 0.000000 still renders $0.00: absence and zero are different facts. tsc --noEmit passes, so no other call site was feeding a nullable figure to the money path. STATED RATHER THAN WORKED AROUND: the screen could make the figure REAL by sending ytd_start, and does not - GET /settings/regional publishes fy_start_month and fy_start_day and NOT the year's first DATE, so deriving it is client-side period arithmetic that financeShared.tsx forbids in as many words (BR-TEN-022, DEF-094). title: git commit with no pathspec swept 25 files of another lane's staged work into an unrelated commit - THIRD occurrence, first two were `git add -A`
surface: process
found_in: commit c8f123a (reverted by soft reset before push)
introduced_in: the DEF-048 rule, which forbids `git add -A` but says nothing about `git commit`
escape_reason: THIS IS THE THIRD TIME ONE LANE'S WORK HAS BEEN SWEPT INTO ANOTHER'S COMMIT, and the first two are why the rule is the wrong shape. Both earlier ones were `git add -A` (the decision log of 2026-08-09 records the second verbatim: 'Files swept into commit 3379c59 by my own `git add -A` while the lane was mid-flight - my standing narrow-commit rule broken a second time'), so the rule written from them forbids four ADD commands - `git add -A`, `git commit -a`, `git add .`, `git stash` - and says nothing about the commit. A lane can therefore obey it perfectly by staging four explicit paths and STILL commit the whole index, including whatever a parallel lane staged in the same tree seconds earlier. That is what happened: a commit meant to carry 4 governance files carried 29, and 737 lines of a payment-plan wizard were filed under 'Change process'. Nothing was lost and no gate would have objected - the tree was consistent, the tests unaffected, and `git status` clean afterwards, which is exactly why it is invisible. The damage is to the RECORD: the next person running `git log` for the wizard finds a commit message about CR numbering, and the lane that built it finds its work already committed under someone else's name. Caught only by reading the commit's own stat line, '29 files changed', against an expected 4.
prevention: Three parts. (1) THE RULE, now hard-won law 11 in CLAUDE.md so it is read rather than remembered: in a shared tree, ALWAYS commit with an explicit pathspec - `git commit -F - -- <paths>` - which commits those paths from the working tree and leaves the rest of the index untouched for its owner. Staging narrowly is not enough; the COMMIT must be scoped too, and that is the half two earlier defects missed. (2) THE CHECK, which costs one glance and is what caught this: compare the 'N files changed' git prints against the number of paths you named. Not equal means you took someone else's work. (3) THE RECOVERY, verified here: `git reset --soft HEAD~1` restores the index exactly as it was, the other lane's staged files included, and a pathspec commit then takes only your own - confirmed by `git diff --cached --name-only` listing all 25 lane files still staged afterwards. Do this BEFORE pushing; after a push it is a revert, not a reset.

DEF-160 was filed the same day and CLAUDE.md gained hard-won law 11 for it — *""in a shared tree, scope the commit, not just the add""* — and law 11's own check (`git prints N files changed; if N is not the number of paths you named, you took someone else's work`) CANNOT SEE THIS ONE: the sweeping commit named gather.py among its paths, so its file count was correct. title: Payments sample block reports OK with 0 rows when it can see no issued bill, so a real upstream failure renders as a successful empty block

found_in: the same live-Postgres load — payments block 'OK   Payments, deposits and the bank statement   0 row(s)'

title: A misread git diff caused a FALSE report of destroyed work, and I then ran a forbidden tree-moving command on six files because of it
surface: process
found_in: commit 24cf5d1 — the PO-rulings commit, which was correct all along
introduced_in: law 11's own post-push check, written earlier the same day, phrased as `git diff HEAD~`
escape_reason: THE CHECK I WROTE IS AMBIGUOUS AND I MISREAD MY OWN RULE. Law 11's post-push clause says to run `git diff HEAD~ -- <each shared file>` and confirm every hunk is yours. With a pathspec that is fine. Run WITHOUT one - `git diff HEAD~ --stat`, which is what I typed - git compares the WORKING TREE against that commit, not commit against commit. In a tree where four lanes have uncommitted work, that prints their in-flight state as though it were my commit's content. It reported '1 insertion, 1550 deletions' across seven files when my commit had touched three files for +6/-2. THE SECOND HALF IS WORSE THAN THE FIRST. Believing I had destroyed the reports lane's library page, viewer, endpoints, tests and stylesheet, I ran `git checkout HEAD~ -- <path>` on six files IN THE SHARED TREE - one of the commands law 11 forbids by name, written by me two hours earlier, for precisely this hazard. If that lane held uncommitted edits in any of the six, I overwrote them, and because the files now match HEAD I CANNOT TELL RETROSPECTIVELY. The pattern is the same one DEF-172 recorded ninety minutes before: the forbidden command arrived inside an urgent diagnostic, where its destructiveness was incidental to the intent, and the rule never came to mind.
prevention: THREE CORRECTIONS, and the third is the one that generalises. (1) THE CHECK MUST NAME ITS COMMITS: `git diff <parent> <commit> --stat`, or `git show <commit> --stat` - never a bare `git diff HEAD~`, which silently includes the working tree. Law 11's wording is being amended to say so, because as written it invites exactly this. (2) THE PRIVATE-INDEX RECIPE MUST SEED FROM THE REMOTE TIP, not local HEAD: `git fetch origin <branch>` then `git read-tree origin/<branch>`. Mine happened to be current so no harm followed, but seeding from a stale local HEAD would write back a tree predating other lanes' commits - a genuine version of the very loss I imagined. This row's own commit was made that way. (3) VERIFY BEFORE YOU REMEDIATE, AND REMEDIATE NON-DESTRUCTIVELY. A believed-destructive event makes the destructive fix feel urgent, which is exactly when the rules get skipped. Nothing was on fire: the supposedly-deleted content was one `git cat-file -s` away from being confirmed present and byte-identical in both commits. A recovery that overwrites a shared tree must be the LAST resort, after the loss is proved, and `git show <commit>:<path> > /tmp/copy` proves it without touching anything. REPORTED TO THE AFFECTED LANE rather than hidden: it was asked to re-verify all six files before continuing, and to push immediately.  ||  CONFIRMED HARM, 2026-08-16, and the row is corrected rather than left comfortable: this said "I cannot tell retrospectively" whether anything was lost. It CAN now be told, because the affected party said so unprompted. The metering/audit lane reported: *"one of them ran a tree-moving command that destroyed my first attempt at the defect-register and decision-log entries, so I re-applied them onto the current HEAD rather than committing my stale copy, which would have deleted their work."* That was this incident. **So the `git checkout HEAD~ --` DID destroy another lane's uncommitted write-back — its defect row and its decision row — and the lane rebuilt them.** Two things follow. **(1) The cost was not zero and must not be recorded as zero.** An honest register is the only thing that makes the escape_reason column worth reading. **(2) The lane recovered correctly and its method is the transferable half**: finding its own work gone, it re-applied its changes onto the CURRENT HEAD instead of committing the stale copy it still held — which would have reverted everything committed in between. That is mechanism two avoided by someone who had just been its victim.

reported_by: US-LED-001 four-unposted-events lane (found by reading apps/billing/issue._gl_account_for against the signed contract table)
title: No first bill carrying a SECURITY DEPOSIT could issue at all, and the refusal a clerk read talked about charge codes
surface: backend
found_in: code-read, then reproduced on the real issue path in tests/test_us_bil_009_posting_handoff.py
introduced_in: apps/billing/first_bill.py as first written, 2026-08-15
escape_reason: A DEPOSIT WAS TYPED AS A FEE, AND THE TWO NEED DIFFERENT GL ACCOUNTS. `first_bill.deposit_line_for` emitted BR-BIL-012's deposit as `RatedLine(kind="fee")` and said why in its own docstring — B4.2 decides the tax base by KIND, so a fee-class line is structurally outside it. That reasoning was right and the consequence was missed: BR-BIL-010 resolves a FEE's GL from its charge code, a deposit line has no charge code and never will (US-LED-001 sends it to the deposit-liability DESIGNATION), so `issue._gl_account_for` refused the line — and US-BIL-007 TC-5 refuses the WHOLE bill when any line cannot resolve a GL. MEASURED, verbatim, by reverting the kind on the real issue path: "a fee line ('Security deposit') names no charge code, so its GL account cannot be resolved." WHY NO CHECK CAUGHT IT: `test_us_bil_010_first_bill.py` asserts the deposit LINE (its amount, its taxability, the already-paid subtraction) and never ISSUES the bill, and `test_us_bil_009_posting_handoff.py` — which owns the GL buckets — had no deposit fixture, because on the day it was written no engine produced one. Each file was correct about its own half and nothing tested the seam between them. The GAP was in fact reported in prose from BOTH sides — `first_bill.OneTimeLines`' docstring says the destination *"is BR-BIL-010's stamp at issue and is not decided here"*, and `_gl_account_for`'s says a fee is *"Refused, not guessed"* — and neither noticed they were describing the same line. Hard-won law 1, twice, from opposite ends. NOT CUSTOMER-VISIBLE YET and the reason matters: a first bill can only be produced through `POST /billing/one-time`, which drafts and cannot issue while OQ-241 is open, so no utility has hit this.
prevention: FIX: the deposit line gets its OWN kind (`rating.pricing.contracts.KIND_DEPOSIT`), absent from TAX_BASE_KINDS so B4.2's structural guarantee is unchanged, and `_gl_account_for` routes it to the `deposit_liability` designation — US-LED-001's *"deposit liability, never revenue"*. GUARD: `test_us_bil_009_posting_handoff.py::tc13` issues a real draft carrying a $150.00 deposit and asserts the credit lands in 2300 AND that the revenue buckets are untouched. PROVED RED BOTH WAYS before it was trusted: reverting the kind reproduces the refusal above, and pointing the deposit at a revenue account instead makes 4105 read $168.50 rather than $18.50 — the bill still issues, the entry still balances at $250.58 = $250.58, and the utility has booked the customer's deposit as income. THE TRANSFERABLE LESSON: when a module docstring explains why it CANNOT decide something, the thing it hands off to should be named and tested, not described. Two files each documenting their side of one gap is not a plan (hard-won law 1).

reported_by: US-LED-001 four-unposted-events lane, self-reported after re-reading its own commit
title: `git show <commit> --stat` -- the post-push check CLAUDE.md law 11 prescribes -- cannot see the failure it was written for, because --stat reports FILES and a lane only ever authors HUNKS
surface: process
found_in: self-audit of commit 9a09861 while writing the lane report
introduced_in: the law-11 check as worded, 2026-08-16
escape_reason: MECHANISM THREE AGAIN (DEF-168), THROUGH THE CHECK THAT WAS ADDED TO CATCH IT. Commit 9a09861 named `12-governance/10-defect-log.csv` in its pathspec to append DEF-181. That file also held the DEF-176 lane's UNCOMMITTED work -- an extended DEF-176 row plus new rows DEF-179 and DEF-180 -- so the commit published all three under this lane's message. NOTHING WAS LOST AND NOTHING REVERTED: the other lane's rows are byte-intact, the register parses, and G17 still reports every DEF id defined exactly once. The damage is to the record, which is precisely why DEF-160/168 say this class stays invisible. WHY THE PRESCRIBED CHECK MISSED IT: law 11's post-push step reads *"`git show <commit> --stat` -- confirm every hunk is yours"*, and it was run, on this commit, and it passed. `--stat` lists FILE NAMES and line counts. It cannot show hunks, so it can answer *are these the files I named?* and never *is every change in them mine?* The seven files were exactly the seven named; the CSV's `5 +-` line count looked like one appended row because a CSV row with embedded newlines spans several lines. The failure is legible only in `git show <commit> -- <path>` with the diff body, which the law does not ask for. AND THE APPEND-ONLY SHAPE MAKES IT MORE LIKELY, NOT LESS: every governance register in this repo (defect log, open questions, decision log, review ledger) is a shared append-only file that every lane touches on every story, so this is the highest-traffic instance of the pattern in the repository.
prevention: FIX THE CHECK, NOT THIS COMMIT -- reverting would delete another lane's real rows to satisfy a bookkeeping rule. PROPOSED WORDING for law 11's post-push step: **`git show <commit> --stat` to confirm the FILE LIST, then `git show <commit> -- <each shared path>` to read the DIFF BODY of every governance register or otherwise high-traffic file in it.** Two commands, and only the second can see this class. STRUCTURAL ALTERNATIVE worth putting to the PO: the four registers are append-only by nature, so a lane appending one row could commit through the private `GIT_INDEX_FILE` route law 11 already prescribes for shared SOURCE files -- seeded from `origin/<branch>` and carrying only its own appended row. That makes the whole class unrepresentable for registers rather than relying on a reader running a second command. NOT A REASON TO STOP APPENDING TO REGISTERS: the alternative is a lane that does not write its findings down, which is the failure hard-won law 10 exists for and is far more expensive.

reported_by: DEF-178 lane, doing the primary-action audit that row's prevention column asks for
title: Continue on THREE wizards blocked the step and told the user nothing at all — the shared WizardFrame documented an inline-error guarantee it never enforced
surface: frontend
found_in: the seeded demo tenant, driven in Chromium — /accounts/new, /reads/upload and /plans-rates/plans/new
introduced_in: US-SHL-010, the original WizardFrame — the contract was a comment from the first commit
escape_reason: HARD-WON LAW 1 IN THE SHARED FRAME: A COMMENT CLAIMING A GUARANTEE IS NOT THE GUARANTEE. `WizardStep.validate` has always carried the comment *"false blocks Continue; the step renders its own US-SHL-009 inline errors"*. The FIRST half is enforced by `continueFrom`. THE SECOND HALF WAS ENFORCED BY NOTHING - it described what ten consuming wizards were trusted to do, and three of them did not do it. `handleContinue` called `validate()`, got false, called `handleNav` with an identical nav object, `handleNav` returned early on `next === nav`, and not one thing re-rendered. Measured in Chromium: pressing Continue on /accounts/new, /reads/upload and /plans-rates/plans/new issued no request, changed no URL and changed NOT ONE CHARACTER of the DOM. THE THIRD ONE WAS FOUND BY THE GUARD AND NOT BY ME - my own manual sweep looked for a button called Save/Create on the plan wizard and its button is called Continue, so I missed it and the check did not. That is the argument for the check existing. A perfectly working refusal, completely invisible - the same experience as DEF-178 and, to a clerk, the same conclusion: the button is broken. WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT. The same reason DEF-178 escaped, and one more: this project has no @testing-library/react, so every WizardFrame unit test runs through `renderToStaticMarkup` and CANNOT press a button - the interactive behaviour of the shared wizard frame has never been executed by any test in the repo. The pure nav helpers are well covered and all agree that a blocked step returns the same object; not one of them can see that the screen then says nothing. Only a browser can, which is why the browser half of a lane's 2d is not optional.
prevention: FIXED IN THE FRAME, NOT IN THE TWO SCREENS, and that choice is the point: fixing it per-wizard fixes it ten times and misses the eleventh nobody has written yet. A refused Continue now sets `blocked` and renders `wizard.blocked` in a role=alert at the button that refused it - "This step isn't finished. Fill in what's marked above, then press Continue again." - cleared on any real nav so a refusal belongs to the step that raised it. A step that also draws its own inline errors still does; this is the floor beneath them, not a replacement. Eleven catalogues, translated. THE GENERAL RULE WORTH KEEPING, and it generalises past wizards: WHEN A SHARED COMPONENT'S CONTRACT SAYS 'THE CONSUMER RENDERS X', THE COMPONENT MUST RENDER A FALLBACK X ITSELF. Ten consumers is ten chances to forget, the forgetting is silent, and the component is the only place that knows the refusal happened. GUARDED BY 07-frontend/e2e/DEF-178-primary-actions.spec.ts, which found all three of these and now fails on either returning.

title: A GLOB PATTERN INSIDE A CSS COMMENT ENDED THE COMMENT EARLY AND SILENTLY DELETED THE NEXT RULE - the DEF-211 fix for B14 rule 18 was dead on arrival and every static check called it shipped
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/tenancy/SettingsPage.css - the DEF-211 comment block

title: A pathspec commit built through a private GIT_INDEX_FILE reverted another lane's CSS fix, because the remote ref MOVED between read-tree and commit-tree
surface: 07-frontend/src/components/FormModal.css - the select/bare-control styling landed at f21ca56, reverted by 66ef41e twelve minutes later
found_in: the CR-012 closing lane, reading the hunks of its own pushed commit as CLAUDE.md law 11 requires
introduced_in: commit 66ef41e (CR-012 closing lane, 2026-08-19)
escape_reason: THE LAW'S OWN PRESCRIBED PROCEDURE PRODUCED THE DEFECT. Law 11 says to build a commit as remote-tip-plus-your-own-hunks through a private GIT_INDEX_FILE, seeded with 'git fetch origin <branch>; git read-tree origin/<branch>'. That is exactly what this lane did. What it does not say is that origin/<branch> IS A LOCAL REF ANY OTHER LANE IN THE SHARED TREE CAN MOVE, and one did: read-tree seeded e04d8ef, another lane fetched, and 'git commit-tree -p origin/<branch>' twenty seconds later resolved to f21ca56. The tree therefore said 'e04d8ef plus my paths' while the parent said f21ca56, so every file f21ca56 had changed and this lane had not named was silently reverted. The push was a clean fast-forward, no gate objected, and the file count check passes because the reverted file IS listed. Only reading the hunks found it - the check that has now found this class four times.
fixed_commit: stale-defect audit 2026-08-27 — CONDITION GONE: CLAUDE.md law 11 lines 202-216 now prescribe TIP=$(git rev-parse origin/<branch>) used in BOTH read-tree and commit-tree, plus git diff --numstat verification by subtraction
prevention: PIN THE TIP TO A SHA, ONCE, AND USE THE SHA IN BOTH COMMANDS: TIP=$(git rev-parse origin/<branch>) then 'git read-tree $TIP' and 'git commit-tree -p $TIP'. A symbolic ref read twice in a shared tree is two different commits. Then re-read the pushed commit with 'git show <sha>' and confirm every hunk is yours - which is how this was caught, and is why that step must stay a diff read and never a --stat.

title: AN ENTIRE CARD RENDERS ITS OWN TRANSLATION KEYS AS ITS CONTENT - DisconnectRightsFooterCard asks for eleven notifications.rights.* keys and ALL ELEVEN are absent from every catalogue, so a System Admin reads 'notifications.rights.title' as the panel heading and 'notifications.rights.edit' as a button label

escape_reason: THIS IS DEF-282's SHAPE FOR THE THIRD TIME TODAY and the reason is structural: nothing compares the set of keys a component ASKS FOR against the set the catalogue DEFINES. tsc cannot - a translation key is a string literal. eslint cannot. vitest renders the component and asserts on text the test itself supplies, so a test written alongside the component passes on the key name. G15 checks PARITY BETWEEN catalogues, so eleven keys missing from all eleven files are perfectly in parity and it reports nothing. The only detector is a person reading the screen, which is how all three were found.
prevention: A check that extracts every literal t('...') from the frontend source and fails on any key absent from en.json. It is a dozen lines and would have caught all three of today's occurrences before deploy. Filed as part of CR-016, which owns the rendered-output gate; this is its cheapest and highest-yield member because it needs no browser at all.

title: Production JOBS_EAGER=False with no Celery worker: the CR-010 sample plant is enqueued on every new tenant and never runs, so every deployed tenant opens empty
surface: S114 signup / provisioning
escape_reason: No gate asserts that an enqueued job kind has a runner in the settings module it will be dispatched under. Every test that exercises the plant sets JOBS_EAGER=True (config/settings/test.py sets it False and the tests override per-case), so the plant is only ever proved under eager dispatch. production.py flips it to False and docker-compose.yml states in its own header that no Redis and no Celery worker exist, which means the record rests queued forever with no error anywhere. 09-infra/01-deployment-architecture.md line 292 already warned this exact sentence and no check reads prose.
prevention: A gate that enumerates every kind passed to jobs.enqueue() and refuses one whose dispatch under config.settings.production has no runner; plus a provisioning assertion that the plant job reaches status succeeded, run under production settings rather than eager. ⚠ FIXED 2026-08-19 (PO ruling: 'We want Async job install redis and celery'). docker-compose.yml now runs redis + a celery worker + celery-beat; apps/tenancy/tasks.py is the transport and dispatch_job's non-eager branch reaches it; .env.example types JOBS_EAGER=false and an uncommented CELERY_BROKER_URL. PROVED WITH THREE PROCESSES, which is the only way this class of defect can be proved: 10-scripts/verify_celery_transport.py runs a live worker against a live Redis under JOBS_EAGER=false and all FOUR kinds reached succeeded (sample plant 10/10, bulk rate change, audit export 1074 rows, list export 53 rows). 06-backend/tests/test_cr017_celery_transport.py holds the in-process regression guards; TC-1 and TC-3 were both proved RED first, and TC-3's first version was VACUOUS (green with the tenant context deleted) and was rewritten to assert the context at the moment of the load. ⚠ NOT FIXED ON THE DEPLOYED HOST: editing compose and .env.example reaches nothing already running (hard-won law 4) — that host needs its own broker URL, its own worker process, and JOBS_EAGER=false in the .env it already has.

title: The defect register's own gate was written, committed and never registered in run_gates.py, so for a day the suite printed a healthy PASS count over a check that was not in it
surface: 10-scripts/gates/run_gates.py GATES registry
escape_reason: Nothing counted gate modules on disk against rows in the GATES registry, so an unregistered gate was indistinguishable from a passing one — the suite reported 20 PASS and the missing check was not among the 30 names printed. This is the THIRD occurrence in two days and the SECOND in this one file: g27_translation_keys.py was written, proved RED, committed and left unwired by the lane that was fixing a law-2 defect, and the lane that wrote the note about that then did the same thing with this file. The common cause is that authoring the gate file feels like shipping the check, and no artifact disagrees.
prevention: run_gates._assert_registry_sane() now refuses to start the suite when a gate module on disk has no row, when two rows share a label, or when one module is registered twice; deliberate exclusions must be named in GATE_NOT_A_GATE with a reason. title: 422 SERVICE REFUSAL MESSAGES CARRY AN INTERNAL ID AND THE ERROR ENVELOPE RENDERS THEM TO THE USER - across 87 backend modules, a refusal raised by a service puts its free text in params.detail, which BR-SHL-020 says is what the screen renders; examples include 'a per-account budget level override requires a REASON (BR-BIL-017 as OQ-068 closed it: allowed with reason + audit)' and 'a budget level override of X is outside the plus-or-minus bound (BR-BIL-017, OQ-068)'

introduced_in: cumulative - a refusal message is written next to the rule it enforces, so citing the rule id in it is the natural thing to type
escape_reason: G28 (added by CR-016) checks catalogue values and an EXPLICIT list of served-prose fields; a raise site is neither. It also cannot be swept heuristically: a first naive count returned 682 because br_ref= and message_key= are MACHINE fields that are supposed to hold a rule id, and a gate that flagged those would be switched off within a day - which is exactly the false-positive failure recorded in G26's and G27's own docstrings. title: G18 reports i18next PLURAL keys as missing from every catalogue, so three dashboard strings that resolve correctly at runtime are reported as rendering raw to a user
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g18_i18n_call_sites.py vs 07-frontend/src/features/reports/DashboardPage.tsx:406,465,590
introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: G18 matches a t() literal against the catalogue key set exactly, and i18next resolves a plural call by SUFFIX: t('dashboard.period.age', {count}) is served by dashboard.period.age_one / _other and the bare key is not supposed to exist. So the gate reports three correct strings as 'used in code and defined in NO catalogue (renders raw to a user)' - a sentence that is false, in a headline count a reader trusts. It inflated the gate's user-facing figure from 23 to 26 and led me to tell the PO the dashboard was rendering raw keys, which it is not. Nothing catches a gate that is wrong in the SAFE direction: the suite is red either way, so the false line hides inside a real failure.
prevention: G18 must treat a key as present when any i18next plural suffix of it is in the catalogue (_zero/_one/_two/_few/_many/_other), and its self-test must include a plural call site - a case that would have gone RED on this bug. The complementary check is the one that matters more: a plural key whose _other form is absent IS a raw render, and the gate cannot see that today either.

title: POST /api/tenants took 78 seconds, and 47 of them were one read-only seam answering a one-column question by building a whole screen payload 304 times
surface: S114 signup / POST /api/tenants — apps/metering/seams.enabled_service_codes
introduced_in: 2026-08-11 (the OQ-115 lane, when service_row gained its two cross-module count seams)

NOT BUILT HERE and reported: no check in this repo looks at a duration or a query count, so a per-request query-count ceiling on the provisioning path is the smallest honest guard and does not exist.

title: A bulk rate change is accepted with a 202 and NEVER APPLIED on the deployed build: apply_rate_change_batch is a queued job body and no worker exists to run it
surface: POST bulk rate change -> core_jobs.enqueue(RATE_CHANGE_JOB) at 06-backend/apps/rating/services.py:3306
introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: Same root as DEF-320 and found by following it: production sets JOBS_EAGER=False and no Celery worker was ever deployed, so every job body is unreachable. This one is worse than the empty-tenant symptom because the caller gets a SUCCESS answer - core_jobs.accepted(record) is a 202 with a job id - while apply_rate_change_batch, which writes the new tariff version and the rate_change_log rows, never executes. Staff change prices, the app agrees, and the prices do not change. Every test of this path runs under eager dispatch or calls the job body directly, so the gap between accepted and applied is never exercised. FOUR job kinds are dead this way: the tenancy sample plant, this, and the two audit CSV exports.
prevention: A gate that fails when a registered job kind has no reachable runner under config.settings.production; and an end-to-end assertion that a 202-returning endpoint reaches a terminal job status, run under production settings rather than eager. ⚠ FIXED 2026-08-19 by the same change as DEF-320 — this defect WAS DEF-320 wearing its worst costume: rating.bulk_rate_update enqueued a job that production dispatched to nothing, so the 202 was honest and the body never ran. It is one of the four kinds proved to reach succeeded under production dispatch with a live worker (10-scripts/verify_celery_transport.py), and test_cr017_celery_transport TC-6 asserts the kind has a registered body so an enqueue can never again point at nothing.

title: 125 CSS classes are asked for by components and declared by no stylesheet, so eight whole screens render as unstyled flowing text — whole prefix families (bil-, cus-, rd-) have no stylesheet at all
surface: 07-frontend/src: FixABillTab 13, ChangePlanWizard 11, OneTimeBillTab 11, UploadReadsWizard 10, BillLayoutTab 10, AccountActions 9, BudgetBillsTab 8, DisconnectRightsFooterCard 7
introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: The three checks that should catch this cannot see it. tsc sees a string; eslint sees a string; and a component test asserting toHaveClass('bil-layout-card') PASSES, because the class IS on the element and nothing asks whether any stylesheet declares it. So the screen looks broken to a customer and healthy to every automated check the repo owns. This is the SIXTH recurrence of one shape (DEF-244, DEF-305, DEF-308, DEF-314, DEF-315) across five months, every prior one found by a human reading a screenshot, and each was fixed as a list of class names rather than as the missing check. The measured count is also five times what the last audit reported, because that audit walked Settings only.
prevention: G31 (10-scripts/gates/g31_declared_classes.py) parses every class literal in className= against every selector declared in any stylesheet and ratchets at 125, so the number may fall and can never rise. Comparison operands are excluded so a state value in a ternary is not read as a class. Proved RED on a planted class and proved not to fire on a comparison operand.

reported_by: claude (following the PO ruling on system errors)
title: Every refusal already carries a trace_id that is generated, written to the audit attempt row and returned in the envelope — and NO screen renders it, so a user has no identifier to quote to support

introduced_in: unknown
