title: G31 COULD NOT SEE THE CLASS AT THE FRONT OF AN INTERPOLATED TEMPLATE - the gate written to catch undeclared classes skipped any className={`a-class${expr}`}, so on the upload-reads wizard it reported is-selected and is-blocked and NOT rd-source-card, the class that actually draws the card
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g31_declared_classes.py (_LITERAL); the missed class was 07-frontend/src/features/metering/UploadReadsWizard.tsx:348
found_in: the DEF-327 fix, by re-reading the gate's own regex before trusting its output
introduced_in: G31 itself, filed with DEF-327 the same day
escape_reason: A GATE CANNOT AUDIT ITSELF, AND NOTHING ELSE AUDITS IT EITHER. The literal reader accepted a backtick string only when it contained no interpolation (`([^`${}]*)`), so a template with a ${} in it contributed NOTHING - its static prefix, which is the whole class name, was discarded. The gate stayed green, its --list output looked complete, and its count of 125 was simply short. This is the same shape as the defects G31 exists to catch, one level up: the check reported success over the thing it was pointed at, and a lane fixing DEF-327 from its output would have declared rd-source-cards, rd-source-name and rd-source-why, left rd-source-card undeclared, and shipped S28 still rendering as flowing text with every gate green.
prevention: G31 now splits each template on ${...} and reads the static chunks, dropping any token that ends in '-' because that is a prefix an interpolation completes (svc-, met-tag-, rcw-consequence-, rd-outcome-, skeleton-, is-) and counting them would be six false positives - and a gate with false positives gets switched off, which is that file's own stated rule. Proved RED on a planted className={`def327-planted-card${s ? ' is-selected' : ''}`} and the old reader proved blind to the same one, before the widened gate was trusted green. THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the reason this row exists rather than a silent patch: when a gate is written FOR a defect, run it against the defect's own worst example and check it sees the whole of it - G31's docstring named .bil-layout-card, which is a plain quoted string, and every hand-check used a plain quoted string.

title: THE SHARED WORKING TREE WAS 126 COMMITTED LINES BEHIND THE BRANCH IN 12-governance/02-decision-log.md - a whole CR-017 ruling was on the branch and absent from the file every lane reads, so any lane appending to it and committing would have reverted that ruling without a single check objecting
surface: 12-governance/02-decision-log.md in the shared checkout (working tree 3276 lines vs origin/claude/cr-status-overview-y0mm4c 3406); local HEAD fac4af7 is ~43 commits behind the branch tip
found_in: the DEF-327 fix lane, on comparing the file against the branch tip before appending to it
introduced_in: the shared-container working model - local HEAD is not advanced when other lanes push, so a file no local lane has rewritten stays at whatever the container last wrote
escape_reason: CLAUDE.md LAW 11 IS ENTIRELY ABOUT WHAT A COMMIT WRITES, AND THIS IS ABOUT WHAT A LANE READS. Its checks - count the files, confirm your own change survived, read every hunk - all pass on an append to a stale file: the count is 1, your paragraph IS present, and every hunk IS yours. The 126 missing lines never appear in the diff, because they are absent from the base the diff is taken against. That is DEF-306's mechanism (reversion by subtraction) arriving through the working tree instead of through read-tree. WORSE, THE LAW'S OWN REMEDY POINTS AT THE WRONG PLACE: it says 'To look at a clean tree, look at HEAD - git show HEAD:<path>', and HEAD in this container is ~43 commits behind the branch, so following that advice reads an even older copy than the working tree. Nothing in the repo says the truth is origin/<branch>.
prevention: Before EDITING any long-lived shared prose or register file - decision log, open questions, defect log, change requests, surface_debt - diff it against the branch tip first: git show $(git rev-parse origin/<branch>):<path> | diff - <path>. If the tree is behind, build the new content as TIP-plus-your-own-hunks and repair the working copy from it rather than appending to the stale one. Done here: the commit blob was built from the tip, and the working copy was replaced with tip+mine after proving by diff that ZERO working-tree lines were lost. AND AMEND LAW 11'S 'look at HEAD' SENTENCE - in this container the authority is origin/<branch>, never HEAD.

title: All 24 RLS policy files use a bare CREATE POLICY with no guard, so 94 policies hard-fail the deploy if the migration is ever re-run against a database that already has them — and the entrypoint's restart loop turns one such failure into an unbootable API
surface: 06-backend/db/rls_*.sql (24 files, 94 CREATE POLICY statements); triggered on smartbillhub.bynry.com at notifications.0012_rls_cr009_in_app_messages
introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: Every RLS migration is proved by running it ONCE against an empty database - migrate-from-empty is the gate, and from empty a bare CREATE POLICY always succeeds. Nothing re-runs one against a database that already holds the policy, which is the only condition that fails, so the defect is invisible to CI by construction. The same files' DOWN path is guarded (drop_rls uses DROP POLICY IF EXISTS on every table) which makes the asymmetry look deliberate when it is not. Compounding it, docker-entrypoint.sh runs migrate under set -e before gunicorn binds, so any migration failure exits the container; with a restart policy that becomes a loop that re-runs migrate from the top on every restart, and the log interleaves four different failures from four different attempts into what reads like one incoherent traceback.
fixed_commit: stale-defect audit 2026-08-27 — CONDITION GONE: 0 unguarded CREATE POLICY across all 30 06-backend/db/rls_*.sql (127 CREATE POLICY, each preceded by its own DROP POLICY IF EXISTS)
prevention: Make every policy file re-runnable: DROP POLICY IF EXISTS <name> ON <table>; before each CREATE POLICY, matching what drop_rls already does. Then a gate that greps 06-backend/db/rls_*.sql and fails on a CREATE POLICY not preceded by its own DROP - ratcheted at 0. Separately, a CI job that runs migrate TWICE against the same database, because once-from-empty cannot see this class at all.

reported_by: PO (deployed build 2.28.0, signup for Silver Creek Water)
title: The signup form stays on screen underneath the provisioning screen: a class rule giving .signup-wizard-frame display:flex out-specifies the HTML hidden attribute, leaving Back and Create utility live under a tenant that already exists
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/tenancy/SignupWizard.css .signup-wizard-frame vs SignupWizard.tsx hidden={committing}; seen by the PO on smartbillhub.bynry.com at 2.28.0
escape_reason: The hidden attribute works through ONE line in the browser's own stylesheet, [hidden]{display:none} - a bare attribute selector at specificity 0-1-0. A class selector is also 0-1-0 and comes later, so any class rule that sets display silently defeats hidden. Nothing here could see it: jsdom honours the hidden attribute and never loads the .css file, so every component test passes; tsc and eslint see a correct boolean prop; and only a real browser renders the attribute and the stylesheet together. THE RULE THAT BROKE IT WAS THE FIX FOR DEF-327, four hours earlier - .signup-wizard-frame was one of the 125 classes referenced and declared nowhere, and declaring it correctly for the spacing it genuinely needed is what defeated the hiding. A class that did not exist could not out-specify anything, so fixing the undeclared-class defect is what created this one.
fixed_commit: stale-defect audit 2026-08-27 — CONDITION GONE: SignupWizard.css is deleted and SignupWizard.tsx:851 carries [&[hidden]]:hidden (0,2,0) beside hidden={committing}; route-b-migrated.txt:2067 records the migration
prevention: Guard the rule: .signup-wizard-frame[hidden]{display:none}. Generally, any class that sets display on an element the markup toggles with the hidden attribute needs that guard - a sweep found this is the only real case today (three other candidates use aria-hidden, a different attribute, and were NOT touched). A browser assertion that the wizard's commit button is not visible while provisioning runs is the only check that can see this class of defect.

title: G28 reads ZERO while two backend fields serve BR-ids, an OQ number and a module path straight onto the Templates screen: set_default_reason and language_selection_reason are not in the gate's named list of served-prose fields
surface: 06-backend/apps/notifications/templates_api.py:670 set_default_reason and :679 language_selection_reason, rendered verbatim by TemplateDetail.tsx:437 and :525; seen by the PO on smartbillhub.bynry.com 2.28.0

So the gate reported 0 violations, the CR-016 audit reported Templates 36 internal strings to 0, and the screen still tells a water utility that the default variant is the row's KEY not a flag on it (BR-NOT-001/BR-NOT-006), that a July letter would claim it was rendered from a row that now says something else (BR-BIL-026), that OQ-252 is with the Product Owner, and that apps/customers publishes no such read. title: Settings > Reference data shows no count for any BILLING card while Reads shows 5 and Payments shows 7, so billing defaults, budget billing rules and document templates read as absent on a tenant that has them
surface: SET-04 Settings > Configure > Reference data, BILLING section; deployed 2.28.0 for Silver Creek Water
introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: The provisioning audit trail for this very tenant records reference.seeded rows with counts for uoms 26, charge_codes 23, tax_jurisdictions 9, asset_types 12, payment_methods 7, read_methods 5 and more - so the seeding happened and is evidenced. What the BILLING cards render is a bare chevron with no number, which is indistinguishable on screen from not-seeded, and sits beside WORK's explicit 'Not set up yet'. Nothing checks that a card which CAN show a count DOES show one: the reference-data completeness gate counts rows in the database, and the screen-level assertion checks the card exists rather than what it says. So a card that has lost its count reads as a configuration gap to the only person who can act on it.
prevention: Assert the rendered count on every Reference-data card that has a countable list, in a browser, against the same reference_data_report() the seeder writes - a card whose count is blank while its list is non-empty must fail. Distinguish three states explicitly on screen: a number, 'Not set up yet', and 'not countable' with its reason.

title: celery and celery-beat restart-loop: compose sets command: without clearing the image ENTRYPOINT, so the worker argv is appended to gunicorn's — and each restart also ran migrate and the tenant sweep from a second container
surface: docker-compose.yml celery + celery-beat vs 06-backend/Dockerfile:84 ENTRYPOINT and docker-entrypoint.sh's trailing exec gunicorn ... $@
escape_reason: The transport verifier that proved all four job kinds reach a terminal status ran a worker DIRECTLY as a process, so it exercised celery and never exercised how compose STARTS celery. Nothing else launches a second service from this image: backend is the entrypoint's only consumer and its command is empty, so the trailing exec gunicorn $@ had no arguments and the collision could not appear. A compose service declaring command: LOOKS like it replaces the entrypoint and does not - it supplies arguments to it - and nothing in this repo reads docker-compose.yml against the Dockerfile. The second half hid for a worse reason: everything above the exec still ran, so the worker container migrated the database and swept every tenant on every restart, and its log was indistinguishable from the backend's.
fixed_commit: stale-defect audit 2026-08-27 — CONDITION GONE: docker-compose.yml:237 (celery) and :336 (celery-beat) both set entrypoint: [] with the reason stated inline
prevention: entrypoint: [] on every service from this image whose command is not gunicorn. Then a check that reads docker-compose.yml and fails when a service uses an image with an ENTRYPOINT, does not clear it, and its command[0] is not what that entrypoint execs. Separately migrations must be provably single-process: the entrypoint should refuse to migrate unless it is the web role.

reported_by: CR-018 Phase 2 lane (found by running `npm run lint` before starting)
title: `npm run lint` was RED on the branch: tailwindTheme.test.ts reads global.css into `globalSource` and nothing uses it — the variable was read for a check nobody wrote, so the one fact three comments call load-bearing (global.css's h1..h6 rule sets NO font-size, which is why Preflight is a whole-product change and why every heading's size comes from the browser) was asserted nowhere
surface: 07-frontend/src/styles/tailwindTheme.test.ts:56; `npm run lint` / eslint @typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars
escape_reason: Nothing in CI runs `npm run lint` on this branch's path — `.github/workflows/gates.yml` installs Python and nothing else, and `ci-frontend.yml` runs `npm ci && npm test`, which is vitest and not eslint. So a lint error shipped and stayed green for a day. The deeper escape is the one hard-won law 1 names: the guarantee was written in three comments and asserted in none, and the dead variable was the only visible trace of the missing check

reported_by: PO (deployed 2.29.4, celery container Up but unhealthy)
title: The celery healthcheck pings a node that cannot exist, so a fully working worker reports unhealthy: CMD runs no shell so $HOSTNAME was never expanded, and CMD-SHELL alone would not have fixed it because dash does not set HOSTNAME
surface: docker-compose.yml celery service healthcheck; deployed 2.29.4, container reported Up (unhealthy) while logging ready
escape_reason: A healthcheck is the one line of a compose file that nothing else exercises: it is not run by tests, not run by any gate, and its failure does not stop the container - it only changes a word in docker ps. The verifier that proved all four job kinds reach a terminal status ran a worker directly as a process, so no healthcheck ran at all. And the bug needed the container to exist before it could show: the same service also failed to start until DEF-338, so the unhealthy status was masked by a restart loop. The second half would have escaped even a careful fix - switching CMD to CMD-SHELL looks like the whole answer and is not, because this image is python:3.12-slim so /bin/sh is dash, and dash does not set HOSTNAME the way bash does. The expansion would have produced the empty string and the check would have kept failing for a new reason while appearing repaired.
prevention: Use $(hostname), not $HOSTNAME, in any container shell on a Debian base. More generally a check that parses docker-compose.yml and fails when a healthcheck in exec CMD form contains a $ - the exec form cannot expand one - and when a CMD-SHELL check references a variable the base image's shell does not set. Both are readable from the file plus the Dockerfile FROM line.

reported_by: claude (OQ-277 lane reported the desync; filed here)
title: The two version literals shipped unequal again — package.json 2.29.7 against pyproject.toml 2.29.6 at commit 8ea7847, the THIRD occurrence, and after 36 gates none reads them
surface: 07-frontend/package.json vs 06-backend/pyproject.toml at 8ea7847 (CR-018 Phase 2c step 1)
escape_reason: Change-process step 7 exists because the PO said this is the step usually skipped, and it made ONE source of truth derived everywhere - but the derivation is a human copying a number between two files in two languages, and nothing compares them. The bump is also the LAST edit a lane makes, when its own checks have already passed, so the one moment the mistake is possible is the one moment nobody is looking. title: Two mobile-first min-width media queries survive in payments.css after desktop-first was ratified, and a sixth breakpoint width (760px) has no name — both are pixel-moving fixes that need a browser

introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: Nothing has ever read a media query's DIRECTION. Thirteen max-width rules and two min-width ones coexisted because each is individually valid CSS and no gate, lint rule or test looks at the shape of a breakpoint - the mismatch only became a defect the moment desktop-first was ratified under OQ-274, which is to say the rule arrived after the code. reported_by: claude (found by the OQ-280 collision, then repeated immediately)
title: An ID minted in the decision log and never written to the registry is invisible to G17, so two lanes allocated OQ-280 for different questions without either being wrong
surface: 12-governance/02-decision-log.md vs 12-governance/01-open-questions.md; g17_duplicate_ids.py
introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: G17 reads the REGISTRY and counts an id as defined once per registry row. An id written only into the decision log has zero registry rows, so from G17's position it does not exist and there is nothing to compare - the gate is not mis-scoped so much as pointed at the allocator while the minting happened somewhere else. Both lanes were correct at the moment they allocated: each read the registry, saw 279 as the highest, and took 280. The collision existed only in prose neither could see. Same shape, immediately afterwards, in this very lane: DEF-345 and DEF-346 were CITED in a decision-log entry and a source comment before either was filed, and file_defect.py then allocated 345 to a different defect - the reference and the reality disagreed until the allocator itself surfaced it.
prevention: Minting an id means writing the registry row in the same commit; prose may only CITE an id the allocator has already issued. Enforceably: extend G17 to also scan 02-decision-log.md and the source tree for OQ-/DEF- references and fail on any that has no registry row - which catches both the double-mint and the cite-before-file, and would have caught all three occurrences today.

reported_by: claude (found by the stop-hook flagging an unpushed lockfile)
title: package-lock.json is a THIRD version literal nobody checks: it reads 2.28.0 on the branch while package.json reads 2.29.13 — thirteen releases of drift, and G35 compares only two files
surface: 07-frontend/package-lock.json vs 07-frontend/package.json vs 06-backend/pyproject.toml
escape_reason: G35 was written for DEF-341 and closed the pair it was SHOWN - package.json against pyproject.toml - because those are the two files that defect named. A check built from one incident is scoped to that incident.
prevention: Extend G35 to read ALL THREE literals and require all three equal - the lockfile carries the version twice, at the top level and in its packages[''] entry, and both mirror package.json. Longer term DEF-341's prescription stands: derive rather than copy, and let the gate assert a derivation instead of a copy.

reported_by: claude (found by ls showing the gates directory ending at g27)
title: A lane's local branch pointer was rewound 240 commits mid-session and node_modules was reinstalled from the 240-commit-old package.json, so every Tailwind-compiler check went red on a healthy repo
surface: local checkout of claude/cr-status-overview-y0mm4c: HEAD moved from 5e9d646 to 757ae43 (DEF-247, 240 commits back) with a clean working tree; 07-frontend/node_modules lost tailwindcss@4; 10-scripts/gates/ lost g28-g37 on disk; 6 tests failed with 'Failed to load url tailwindcss'
introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: Nothing watches the local HEAD. Every Law 11 check in CLAUDE.md is about what a COMMIT contains - the file count, the hunks, re-reading from HEAD after pushing - and all of them assume HEAD is where you left it. This moved the branch POINTER, not any file, so git status was clean, no command failed, and the tree looked healthy. It surfaced only because a directory listing for an unrelated reason ended at g27 where it should have ended at g37. Had the next action been a commit, it would have been built on a 240-commit-old tree - and the private-index procedure would have SAVED it, because that seeds from the remote tip rather than local HEAD, which is why nothing was lost.
fixed_commit: a7f6bb02 - the detector shipped (10-scripts/check_head_current.sh); the environmental rewind it detects is NOT fixed and recurred 6+ times since (DEF-2100)
prevention: Cheap and mechanical: before any commit, and before drawing any conclusion from the tree, compare the HEAD revision against the upstream revision and stop if HEAD is behind. The private-index commit procedure ALREADY fetches the remote tip and pins it, so add the assertion there - it has both values in hand and currently ignores where HEAD is. That is also why nothing was lost here: seeding the index from the remote tip rather than local HEAD means a rewound HEAD cannot reach a commit. Recovery, when the working tree is clean, is a fast-forward-only merge from the remote branch - the form that refuses rather than discards - followed by a dependency reinstall from the lockfile, because a rewind past a dependency change silently reinstalls the old one and every check that needs it goes red on a healthy repo.

reported_by: claude (found in a Phase 5 before/after screenshot, looking for something else entirely)
title: Row-action icons wrap 2x2 in the ACTIONS column on Units and Premises — four 32px icons do not fit the column the text links used to
surface: 07-frontend/src/components/RowActions.tsx (the container is inline-flex + flex-wrap) rendered on /premises/units and /premises, where a row has four actions: edit, assign plan, deactivate, delete. Visible in the browser at 1440px; the ACTIONS column is narrower than 4 x 32px + 3 x 4px gap
escape_reason: EVERY CHECK IN THIS REPO READS ONE ELEMENT AT A TIME. G37 asks whether each row action is an icon with an accessible name - all four are. The before/after census compares each element's computed style - identical, because nothing about the ICONS changed. What changed is that four 32px boxes need 140px where four words needed less, and the column did not grow. A wrap is a property of the CONTAINER and its siblings, and no per-element check can see it. It was found in a screenshot taken to judge Preflight, which is hard-won law 6 almost word for word: nine defects were found by diffing the running app against the prototype and by nothing else. It has been shipped since 2.29.17 and nobody looked.
prevention: Decide what a 4-action row does: allow the column to grow, drop to a '...' overflow after two (which is what B14 rule 15 actually says - 'Max 2 visible + ... overflow'), or shrink the icon box in dense tables. Rule 15's own text prescribes the answer and this lane did not implement that half of it. Then a browser assertion with teeth: for every row-actions container, its rendered height must equal one icon's height - a wrap is exactly a container taller than its children, and that IS checkable per container even though it is not checkable per element.

reported_by: claude (CR-013 PLN-03 r10-conformance lane, from the PO's step 8 screenshot)
title: EVERY SEEDED PLAN HAS NO CUSTOMER CLASS, so PLN-03 step 8 reads "CUSTOMER CLASS - Not set" on a plan the product shipped - and the field is the one CR-013 part 5 calls load-bearing. The review step is reading the RIGHT field: draft.account_type_id comes from PlanDetail.account_type_id, account_type_id is in PLAN_FIELDS and is accepted on write and served on read (DEF-421 wired the picker on 2026-08-21). The gap is in the fixture - _plan_payloads in apps/rating/sample_data.py builds name, code, description, services, charge_rules and tax_rules and never sets account_type_id, so the seeded Residential and Commercial plans are classless. The consequence is not only a blank on step 8: CR-013 part 5 step 1 says the customer class "constrains every later step", so on a seeded plan steps 2 and 3 cannot filter schedules by class and schedulesWithForeignClass - the named gate - has nothing to compare against and can never fire.
surface: [backend] 06-backend/apps/rating/sample_data.py _plan_payloads -> PLN-03 steps 1, 2, 3 and 8 and the S9 plans list
introduced_in: the plan fixture as first written, before account types were served
escape_reason: The seeder's tests assert it writes plans idempotently and that publish succeeds, and both do - account_type_id is optional on write, so a payload omitting it is valid and nothing is red. The screen then renders the absence honestly, which is correct behaviour over incorrect data, and prose is invisible to every gate. Same family as DEF-448 and DEF-444 on the neighbouring steps: the fixture is checked for whether it WRITES, never for whether the screens it exists to fill can be walked.
prevention: FIXED 2026-08-21. Both sample plans now carry the class their own CODE has always claimed — `SCW-RES` residential, `SCW-COM` commercial — resolved through a new read-only seam, `rating.seams.account_type_id_by_code`, because the id is a uuid minted at migration time and cannot be MIRRORED the way rating already mirrors the four class CODES. ⚠ **THE SEEDER NOW REFUSES RATHER THAN WRITING A NULL, and that is the part that keeps this fixed.** A plan with no class is not a cosmetic gap: BR-RAT-108 derives the base from service → ACCOUNT TYPE → meter size and expects exactly one survivor, so a NULL class is a dimension the derivation cannot narrow on. Seeding one quietly is HOW THIS LASTED — it looks like data and behaves like an absence, which is why no test and no gate ever objected. A refusal makes the same condition loud. Set account_type_id on both seeded plans from the tenant's own account_types reference list (Residential for the residential plan, Commercial for the commercial one), resolved by CODE through the lookup selector rather than hard-coded, so a tenant whose list differs is not given a dangling id. Then assert it: a fixture test that reads the seeded plan back and requires a class would go red today.

reported_by: claude (CR-013 PLN-03 r10-conformance lane, implementing BR-RAT-096)
title: BR-RAT-096 SAYS A PLAN BINDS TAX AND FEE *CODES* AND THE COLUMN BINDS A *JURISDICTION*, so step 5 can only bind at the coarser grain the ruling did not describe. PO verbatim in the rule: "we have created Tax and Fee codes in Tax section; in step 5 of the plan we have to bind it". The Tax section mints TAXES (apps/rating tax rows, each with a name, a rate and a jurisdiction). What a plan can store is plan_tax_rules.jurisdiction_id - PLAN_TAX_RULE_FIELDS is exactly ("jurisdiction",) after BR-RAT-094 closed rate_override - so binding one code out of an authority's three is not expressible: binding TX-STATE brings every tax that authority levies on this plan's services, and unbinding one of them is not a write the API accepts. On the seeded catalogue that is invisible because each authority carries one tax; it becomes visible the moment an authority levies a utility tax AND a franchise fee and a plan wants one of the two. Implemented at the grain the write path accepts, with the grain named on the screen, rather than drawing per-tax checkboxes that would silently bind the authority.
surface: [backend+frontend] apps/rating PLAN_TAX_RULE_FIELDS + plan_tax_rules.jurisdiction_id -> 07-frontend/src/features/rating/PlanWizard.tsx step 5 (S10 / PLN-03)

escape_reason: The ruling was put and taken in the vocabulary of the SCREEN a person had just used - the Taxes & fees tab, which lists taxes - and the vocabulary of the STORE was not on the page when it was answered. Nothing reconciles a rule's nouns with the columns that have to hold them; a signature covers what was shown, and a column name was not shown. The seeded fixture hides it because every seeded authority carries exactly one tax, so the coarse and fine readings give identical results on every row anyone has looked at.
prevention: Put the grain question to the PO in plain English with the case that separates the two readings: an authority levying BOTH a 6.25% utility tax AND a franchise fee, and a plan that wants the tax and not the fee. If per-code binding is wanted, plan_tax_rules needs a tax_id (a B2 schema change on the schema route) and the jurisdiction stays as the scope gate BR-RAT-096 explicitly keeps. Step 5 names its grain on screen in the meantime, so nobody infers per-code binding from a screen that cannot do it.

title: A SERVICE-SCOPED PERCENT TAX IS CHARGED ON THE WHOLE BILL, because rating.selectors.plan_tax_rules never serves applies_to_services and gather never puts it on the seam. The seeded reference catalogue already carries the case: lookup_defaults.json TX-CITY City Franchise Fee is percent 1.50 with services [electric, gas]. On design A4 S1 that fee is 1.82 (1.50% of the 121.10 of electric) and production computes 2.83 (1.50% of the 188.90 whole-bill taxable base) - a 1.01 OVER-charge on one bill; A4 S3 is 21.39 correct against 28.41 computed, an over-charge of 7.02. The tax is ATTACHED correctly - selectors.tax_applies_to reads applies_to_services as an applicability gate at line 1990 - so the line appears on the right bills and only its BASE is wrong, which is why it looks right.

reported_by: claude (DEF-438 diagnosis lane, checking whether the live path implements R5)
title: R5's OUTSIDE-CITY MONEY FACTOR CAN NEVER BE ANYTHING BUT 1.0 - the engine multiplies by it on every base and every usage line and NOTHING IN THE PRODUCT CAN SET IT, at any layer. apps/rating/pricing/stages/price_usage.py multiplies both the base line (line 65) and the usage lines (line 96) by source.config.jurisdiction_factor, normalize.py reads it off the tariff with a default of 1, and rating_seam.TariffConfig and pricing/contracts.ModelConfig both declare jurisdiction_factor: Decimal = Decimal('1'). apps/billing/gather.py _tariff_config_for constructs TariffConfig with twenty-odd fields and never mentions this one, so every bill this product has issued priced at exactly 1.0. It is not merely unwired - THERE IS NO STORAGE TO WIRE IT TO: grep for outside_city_factor and outside_city_exempt_services across 06-backend finds them ONLY in apps/rating/resolution.py (the dead R1-R7 chain of DEF-438) and its three test files; there is no column on charges, no column on rate_plans, no tenant setting, and the premises.inside_city_limits flag the factor would be selected by does not exist either (gather._premises_geography reads it with getattr and metering owns the table). So all three inputs the factor needs are absent. r10 draws the feature - 'Premises outside city limits multiply base and variable by 1.5' - and the PO ruled it on 2026-08-19 ('you will ahve to add rate cahnges in base charges and rates'). Design A4 S2 works it: an outside-city electric base of 18.50 bills 27.75 while the sewer base beside it stays 8.00. Today all three bill at 1.0, so every outside-city customer is UNDER-charged by a third of every base and usage line the tenant intended to uplift.
surface: [backend] apps/billing/gather.py _tariff_config_for (never sets jurisdiction_factor) -> apps/billing/rating_seam.TariffConfig.jurisdiction_factor -> apps/rating/pricing/stages/normalize.py:254 -> price_usage.py:65 and :96; and NO storage anywhere for the factor, its per-service exemptions, or premises.inside_city_limits

introduced_in: 2026-08-19, when the PO's R5 correction was implemented in the pricing stages and the seam gained the field; the DB, the settings surface and the gather adapter were never built
escape_reason: A MULTIPLIER THAT DEFAULTS TO THE IDENTITY IS INVISIBLE WHEN IT IS DEAD. Multiplying by 1 changes no figure, so every existing test, every B5 golden and every live bill produces exactly the number it produced before the field existed - the code is executed on every line of every bill and cannot fail. That is strictly worse than an unreached branch, which coverage would at least show cold. The engine's own tests pass a tariff carrying the factor directly, so the arithmetic is proven and the SOURCING is untested, which is precisely the shape of DEF-154 (the schedule-versus-plan base charge that billed 0.00 on every bill for weeks). Nothing anywhere asserts that a field the engine reads is populated by the only caller that builds it, which is the same missing gate DEF-438 and DEF-463 both name.
fixed_commit: lane RATING-WRITE-PATHS 2026-08-28 - THE WRITE HALF IS COMPLETE. Step 0 found four of the five parts already built (PLAN_FIELDS, the serializer, gather._jurisdiction_factor_for and the seeder); what was owed was the SCREEN, and BR-RAT-102's own 2026-08-27 amendment said so. PLN-03 step 2 now draws the plan's factor and a per-service exemption tick. Worked on the seeded estate: 161 Silver Creek Rd, June 2026, 18 kgal - water base 8.00 -> 12.00 and water usage 109.00 -> 163.50, a water subtotal of 117.00 -> 175.50 at the seeded 1.5. Closed with DEF-515.
prevention: THE READ HALF IS BUILT (2026-08-21, DEF-438 cutover step-5 lane): BR-RAT-101 and BR-RAT-102 ruled the storage and the money, rating.selectors.plan_jurisdiction_pricing serves the plan s factor and its per-service exemptions, gather._jurisdiction_factor_for applies the two gates per service and sets TariffConfig.jurisdiction_factor, and price_usage has always multiplied base and usage by it - so an 11 kgal water household on a plan stating 1.15 at an outside-city premises now bills 9.20 base + 67.85 usage against 8.00 + 59.00 inside. A plan stating a factor over a premises whose flag is None refuses THAT ACCOUNT by name and the run continues. Not one figure moves on any real tenant. STILL OPEN: nothing WRITES rate_plans.outside_city_factor or plan_services.outside_city_exempt at any layer (DEF-515) and nothing writes premises.inside_city_limits at any layer (DEF-517), so no utility can yet ask for the surcharge. The original prevention, for the record: Do not wire the multiplier before the PO rules where the factor and its per-service exemptions are STORED - resolution.Catalogue models them as a tenant-level Decimal plus an exempt-service list and ChargeCode.outside_city_applies, and none of the three has a column, so this needs a schema decision and not a lane's choice. premises.inside_city_limits is a metering-owned column that must land first (DEF-292 already blocks the tax half of the same flag on the frontend). Until then the honest state is a named refusal or a documented 1.0, not a silent identity. The gate that would have caught it: for every field a pricing contract declares and the engine reads, assert some production caller writes it - the backend twin of G13 that DEF-438 asks for.

reported_by: claude (costing the three migration options the PO asked for, and checking them against Silver Creek's actual plan data)
title: A BASE CHARGE CODE CANNOT VARY BY CUSTOMER CLASS, AND SILVER CREEK'S REAL DATA ALREADY NEEDS IT TO. rating.Charge has code, name, charge_type, service, amount_rule, amount, percent, min/max, gl_account_id, is_base, taxable_default, auto_apply - and NO customer-class column. ChargeCodeAmount varies by SIZE only. But resolution.ChargeCode carries customer_classes and R4 narrows on it, so the engine expects a scoping the database cannot express. Silver Creek's water base is $8.00 on Sample-Residential and $15.00 on Sample-Commercial: ONE service, TWO bases, and a single BASE-W code can hold neither pair.
surface: [backend] apps/rating/models.Charge -> BR-RAT-088's migration path -> resolution.resolve_charge_codes

escape_reason: BR-RAT-088 was ruled and recorded against resolution.py, where ChargeCode.customer_classes DOES exist - so the rule reads as implementable and the gap is one layer down, in the table. Nothing compares the resolution dataclass's fields to the model's, and the chain has no production caller (DEF-438) so no bill has ever exercised the narrowing. The seeder writing no base codes (DEF-455) kept it inert from the other end too.
prevention: Surfaced while costing BR-RAT-088's migration story for the PO: any migration copying plan_services.base_charge into a charge code hits this immediately, because the plan column is per PLAN and the code is per TENANT. Either Charge gains class scoping, or a tenant mints one code per class (BASE-W-RES / BASE-W-COM) and the naming convention becomes load-bearing - which BR-RAT-088's own docstring warns against, since matching BASE-<service> by name fails silently.

reported_by: Product Owner (questioning how one base is derived from many, 2026-08-21)
title: THE BASE CHARGE WAS PICKED BY CATALOGUE ORDER WHEN TWO CODES MATCHED. resolve_base_charge returned on the FIRST code whose is_base was set for the service and never asked whether a second applied - so an account matching two base codes was billed by tuple order, silently. Nothing in the schema prevents two: charges.is_base is a bare boolean with no uniqueness constraint of any kind. On Silver Creek's own figures a residential water account would bill $8.00 or $15.00 depending on which row the catalogue listed first.
surface: [backend] apps/rating/resolution.resolve_base_charge -> R4 -> every bill's base line

escape_reason: Every existing test configures ONE base charge code, so first-match and only-match are indistinguishable to the whole suite - and they will stay indistinguishable for as long as nobody writes the two-code case. The narrowing R4 does (service, customer class, size) reads as though it guarantees uniqueness and does not: it FILTERS, and a filter returning two is a perfectly ordinary outcome that this function treated as one. The chain also has no production caller (DEF-438), so no bill has ever exercised it.
prevention: Raised by the PO while costing BR-RAT-088's migration: "based on Asset and Account type you will have select 1 base charge out of so many charges - then you need to derive which base rate to select". Selecting one of several is exactly where a first-match wins by accident. It now REFUSES and NAMES every matching code, the same posture R3, R4 and R5 already take. A test asserts the two orderings refuse IDENTICALLY - if that ever passes with a price, the first-match has come back.

reported_by: claude (BR-RAT-088 migration lane, checking what happens to a cleared column on the next ordinary plan save)
title: AFTER BR-RAT-088's MIGRATION, RE-SAVING A PLAN RE-INSTATES A BASE OF $0.00 AND EVERY BILL FOR THAT PLAN THEN CHARGES NO BASE. Two halves that are each individually correct. (a) apps/rating/services._validate_plan still requires base_charge on EVERY service row (required=True, services.py:648), so the write path demands the figure BR-RAT-088 says a plan may not define. (b) PlanWizard.planPayload sends base_charge: decimalOut(line.base_charge) ?? "0" (PlanWizard.tsx:563) and decimalIn(null) is "", so a plan whose column this migration CLEARED sends the literal "0" on the next ordinary save - a rename, a description edit, adding a charge rule. A stored 0.00 is a PRICE, not an absence (PO ruling 2026-08-19 'print $0.00'), so gather._base_charge_for then returns 0 and the base line prints $0.00. On Silver Creek that is $8.00 residential water, $15.00 commercial water and $18.00 trash silently becoming zero on the next plan edit - DEF-154 exactly, reintroduced by a screen nobody would associate with money.
surface: [backend] apps/rating/services._validate_plan:648 + [frontend] features/rating/PlanWizard.tsx:563 -> plan_services.base_charge -> billing/gather._base_charge_for
introduced_in: BR-RAT-088 (2026-08-20) moved the base off the plan; neither the plan write validator nor the wizard payload followed
escape_reason: Both halves are individually correct and were each written for a good reason. The validator's required=True predates BR-RAT-088 by weeks and nothing re-reads a validator when a rule is superseded. The wizard's ?? "0" was added BY DEF-422's fix, whose own comment argues the round-trip 'destroys no stored figure' - true while the served value is non-null, and false the moment a migration nulls it. No test covers 'save a plan whose base is NULL', because until BR-RAT-088's migration exists no plan can have one. The failure is therefore invisible until the migration runs, and then invisible again because a $0.00 base is a well-formed row on a bill that is produced.
prevention: Two changes, both small: drop required=True on the plan service base (or refuse a non-null one outright, which is what BR-RAT-088 actually says), and stop the wizard defaulting a blank to "0" - omit the key. Then a test that saves a plan whose base is NULL and asserts the column is still NULL afterwards. The migration command's dry run reports this as a precondition.

DEF-400 was found by a lane building the wizard and noticing its own two buttons had nowhere to post; the six here have no wizard yet, so nobody was standing in front of them. record_grant is the one legitimate member - the bill run calls it, like suspend_discount_for_funding - which is exactly why the check must carry a NAMED-CALLER allowlist rather than a count.

The fix proper is a screen and a route per act, sequenced with the story that needs it (enrolment is the account panel, attachment is PLN-03 step 6, retire is the definition detail's third button) - not six routes with no screen, which is this defect from the other end. || 2026-08-27 (rating critical/high lane) — STILL OPEN BUT NARROWER: one of the six now HAS a caller. apps/customers/discounts.py:667 resolves seams.resolve('rating','enrol_account',kind='discount_services'), so enrolment is reached from the move-in path rather than from a rating route. The probe still lists it because tests/test_def400_discount_lifecycle_routes.py compares write services against rating's OWN api.py only — a service reached cross-module by a seam reads to it exactly like one reached by nothing. THAT IS A GAP IN THE PROBE, not a false alarm: REACHED_ELSEWHERE already carries a named-caller allowlist for precisely this case, and enrol_account's entry still says 'the account discount panel is not built', which is now only half true. The other five (end_enrolment, verify_enrolment, attach_discount_to_plan, retire_discount) are unchanged; record_grant remains the legitimate member. Not re-fixed here — the fix proper is still a screen and a route per act, sequenced with the story that needs it.

title: ACTIVATE ACCEPTS A DRAFT VERSION, SO THE SECOND APPROVAL CAN BE WALKED AROUND - apps/rating/discount_services.activate_discount_version admits VERSION_SCHEDULED **or VERSION_DRAFT**, and the second-approval requirement BR-RAT-077 computes is written at SUBMIT. A version that never goes through submit therefore carries second_approval_required=NULL and can be made the version in force by one System Admin acting alone. A discount with NO budget cap - the case the PO ruled ALWAYS needs two people, because unbounded is the largest commitment there is - is the case this bypasses most cleanly.
surface: [backend] 06-backend/apps/rating/discount_services.py activate_discount_version (the status tuple) -> POST /discounts/{id}/versions/{vid}/activate (mounted 2026-08-21 by DEF-400) -> CHG-01.discount status cluster
found_in: 2.29.62 - Wave C DEF-400 lane, reading the state machine before mounting a route onto it
introduced_in: 2026-08-19, when the three lifecycle services were written; latent while no route reached activate_discount_version
escape_reason: It was UNREACHABLE, which is DEF-400, so no test could exercise the hole and no screen could open it - a defect hiding inside a defect. The service tests drive submit->approve->activate in order and test_activation_refuses_a_type_no_engine_can_price activates a version straight from DRAFT to reach the type gate, so the draft branch is exercised as a SETUP STEP and asserted on for a different reason. BR-RAT-083 says only Owner/Admin may activate and @require_role(SYSTEM_ADMIN) satisfies that exactly, so the base rule reads as enforced; what is unenforced is BR-RAT-077's SECOND approval, which lives in a different rule and is stored on a column nothing checks at activation.

title: A RATE CHANGE THAT TAKES EFFECT MID-PERIOD IS NOT SPLIT ON AN ORDINARY BILL RUN - one version prices the whole period, chosen at the service date, while the back-bill path already prices per sub-period against the version in force THEN

escape_reason: TWO CONFIRMED RULES DESCRIBE DIFFERENT BEHAVIOUR AND NOTHING RECONCILES THEM. BR-RAT-007 says historical invoices reprice against the tariff version in force ON SERVICE DATE - singular - and apps/billing/gather.py implements exactly that, refusing with tariff_has_no_version_in_force_at_service_date when none matches. BR-BIL-018 says back-bills price PER SUB-PERIOD against the tariff version in force THEN. So the product already knows how to split a period across a rate change; it does it on the back-bill path and not on the ordinary one. Neither rule is wrong on its own and neither mentions the other, so no gate, test or review could see the disagreement - it is only visible when someone asks what happens on the fifteenth of a month whose rate changed. ⚠ AND THE MONEY DIRECTION IS NOT NEUTRAL: whichever version wins prices the WHOLE period, so a rate rising mid-month either over-charges the days before it or under-charges the days after, by the full difference, on every affected account

So this is applying a built capability to a second caller rather than designing a new one. What it needs first is a ruling, because BR-RAT-007 is CONFIRMED and says the opposite: either an ordinary run splits like a back-bill (and BR-RAT-007 is amended to say ON SERVICE DATE means per sub-period), or it deliberately does not (and the rule gains a sentence saying so, with the money consequence stated, so the next reader does not assume it splits). ⚠ Whichever is chosen, tier thresholds must scale with each sub-period - BR-RAT-002 already rules that thresholds scale with a prorated period, and a split period is a prorated period

title: ONE GUARD KILLS THREE BEHAVIOURS: import_runs._run() refuses every run whose status is loaded or rolled_back, and three functions that exist to work on exactly those runs open with it. (3) rollback() opens with _run(locked=True) and its own 'status != loaded' guard is dead code, so NO RUN CAN EVER BE ROLLED BACK - while r10's PRM-04 draws a rollback icon on every row and prints 'A run can be rolled back as one unit for 30 days'.

That is DEF-322's exact shape inside the gate written to end it, and approval_required is BR-MET-098's own refusal, so the rule the PO ruled on 2026-08-21 could not have spoken to a user at all.

title: THE APPROVAL PERCENTAGE BAR FIRES AT EXACTLY 5 PERCENT, AND BR-MET-098 SAYS 'EXCEED'. import_runs.dry_run computes (rejected * 100) >= (APPROVAL_PCT * checked), so a run at precisely 5.00 percent - 1 reject in 20 rows, or 25 in 500 - stops for an Owner-or-Admin approval that the rule as written does not require. One row's difference on one batch size, and in the safer direction, so this is filed rather than changed: the rule's own worked reasoning is about SMALL files ('5 percent of a 20-row batch is 1 row') and 20 rows is exactly where the tie bites, which is the case the PO reasoned about out loud. title: THE `unit` NUMBER SERIES STANDS BEHIND THE UNITS THAT EXIST, SO CREATING A UNIT THROUGH THE REAL SERVICE FAILS WITH A DUPLICATE KEY. Measured on the demo database: number_series for tenant brazosbend reports series='unit', next_number=102, while `units` already holds numbers up to U-00420 (209 rows, min SCW-U-001, max U-00420). Creating units through `metering.services` therefore succeeded until the counter reached 102 and then raised `django.db.utils.IntegrityError: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "uq_units_tenant_unit_no" DETAIL: Key (tenant_id, unit_no)=(01a0258b-6153-7f0b-a080-d3427a50053a, U-00102) already exists.` Some path creates units WITHOUT allocating from the series - the BR-TEN-063 sample plant and/or the CR-023 import runner are the candidates, both of which create units in bulk - and every later creation through S16 collides until an operator clicks through the failures one at a time. Customer-facing shape: 'Add unit' fails with a 500 on a tenant that has ever imported or been sample-seeded
surface: 06-backend/apps/metering (unit creation) + the number_series allocation - the collision is visible from any caller
found_in: fixture-build
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: Nothing compares a number series against the highest value that actually exists in its table. Every test creates a handful of units on a fresh tenant, where the counter and the data start together and stay together; the divergence needs BULK creation first and ORDINARY creation second, which is the order a demo stack has and no test does. It surfaced only because a fixture needed 340 units in one pass and walked the counter straight into the pre-existing block
prevention: Reported, not fixed - metering/tenancy are not this lane's territory. The cohort works around it through `tenancy.services.save_number_series`, which is the S63 act an admin would perform and is forward-only by rule (BR-TEN-035: issued numbers are never renumbered), advancing the counter past the highest existing unit before it creates any. The durable fix is either (a) the bulk paths allocate from the series like every other path, or (b) a guard that fails when any series' next_number is at or below the highest value in its own table - which is a cheap query and would have caught this on the day the divergence was created. The general rule worth keeping: a counter and the rows it numbers are two sources for one fact, and nothing in this repo checks that they agree

title: TWO LANES HOLD DEF-571 AND DEF-572 — the defect register's id-collision guarantee failed on the day it was tested by six concurrent lanes. 10-scripts/file_defect.py allocates 'against the REMOTE TIP as well as the working tree' so a lane 'cannot take an id another lane has already pushed, and cannot take one a sibling has staged locally either'. Both halves were true and it still collided: the master-account bill-assembly lane allocated 571/572 and COMMITTED them at 08:35 (commit fb60750 — the master bill's under-charge and its phantom exception row); the W11 CR-014 journey-fixtures lane committed 571/572 for the finance-period seeder family at 09:01 (commit 16d12d0). The register now carries four rows under two ids, and every citation — code comments, commit messages, business-rule stamps, decision-log rows — is ambiguous between them.
surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv (four rows, two ids) · 10-scripts/file_defect.py (the allocator) · every citation of DEF-571/DEF-572 in apps/billing, apps/customers and 08-qa
found_in: master-account bill-assembly lane (self-found, 2026-08-22 — reading the branch log after committing, while checking that no other lane's work had been swept up)
introduced_in: 2026-08-22, two lanes allocating within the same window while both rows were uncommitted in a shared tree
escape_reason: The allocator reads three sources — working tree, HEAD and @{upstream} — and prints what it read ('535 · 535 · 535' on this lane's first call). A lane that allocated BEFORE another lane's row reached any of those three, and wrote LATER, defeats all three reads: the guarantee is about the moment of ALLOCATION and the collision is created in the gap between allocating and appending. Nothing re-checks the id at append time, and nothing checks the register for duplicates at all — no gate reads the file for uniqueness, which is why four rows under two ids sit there passing every check.
prevention: NOT FIXED by this row, and the fix is not this lane's to choose: the register is append-only by design and renumbering another lane's COMMITTED rows is exactly the shared-tree edit CLAUDE.md law 11 forbids. Recorded so the next reader knows which is which — the EARLIER commit (fb60750, 08:35) is the master-account pair and the LATER (16d12d0, 09:01) is the CR-014 seeder pair. The durable fix is a uniqueness check: either file_defect.py re-reads and re-allocates immediately before writing, or a gate fails on a duplicate id in the register.

title: THE ROUTE/CYCLE WIZARD'S EMPTY-STATE CELL HAS NEVER BEEN CENTRED, AND ITS 24px PADDING HAS NEVER APPLIED. `.rcw-empty { text-align: center; padding: 24px 8px }` is (0,1,0) and the only three elements that carry it are `<td>`s inside `.rcw-table`, whose `.rcw-table th, .rcw-table td { text-align: left; padding: 6px 8px }` is (0,1,1) and sets both properties. The `.rcw-empty .rcw-desc` child override (0,2,0) DID apply and is preserved. NOT folded into the round-4 migration (CR-018 §6): the port carries only the live child override, so the screens render exactly as they do today, and this row is the fix request. The fix is one line — write the centring on the cell at a rank that wins, or move the empty state out of the cell into a block the table rule does not reach
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/tenancy/RoutesCyclesWizards.tsx — the three empty-state cells (SET-06 step 2 premises picker, SET-06 step 3 meters picker, SET-07 step 2 routes picker)
found_in: CR-018 long tail round 4 (W14 lane, 2026-08-22) — counting specificity on every rule before porting it, after the same count caught a near-regression on .cell-num in the same file
introduced_in: CR-006 (the SET-06/07 wizards) — present since the stylesheet was written; the two rules were authored in the same file and never compared
escape_reason: Two rules in ONE stylesheet, both valid, both compiling, and the loser is invisible to every check this repo has: no gate reads rendered output (hard-won law 6), G31 sees a declared class that is referenced, G34 sees no literal, and the e2e specs assert TEXT in the empty state rather than its alignment. A dead declaration in the same file as the one that kills it is the hardest kind to see by reading, because both look intentional

A cheap mechanical check exists: for every rule of the form '.parent el { … }' in a stylesheet, list the single-class rules in the same product that target elements matching it and report any property both set — that would have printed this pair. title: A PREMISE'S AREA AND SUB-AREA CANNOT BOTH BE NAMED FROM THE PAYLOAD — the parent's NAME exists only inside the display string `area_path`, so a screen that wants r10's two separate facts has to SPLIT a joined sentence

title: A STATED ABSENCE RENDERED INSIDE A FACT LIST BLOWS THE FACT LIST'S LABEL COLUMN TO FULL WIDTH — every value on the screen is squeezed into a ~90px ribbon down the right-hand edge
surface: `.met-facts` (metering.css:46) is `display:grid; grid-template-columns: minmax(140px,auto) 1fr` over `<dt>`/`<dd>` pairs. `ArrivesWithField` (features/rating/ratingShared.tsx:429) renders a `<div class="rating-arrives">` — neither a `dt` nor a `dd`, but still a GRID ITEM, so it lands in the label column and `auto` grows that column to the width of a full-width dashed callout. title: THE BILL'S PER-SERVICE GROUP HEADER LOST ITS EXTRA TOP PADDING WHEN PlainTable BECAME UTILITIES — DEF-581's mechanism again, from a different component. `.bil-linegroup th { padding-top: var(--space-3) }` (billing.css, 12px) is (0,1,1), and `PlainTable`'s own `[&_th]:p-2` is ALSO (0,1,1) — a `padding: 8px` shorthand that sits in the utilities sheet, which the bundle emits last (byte 132188 against 44583). title: EXPORTING GIT_INDEX_FILE AND THEN RUNNING AN ORDINARY GIT COMMAND IN THE SAME SHELL LEAVES THE SHARED INDEX STALE - AND THE STALE STATE IT LEAVES SAYS 'DELETE'. Law 11's commit-tree recovery says to build the tree against a private GIT_INDEX_FILE, which is right. What it does not say is that the variable is EXPORTED for the rest of that shell invocation, so a following `git reset --mixed <sha>` in the same call writes to the PRIVATE index and leaves .git/index untouched at its pre-lane state. `git status` then reports D (deleted) for every file the lane had just created and pushed, because the real index predates them. A bare `git commit` at that moment would have committed the deletion of four files that were live on the branch thirty seconds earlier. Happened TWICE in one session; the first time the stale entry was benign (one modified file), the second time it held deletes for import_writer.py, two migrations and a 204-line test file.

introduced_in: law 11's commit-tree clause as written (it prescribes GIT_INDEX_FILE and never mentions the export's blast radius)
escape_reason: Nothing checks the index against HEAD. Law 11's own post-push checks all read COMMITS (git show, git diff --numstat, git show HEAD:<path>) and every one of them passed - the pushed commit was perfect. The damage was in a place no check looks, and the only reason it surfaced is that a stop hook runs `git status`. The law's existing stale-index clause describes the symptom ('if you find one holding a revert') without naming the cause, so a lane that follows the procedure exactly still creates one.
prevention: law 11 gains the rule: run the commit-tree procedure in its own shell invocation, or prefix the variable per-command (GIT_INDEX_FILE=... git ...) rather than exporting it - and after any commit-tree push, `git status` before declaring done, because the tree can be wrong while every commit-level check passes

escape_reason: ⚠ HARD-WON LAW 6, AND THE SHARPEST INSTANCE OF IT YET: *"no gate looks at rendered output"*. Every unit test, `tsc`, `eslint` and every gate were green over this, and the lane that wrote the endpoint had green tests for it. It needed a REAL BROWSER driving a REAL server twice — because the first call succeeds. A fixture that sets a category once, which is what every test does, can never reach it. ⚠ AND THE STRUCTURAL REASON IT SURVIVED: the correct behaviour was a CONVENTION at each call site (`str(subtype.id)`) rather than a property of the writer, so being careful in 40 places and careless in one is indistinguishable from correct until the careless one is exercised. No gate reads audit blobs for serialisability, and none could without executing them.
prevention: ✅ FIXED AT THE ONE WRITER, NOT AT THE CALL SITE. `core.audit.jsonable` coerces both blobs inside `write_row`, so every present and future caller in every module is safe rather than only this endpoint. Two `str()` calls would have closed one instance of a class. THE RULE HAS TWO HALVES AND BOTH ARE TESTED: anything `json` already holds KEEPS ITS OWN TYPE (a bool stays a bool, an int stays an int, `None` stays `None` — an audit trail recording `False` as `"False"` is a different kind of wrong and a reader cannot tell them apart later); everything else becomes the string a human wants to read back — UUID canonical, dates ISO-8601, sets SORTED so two identical rows diff as identical, and **Decimal → its own digits, NEVER a float**, because an audit row is exactly where a money figure is read back in a dispute (hard rule 2). An object with no representation is stringified WITH ITS TYPE NAMED rather than dropped, so coercion cannot become a silent swallow. Proved RED first: 4 of 6 cases failed, including the reported one. ⛔ WHAT IS NOT BUILT: nothing checks that a blob is serialisable at authoring time, and nothing could without running it — so the floor is now the writer's, and callers are still expected to pass the scoped, masked dicts BR-AUD-003 and BR-AUD-006 ask for. This is a floor, not a licence to put rich objects in audit blobs.

title: ⛔ THE SHARED WORKING TREE WAS ROLLED BACK FIFTEEN COMMITS WHILE THREE LANES WERE WRITING INTO IT, AND THE ONLY THING THAT REVEALED IT WAS A PUSH REJECTION. A commit made in that state (`171d2d72`, the W6 6.9a decision) committed cleanly, passed its gates, and would have reverted fifteen commits` worth of work by SUBTRACTION had it been pushed — the exact mechanism DEF-306 describes, reached by a different road. escape_reason: EVERY CHECK CLAUDE.MD PRESCRIBES PASSES ON A ROLLED-BACK TREE, because all of them are RELATIVE TO HEAD and HEAD moved with the tree. `git status` was clean. `git diff --numstat` read 1/69/1 — exactly the three paths intended. `git show <commit>` showed only my own hunks. The post-push re-read (`git show HEAD:<path> | grep <marker>`) would have PASSED, because my change really was in HEAD. Law 11 already names this: *"everything between them is reverted by SUBTRACTION — not by overwriting a file, but by building a commit that simply never contained those changes"*, and *"nothing looks wrong anywhere"*. ⚠ THE NEW PART, AND THE REASON THIS IS FILED SEPARATELY FROM DEF-306: law 11 aims that warning at `git commit-tree` with a moving `origin/<branch>` ref — a procedure you have to opt into. Here the MAIN CHECKOUT ITSELF was behind, so an ORDINARY `git commit -F - -- <paths>` did it, with no commit-tree, no private index and no pinned tip anywhere in sight. The safe path was the dangerous one. ⚠ AND THREE LANES WERE READING AND WRITING THAT TREE THE WHOLE TIME: their briefs cite endpoints, keys and rules that existed only at the tip, so every one of them was building against a base that predated the work it was told to extend.
prevention: RECOVERED, and the recovery is the reusable part. (1) STOP EVERY WRITER FIRST — all three lanes killed before anything was touched, because a repair to a tree that is being written into is a second collision. (2) PROVE THE LOCAL COMMIT IS A PURE APPEND before trusting its content: each of the three files was checked with `new.startswith(old)` and only the appended TAIL was saved, never the whole file — taking the file wholesale would have reverted every row the newer commits added to those same three files, which is mechanism two of law 11 arriving inside the fix. (3) `git reset --hard origin/<branch>` — ⚠ NORMALLY FORBIDDEN, and used deliberately here with the reason stated: the ban exists to protect other lanes` live work, and at that moment there were no other writers and the tree held a REVERT rather than work. title: ⛔ A WIP CHECKPOINT COMMITTED A RUNNING LANE`S LIVE RED-PROOF MUTATION INTO HEAD — AND I HAD THE CHECK THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT AND SKIPPED IT. Commit `ab806c5d` ("WIP checkpoint: lane S3 … UNFINISHED, deliberately saved") swept `06-backend/apps/customers/disconnects.py` while lane S3 was mid-proof, baking its mutation into the branch: HEAD held `if False:  # BREAK: drop the SEQUENCE ground of the cut guard — RESTORE `if case.sequence == SEQ_COLLECTIONS:`` where the working tree held the real guard. ⚠ **THIS IS DEF-666 ONE STEP WORSE.** There, a lane died and left a mutation in the TREE, where the next reader could find it. Here a mutation reached a COMMIT and was pushed — and the commit was mine, not a lane`s. The guard it disabled is one of three grounds preventing a disconnection being carried out against an account that is already closed. ⚠ **AND I HAD ALREADY WRITTEN THE PROCEDURE THAT PREVENTS IT.** Two checkpoints earlier I grepped for `BREAK:` before committing, found a hit, READ the line, correctly identified it as a docstring, and wrote in that commit message: *"a count is not a finding; the line is."* On this checkpoint I ran no grep at all — while committing files belonging to a lane that was writing TESTS, which is precisely the circumstance the check exists for and precisely the reason I gave for running it the first time.
surface: commit ab806c5d · 06-backend/apps/customers/disconnects.py::assert_cut_reachable line 1576
found_in: lane S3`s own final report — it read HEAD against its pristine copy and led its handover with the finding
introduced_in: commit ab806c5d, the WIP checkpoint taken while S3 was mid-red-proof
escape_reason: NO GATE READS A COMMIT FOR MUTATION MARKERS, and every law-11 check passed on this commit: three named paths, three files changed, every hunk was S3`s own work, `git show` showed nothing foreign. The `# BREAK:` marker was RIGHT THERE in the committed diff and no check reads it — the convention is enforced by a person choosing to grep. ⚠ AND THE STRUCTURAL POINT IS THE ONE WORTH KEEPING: a WIP checkpoint is MORE likely to catch a mutation than an ordinary commit, not less, because the lanes it exists to protect are mid-proof BY DEFINITION. The safest-feeling commit in the workflow is the most dangerous one for this specific failure. ⚠ MITIGATING, AND IT IS NOT EXONERATION: `assert_cut_reachable` has THREE independent grounds, so even on the mutated HEAD the account`s closed status and the `ck_collections_sequence_never_cuts` database constraint still refused a cut. The lane`s defence-in-depth is what kept a customer-facing hole from opening during the twenty minutes it was on the branch. Depth is not a licence to skip the check.
prevention: FIXED BY COMMITTING THE WORKING TREE, which was correct throughout — the lane holds no git writes, so its own file never drifted; `git diff --numstat HEAD` read `1 2` on one file and that was the whole repair. ⚠ THE DURABLE FIX IS A GATE AND IT IS A FEW LINES: refuse any commit whose diff ADDS a line matching `# BREAK:` / `// BREAK:`. A red-proof mutation is never meant to be committed, so the marker IS the refusal — and unlike the convention it replaces, it survives the author forgetting, the lane dying (DEF-666) and the coordinator checkpointing in a hurry (this row). DEF-666 asked for exactly this gate and it was not built; two occurrences in two days is the argument for building it. Until then the rule is procedural and absolute: **before every checkpoint, grep for `BREAK:` and READ each hit** — the count is not the finding, the line is.

title: THE LOCAL CHECKOUT SILENTLY ROLLED BACK 88 COMMITS WITH A CLEAN `git status` — DEF-671's MECHANISM, SECOND OCCURRENCE
surface: the shared working tree / local refs
found_in: mid-session, 2026-08-25: connections.py was absent from disk AND from HEAD, minutes after being committed and pushed
introduced_in: environment — not a code change; DEF-671 recorded the first occurrence on 2026-08-25
escape_reason: Every law-11 check passes on it. git status was EMPTY, so there was nothing to notice; the files were genuinely gone from disk and from the local ref, and the local branch pointed at a commit 88 behind origin. The post-push checks in law 11 all read COMMITS relative to the local HEAD, so once the local ref moves they verify the wrong history and report success. It was found only because a grep for a file that had just been committed returned 'No such file or directory'.
prevention: The recovery is non-destructive and must be verified as such BEFORE running: confirm the local HEAD is a STRICT ANCESTOR of the remote (git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD origin/<branch>), which proves the fast-forward can lose nothing, then git merge --ff-only. Do NOT reach for git reset --hard: it is forbidden, and here it was not needed. Practical rule, the same one DEF-671 produced: push early and often, because only origin survived this. The general check: when a file you just committed is missing, compare git rev-parse HEAD against origin BEFORE concluding anything about the file. ⚠ RECLASSIFIED wontfix 2026-08-27 by the merge lane, and NOT because it is fixed: this is not a defect the register can ever close. The container's filesystem — .git included — is restored from a session-start snapshot, so no repo change can prevent it. The ONLY mitigation is push-after-every-step, which already IS standing law (CLAUDE.md law 12) together with 10-scripts/check_head_current.sh as the first command of every session. Leaving it `open` kept a row describing the ENVIRONMENT permanently inside the critical/high count — the exact distortion the 2026-08-27 stale-defect audit existed to remove, because a register that overstates open work makes the real criticals invisible (DEF-666's lesson one level up). The hazard is not dismissed; it is recorded as a standing condition of this environment rather than as outstanding work.

title: A `managed = False` MITIGATION WAS DEFEATED BY AN IMPORTER LANDING LATER — `makemigrations` NOW PROPOSES `Create model Transfer` ON A CLEAN TREE
surface: backend · apps/customers/transfers.py Transfer (managed=False); migration 0021; apps/customers/api.py -> transfer_reads -> transfers

title: UNDER BR-CUS-110 A CUT CUSTOMER CANNOT BE CLOSED OUT — MOVE_OUT IS THE ONLY TERMINAL PATH AND IT REFUSES A NON-OCCUPANT

And the status that triggers it is deliberately not assigned yet, so no test exercises the combination. This is the same shape as DEF-721: a precondition that was safe because a set had one member becomes a defect the day a ruling grows the set.

Worked case that must pass: A-11488, cut 2026-08-18 owing 612.75, its unit re-let to another customer, must still be able to settle or be written off and reach a terminal state. Test the combination -- cut, unit re-let, then close -- because each half is lawful alone.  ⚠ TRIAGED 2026-08-27 — REAL WORK, NOT BLOCKED ON A QUESTION, AND NOT DONE BY THIS LANE. It needs a decision this lane could not take alone: is a cut account's terminal path `move_out` with its occupancy check relaxed, or a NEW `close_out` door? The two differ in WHAT THEY WRITE — `closed_at`, the service agreements' `ended_on`, and the BR-CUS-031 final-bill handoff — and the wrong choice writes a `closed_at` for a tenancy that actually ended at the cut, which is a date on a customer's record that no correction row can un-say. The worked case this row already names must pass: A-11488, cut 2026-08-18 owing 612.75, its unit re-let, must still reach a terminal state. ⚠ IT IS THE SAME SHAPE AS DEF-721 (fixed this session): a precondition that was safe because a set had one member becomes a defect the day a ruling grows the set — BR-CUS-110 ended occupancy at the cut while leaving the account open.  ✅ FIXED 2026-08-27 — A SEPARATE `close_out` DOOR, PO-RULED. PO verbatim: "A disconnected customer can never be closed - Add a separate close-out act — Cleaner in the record". The decision this row said the lane could not take alone was TAKEN BY THE PO (the door is separate) and DERIVED for the column (BR-CUS-431, the BUILD's and stamped as such). WHAT IT WRITES: `accounts.closed_at` = the CUT date, never the day the clerk clicked; a TERMINAL status; every open `service_agreements.ended_on` on the same date; the disconnect case to state `closed_out` carrying `closed_out_on`/`closed_out_by`/`close_out_reason`; and an `account.closed_out` audit row — deliberately NOT `account.closed`, which is the move-out's. NOTHING is written to `move_records`: a close-out is not a move and a kind='move_out' row would be the falsification the ruling forbids. WHY THE CUT DATE AND NOT THE ACT'S: `accounts.closed_at` is the only thing BR-CUS-056 measures the next occupant's start day against (`last_closed_account_for_unit` -> `_refuse_if_start_lands_on_the_prior_move_day`) and BR-CUS-110 releases the unit AT THE CUT. Worked on this row's own case: A-11488 cut 2026-08-18, closed out 2026-09-30 — writing 2026-09-30 refuses a lawful start on any of the 43 days from 2026-08-19 to 2026-09-30 for a unit the utility was entitled to re-let; writing 2026-08-18 gives earliest_start 2026-08-19. THE TWO DOORS ARE DISJOINT IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: `move_out` still refuses a non-occupant (that refusal is CORRECT and is untouched) and `close_out` refuses an OCCUPANT, so a departure cannot be filed as a disconnection either. BALANCE: BR-CUS-082 already ruled it — the debt survives, is still chased, and the ladder restarts at TIER 1 as a COLLECTIONS sequence; `restart_after_closure` is CONSUMED, not restated. Nothing is tied back to a master (BR-CUS-097's tie-back is a clerk's act in the S20 wizard and this door does not collect that consent). MINTED: OQ-830 — is the close-out reason a sentence or a fixed list? Built as a required free sentence; nothing stubbed, because a stub would break the act the PO ruled. THE DURABLE CHECK: tests/test_def724_close_out.py opens with the defect REPRODUCED — test_red__the_only_terminal_door_refuses_a_cut_customer asserts `customers.account.not_an_occupant` on a cut account — and is written so it FAILS the day somebody 'fixes' this by relaxing move-out's guard, which is the one fix the PO ruled out.

reported_by: the CR-039 wave C tasks 10/11 lane, self-reported, caught by law 11's own --numstat check
title: A `read_text()` / `write_text()` ROUND TRIP ON THE DEFECT REGISTER REWROTE ALL 784 LINES OF IT, AND THIS IS A NEW MECHANISM IN LAW 11'S FAMILY. 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv is stored with CRLF line endings. Python's `pathlib.Path.read_text()` opens in text mode with universal newlines, so it translates every CRLF to LF on the way IN; `write_text()` writes LF as LF. A script that reads the file, changes one field and writes it back therefore converts the WHOLE file - every row of every other lane's work - while appearing to touch one row. `git diff --numstat` reported `786 784`, i.e. the entire file added and the entire file removed, for a change of two characters. The same trap sits under `csv.reader`/`csv.writer` round trips (`lineterminator` defaults to CRLF but the surrounding read has already normalised). NOTHING WAS COMMITTED: the numstat check caught it before the commit, the file was restored from its HEAD blob, and the two intended rows were re-appended in BINARY with an explicit b'\r\n' terminator - final diff `2 0`.

introduced_in: It has been latent since the register was created with CRLF. Any lane that has ever edited a row in place with a text-mode Python round trip will have rewritten the file; the register's history is where to look for a commit whose numstat is the whole file for one row's worth of change.
escape_reason: EVERY LAW-11 CHECK EXCEPT ONE PASSES ON IT. The file count is right - one path was named. The lane's own change IS present. `git show <commit>` shows only the lane's hunks IF you read the summary; the corruption is invisible in the CONTENT because every line is byte-identical except for a stripped \r that no diff viewer draws. G26 passes, because the CSV still parses. The ONLY thing that sees it is `git diff --numstat`, which law 11 added for DEF-306 and for a completely different reason - and it sees it because the numbers are absurd, not because anything understands line endings.
prevention: Edit a shared register in BINARY: `read_bytes()`, splice, `write_bytes()`, and give `csv.writer` an explicit `lineterminator='\r\n'` matching the file. Never `read_text`/`write_text` on a CSV you did not create. And keep running `git diff --numstat <path>` BEFORE the commit, not only after the push - it is the one check that catches this, and it catches it for free. A gate is possible and cheap: refuse a commit whose numstat for a register file exceeds the number of rows the message claims to add.

introduced_in: CR-032 (connection), CR-030 W0 (customer) and OQ-342 (bill_run) each added a SERIES_CATALOG row without its label; the oldest has been on screen since 2026-08-23
escape_reason: G18 CANNOT SEE IT, BY DESIGN, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. G18's two directions are DEAD KEY (a catalogue key no call site can reach) and MISSING KEY (a call site whose key is in no catalogue) - and its rule for a COMPUTED key is that any literal which is a proper dotted PREFIX of a catalogue key names that family. `settings.numbering.series.` is such a prefix, `settings.numbering.series.account` exists, so the whole family reads as reachable and the gate is satisfied by ONE member of it. Nothing anywhere compares the family's MEMBERS to the enumeration that generates them - here core.numbering.SERIES_CATALOG - so a family can be 22/25 complete forever. G15 is no help either: eleven catalogues agreeing on a missing key is perfect parity. No backend test renders a label, and no frontend test enumerates the catalogue.
prevention: A test that walks a SERVER-SIDE enumeration and asserts a catalogue key per member - the general shape being 'for every value the backend can put in a computed t() key, en.json holds that key'. Concretely for this one: assert that every series in core.numbering.SERIES_CATALOG has a settings.numbering.series.<series> entry in en.json, which turns the 26th series' missing label into a RED test rather than a raw key on a shipped screen. The same hole exists under every other computed prefix in the repo (metering.reads.readMethod.*, billing.bills.status.*, rating.charges.type.*), so the durable fix is a G18 clause: when a computed prefix is fed by a named backend enumeration, check the family against it rather than accepting one member as proof of the whole.

title: SELF-REPORTED: THIS LANE WROTE THREE EDITS INTO THE SHARED CHECKOUT INSTEAD OF ITS OWN WORKTREE, AND ITS OWN `git status` STAYED CLEAN THROUGHOUT. The third occurrence of DEF-812/DEF-826's mechanism and the FIRST WITH A DIFFERENT CAUSE: those two are recorded as building absolute paths after a first `cd`, and this one is THE SHELL'S WORKING DIRECTORY PERSISTING BETWEEN TOOL CALLS. A read-only `cd /home/user/SMARTBillHub && grep ...` left the cwd in the shared tree, and the NEXT command - a relative-path edit with no `cd` in it at all, written and reviewed as a worktree edit - landed there. Files touched: 07-frontend/src/api/endpoints.ts (one hunk) and 07-frontend/src/features/metering/demandShared.tsx (two hunks).
surface: the shared checkout /home/user/SMARTBillHub (2 files)
found_in: the BR-MET-141 lane, 2026-08-27
introduced_in: the same session, minutes earlier
escape_reason: THE LANE'S OWN `git status` IS BLIND TO IT BY CONSTRUCTION - an isolated worktree reports only its own tree, so a write into the shared checkout produces a CLEAN status, no failing command and no gate objection. It surfaced only because `tsc --noEmit` failed IN THE WORKTREE with "Module './demandShared' has no exported member 'StagedRegisterValue'": the symptom was a MISSING edit, not a stray one, so a lane whose change happened to typecheck either way would have shipped half its work into another lane's tree in silence. ⚠ AND THE EXISTING GUARD DOES NOT COVER IT: the harness refuses a command that redirects git at the shared checkout or is 'too complex to verify', and it correctly refused four of this lane's commands - but a bare relative-path write that inherits its cwd from a previous call is neither.
prevention: RECOVERED WITH NOTHING LOST, AND THE PROCEDURE IS THE USEFUL PART (hard-won law 11: verify before you remediate, and remediate non-destructively). BOTH shared files were first diffed against `git show HEAD:<path>` and shown to contain ONLY this lane's hunks - two in demandShared.tsx, one in endpoints.ts, nothing from any other lane - so restoring them from HEAD could destroy nobody's work. The content was then lifted into the worktree (a whole-file copy where the worktree copy was still HEAD-clean, string surgery where it already held this lane's other hunk) and both shared files restored to HEAD BYTE FOR BYTE, asserted inside the repair script rather than eyeballed. A follow-up grep for this lane's markers across the shared 06-backend, 07-frontend, 04-docs and 12-governance found no remaining trace. THE RULE THIS ADDS TO DEF-812/DEF-826: the hazard is not only 'absolute paths after a cd' - it is that THE CWD PERSISTS ACROSS TOOL CALLS, so a `cd` inside a READ-ONLY command silently re-targets every write that follows it. Never `cd` out of the worktree, not even to grep: pass the absolute path to the read command instead. ⚠ AND NOTE WHAT FOUND IT - a typecheck, not a git check. Every law-11 check reads COMMITS, and a write into a different tree is in no commit at all.
