title: A DUPLICATE-OWNER REFUSAL RAISED TransactionManagementError INSTEAD OF THE HELPFUL ANSWER IT WAS WRITTEN TO GIVE. `premises_owners.create_premises_owner` catches the `uq_premises_owners_tenant_name_ci` IntegrityError and calls `_duplicate_name_error`, which QUERIES for the party that already exists so the message can name it and the clerk can link to it instead. prevention: RUN THE NEIGHBOURS' TESTS, NOT ONLY YOUR OWN, WHENEVER YOU ADD A CONTROL TO A SHARED FORM - `vitest run` over every test file that mounts the modified component, which is how this was found. And in the control itself: any async list feeding a `.map()` coalesces to `[]` at BOTH ends (the setter and the render), because the two failure modes are different - a bad response and a caller that passes nothing - and a single guard leaves the other one live. The rule underneath is hard-won law 3 pointed at the UI: the failure mode of an optional convenience must be its own absence, never the loss of the record the form exists to save.

escape_reason: NOTHING IN THIS REPO READS PROSE FOR TRUTH, AND THAT IS r11 STEP 0'S WHOLE REASON FOR EXISTING ('Keep this human - nothing automated reads prose for truth'). The ruling stands; its evidence sentence does not, and the next agent reads the ruling. reported_by: the CR-039 wave D 16-19 lane, after its own new test failed three times on what looked like a product bug
title: `monkeypatch.undo()` IN A TEST SILENTLY DISARMS AN AUTOUSE FIXTURE, AND THE FAILURE LOOKS LIKE A BROKEN TRANSACTION. tests/test_us_ten_helpers.sqlite_guc is an AUTOUSE fixture that patches core.tenancy.connection with a recording fake, because sqlite has no set_config; it does so through the same function-scoped `monkeypatch` instance every test in the file shares. A test that calls monkeypatch.undo() to lift its OWN patch therefore ALSO lifts the autouse one - core.tenancy.connection becomes the real sqlite connection, and the very next tenant_ctx raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: no such function: set_config`. THE SYMPTOM POINTS AT THE WRONG PLACE: the traceback names the `with tenant_ctx(...)` line, so it reads as a connection soured by a rolled-back transaction, and the first two fixes attempted (raise-instead-of-create, then splitting the test into three tenant_ctx blocks) were both workarounds for a diagnosis that was wrong. FIXED by taking a private pytest.MonkeyPatch() and undoing it in a finally - the shape tests/test_us_bil_surface_apis.py already used, which is the only prior undo() in the suite and had got it right.
surface: [backend] 06-backend/tests/test_us_ten_helpers.py::sqlite_guc (autouse, patches core.tenancy.connection) -> any test in the suite calling monkeypatch.undo() -> core.tenancy.set_current_tenant's `SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', %s, false)`
found_in: 2.58.0 - this lane, in its own new test; NOT a product defect and nothing shipped is affected
introduced_in: The trap has existed since sqlite_guc became autouse. It has never fired because this is only the SECOND test in the suite ever to call undo(), and the first one used a private instance.
escape_reason: NOTHING COULD HAVE CAUGHT IT, AND THAT IS THE POINT WORTH KEEPING. `undo()` reads as local - the author's mental model is 'lift MY patch' - and pytest's API gives no signal that the instance is shared with fixtures. ruff and black see valid code; no gate reads fixture scope; and the runtime failure names a DIFFERENT file (core/tenancy.py) and a DIFFERENT operation (the GUC statement) than the line that caused it. It is the same class as DEF-182's 'a check whose output cannot distinguish pass from fail': here the FAILURE cannot distinguish its own cause, so it sends the reader to the product.
prevention: TWO THINGS. (1) The rule, which is one line: NEVER CALL `monkeypatch.undo()` ON THE FIXTURE INSTANCE IN THIS SUITE - take a private `pytest.MonkeyPatch()` and undo THAT in a finally, exactly as test_us_bil_surface_apis.py does. Both current uses now follow it. (2) The durable one: a lint or gate clause that flags a bare `monkeypatch.undo()` in 06-backend/tests and points at this row, because the cost of learning it the hard way is three wrong fixes and about twenty minutes of test runs, and the suite's autouse fixtures (sqlite_guc, audit_rows, series_sink) are exactly the machinery a test cannot afford to have silently removed.

reported_by: the CR-039 wave E tasks 20-21 lane, self-reported after nearly reporting a clean run on truncated evidence
title: run_gates' ONE-LINE DETAIL SHOWS 5 OF N PROBLEMS, SO A LANE THAT GREPS THE RUN OUTPUT FOR ITS OWN FILES GETS A FALSE ALL-CLEAR. `common.summarize(items, limit=5)` prints the first five problems and '(+N more)'. On a gate with a large standing backlog that is a 1.7% sample: G1 packet reported '5 shown (+293 more)' - 298 problems - and THIS LANE'S NEW FILE `apps/tenancy/service_size_classes.py` was one of them, missing its Lifecycle trailer entirely. The lane grepped the full run_gates output for its own filenames, got zero hits, and was one step from reporting 'every FAIL is pre-existing and none names this lane'. The list is alphabetical-ish by walk order, so a file late in the walk is structurally invisible; `apps/tenancy/...` sits behind `apps/assets`, `apps/audit`, `apps/billing` and `apps/customers`. The finding was recovered only by re-implementing each gate's predicate in a scratch script and reading the UNTRUNCATED list. NOTE THE SHAPE: the summary is not lying - it prints an honest count - but the count is the one part a grep cannot search, and a grep over the output is the natural thing for a lane to do.
surface: [gates] 10-scripts/gates/common.py::summarize (limit=5) as consumed by 10-scripts/gates/run_gates.py's table; every gate that calls it
found_in: the working branch, 2026-08-27, running run_gates for CR-039 wave E tasks 20-21
introduced_in: not a regression - summarize() has capped at 5 since the gate suite was built; it became a false-clear the day a gate's backlog grew past a handful, and G1 is at 297
escape_reason: THIS IS DEF-182 IN A NEW PLACE, AND DEF-182'S OWN SENTENCE IS THE DIAGNOSIS: 'a check whose output cannot distinguish pass from fail is worse than no check, because it is trusted.' Here the GATE was right - G1 correctly held 298 problems including this lane's file - and the RUNNER's presentation hid it. Nothing is broken in either component; the failure is at the seam, and it only bites the specific question a lane asks at step 3 ('is any of this mine?'), which is not the question the summary was designed to answer ('how bad is it?'). It also cannot be caught by a gate, because the gate is the thing being summarised. Two accidents made it recoverable: G1 was the ONLY gate this lane was failing, and the lane happened to re-implement the predicate to be sure.
prevention: TWO FIXES, and the first is small. (a) HAVE run_gates WRITE THE FULL LISTS TO A FILE - one line per problem, per gate, e.g. 10-scripts/gates/last_run_problems.txt - and name that path in the summary line. The table stays readable, and 'grep the output for my files' becomes a correct method instead of a trap. (b) BETTER, and it is what a lane actually needs: teach run_gates a --mine <path>... filter that reports, per gate, only the problems naming the paths given, and prints 'N problems, 0 yours' explicitly. Until either exists, the lane-level rule is the one this defect was found by: NEVER conclude 'no gate names my work' from a grep over run_gates output - re-run the individual gate and read its full list, because the runner shows five.

introduced_in: the seam mechanism itself - every block has always resolved through the SERVICE layer; the trap appears the moment a lane adds a block, which is rare enough that nobody had written it down
escape_reason: THE GUARD EXISTED AND THE LANE DID NOT RUN IT. found_in: 2.61.1, on the CR-040 wave A/D lane branch

reported_by: this lane's own test, before merge (DEF-901/902/CR-040-A1 lane) — never on a branch and never seen by a user
title: READING `row.code` OFF A LOOKUP HANDLER'S QUERYSET IS A 500 FOR `tax_jurisdictions`, WHICH HAS NO `code` COLUMN. The new BR-TEN-161 fixture-gap read compared the tenant's rows to the platform fixture by taking `row.code` off `handler.search(None)`. Every other reference list has a `code` column and it worked; `tax_jurisdictions` does not — BR-TEN-037 makes it tenant-entered with the NAME as its identity, and its handler's `serialize` is the only thing that publishes `code: row.name`. So `GET /lookups/tax_jurisdictions/fixture-gap` answered `AttributeError: 'TaxJurisdiction' object has no attribute 'code'` — an HTTP 500 on the one list in twelve that is shaped differently.
surface: [backend] apps/tenancy/services.reference_list_fixture_gap — the held-codes read
found_in: unmerged, on this lane's own branch — the case that caught it was written before the code it caught
introduced_in: 2026-08-27, in the first cut of the DEF-902 fixture-gap read
escape_reason: A LOOKUP HANDLER IS DUCK-TYPED AND NOTHING TYPES ITS ROW. `LOOKUP_LISTS` holds twelve handlers from five modules, each wrapping a different model, and the contract between them is prose — there is no Protocol, no ABC and no annotation that says a row has a `code`. `mypy` is not run on this repo and would not have known either. Eleven of the twelve models DO carry `code`, so any test written against a normal list passes and the odd one out is invisible: `tax_jurisdictions` is the single exception and the module docstring records it as 'gap 2'. ⚠ AND THE CORRECT READER ALREADY EXISTED SIX HUNDRED LINES AWAY: `reference_sweep._held_codes` reads every list through `handler.serialize(row)['code']` for precisely this reason, and its docstring says so. The defect was writing a SECOND reader rather than reusing the one that had already learned this — which is the same shape as hard-won law 1, one layer down: a rule that is written in a function nobody is required to call is not a rule.
fixed_commit: this lane, same session — `reference_list_fixture_gap` now calls `reference_sweep._held_codes(list_code)` rather than re-deriving codes, so the held side and the sweep's own plan read the SAME codes through the SAME handler contract and cannot disagree about one list. The fixture side was already changed to `reference_sweep._fixture_entries` for the mirror-image reason (`tax_jurisdictions` is a dict keyed by STATE, and iterating it naively reports a gap of zero for a list that has one). `tests/test_def_902_reference_freshness.py::test_the_state_keyed_list_resolves_through_the_SWEEPS_OWN_RESOLVER` is the case that caught it and is what keeps it caught.
prevention: WHEN A READ NEEDS A FACT ABOUT EVERY REFERENCE LIST, CALL THE FUNCTION THAT ALREADY ASKS FOR IT — do not write the query again. `reference_sweep._held_codes` and `_fixture_entries` are the two readers that have already met every exception in this family (`tax_jurisdictions` twice over, `premises_types`' missing handler, `import_mappings`' generated entries), and each of those exceptions cost a defect to learn. A cheap machine check is possible and is NOT built here because it belongs to the handler framework rather than to this lane: give `LOOKUP_LISTS` handlers a typing `Protocol` naming `search`/`count`/`serialize`/`used_by`, and a test that walks every registered handler, serializes one row of each and asserts the published `code` is a non-empty string. That test would have gone red on this in under a second, and it is twelve lines.

reported_by: the DEF-901/902/CR-040-A1 lane, incidentally — a test asserting something else printed the mismatch
title: THE DEMO TENANT RECORDS ITS STATE AS "Texas" AND THE PLATFORM FIXTURE KEYS ITS TAX ROWS UNDER "TX", SO THE FIVE TEXAS JURISDICTIONS CAN NEVER REACH IT FROM THE FIXTURE. Measured: `apps/tenancy/fixtures/lookup_defaults.json` carries `tax_jurisdictions` as a dict with exactly two keys — `TX` (5 rows) and `ALL` (3 rows: County, City, Special district, no rate). `services.tax_jurisdiction_entries(fixture, state_code)` resolves `keyed.get(state_code or "", []) + keyed.get("ALL", [])`. `apps/tenancy/management/commands/seed_demo.py` provisions with `"state": "Texas"` (two sites, lines 90 and 123) and `tests/test_us_ten_helpers.brazosbend_payload` does the same, and NOTHING normalises the value — a test asserted `tenant.state` and got the literal `'Texas'`. So the resolver returns **3 rows, not 8**, and Texas State, the Local rate, the PUCT, the City franchise fee and the TWDB surcharge are delivered by the fixture to NOBODY. ⚠ THE DEMO IS NOT VISIBLY BROKEN because `seed_demo` plants its own `{"name": "Texas State", "level": "state"}` jurisdiction separately (line 284) — so the tenant HAS Texas tax and the FIXTURE path is the thing that is dead. That is the dangerous half: a second delivery mechanism is hiding a broken first one.
surface: [backend] apps/tenancy/services.tax_jurisdiction_entries against seed_demo's `state` value; the same mismatch reaches provisioning, the sweep and the `--tenant` repair door
found_in: v2.63.0 on the branch; the mismatch is older than this lane and reaches any tenant whose state is spelled out
introduced_in: whenever the fixture adopted two-letter state keys while the signup payload kept full state names — the two have never been checked against each other
escape_reason: NOTHING COMPARES THE FIXTURE'S KEYS AGAINST THE VALUES ANY TENANT ACTUALLY RECORDS, and the miss is invisible from both ends. From the fixture's end `TX` is obviously right — it is how the corpus writes a state. From the signup form's end `Texas` is obviously right — it is what a person types, and `tenants.state` is a free-text column with no choices behind it. DEF-444 already taught this family its lesson and taught it ONE CASE TOO NARROW: it fixed the tenant that records NO state, and the tenant that records a state the fixture does not recognise takes the SAME silent path — `keyed.get(state_code, [])` returns `[]` for `'Texas'` exactly as it does for `''`, and the `ALL` scaffold arrives either way so the list is never empty and never looks wrong. ⚠ AND THE DEMO SEEDER PLANTS ITS OWN TEXAS JURISDICTION BY ANOTHER PATH, which is why no walkthrough, no browser check and no screenshot has ever shown the gap: the product a person looks at is correct and the mechanism under it is not. Found only because a test in an unrelated lane asserted `tenant.state` and printed `'Texas'` where the author expected a key that would resolve.
prevention: A GUARD THAT COMPARES THE TWO SIDES, WHICH IS CHEAP BECAUSE BOTH ARE ALREADY MACHINE-READABLE: assert that every state value the seeders and signup fixtures write resolves to a NON-SCAFFOLD set through `tax_jurisdiction_entries` — i.e. that `len(entries(fixture, state)) > len(entries(fixture, ""))` for every seeded tenant. That is one assertion and it goes red on this today. ⚠ AND THE REAL FIX IS A RULING, NOT A CODE CHANGE, WHICH IS WHY THIS ROW IS OPEN: `tenants.state` is free text with no choices behind it, so 'Texas', 'TX', 'texas' and 'Tx' are all reachable through the signup form and only one of them resolves. Either the column becomes a two-letter code with a picker (a schema + screen change that touches signup), or the resolver normalises (which needs a signed mapping — 'which spellings mean TX' is a decision nobody has made). Choosing either one here would be inventing law. ⚠ AND DO NOT 'FIX' IT BY EDITING seed_demo TO SAY 'TX': that repairs the demo and leaves every real customer who types their state name in the same hole, which is the shape DEF-444 warns about in its own row.

title: THE FIX FOR DEF-896'S THIRD SITE WROTE TAILWIND UTILITIES INTO A FILE THAT IS NOT ROUTE B, SO THE TOOLBAR IT REPAIRED WOULD HAVE RENDERED WITH NO LAYOUT AT ALL. reported_by: the Product Owner, on the live deployment at v2.61.1, with a screenshot of bill BL-2607-000001
title: EVERY SEEDED BILL SHOWS THE MONEY-INTEGRITY ALARM IN RED - 'No - these do not match. Do not treat this bill as settled until someone has looked at it.' - AND THE MONEY MATCHES. The evidence the panel prints beside it is the diagnosis: 'Saved bill: 64.570000 USD over 0 line(s). Charge lines: 64.570000 USD over 6 line(s).' The TOTALS are equal; only the LINE COUNT differs, and it differs because the saved payload's line set is read as EMPTY. pipeline._payload_lines looks for a list under 'lines', 'invoice_lines' or 'charge_lines', or under services[].lines, and returns [] for any other shape - deliberately, so an unrecognised payload fails the tie-out loudly rather than passing quietly. DocumentTieOut.ties_out then requires payload_line_count == row_line_count, so 0 != 6 turns BR-BIL-032 red on a bill whose figures are correct. Either the seeded payload is stamped in a shape _payload_lines does not recognise, or it genuinely carries no lines; both are defects and they are different ones. THE COST IS THE ALARM ITSELF: this is the one check that would catch a customer seeing one number while the trial balance shows another, and a clerk who meets it on all 47 bills learns to scroll past it

The seeder writes its payload by a different path and nothing compares the two. The failure is also SILENT IN THE RIGHT DIRECTION for a test: ties_out returns False, which is what a test asserting a REFUSAL wants to see, so the defensive branch is well covered and the healthy branch on real seeded data is covered by nothing. And no gate reads rendered output (hard-won law 6), so a red panel on 47 of 47 bills is invisible to CI
prevention: A guard that opens a SEEDED bill - not a hand-built payload - and asserts the tie-out is GREEN, non-vacuously: payload_line_count > 0 AND equal to row_line_count on the same invoice. That is DEF-828's shape (the empty set and the non-empty set asserted together) and it is the only form that can tell 'recognised and equal' from 'unrecognised and therefore zero'. Second, _payload_lines should say WHICH keys it looked for when it finds none, so the panel's evidence line names the shape mismatch instead of reporting a count of zero as though it were a fact about the bill

title: A MERGE COMMIT SHIPPED CONFLICT MARKERS BECAUSE A SHELL `while read` LOOP SILENTLY DROPPED ITS LAST LINE. title: A WORKTREE-ISOLATED LANE WROTE TWO OF ITS OWN WRITE-BACKS INTO THE SHARED TREE, AND THE REVERSAL THEN TRUNCATED 33 KB OF ONE OF THEM FOR FORTY SECONDS. Two documentation edits - B14's two stale 'RATIFIED and UNCHECKED' lists, and CR-041's own outcomes table - were applied under `/home/user/SMARTBillHub/` instead of `/home/user/SMARTBillHub/.claude/worktrees/agent-aee3a7b2d0401020c/`. MECHANISM: the lane ran `cd /home/user/SMARTBillHub && grep ...` to READ a document that its own worktree also holds, and the next few commands were heredoc python scripts using RELATIVE paths. The Bash tool resets cwd between calls, but a compound `cd X && python3 - <<PY` runs the script in X - so a read in the shared tree silently became a write in the shared tree one command later. NEITHER EDIT WAS EVER COMMITTED AND NEITHER WAS LOST: both were reproduced in the worktree and both shared files are byte-identical to HEAD again, verified by comparing the full text against `git show HEAD:<path>`. ⚠ THE SECOND HALF IS THE WORSE ONE. Reversing the change-register edit was written as `text[:start] + <the original sentence>` on the assumption that the inserted block ran to end of file. It did in the WORKTREE's copy, whose branch is 3 commits behind; in the SHARED tree, three later CR sections sat after it, and the slice deleted all of them - 991,943 bytes down to 962,397. Caught by the script's own `assert live == HEAD` on the very next line, and restored from `git show HEAD:<path>` immediately.
surface: [repo] /home/user/SMARTBillHub 04-docs/02-decisions/14-ui-conventions.md + 12-governance/11-change-requests.md, the shared working tree six other lanes read
found_in: the lane's own post-write verification - grepping BOTH trees for the sentence it had just written, and finding it in the wrong one
introduced_in: 2026-08-27, this lane, twice within about fifteen minutes
escape_reason: EVERY CHECK IN CLAUDE.md LAW 11 IS ABOUT WHAT A COMMIT CONTAINS, AND THIS NEVER REACHED A COMMIT. The file count, the hunks, `git show HEAD:<path>`, `git diff --numstat` against the tip - all of them read COMMITS, and an uncommitted edit in a tree you do not own is invisible to every one. `git status` in the worktree was clean and correct throughout, because the worktree genuinely had no such change. The lane's own commits were all correctly scoped. Law 11's actual warning covers the mirror case - another lane's work being swept INTO your commit - and says nothing about YOUR work landing in THEIR tree, where the next lane to run `git add` on that path would have committed a stranger's paragraphs under its own message (mechanism five, from the other end). ⚠ AND THE TOOL-LEVEL GUARD DID NOT FIRE: this session refuses commands it judges too complex to verify as staying inside the worktree, and it passed `cd /home/user/SMARTBillHub && python3 - <<PY` because the path is explicit and legible. It is legible and it is the wrong tree.
fixed_commit: this lane - both shared files restored and verified byte-identical to `git show HEAD:<path>`; both edits reproduced in the worktree and committed there
prevention: READ FROM THE WORKTREE TOO. There is no reason to `cd` out of an isolated worktree to read a shared document: the worktree holds every tracked file, and the only thing the shared copy offers is commits this branch has not merged - which `git show <ref>:<path>` answers WITHOUT changing directory and without any possibility of a write. So: never `cd` to the shared tree at all, and prefer ABSOLUTE paths in every heredoc script, which is what this lane did for its other twenty edits and exactly why those were correct. ⚠ AND THE SECOND LESSON IS SHARPER THAN THE FIRST: A REVERSAL COMPUTED FROM ONE COPY OF A FILE MUST NOT BE APPLIED TO ANOTHER. `text[:index]` is safe only if you know what follows the index IN THE FILE YOU ARE WRITING; here the two copies were three commits apart and the tail differed by 33 KB. Reverse an insertion by replacing the EXACT inserted string with the EXACT original string - a bounded, symmetric edit that cannot reach content it did not touch - and assert byte-equality with `git show HEAD:<path>` before believing it. The assert is what turned this from data loss into a forty-second window.

surface: 12-governance/13-change-process.md step 7 - and 10-scripts/gates/g35_version_lockstep.py
found_in: 2026-08-27 on the integration branch, after four lanes merged
introduced_in: the merges of 2026-08-27 - no single commit dropped it
escape_reason: G35 CHECKS THAT THE FOUR LITERALS AGREE WITH EACH OTHER, WHICH IS ALL IT CAN CHECK, AND THEY DID. A version that never moved is internally consistent; so is one whose bump was reverted. The gate has no notion of what the branch CONTAINS, so it cannot ask whether shipped work is covered by a version, and no other gate asks either. It also cannot see that two lanes chose the same number - the same cross-branch blindness as DEF-977's id race, one file over. And a version literal is a one-line change in four files, which is the exact profile of a hunk that loses a three-way merge without anyone reading it.
prevention: The narrow fix is this cut: 2.65.0, carrying both lanes' work with a changelog entry that names what was lost and why. The durable one is that a version is not a number in a file, it is a CLAIM ABOUT WHAT SHIPPED - so the check that matters is whether the newest changelog entry names the CRs and defects that landed since the previous entry, which is answerable from the register and the git log. Worth building; until then, the merge lane cuts the version, because the merge lane is the only actor that can see all the lanes at once.

reported_by: the merge lane, after disarming it by hand five times in one session
title: MERGING OFF-TREE LEAVES THE SHARED INDEX HOLDING A REVERT OF THE MERGE, AND LAW 11'S OWN REMEDY DOES NOT APPLY. Six lanes share one checkout and one INDEX. A merge computed with git merge-tree and committed with commit-tree - the only way to merge while the others are writing - moves HEAD and does not touch the working tree, so the index still holds the PRE-merge blob for every file the merge changed. A bare git commit by any lane then commits those, reverting the merge file by file in a commit nobody meant to make. It happened five times on 2026-08-27; the largest instance staged a revert of 24 files including WizardFrame.tsx and BillRunWizard.tsx - the fix for a blocker that had stopped the Product Owner billing anybody, landed minutes earlier - plus DateCell, FormModal and the whole CR-042 import set. THE LAW'S REMEDY CANNOT BE FOLLOWED HERE: CLAUDE.md law 11 says 'confirm git diff HEAD is empty, then git reset to disarm it', and in a six-lane tree git diff HEAD is NEVER empty, so the precondition never holds and a blanket reset would throw away five lanes' staged work. The question has to be asked PER PATH.
surface: the shared git index at /home/user/SMARTBillHub - every path an off-tree merge touches
found_in: 2026-08-27, five times during the CR-039..043 merges
introduced_in: the off-tree merge procedure itself - it is inherent to merge-tree plus commit-tree, not a mistake in using them
escape_reason: EVERY LAW-11 CHECK READS COMMITS AND THIS HAZARD LIVES IN THE INDEX. git show, git diff --numstat against the tip, re-reading each file from HEAD - all of them pass, because the commits ARE correct; it is the index that is wrong, and nothing looks at it. git status does show the entries, as ordinary M lines indistinguishable from five lanes' real staged work, which is why they were scrolled past four times before the fifth was noticed. And the signature is counter-intuitive: a STALE entry is one where the working tree matches HEAD and the index does not, which reads like the file is fine.
prevention: 10-scripts/check_stale_index.py, added with this row. It asks the question per path - worktree == HEAD and index != HEAD, a combination that is never deliberate because nobody stages a version identical to a base they have already moved past while holding the newer one on disk - and --fix runs git reset on exactly those, touching the index and never the working tree. Exit 1 when any are found, so it can be a gate or a pre-commit hook. RED-proved by staging a genuinely older blob (the first attempt used a blob that was identical across three commits and did NOT go red, which is why the proof was run at all - hard-won law 7). A merge lane should run it after every off-tree merge, and law 11's remedy paragraph should say that its git diff HEAD precondition assumes a single-lane tree.

A --block flag (or a --lane naming a row in 14-id-reservations.md) so next_id allocates INSIDE the caller's reservation and refuses when that block is exhausted - which is the only thing that can distinguish 'this block is mine' from 'this block is somebody else's'. So the walk goes UP instead: from max+1, jump to high+1 for any ACTIVE block containing the candidate, and repeat. It terminates because the blocks are finite, it never returns an id below the frontier, it cannot land in a reservation, and it always returns an id. Refuse the BAD ID, never the FILING — the one refusal kept is a caller whose own --block is full, where there genuinely is no good id and inventing one outside the reservation is what --block exists to stop. escape_reason: NO TEST COMPARES WHAT A TENANT SELLS AGAINST WHAT ITS PLANS PRICE. The seed tests assert that seeding twice adds nothing (which is BR-TEN-063 working exactly as designed) and the rating tests assert that an ENABLED service seeds its schedule — so the failing case, enable-AFTER-seed, is the one combination neither suite constructs. The idempotency that makes the seed safe is the same property that makes this permanent, which is why it reads as correct in both files  ||  ⚠ THE MECHANISM ABOVE IS HALF STALE AND WAS CORRECTED AT THE FIX (2026-08-28). (1) 'metering.sample_data seeds trash SERVICE POINTS regardless of the flag' has not been true since CR-039 wave A (DEF-795) replaced the literal water/sewer/trash intersection with fixture.estate_plan(enabled...) - the two seeders already agree about the flag, so 'making them agree' was not available as the smaller fix. reported_by: the display-truth lane, self-reported — CLAUDE.md law 11's *"if you do it anyway … then file it"*
title: LAW 11's `commit-tree` RECOVERY PUBLISHED ANOTHER LANE'S IN-FLIGHT WORK TWICE IN ONE SESSION — DEF-168's MIRROR IMAGE, AND THE PROCEDURE PRESCRIBED TO PREVENT IT IS WHAT DID IT. Occurrence 1: a pathspec commit of `12-governance/10-defect-log.csv` carried the CR-044 lane's uncommitted `DEF-1180` row. Occurrence 2, ninety minutes later: the `commit-tree` procedure — seeded from a pinned remote TIP exactly as law 11 prescribes — carried 44 lines of the customers lane's uncommitted `MoveOutWizard.test.tsx` (their DEF-669 work) into a commit about display formatting. NOTHING WAS LOST in either case and no test broke; the damage is to the record, which is why both were invisible until the diff was read.
surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv · 07-frontend/src/features/customers/MoveOutWizard.test.tsx — commits 332c1a8 and 6e3fe9a
found_in: the shared working tree, 2026-08-27
introduced_in: not a regression — this is law 11's known mechanism recurring for the ninth and tenth time
escape_reason: ⚠ **LAW 11's OWN CHECK CANNOT SEE THIS ONE, AND THE LAW SAYS SO WITHOUT SAYING IT LOUDLY ENOUGH.** The file COUNT was right both times (I named 4 paths and 20 paths and got 4 and 20). My own change WAS in HEAD both times. `git diff --numstat` showed deletions only where I intended them. The clause that catches it is the DEF-182 one — *read the hunks, and confirm every hunk is YOURS* — and on a 20-file, 1,136-line commit nobody reads 1,136 hunks, which is precisely DEF-182's own complaint about `--stat` restated one level up. ⚠ **AND THE SECOND OCCURRENCE HAS A CAUSE THE LAW DOES NOT MENTION AT ALL: A RACE.** I ran `git diff --stat -- MoveOutWizard.test.tsx` before committing and it printed `1 insertion` — mine. The customers lane wrote to that file in the ~4 minutes between that check and `git update-index`, and `commit-tree` reads the WORKING TREE, so the pinned-TIP procedure inherited their edit. The pin protects the PARENT and the BASE TREE from moving; it does nothing about the FILES, and a check performed before the read is a check of a different tree.
prevention: THE ONLY CHECK THAT SURVIVES A RACE IS ONE TAKEN FROM THE COMMIT ITSELF, AFTER THE FACT, PER FILE: `git show <commit> -- <path>` for each path, read the hunks, and confirm each is yours. That is what found both of these. **What would make it cheap enough to always do** is a script — the register already has `10-scripts/file_defect.py`, written for exactly this problem in exactly this file, and the general version does not exist: given a commit and an author's intent, list the hunks in it that the author did not write. Filed rather than built here because it is a tooling story, not a display defect, and this lane must not silently widen its own scope. **The narrow, free mitigation meanwhile:** commit ONE concern's files at a time and read that diff — a 4-file commit's hunks can be read; a 20-file commit's cannot, and the 20-file commit is where both of these hid.

title: THE ELEVEN MESSAGE CATALOGUES ARE NOT IN THE FORM i18n_fanin.py WRITES, SO EVERY KEY ADDED THROUGH THE REPO'S OWN TOOL REFORMATS TEN FILES - and parity is ALREADY broken on the branch: en.json holds 9374 keys and the other ten hold 9422, a gap of 48. Two findings, one file set. (a) i18n_fanin.py re-serialises each catalogue as json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) and writes the whole file. Ten of the eleven are not currently in that form, so adding three keys through the tool produces roughly 47 changed lines per file for a 3-line change. Measured directly: re-serialising de.json's own UNCHANGED content is not byte-identical to the committed file. That is a whole-file write wearing an append's costume - the exact mechanism file_defect.py's docstring was written about - and its diff is indistinguishable from corruption, so a reviewer cannot tell an added key from a mangled catalogue. (b) Independently, en.json is 48 keys SHORT of the other ten at the branch tip, which G15 exists to refuse. Neither was caused by this lane; both were found by a build-time guard added while landing three keys, which refused to write a file whose re-serialisation did not round-trip.
surface: [frontend] 07-frontend/src/i18n/locales/*.json (ten of eleven off-format; en.json 48 keys short) and [tooling] 10-scripts/i18n_fanin.py's write step
found_in: branch claude/meter-reads-70rxcc at 6e3fe9a (CR-044 lane)
introduced_in: unknown and probably gradual - a catalogue drifts off-format the first time a key is added by hand instead of through the tool, and nothing since has compared the file against what the tool would write
escape_reason: G15 asks whether the eleven hold the SAME KEY SET and never whether a catalogue is in the canonical FORM, so a file can be off-format indefinitely with every check green - and the first lane to add a key through the tool then ships a 470-line reformat it did not intend and cannot see the meaning of. The parity half is worse: G15 is the check for exactly that and the branch tip is red on it right now, which means either the gate is not run on this branch or its failure is being read as one of the several that fail on HEAD for unrelated reasons (DEF-973's hazard, a truncated summary treated as noise).
prevention: Two, and the first is cheap. (a) Give i18n_fanin.py a --check mode that re-serialises every catalogue unchanged and refuses when the result is not byte-identical, then run it as part of G15 - that turns 'off-format' from invisible into a named failure, and it is the guard this lane wrote inline and then had to throw away. (b) Normalise the ten once, in a commit that does nothing else, so the reformat is reviewable as a reformat rather than riding inside somebody's feature. Do NOT normalise inside a feature commit: this lane deliberately inserted its three keys line-by-line at their sorted positions instead, which is 3 added and 0 deleted per file, precisely so the two changes stay separable.

title: ⛔ TEN CATALOGUES RESOLVED TWO MESSAGE KEYS THAT ENGLISH DID NOT — A PATHSPEC COMMIT OVER A SHARED WORKING TREE PUBLISHED MY UNCOMMITTED ROWS INTO TEN FILES AND LEFT THE ELEVENTH
surface: 07-frontend/src/i18n/locales/*.json — customers.account.type_is_legacy · customers.account.activate_wrong_starting_status
found_in: lane customers-high-severity, 2026-08-27, rebuilding its locale blobs from the remote tip before committing them — the tip already held its own rows in ten files
introduced_in: another lane's pathspec commit over the shared working tree, the same day
escape_reason: LAW 11 MECHANISM FIVE, AND EVERY CHECK IN THE LAW PASSES ON IT. A pathspec commit takes the whole WORKING-TREE content of every path it names, so a lane committing locale files for its OWN rows also shipped mine, which were sitting uncommitted in the same copies. The committing lane's file count was right and its own change WAS present — the law's two headline checks — and reading the hunks of an eleven-file catalogue diff is not something anyone does. ⚠ THE ASYMMETRY IS WHAT MADE IT A DEFECT RATHER THAN A LUCKY EARLY LANDING: ten of the eleven copies had been touched by that lane and were swept; en.json had not, so it alone was left behind. The result is a catalogue set where ten languages resolve a refusal that ENGLISH does not — G15 reads that as a parity break and G32 as a key that renders raw. Neither gate had run between the sweep and the discovery. Nothing in the repo compares WHO AUTHORED a row against WHO COMMITTED it.
prevention: The durable form is the one file_defect.py already proves for the register: make APPENDING the only easy operation, so a shared file cannot be committed as a whole. For catalogues that means a per-key append tool and a gate that refuses a locale commit whose diff spans keys the committing lane does not name. Until then the narrow rule is the one that found this: BEFORE committing a shared file, rebuild its content from the REMOTE TIP plus your own hunks rather than committing the working-tree copy — the working tree is every lane's, the tip is nobody's.

reported_by: merge lane, diagnosing DEF-1080 for the Product Owner
title: Every 500 in production was discarded unlogged - no LOGGING config, so Django's default filtered the traceback away
surface: 06-backend/config/settings - all deployed environments, every unhandled exception
found_in: v2.73.0, surfaced by DEF-1080
introduced_in: the original settings module - LOGGING was never defined, so this has been true since the first deploy
escape_reason: Nothing was broken in a way any test or gate could see: the app answered requests, gates passed, and the ONLY symptom was the absence of a log line nobody had a reason to look for. Django's DEFAULT_LOGGING discards an unhandled exception under DEBUG=False by three mechanisms at once - the console handler is declined by its own require_debug_true filter, mail_admins mails an unset ADMINS, and logging.lastResort does not fire because a handler WAS found and then declined. Django catches the exception itself and returns a response, so it never escapes to gunicorn either, and --error-logfile - saw nothing.
fixed_commit: stale-defect audit 2026-08-27 — CONDITION GONE: 06-backend/config/settings/base.py:236-273 defines LOGGING wiring django.request to an unfiltered StreamHandler, and tests/test_def1080_unhandled_errors_are_logged.py keeps the RED half
prevention: A LOGGING dict in base.py wiring django.request to an unfiltered StreamHandler - stderr IS the container log because docker-entrypoint.sh already runs gunicorn with --error-logfile -. Pinned by tests/test_def1080_unhandled_errors_are_logged.py, which keeps the RED half permanently: it asserts Django's default really does filter its console handler, so the reason this config exists cannot be forgotten. Deliberately a settings module and NOT an env var, because hard-won law 4 says a template change never reaches a host that already has a .env.

reported_by: Product Owner (deployed traceback) - diagnosed by the merge lane
title: Asset import 500 is a GUNICORN TIMEOUT: ensure_reference_catalogs() runs 96 times per row, 1920 queries for a 20-row file
surface: Assets - Import, stage 4 Load. apps/assets/services.py type_by_code/stage_by_code/_flat_catalog_row each re-seed the four catalogs
found_in: v2.73.0 - traceback supplied by the PO from the deployed backend log, 2026-08-27 12:00:14 UTC
introduced_in: the BR-AST-043 gap lane 2026-08-09, which made ensure_reference_catalogs() the guarantee that creation works on a tenant provisioned after the W1 migrations - correct, but placed inside every lookup
escape_reason: It is invisible at test latency and fatal at network latency. 96 reference queries per row x 20 rows = 1920 round trips; at 0.2ms locally that is 0.4s and every test passes, at 15-20ms against a remote database it is 29-38s and the 60s gunicorn timeout kills the worker mid-row. The traceback shows handle_abort/SystemExit inside type_by_code, which is the arbiter SIGABRT, not an application exception - so no error taxonomy, no refusal and no test could have surfaced it. title: A MIGRATED DEPOSIT IS A LIABILITY THE BALANCE SHEET NEVER HEARS ABOUT: create_from_import writes accounts.deposit_on_file and posts nothing, so the seeded estate carries a deposit register of $750.00 against a 2300 deposit-liability GL of $0.00 -- the exact MIRROR of DEF-177

DEF-177 filed the same COLUMN in the opposite DIRECTION on 2026-08-16 and its own prevention text predicts the row would read 'books $150.00 / register $0.00'; nobody checked whether a door existed that produced the reverse. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE DEMO: a migrated deposit is money the utility owes back to the customer. title: THIS LANE REVERTED ANOTHER LANE'S DEFECT ROW BY SUBTRACTION - DEF-1713 left the register twenty seconds after it landed, and the commit-tree procedure CLAUDE.md law 11 prescribes is what did it
surface: process
found_in: review
escape_reason: Law 11's commit-tree procedure pins the TIP to a SHA once and uses it for read-tree and commit-tree, which closes DEF-306's race between those two lookups. It does NOT close the gap between when a lane BUILDS ITS BLOB from a file and when it pushes: the blob was cut from 136b961, a sibling lane appended DEF-1713 at f2b6b74 four minutes later, and the push wrote a whole-file blob that had never contained that row. Every one of law 11's checks passes on it - the file count is right, my own rows are present, git show's hunks are all mine - because the reverted row is not in the diff at all, it is missing from the tree the diff is taken against. The ONE check that saw it is law 11's last one, git diff --numstat TIP..COMMIT read as SUBTRACTION: '2 insertions 1 deletion' on a two-row append is arithmetic that cannot be explained, and that is what found it, twenty seconds after the push.
prevention: Recovered non-destructively: took the file from the pinned tip that HAD the row, re-appended this lane's two rows, pushed again - nothing was rewritten and nothing was force-pushed. THE DURABLE HALF IS ONE LINE IN THE PROCEDURE, and it is not another post-push check: RE-DERIVE EVERY BLOB FROM THE PINNED TIP AT PUSH TIME, never from an earlier read of the same path. A lane that reads a file, works for ten minutes and then pushes is holding a stale whole-file blob, and the append-only registers (10-defect-log.csv, 11-change-requests.md, 02-decision-log.md, 01-open-questions.md) are exactly the files six lanes append to concurrently. Law 11 tells lanes to pin the tip; it does not tell them their own working copy has an age. Post-push, the arithmetic check must be stated as arithmetic: for a pure append of N rows the numstat MUST read 'N 0', and any deletion at all is this defect until proven otherwise.

title: CR-045 WAVE B TASK B.3 IS UNBUILDABLE AS COPY AND THE ROW SAYS THE OPPOSITE. prevention: A wave and its tasks need a countable home - one line per task with a state, in a file a script can read, the same way defects live in 10-defect-log.csv. title: A CONTAINER REWIND LEFT 117 FILES IN THE SHARED TREE HOLDING A 276-COMMIT REVERT, UNDER TWO RUNNING LANES - and CLAUDE.md law 12 told the session to leave it that way. Session start reported HEAD 276 commits behind origin/claude/meter-reads-70rxcc (374bbb0 vs 9ed8d21) with a dirty tree, so law 12's own advice fired: if the tree is NOT clean, someone is mid-edit, leave it and say so. That advice is wrong after a rewind, because the tree is not one state but two. Measured: 166 files differed from the tip; 117 of them were byte-identical to the stale HEAD, meaning no lane had touched them and they held PRE-TIP content, a revert of up to 276 pushed commits; the other 49 were genuine in-flight lane edits. 06-backend/apps/billing/resolution_shadow.py (712 lines at the tip, and put on 10-scripts/gates/human_owned.txt by PO ruling the same morning) did not exist in the tree at all; nor did the g45-g52 gate modules, sixteen tests, or six migrations. 06-backend/apps/customers/api.py held the pre-DEF-1702 version, i.e. with the list filters removed. Both running lanes (DEF-2000-2029 meter-size doors, DEF-2060-2089 size refusal) were building on that base: 47 of the 49 live files sat on stale content, including 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv, 01-open-questions.md, 02-decision-log.md, 09-human-review-ledger.md, 14-id-reservations.md and CLAUDE.md itself. Nothing had yet been pushed, so no work was lost.
surface: process
introduced_in: environment
escape_reason: The detector worked and the INSTRUCTION it gives is what failed. 10-scripts/check_head_current.sh correctly reported behind-and-dirty; law 12 then classifies the tree with a single boolean, clean or not, where clean means recover and not-clean means someone is mid-edit, leave it. After a rewind that boolean is meaningless: the dirtiness IS the staleness for most files and IS live work for the rest, and no check in the repo distinguishes them. Law 11's post-commit checks cannot catch what follows either, and that is why the exposure is critical rather than high - a lane committing a stale path gets the right file count, finds its own hunks present, and reads a diff that never mentions the pushed work it is subtracting. It is the DEF-306 mechanism with a container rewind as the cause instead of a moving ref.
fixed_commit: 2.79.6 8b20ea6 + 9857e71 — 8b20ea6 restored the first 117 stale files and wrote the mix into law 12; 9857e71 corrected the method after it missed 35 more, and the content-addressed test then found the last 15 (every i18n locale, endpoints.ts, ImportWorkflowPage.tsx, and the defect register itself missing 992 lines). Tree verified byte-clean against the tip afterwards; both lanes had worked in private worktrees and lost nothing.
prevention: Two things, one mechanical and one written down. Mechanical: the stale half is computable as the set difference of `git diff --name-only <tip>` and `git diff --name-only HEAD` - everything wrong, minus everything a lane has touched - and that difference is safe to restore because by construction nobody is editing it. All 117 were restored by writing the tip's bytes (git show <tip>:<path>), which also recreates the files the rewind deleted, rather than by git checkout, which law 11 bans and which would have taken the 49 live files with it; then git reset --mixed <tip> moved HEAD and the index without touching a file. Verified byte-for-byte: 117/117 match the tip, 49/49 lane files untouched, and both lanes were sent the pinned tip SHA with instructions to rebuild their edits on it. Two traps found in the doing and now recorded in law 12: git diff still reports a restored file as deleted when it postdates the stale HEAD (untracked, so the diff is not the check - compare bytes), and a plain write drops the executable bit, which no content check can see. Written: law 12 now carries the mix, the two-command separation, the restore form, and the obligation to tell the running lanes the tip SHA. CORRECTION, same hour: that set difference is INSUFFICIENT and left 35 more stale files in place, every shared register among them (02-decision-log.md, 01-open-questions.md, 09-human-review-ledger.md, 11-change-requests.md, 14-id-reservations.md, CLAUDE.md, CHANGELOG.md) plus customers/api.py still holding the pre-DEF-1702 form. The difference only catches files matching the stale HEAD exactly, and a rewind can leave a file at an INTERMEDIATE version, which then hides in the do-not-touch half. The conclusive test is content-addressed: git hash-object <path>, then walk git log --format=%H -- <path> and compare git rev-parse <commit>:<path>. A hit proves the content is a version this repo already had, so no lane authored it and it is safe to restore; a miss proves nothing and must be left alone. All 35 were restored on that evidence and verified byte-for-byte, and the survivors were confirmed SUPERSETS of the tip by diff <(git show <tip>:<path>) <path> showing additions only. Law 12 carries both the content-addressed test and the superset confirmation.

title: A ROUTE SERVING A READ ABOUT AN ACCOUNT ANSWERS 200 FOR AN ACCOUNT ID THE TENANT CANNOT SEE. Found by this lane's own cross-tenant test on the routes it had just mounted; the engine reads predate the routes and were unreachable until now, which is why nothing had ever asked them this question.

title: THE REGISTER FILLS WITH FINISHED WORK THAT READS AS OUTSTANDING, AND THE OBVIOUS GUARD FOR IT WOULD CRY WOLF - MEASURED, AND DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT. G51 asks the FORWARD question - a defect a source file marks `DEF-nnn ✅` must be closed in the register - and nothing asks the REVERSE, so a row a lane forgets to flip is invisible. DEF-1250's lane hit it: its code comments, its business rule, its changelog entry and its decision-log row all said fixed while the register row still said open, hours after shipping. That is the mechanism behind the register's measured ~20% staleness (random sample of 15 open highs, 3 already fixed, Wilson 95% CI 7-45%), which cost a full lane-day aimed at work that was already finished. TWO CANDIDATE SIGNALS WERE MEASURED AND BOTH FAIL. (1) `fixed_commit` non-empty while status is open: only 4 rows in 1,030, and three of those are honest non-fixes reading 'pending', '(none - process)' and '(not fixed)' - the column is used loosely, so a gate on it is noise. (2) a defect id named in the shipped CHANGELOG while its register row is open: 24 of the 110 ids the changelog names. But a changelog entry legitimately NAMES a defect it FILED and did not fix - DEF-2430 and DEF-2431 are the discount lane's two honest deferrals, DEF-2312 the trash base it reported rather than fixed. A crude 'does the surrounding sentence say filed / not fixed / still' test puts at least 7 of 27 in that class, a false-positive rate of 26 percent, and the test is crude so the real rate is higher.
surface: process
introduced_in: implementation
escape_reason: The forward direction is mechanical and the reverse is not. G51 can be exact because `DEF-nnn ✅` in a source file is a CLAIM a machine can read. The reverse asks whether a fix has SHIPPED for a row still marked open, and the only evidence outside the row is prose - a changelog paragraph, a decision-log entry, a docstring - which is exactly what CLAUDE.md's hard-won law 1 says nothing reads for truth. So the escape is structural rather than an oversight: there is no artefact that says 'this is fixed' in a form a check can trust, other than the register row itself, which is the thing being checked.
prevention: NOT BUILT, ON PURPOSE, and the measurement above is the reason - a 26 percent false-positive floor is the profile of a gate that is red from birth, earns a noqa instead of a fix, and then makes its own true findings invisible. This lane shipped G53 the same day on the opposite profile (a NAMED baseline equal to reality on the day it landed, so the 51st arrival is the only thing that goes red) and criticised G18 the same afternoon for reporting a correctly-translated string as raw, so shipping this one would have been the exact fault it had just written up. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT is a structural change rather than a cleverer regex: give the register row the same treatment as the version field - a lane that ships a fix must flip the row in the SAME commit, and a check can then compare the row against the commit that names it, which is a machine-readable claim rather than prose. That is a change to the process file and the r11 step-4 checklist, not a gate, and it is the PO's to weigh because it adds a step to every lane's close-out. Filed with the numbers so the next lane does not re-derive the two dead ends.

reported_by: claude (the DEF-2310 service-declaration lane, on its own push)

Nothing looked wrong: the file count was exactly the 42 paths named, my own hunks were all present, `git show` displayed only my changes, `git status` was clean, tsc and every suite were green. THE ONLY THING THAT SAW IT was `git diff --numstat <pinned-tip> <commit>` READ AS ARITHMETIC — the register said `2 insertions, 4 deletions` where exactly two rows had been edited in place, so two deletions belonged to somebody else. surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv (DEF-2400, DEF-2401) · 12-governance/14-id-reservations.md (the DEF-2490 block's RELEASED state) · the lane's own push helper
introduced_in: 2026-08-28, at this lane's first push — the worktree was created at 178aac8 and the tip had advanced to a1f5a46 by the time the push ran, roughly forty minutes later
escape_reason: CLAUDE.md law 11 already describes this exactly — DEF-1706/DEF-1782, 'PINNING THE TIP DOES NOT PROTECT YOUR BLOB — IT ONLY PROTECTS THE TREE' — and this lane had read it and still shipped it, which is the useful part. The reason is that the law's remedy is a PARAGRAPH a person has to remember at the one moment they are busiest, and its own last line says the durable fix is a helper that REFUSES. This lane's helper did not have that check because it was written for the first push, when base and tip were the same commit, and a check that is correct on the first run is not tested by it. Nothing automated could have caught it either: no gate reads a commit's parent against a lane's base.
fixed_commit: ef5c2c3 (both files restored) + the same commit's push-helper change: the helper now resolves BASE=$(git rev-parse HEAD) and TIP once, runs `git diff --name-only $BASE $TIP -- <the named paths>` and EXITS rather than building a tree when that is non-empty. It refused nothing on this lane's next push because the paths had not moved, which is the correct green.
prevention: Make the refusal the helper's job, never the lane's memory — law 11 asks for exactly this in its own words ('make your push helper REFUSE when a named path moved between your blob's base and the tip — that is a check the next lane inherits instead of a paragraph it has to remember'). The general form worth building once: a shared push script in 10-scripts/ that every lane sources, so the check is not re-derived per lane and cannot be written for the first push and never re-tested. Until then, the arithmetic reading of `--numstat` is the last line of defence and it works — read it as numbers, not as a glance.

reported_by: merge lane, tracing the account upload for the PO
title: A signed rule says an account import skips errored rows and reports 'N created, N failed'; the code loads the whole file in ONE transaction, so one refused row rolls back every account that had already landed
surface: backend
found_in: code read, 2026-08-29, tracing the account upload end to end for the PO walkthrough
introduced_in: CR-030 W1 - the accounts target was added to the shared ETL runner, which had always been all-or-nothing because its other five targets have no write-time business refusals
escape_reason: NOTHING COMPARES A SIGNED RULE'S TEXT TO THE BEHAVIOUR THAT IMPLEMENTS IT. BR-CUS-051 is CONFIRMED and reads 'Import mechanics = the standard: staged -> per-row errors -> skip-errors ON -> N created, N failed summary -> 10,000-row cap'. The runner's stage 4 is one transaction.atomic() around the whole file (import_runs.py:5265 _load_apply) and _load_accounts_rows (6150-6420) has NO try/except and NO savepoint anywhere in its row loop. Four failure modes ARE handled row by row - no unit, no account number, on-file-and-inserting, on-file-and-updating - because each is checked BEFORE the write is attempted; anything the customers writer itself refuses escapes the loop and aborts the run. THREE such refusals exist and NONE has a stage-3 counterpart: _require_plan_on_unit (services.py:1622, BIZ_COMPLETENESS), _refuse_if_unit_occupied (services.py:1620, BIZ_STATE) and the opened_at-is-None refusal (services.py:1628, BIZ_COMPLETENESS). So a run can pass validation with a clean bill of health and still write nothing at all: a 1,213-row migration in which row 63 names a unit with no rate plan leaves ZERO accounts on file, one error message and no receipt. Every gate is green over it - the rule is prose in a markdown table and no check reads prose.
prevention: FIX (CR-047 tasks 8-12): a savepoint per record so a refusal undoes that record and nothing else; the refusal's sentence and fix written onto the row exactly as the four handled cases already do; and the three write-time refusals moved to stage 3 as named rules so they reject a row in the rehearsal instead of aborting the commit. PREVENT, and it is the transferable half: this is hard-won law 1 in the rule layer - a signed rule that no test asserts is a comment. Every CONFIRMED rule that describes RUNTIME BEHAVIOUR (as opposed to a figure) needs one test that fails when the behaviour changes; BR-CUS-051's would be 'a file with one refused row still loads the other N-1', which is a three-line test that has never existed.

reported_by: merge lane, answering the PO's inheritance question
title: An account created by the import inherits its unit's services, plan and meters ONLY when its status is a billing status - a blank status cell loads an account wired to nothing, counted on the receipt as created
surface: backend
found_in: code read, 2026-08-29, answering the PO's question 'what all data you have to inherit from units'
introduced_in: the original _open_account design - the import path reuses the S18/S19 door, and that door only creates service agreements for an occupying account, which is correct for a hand-typed draft and wrong for a migration
escape_reason: NO GATE COMPARES WHAT AN IMPORT CREATES AGAINST WHAT THE SAME RECORD WOULD CARRY IF TYPED BY HAND. services.py:1758 reads 'if is_occupying(status): _make_occupying(account, unit, warnings=warnings)' and _open_service_agreements - the ONLY writer of service_agreements on this path - is inside it. OCCUPYING_BEHAVIOR_CLASSES is (billable, billable_base_only); a row whose status cell is EMPTY resolves to pending_activation (services.py:1358), which is non_billable, so the branch is skipped entirely. The Status column is OPTIONAL in the published template and ACC.STATUS_IN_LOOKUP only WARNS, and only on an unknown value - never on an absent one. So the easiest file to produce - name, unit, account number, balances, no status column - loads N accounts with no service agreement, therefore no service, no route, no cycle, no plan and no meter, and the receipt counts every one of them under 'Accounts created' beside the good ones. Nothing distinguishes the two on any screen. The failure surfaces a month later as a bill run that finds nothing to bill, at which point the fix is a second pass over every migrated account. Measured on the seeded estate: the template's own worked row carries status 'active' so the sample file hides it completely.
prevention: FIX (CR-047 tasks 10-11, under new rule BR-CUS-672, PO ruling 2026-08-29 'if account is created then we need to inherit details form units - otherwise upadling it later will be big tasks'): write the service links for EVERY account this upload creates, whatever its status, and move the plan-required-at-activation check (BR-MET-040) out of the import path to activation where the rule's own wording already puts it. Verified safe: the bill run selects accounts by billing status, so a draft's links are read by nothing until its status changes - which is exactly the property that makes switching a draft on a status change and nothing else. PREVENT: the receipt must report how many accounts took services from their unit as a figure BESIDE 'created', because a count that adds a wired account to an unwired one is the thing that made this invisible.

reported_by: CR-047 frontend lane; filed by the merge lane
title: Three metering-import refusals were written with SINGLE braces, so a clerk read the placeholder's NAME instead of the value - 'Your changeover date ({given}) is in the future'
surface: frontend
found_in: the CR-047 frontend lane, building the changeover-date door - the first thing in the product that could reach these three refusals
introduced_in: whenever each refusal's English copy was written; the keys predate the screen that can trigger them, which is why no human had ever seen one render
escape_reason: THREE CHECKS PASSED OVER IT AND EACH WAS ASKING A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM THE ONE THAT MATTERED. i18next interpolates {{name}}, not {name}. (1) G18 compares code to catalogue in both directions and is merge-blocking - it asks whether a KEY RESOLVES, and never whether the key's PARAMETERS resolve, so a key with a perfectly good English sentence and unusable placeholders is indistinguishable from a correct one. (2) G15 proves the eleven catalogues agree with each other, and all eleven agreed perfectly - because all eleven were translated from the same broken English, so the parity check confirmed the defect eleven times over. (3) No test had ever rendered these three refusals, and could not have: until the changeover door was built, NOTHING IN THE PRODUCT COULD REACH THEM. That is the escape underneath the other two - an unreachable refusal's copy is unverifiable by construction, and this repo has no gate that counts refusals nothing can trigger. Proved before fixing by prefixing the value with a probe string; the probe interpolated nothing, which is the same evidence a clerk would have had.
prevention: FIXED in the CR-047 frontend lane (double braces, plus an assertion pinning both interpolated dates so a regression goes RED). THE DURABLE FIX IS A GATE AND IT IS CHEAP: extend G18 to parse each catalogue VALUE for brace placeholders and fail on any single-brace {token} - it is a regex over strings the gate already reads, it names the whole class rather than these three, and it can be proved RED on this very defect today. WORTH SAYING SEPARATELY, because it is the bigger finding: a message_key that no code path can currently reach is copy nobody has ever read. G18 knows which keys are raised and which are defined; it does not know which are REACHABLE. A count of unreachable refusals would have flagged these three as unverifiable before anyone built the screen.

title: The sample-data seeder cannot create its payment-plan block, so provisioning lands SHORT and eight accounts-import end-to-end tests fail on a cause that has nothing to do with importing accounts
surface: backend
found_in: CR-047 merge lane, 2026-08-29, verifying whether the customers lane had broken these tests - it had not
introduced_in: unknown; the seeder's own refusal message names the likely cause - the payments block that is supposed to leave CASE_PAYMENT_PLAN's June bill wholly unpaid
escape_reason: NOTHING RUNS THE SEEDER AS A GATE, so a broken sample tenant is invisible until a test that provisions one happens to fail - and then it fails wearing the name of whatever that test was about. customers/sample_data.seed_sample_payment_plans raises BlockCannotRun: 'no payment plan was created: the books say this account owes 0, and the fixture's plan spreads its UNPAID June bill'; payments/sample_data.seed_sample_plan_payments then raises because no live plan exists; and tenancy reports 'the sample set landed SHORT at provisioning - identity: exception; billing: exception; payments: exception; payments: exception; billing: exception; billing: exception; customers: exception; payments: exception'. EIGHT tests in tests/test_cr030_w1_accounts_import.py fail as a result, every one of them named for account-import behaviour (a migration landing balances and a balanced entry, the opening entry tying out, the changeover date holding the books, confirming the date posting once, a future date refused by name, a row naming no unit erroring, a negative bucket carrying a credit, an unmappable account type not loading a typeless account). NONE of those behaviours is broken. MEASURED BOTH WAYS to prove the attribution: the same single test fails identically at 5344618 (before this CR's inheritance change) and at c637fa6 (after it) against the same database - 42s and 126s, same failure - so the change is exonerated and the cause predates it. THE ESCAPE IS THE MIS-ATTRIBUTION, exactly as DEF-054: a lane reading this failure list concludes its own work broke the account import, and either reverts correct code or spends a cycle proving it did not. This lane spent that cycle.
prevention: TWO HALVES. (1) FIX: the seeder's own refusal names the block to look at - payments' _share_for is supposed to return None for CASE_PAYMENT_PLAN's June bill, leaving it wholly unpaid for the plan to spread; something changed that and the plan block broke with it, exactly as its message predicted. That message is the model for how a fixture should fail and is why this was diagnosable at all. (2) PREVENT, and it is the durable half: a gate that PROVISIONS A SAMPLE TENANT AND REFUSES ON ANY BlockCannotRun. tenancy.sample_data already reports every failed block by name and S62 renders them, so the information exists and nothing acts on it - hard-won law 1 in the fixture layer. Such a gate would fail on the commit that broke the block rather than eight tests later under someone else's name, and it can be proved RED on this defect today. Related: DEF-110 asked for the same class of fixture completeness check and is still open.

title: An account import over 5,000 rows dies with an AUTH error in Insert-and-update mode: the work moves to a background worker that carries no role, and customers.update_from_import demands one
surface: backend
found_in: PO report, 2026-08-29: 'When we tried to upload accounts yesterday with 9000 accounts - it gave us Auth error and then 500'
introduced_in: CR-046 C4, which added update_from_import with an @require_role decorator copied from the hand-typed doors - the import door's own creator, create_from_import, is deliberately UNDECORATED for exactly this reason and the difference was never noticed
escape_reason: EVERY TEST USES A SMALL FILE, AND THE DEFECT ONLY EXISTS ABOVE 5,000 ROWS. ASYNC_ROW_BAR is 5_000 (import_runs.py:152): at or below it the load runs on the request, which carries a real actor with a real role, and everything passes. Above it the stage is deferred and the worker carries _JobActor - '__slots__ = ("id",)', an id and NO role, by design and correctly so (import_runs.py:2840). apps/customers/services.py:4246 declares @require_role(SYSTEM_ADMIN, BILLING_CLERK) on update_from_import, which _load_accounts_rows calls at import_runs.py:6506 for every row matching an account already on file. core/permissions.require_role reads getattr(actor, 'role', None), gets None, and raises AuthError AUTH-002 - its own docstring says 'job callers get the same exception and their runner records it'. Under the all-or-nothing transaction the whole run then dies with not one row written. MEASURED: of 220 role-guarded functions in the backend, EXACTLY ONE is reachable from the import load path, and it is this one - so the class is a single line, and nothing looks for it. The shape is DEF-1108 repeating in a different function: that defect moved the approver check out of the worker and its docstring says 'rebuilding a role in the worker would be a second, weaker place for that decision to live'; this decorator was added independently afterwards and nobody re-asked the question. It bites only in Insert-and-update mode, which is the mode a corrected re-run uses - so it hits hardest on the second attempt at a migration, when the operator has already fixed their file.
prevention: FIX: remove the decorator from update_from_import, exactly as create_from_import already stands. The role IS checked - @require_role sits on transform/validate/load at the door, on the request that enqueues the stage, plus BR-MET-098's approver check in the API layer. A second check in the worker is not defence in depth; it is a check that can only ever produce a false refusal, because the worker is architecturally incapable of carrying a role. PREVENT, and this is the durable half: a gate that walks every function reachable from a DEFERRED stage body and fails on any @require_role among them. The data is all static - the seam table names the callees, and the deferred bodies are three named functions - and it can be proved RED on this defect today. Without it the next decorator added to a customers or assets import writer reproduces this exactly. ALSO OWED: at least one test above ASYNC_ROW_BAR. Every existing import test uses a handful of rows, so the entire deferred path - the one a real 9,000-account migration always takes - is untested end to end.

reported_by: CR-048 B2 lane; filed by the merge lane
title: A reissued bill document - the name or address fix a customer actually receives in the envelope - leaves no delivery row at all, so nothing is ever queued for it
surface: backend
found_in: CR-048 B2 lane, wiring billing's queue call to fire its notification event
introduced_in: apps/billing/document_correction.py as first written - OQ-103 option (a), the document-only correction path; it was built to restate the DOCUMENT and delivery was never part of its scope
escape_reason: NOTHING COUNTS THE PATHS THAT SHOULD QUEUE A DOCUMENT AGAINST THE PATHS THAT DO. apps/billing/document_correction.py contains no reference to delivery, notifications or the queue - measured by grep, not inferred. It is the OQ-103 option (a) path: a name or address fix that produces a corrected DOCUMENT for the customer without touching money, which is precisely a document a customer is supposed to receive. It never queued anything, so no test could regress and no gate could notice: G13 reads props, G20 reads seams, and none of them asks 'which code paths produce a customer document, and do they all reach the one write path into the queue'. The CR-048 wiring made it visible only because that lane went looking for every billing call site and found exactly one - issue.py:1688 - which means every OTHER path that ought to produce a delivery does not.
prevention: NOT FIXED, AND THE REASON IS A RULE-6 JUDGMENT RATHER THAN SCOPE. The queue's idempotency key is (tenant, source_type, source_id, channel, copy_no) and the ORIGINAL issue already holds that key for this invoice. So a naive queue_document call from the reissue path writes NOTHING - silently, because a duplicate key is the queue working correctly - and the operator would see a reissue that appears to succeed and never arrives. Making it work needs a copy_no decision: is a reissued document copy 1 of the same invoice, or a new source? That decides whether the customer can hold two documents for one bill and which one a reprint resolves to, so it is a ruling, not an implementation choice. bill_corrected is the event it would fire once that is settled. PREVENT: the durable check is a gate that walks every path producing a customer-facing document and asserts it reaches queue_document - the same shape as CR-047's DEF-2515 test that walks the import seam surface for role gates, and buildable the same way.

title: The failures CSV returns the operator's own row in the WRONG COLUMN ORDER, because the code takes the order from a jsonb object and Postgres does not preserve object key order
surface: backend
found_in: CR-047 merge, 2026-08-29 - two tests red on the merged branch that were green in the authoring lane's own worktree
introduced_in: CR-047 task 13, the results.csv endpoint, whose _source_headers derived the column order from row 1's stored 'raw' keys
escape_reason: HARD-WON LAW 1 IN THE DATA LAYER: A DOCSTRING CLAIMED A GUARANTEE THE DATABASE DOES NOT GIVE. _source_headers returned the keys of row 1's 'raw' on this stated reasoning: 'extract builds every row's raw as {header: value for header in headers} from one csv.DictReader, so row 1's key order IS the file's column order'. That is TRUE of a Python dict and FALSE after a round trip - 'raw' is a JSONField, Postgres stores it as jsonb, and JSONB DOES NOT PRESERVE OBJECT KEY ORDER: it re-sorts by key length then bytewise. A file whose first column is UNIT_REF came back starting ACCT, NAME - the four-letter keys first. NOTHING COULD CATCH IT: the type is right, the values are right, every row carries the same keys, and only the ORDER is wrong, which no schema check and no type checker models. AND IT PRESENTED AS FLAKINESS ACROSS LANES, which is the expensive part: the same file reported 23/23 green in the authoring lane's worktree, 2 failures from a sibling lane, and 4 on the merged branch. Same code; different key ordering coming back from a different database state. Three honest reports, three different answers, and the natural conclusion at each step was that somebody else's change had broken it.
prevention: FIXED: the file's column order is now written at EXTRACT into mapping_spec['source_headers'] as a JSON LIST - jsonb ARRAYS are ordered and only objects are not, so it is the same store in a shape it can keep. Stage 2 replaces mapping_spec wholesale and now carries the key forward explicitly; dropping it there would restore the defect at the exact moment a run becomes downloadable. The old derivation stays as a NAMED fallback for runs extracted before this change, documented as approximate rather than silently returning a wrong order that looks right. RED-PROVED BOTH WAYS: removing the stored read gives 'At index 0 diff: ACCT != UNIT_REF'; restoring it passes, 2 passed in 89s. WHY IT MATTERS rather than being cosmetic: BR-CUS-673 requires the failures file to be the original row byte-identical and NOT RE-ORDERED, because the operator's whole workflow is to fix two cells in the spreadsheet they already know and upload that file again. Re-ordered columns make it unusable for its only purpose. PREVENT: treat any ORDER read out of a JSONField as a defect on sight - store order as a list, or not at all. Worth a gate that greps for iteration over a JSONField's keys where the resulting order is then used.

title: Every payment-plan notice shared one idempotency key, so a customer was chased once and never again
surface: backend
escape_reason: Nothing looked wrong at any layer. apps/payments/notices.py passed the PLAN as source_id, so the reminder, the missed notice, the second notice and every instalment of a twelve-month plan all produced the same (tenant, 'plan', plan_id, channel, copy_no) tuple. The second write found the first row and returned created=False - which is the CORRECT behaviour of an idempotent queue and is indistinguishable from a replay. No exception, no gap in the audit trail, no failing test: the suite asserted that a notice was queued, and one was. So the product can record that a customer signed and cannot produce what they signed. reported_by: CR-048 task E9 lane / merge lane, 2026-08-30
title: Nothing actually prevents deleting a template version a sent document points at, and the two sides refuse different things
surface: backend
escape_reason: BR-NOT-025 says a template version any sent document points at is ARCHIVED and NEVER DELETED. Adding the archived_at column (CR-048 task E9) is half of it; nothing enforces the other half. BOTH PINS ARE PLAIN COLUMNS RATHER THAN FOREIGN KEYS - invoices.template_id/template_version and outbound_messages.template_id/template_version - so the database will not refuse the delete, and the two application-level checks DISAGREE about what they refuse: the letter side refuses to delete any version that is not a draft, while the bill side refuses only a version that is published or pinned. SO AN ARCHIVED BILL-TEMPLATE VERSION THAT NO ISSUED BILL HAPPENS TO POINT AT CAN BE DELETED TODAY. And a shell, a data migration or a future endpoint bypasses both checks either way. Found by the lane that added the column, which correctly declined to narrow a delete path on its own - narrowing what a rule permits is a change to the rule.
prevention: FIXED 2026-08-30 with (b), the delete trigger, and (a) was rejected on a MEASUREMENT rather than on cost: outbound_messages.template_id is POLYMORPHIC and nothing said so - of its 181 rows, 94 carry a BILL template's id (every one a pdf_print row whose source_type is invoice, all 94 resolving against bill_template_versions) and 87 carry a notification template's id. A single foreign key cannot point at two tables, so ADD CONSTRAINT would be REFUSED today on 52 percent of that table. The version tables' unique key is also three columns (tenant_id, template_id, version_no), so even the invoices side would need a raw three-column composite FK whose MATCH SIMPLE semantics leave a template-without-version row unchecked; and both are money-path tables, so ADD CONSTRAINT takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and a full validation scan. BUILT: billing/0025_def2496_bill_version_pin_lock.py counts BOTH invoices and outbound_messages; notifications/0017_def2496_notification_version_pin_lock.py counts outbound_messages alone. Neither is SECURITY DEFINER and both fail CLOSED under RLS in every reachable case, argued in each migration docstring. This deliberately overturns billing/0019's reasoning (a trigger would be a second implementation of the rule) - the notification side had already answered that in notifications/0006, where a service check and a trigger run together on purpose and say why. A SECOND LIVE HOLE FELL OUT OF THE SAME MEASUREMENT AND IS FIXED HERE TOO: templates_service.pin_count counted invoices ALONE, so a bill layout pinned by a printed bill and by no issued invoice read as UNPINNED and delete_version - the function whose whole job is to refuse that - allowed it; it now asks notifications by name through delivery_seam.template_print_pin_count, and an UNASKABLE count RAISES rather than returning the invoice figure alone (DEF-127's mistake pointed at a document instead of money). PROVED RED FIRST on live PostgreSQL with no trigger present: Failed: DID NOT RAISE Exception for a bill layout an issued bill pinned, the same verbatim for a DRAFT a queued message pinned (the hole notifications/0006 left by construction - it refuses only NON-DRAFT deletes), and assert 0 == 1 on the print-row pin. GREEN after: 5 cases; template suites 26 passed / 12 skipped on sqlite and green on Postgres. NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY, AND ON THE AGENDA: the two sides still refuse different things for an UNPINNED version - the letter side refuses any non-draft delete (NFR-8), the bill side lets an archived-but-unpinned layout go. Harmonising them would NARROW a ratified delete path, which is a change to a rule and not a defect fix. BR-NOT-025 protects a version a document POINTS AT and is silent about one nothing points at, so both sides are lawful today. Flagged in the human-review-ledger row instead. Test: 06-backend/tests/test_def2496_pinned_version_delete_guard.py

title: Two lanes in private worktrees both took DEF-2503, and the allocator was right both times
surface: governance
escape_reason: The send-test lane and the thirteen-events lane both allocated DEF-2503, minutes apart, and file_defect.py printed an accurate line to each. It reads the working tree, HEAD, @{upstream} and every refs/remotes/origin ref - which is the PUSHED world plus the caller's own checkout - and a sibling working in its own git worktree has rows in NONE of them until it pushes. So both lanes correctly computed max+1 and correctly got the same number. CLAUDE.md law 11 predicted this exactly (DEF-1787, 2026-08-27) and the mitigation it prescribes - re-derive the ids at PUSH time and renumber if one is taken - is a paragraph a lane has to remember, which is the category of check that fails. NOTHING DOWNSTREAM WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT: a duplicate id in a 1,055-row register reads as a register, not as an error. Caught only because the two rows collided in a git merge conflict and the merge lane parsed both sides before resolving.
fixed_commit: 6afd94ea - the duplicate id was renumbered; the durable check is NOT built (file_defect.py still has no --verify mode)
