THE DURABLE FIX IS A CHECK, NOT A PARAGRAPH, and it is small: file_defect.py already knows how to compute the next free id, so it should also offer a --verify mode that re-reads the register and fails if an id the caller holds is now taken - and the push helper should call it. That converts 'remember to re-derive at push time' into something the next lane inherits. Cheaper still and worth doing alongside: make the allocator RESERVE its id in 14-id-reservations.md as its first act, so a sibling reading the register sees the claim even before the row exists.

reported_by: the Product Owner, on the live deployment at v2.81.1
title: Both redesigned notification screens are nested inside a legacy equal-column card grid that crushes them
surface: frontend
escape_reason: MEASURED IN A REAL BROWSER at 1728px, which is the only thing that could see it. `.settings-grid` is `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(320px, 1fr))` - a legacy EQUAL-COLUMN card grid - and both redesigned screens are still nested inside it. TEMPLATE DESIGNER: the frame renders at 448px inside a 1424px page, because it lands in ONE 448px cell of that grid rather than spanning the page. Its own 1fr:3fr split is then applied CORRECTLY to 448px, giving a 108px control rail - which is why 'Save as new version' wraps onto four lines and the body box is a few characters wide. NOTIFICATIONS: ten cards all forced to 330px, widest:narrowest exactly 1.00:1, where the teardown's agreed shape is three cards and a rail. WHY THREE WEEKS OF FIXES DID NOT CONVERGE, and this is the real finding: every fix was made INSIDE the new components, and the thing crushing them is the old page wrapper one level up that no lane owned or touched. NOTHING COULD SEE IT. Every gate reads source. Every screen test runs in jsdom, which performs NO LAYOUT AT ALL - so a column collapsed to 108px passes an assertion that its class is present, and the class IS present and IS correct. title: Syncing the local ref after a commit-tree push with git reset --mixed leaves the whole working tree at pre-push content, and git status reports clean

introduced_in: the law 11 commit-tree procedure itself
escape_reason: EVERY CHECK IN LAW 11 PASSES ON IT. The commit-tree push is safe by construction - it reads the pinned tip, not the working tree - so the file count is right, the author's own hunks are present, git show prints only those hunks, and git diff --numstat against the tip shows deletions nowhere. The damage is not in the commit at all; it is LEFT BEHIND in the tree. git reset --mixed moves HEAD and the index and touches no file, which is exactly what law 12 prescribes as the LAST step of a rewind recovery - after the tip's bytes have been written. Used alone, to sync a local ref after pushing, it does the opposite: HEAD advances past three lanes' pushed commits while the files stay where they were, and git status then reports CLEAN because the index matches the tree it was told to match. The tree held a latent revert of 39 files for as long as it went unnoticed, and the first ordinary pathspec commit in it would have published that revert with a correct file count. Nothing in this repo looks at the shared tree after a push; the post-push checks all read COMMITS.
prevention: Diagnosed by law 12's content-addressed test and repaired by its procedure: git diff --name-only against the pinned tip gave 39 files; git hash-object plus a walk of git log per path proved 38 of them were older versions of their own path and the 39th did not exist locally at all because it was created after the stale content; all 39 restored by WRITING the tip's bytes - git show TIP:path - which also recreates the missing file, then modes re-set from git ls-tree, then verified byte-for-byte rather than by diff. The durable rule, and it belongs beside the commit-tree procedure in law 11: A COMMIT-TREE PUSH DOES NOT UPDATE YOUR WORKING TREE, SO SYNCING THE REF ALONE LEAVES IT STALE. After pushing, either fast-forward with git merge --ff-only, which moves the files too and refuses rather than discards, or run the reset and then write the tip's bytes over every path that differs. Verify with git diff --numstat against the tip printing NOTHING - a clean git status is not the check, because a clean git status is the symptom.

title: The geometry harness measures a live stack and nothing asserted the stack was current, so it reported detailed failures over screens that were already correct
surface: 10-scripts/render-checks/cr048-notifications-geometry.mjs
introduced_in: the harness itself
escape_reason: The harness drives a real browser against a vite build served by 07-frontend/server.mjs proxying to a Django runserver. NEITHER REBUILDS ITSELF and the backend runs --noreload, so it can never pick up a source change - yet nothing in the harness compared what it was measuring against what the source says. A stale stack therefore produces the one output a check must never produce: a confident, detailed, entirely accurate report about an app nobody is running. It bit twice in one hour and the SECOND time was after the first was understood. First: dist/ was 2.5 hours old and 17 assertions failed, every one of them a fix that WAS in the source. Second: the frontend was fresh, the backend had been up five hours, and 6 assertions failed on strings the backend source no longer contains. Both times the natural reading was that a lane had reported work it had not done. No other check in this repo could have caught it either, because every one of them reads SOURCE - which was correct throughout.

Frontend: the served build's app-version chip against 07-frontend/package.json - and it runs AFTER sign-in, because the shell is not drawn on the sign-in page and the first draft ran there and reported not-checked on every run. Backend: it has no version endpoint, so it is checked by AGE, and the right server is RESOLVED rather than guessed - BASE's port, to the server.mjs process serving it, to that process's own API_PROXY_TARGET out of /proc/pid/environ, to the runserver on that port. Six runservers are typically up, one per lane, and an earlier draft refused on a server this harness does not talk to. Where any step cannot be resolved it SAYS SO on stdout rather than passing silently. BOTH HALVES PROVED RED FIRST: bumping package.json gave STALE FRONTEND exit 2 naming both versions; touching apps/notifications/rendering.py gave STALE BACKEND exit 2 naming the pid, its start time and the changed file. Green after a rebuild and a restart.

title: A TAMPER TEST CORRUPTED WHICHEVER FILE THE FILESYSTEM YIELDED FIRST, SO IT FAILED ON ONE STACK AND PASSED ON ANOTHER FROM THE SAME COMMIT - test_cr049_t3__corrupting_the_stored_bytes_makes_the_route_REFUSE took next(p for p in docs_dir.rglob('*') if p.is_file()). It passed 3 runs locally including with -p no:randomly, and failed on the merge lane's stack, from an identical commit. title: The production frontend build was broken on the branch by a test file importing ApiClient from the wrong module, and every local check passed over it
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/notifications/templateChangeTrail.dom.test.tsx
introduced_in: the CR-049 task 8 lane
escape_reason: THE PO FOUND IT BY RUNNING docker compose build - it is the FIRST failure today that no check in this repo could see, and it stopped a deploy. The lane reported tsc clean and it was telling the truth about the command it ran; vitest also passed, because vitest never type-checks. What breaks is the PRODUCTION build's own command, tsc --noEmit && vite build, which type-checks the test files too. The durable ask, which this lane did NOT do and which is worth a story: run the image build's exact command in the gates, because a check that runs a DIFFERENT command from the one that ships is the class of failure this repo keeps paying for - a gate that cannot fail on the thing it is pointed at.

title: TWO TEMPLATE COLUMNS ACCEPT THE SAME HEADER WORD 'register', SO WHICH FACT IT SUPPLIES DEPENDS ON WHAT ELSE IS IN THE FILE
surface: 06-backend/apps/metering/read_import.py TEMPLATE_COLUMNS - 'register' is an alias of BOTH the 'reading' target and the 'channel' target
found_in: 2026-08-30, by the CR-054 W1 reading-sheet lane, while choosing header words for the generated sheet that could not collide with an importer alias
introduced_in: unknown - both aliases have been in TEMPLATE_COLUMNS since BR-MET-032's template was written; the collision was never noticed because detect_mapping is order-dependent and always produces SOME answer
escape_reason: detect_mapping walks TEMPLATE_COLUMNS in dict order and takes the first alias that matches, so it can never fail or warn - it simply resolves the ambiguity silently and differently depending on which OTHER headers the file carries. A file headed meter,date,register maps register to the READING; add a 'reading' column and the same word now maps to the CHANNEL instead, so every register value becomes a channel name and every row errors channel_unknown. No test asserts what 'register' means, and no check looks for a word appearing in two alias tuples.
prevention: A test that asserts no header word appears in more than one TEMPLATE_COLUMNS tuple, in both importers - it is four lines and it would have caught this the day the alias was added. The FIX itself needs a ruling, not a lane's guess: 'register' most naturally means the reading value on a meter export and the register NAME on a rate export, and picking one changes how existing customer files parse.

title: A WORKTREE-ISOLATED LANE'S UNCOMMITTED WORK APPEARED IN THE SHARED CHECKOUT — TWICE IN ONE SESSION, BY TWO DIFFERENT LANES — AND THE SHARED TREE WAS SITTING ON A SIX-ROW REVERT OF THE DEFECT REGISTER
surface: /home/user/SMARTBillHub (the shared checkout) vs .claude/worktrees/agent-*; 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv, 06-backend/apps/metering/validation.py, 06-backend/apps/metering/services.py
found_in: 2026-08-30, by the orchestrating session running law 12's check before its next commit: `git status` in the shared tree showed 10-defect-log.csv modified, and `git diff` against the branch tip showed the file was MISSING six rows that exist on the tip (DEF-2450..2455) while carrying one row that does not (DEF-2449, authored by the CR-051 backend lane, which is worktree-isolated and had not pushed it)
introduced_in: 2026-08-30, when lanes were first dispatched into git worktrees per CLAUDE.md law 12 and given edit freedom inside them
escape_reason: THE WORKTREE IS THE MITIGATION AND IT HAS A HOLE IN IT. The Edit tool and the git wrappers both refuse a shared-checkout path from a worktree-isolated lane, and that refusal is what makes a worktree safe — but a bare `python3 - <<PY` or `bash` heredoc carrying a literal `cd /home/user/SMARTBillHub` goes through NEITHER, so the one editing route with no guard is the one a lane reaches for when it wants several replacements at once. The CR-054 W1 lane self-reported this as DEF-2455 the same hour; this row records that a SECOND lane did it independently, which makes it a property of the setup rather than one lane's slip. Compounding it: the shared tree was 31 files behind the tip with no local edit to any of them, so a pathspec commit on the defect register would have published a six-row deletion with a correct file count and its own hunks present — every check in law 11 passes on it, which is law 12's own warning arriving in practice.
prevention: THREE THINGS. (1) A lane must never write a literal repo path in an edit script: resolve the root once with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` and build every path from it, so a wrong tree is a missing file rather than a silent write — this is the only half a lane can fix for itself and it belongs in every dispatch brief. (2) The durable half, which no lane can build for itself: a guard that refuses a write whose resolved absolute path is outside the caller's own worktree, applied to the heredoc route as well as the Edit tool — the hole is that one route is unguarded, not that lanes are careless. (3) The repair, which is the part worth copying: NEVER `git checkout`/`stash`/`reset --hard`/`clean` in a shared tree (law 11 forbids all four). Separate the halves first — `git diff --name-only <tip>` is everything wrong, `git status` is what a lane actually touched — then preserve the live row to a file, write the tip's bytes over the stale file, `git merge --ff-only <tip>` so the FILES move and not just HEAD, and verify by SUBTRACTION: `git diff --numstat <tip>` must print nothing. A clean `git status` cannot tell you this and never could.

title: THE ONE THING BLOCKING BR-CUS-107's `Disconnected` STATUS IS NAMED WRONG IN FOUR PLACES -- IT IS CUSTOMERS' OWN SCOPE SEAM, NOT BILLING'S STAGE 1 -- AND THE GUARD THAT ASSERTS IT CANNOT GO RED FOR THE THING IT GATES

escape_reason: EVERY COPY AGREED WITH EVERY OTHER COPY, WHICH IS WHAT A MEASUREMENT LOOKS LIKE WHEN IT IS NEVER RE-TAKEN. Four files say a Disconnected account 'raises BillingRuleError and lands on every run's phase-3 exception list as a NON-RETRYABLE break' because billing.stages.resolve_subscription.CLASSES_THAT_BILL excludes non_billable, and that closing DEF-701 is therefore 'a billing change and customers may not make it (B2 section 2)'. On an account walked through the REAL ladder to a real cut it reads ACTIVE -- marked_disconnect appears in apps/customers in exactly two places, SEED_ACCOUNT_STATUSES and one comment, and NO code path writes it, so the ladder does not move the status either.

title: METERING'S DOCUMENTED OCCUPANCY DOOR CAN NEVER BE OPENED -- `customers.selectors.occupying_status_codes` IS UNAUTHORED, AND METERING'S DOOR-1 BRANCH ITERATES THE RESULT SO IT CANNOT CARRY THE `None` ITS OWN CONTRACT REQUIRES
surface: 06-backend/apps/metering/seams.py :: occupying_account_status_codes (the door-1 branch, ~line 807)
found_in: the CR-052 W0 lane, 2026-08-30, looking for the occupancy seam CR-052 task 2's consequence must travel through
introduced_in: CR-047 stage 3 -- the seam was written with door 1 as an interface customers would author later, and nobody did
escape_reason: THE FALLBACK WORKS, SO NOTHING IS RED. occupying_account_status_codes documents two doors and prefers door 1, apps.customers.selectors.occupying_status_codes() -- 'the documented contract, and the ONLY one that can see a status this tenant added or renamed'. Customers has never authored it, so every caller has always fallen through to door 2, the seeded CONSTANTS, which by metering's own admission cannot see a tenant-added status or a seeded one whose behaviour class a tenant changed. For BR-CUS-107's platform-seeded 'disconnected' row door 2 is right, which is why CR-052 task 2 passes today and why this has stayed invisible. AND DOOR 1 CANNOT SIMPLY BE PUBLISHED: the seam's own docstring requires None -- NOT an empty set -- when customers cannot answer, because frozenset() would say 'no status occupies a unit' and silence two import rules with a fabricated answer. But the branch reads if published is not None: return frozenset(... for code in published() ...), which iterates the RESULT, so a customers function returning None raises TypeError inside metering. The contract as written cannot express the answer the contract as documented demands. REPORTED, NOT REACHED: apps/metering is not this lane's fence (B1 / B2 section 2), and publishing door 1 from customers alone would hand metering a value it cannot handle.
prevention: Two changes, and they must land in this order or the fix is the bug: first make metering's door-1 branch tolerate None (fall through to door 2, or return None), THEN customers publishes selectors.occupying_status_codes() reading the tenant's account_statuses rows rather than the seeded constants. Publishing first is what turns a silent correct fallback into a TypeError. Asserted meanwhile by 06-backend/tests/test_cr052_w0_disconnected_at_the_cut.py::test_metering_reads_the_same_vacancy_through_the_published_seam, which checks BOTH that the seam answers correctly for 'disconnected' and that door 1 is still unauthored, so the day somebody publishes it the test says which half moved. THE DURABLE ASK: a seam documenting a door nobody has built should carry the same stated-absence shape this repo already uses in services -- a named constant with a tracks id -- so the gap is a row somebody can count, not a paragraph in a docstring.

title: A W7 GUARD IS RED ON THE UNTOUCHED BRANCH TIP AND IS RED ON PROSE -- IT GREPS FOR A NAME, NOT A CALL, AND IT GREPS THE SHARED CHECKOUT BY HARDCODED PATH SO NO WORKTREE CAN RUN IT HONESTLY

The case asserts grep -rl new_service_block_for apps == ['apps/customers/disconnects.py'] to prove hard-won law 2's other half -- that the block is computed and consumed by nobody. It now finds TWO files, and the second, apps/customers/transfer_disconnect_api.py, contains the name only in a docstring and a lifecycle comment, both of which SAY 'Nothing here reads new_service_block_for()'. So the absence the guard defends is still TRUE and the guard reports it FALSE -- a file that documents not calling something is indistinguishable, to this check, from a file that calls it. (2) IT READS SOMEBODY ELSE'S TREE. The subprocess passes cwd='/home/user/SMARTBillHub/06-backend', a hardcoded absolute path to the SHARED checkout, so a lane running it from a git worktree greps a tree it is not testing -- DEF-2556's class, in a test rather than in a heredoc. A lane in a worktree can therefore neither reproduce nor clear it. AND IT WAS LEFT STANDING RED ON THE BRANCH, which is DEF-2469's escape_reason repeating: the next lane reads a failure it did not cause and either attributes it to itself or learns to ignore a red suite.
prevention: Two lines, both in the test, and neither is this lane's to choose because the assertion's SHAPE is the W7 lane's judgement about what 'consumes' means. (a) Grep for a CALL, not a name -- new_service_block_for\( -- or exclude comment and docstring lines; the measured fact is that both hits in transfer_disconnect_api.py are prose asserting the opposite of what the guard concluded. (b) Resolve the corpus with git rev-parse --show-toplevel instead of the hardcoded /home/user/SMARTBillHub path, so the check reads the tree it is run in. REPRODUCED AT THE TIP rather than attributed: both prose hits are present at 49e7edf5 and at 13dac314 with no lane edits, so CR-052 did not cause this. A lane repairing ONE row by hand does not reach for that tool, reads the file with pathlib.Path.read_text, and gets universal-newline translation it never asked for. The register is left pure-LF rather than churned a second time to restore 11 anomalous carriage returns: reverting a cosmetic normalisation with another unintended-change commit is worse than recording it, and file_defect.py's terminator detection now sees a consistent file. Recorded rather than quietly kept.

title: THE LAW-11 PUSH HELPER STAGED THREE FILES THIS LANE NEVER TOUCHED, ONE OF THEM AN 816-LINE REVERT OF A SIBLING'S CHANGE REQUESTS

(2) The helper staged `find . -type f` rather than the paths it had itself derived, so it committed the union of both lanes' work. title: Two DEF-629 guards fail on exactly one day of the year, and today is that day: GT16_CUTOVER_ON is date(2026, 8, 31) and the seed-time cutover they assert it differs from is the tenant's today
surface: Backend test suite — tests/test_def629_seed_cutover.py (no product surface)

title: MOVING A WORKING TREE TO THE TIP WRITES THE TIP'S BYTES AND NEVER REMOVES A FILE THE TIP DROPPED, SO A RENAMED MIGRATION LEAVES TWO LEAF NODES AND EVERY TEST IN THE PROCESS ERRORS BEFORE IT RUNS

The mirror case is a file the TREE has and the TIP does not, and nothing in the law names it. The damage is again in what was LEFT BEHIND rather than in what was pushed - DEF-2474's sentence, one mechanism along.

UNPROVEN AND SAID SO: no failing run has been observed, the branch needs a genuine race between two requests on one cycle-period, and whether Django marks the outer block for rollback here depends on how the model save wraps its INSERT - which is why this is filed with what would settle it rather than fixed on a reading

title: Switching R3+R4 on stops bills in fixtures lacking EITHER a base charge code (R4) or a recorded connection size (R3) - 15 failures proved ours, 3 proved NOT ours, ~59 still unattributed of the ~77 seen

R3 cannot be resolved and a size may not be guessed" - that is R3 ITSELF, the flip and not the gate, refusing electric accounts whose assets carry no size_class. fixed_commit: v2.120.1 (436f043c) — FOUR mechanisms, not the two this row named. (A) is_base charge code declared per service the tenant bills, in tests/test_us_rat_helpers.py, from core.sample_fixture's signed figures ([W] §1 water $8.00, electric $12.00). prevention: ⚠ THE TRIAGE RULE FIRST, because it costs a grep and has held on every file tested: A TEST THAT BILLS AN ACCOUNT FAILS BECAUSE OF US; A TEST THAT DOES NOT, DOES NOT. Proved twice - test_br_cus_068_master_bill.py (prices a master bill) fails 2/2 with the pair on and 0/2 with it off, so it is OURS; test_br_ast_049_external_ref.py (the asset identifier law, prices nothing) fails 3/3 BOTH ways, so it is PRE-EXISTING and must not be charged to this change. Its verdict reads MET while it has never looked at a service the deployment bills; it should name the services measured beside the count so a reader can tell 'nothing wrong' from 'nothing looked at'. A utility billing ELECTRIC on meters with no recorded size would have every electric bill refused and this report would still say MET. title: THE SEED STILL HANDED IN THREE MONTHS OF METER READINGS IN ONE PASS BEFORE ANYTHING WAS BILLED - MOVING ONLY THE THIRD MONTH OUT FIXED ONE PERIOD AND LEFT THE SAME FAULT ONE PERIOD EARLIER

found_in: 2.114.0, the release that moved the third cycle's walk into its own step
introduced_in: not a regression - the reads block has planted every period in one pass since it was written; 2.114.0 moved one of the three out and left the other two together
escape_reason: THE FIX WENT HALF WAY AND NOTHING COULD SEE THE OTHER HALF. 2.114.0 moved the third cycle's walk into a step of its own, correctly and for the PO's own reason, and left seed_sample_reads looping (opening, *_billed_periods()) - so the opening set, June AND July were still posted in one pass, before June had been billed. PO verbatim on seeing it: 'reading data when you seed first time add reading then bill it, then add reading data again, then bill it and then again add reading data - you can not add reading data once for 3 months'. No gate or test could catch it: every row, register value and read date is identical either way, so nothing that counts rows or compares figures can tell the two orders apart - the only thing that differs is WHICH STEP plants which period, and the one test that asserts block ORDER (test_us_ten_019_sample_records::test_the_money_blocks_run_between_the_two_billing_blocks) asserts it for the money blocks and not for the reads. The cost is not to any figure: it is that the seeded tenant could not be read as a sequence of cycles, and the step a person would point at and say 'that one prepares my run' did not exist for cycle two.
fixed_commit: 6794c673 — the three reads blocks partition fixture.PERIODS (opening + first billed / the rest of the billed / the unbilled), a new metering:seed_sample_second_cycle_reads block sits between the correction and the second bill run, and the second run's declared dependency was re-pointed at it. Live readings 221 under both orderings; only a superseded intermediate row on the overcharge meter is no longer created.
prevention: The three reads blocks now partition fixture.PERIODS between them - seed_sample_reads takes the opening set plus the FIRST billed period, seed_sample_second_cycle_reads takes the rest of the billed ones, seed_sample_next_cycle_reads takes the unbilled ones - so every period is planted by exactly one block and the order is reads, bill, money, reads, bill, reads. The partition is derived from the fixture rather than listed, so a fixture that ever declares a third billed period is walked by the second-cycle block instead of dropped. What is still missing and is worth building: the block-order test covers the money blocks only, so nothing asserts that a reads block precedes the bill run it feeds. That assertion is what would have failed on this.

title: THE JUNE COLLECTIONS BLOCK PAYS EVERY ISSUED BILL IT CAN SEE, NOT ITS OWN PERIOD - SO PRESSING LOAD SAMPLE DATA A SECOND TIME RECORDS 82 DUPLICATE PAYMENTS AND A SECOND REFUND, AND HARD RULE 4 MEANS THEY CAN NEVER BE DELETED
surface: 06-backend/apps/payments/sample_data.py::seed_sample_records (the 'Payments, deposits and the bank statement' block) + its consequence in seed_sample_refund - Settings > Company profile > Load sample data, and manage.py load_sample_data

introduced_in: not a regression - the block has never had a period filter; it was invisible because on a first run June is the only issued cycle
escape_reason: THE BLOCK IS CORRECT ONLY BECAUSE OF WHEN IT RUNS, AND NOTHING SAYS SO. Its docstring is 'June ~95% collected', but _bills_by_account() returns EVERY invoice with status=issued and the loop pays each one; the June scope is an accident of block order - payments runs between cycle one and cycle two, so at that moment June is the only issued cycle. Its idempotency is real but narrow: the key is sample:{invoice_no}, so it will not pay the SAME bill twice - and a bill issued since the last run has never had that key used, so it is paid in full as though it were June. Nothing measured a replay: BR-TEN-063 says a replay changes no count, no test runs the load twice against a tenant that has since billed another cycle, and the panel prints OK beside the count so 82 new payments read as success. MEASURED on a PostgreSQL 16 database seeded end to end and then billed for a third cycle, 2026-09-01: a second load wrote 84 rows - payments 79 -> 161, allocations 88 -> 170, refunds 1 -> 2 - and the new payments settled Jun 2026 (46 allocations, 3652.87), Jul 2026 (31, 1806.91) and Aug 2026 (53, 2981.09). The second refund is a CONSEQUENCE and not a separate fault: seed_sample_refund derives its idempotency key from the payment, the duplicate overpayment is a new payment, so a new 93.88 refund was requested, approved, issued and cleared beside the original 44.47. CLAUDE.md hard rule 4 makes issued payments append-only, so none of it can be removed - the tenant is permanently wrong.
fixed_commit: 6794c673 — seed_sample_records is scoped to _first_cycle_periods() and skips any invoice whose own period is outside it, the same shape seed_sample_cycle_collections already used. A second load writes 1 row instead of 84; the residue is the correction's June rebill and is described in this row's prevention.
prevention: Scope the block to its OWN period the way the sibling block added the same day already does: apps/payments/sample_data.seed_sample_cycle_collections reads each invoice's own period off the bill (_invoice_window) and skips anything outside the windows it owns, so its replay wrote 0. The same three lines in seed_sample_records make the June scope a STATED fact rather than a property of block order. Worth pairing with a test that runs the load twice with a bill run in between and asserts every block reports 0 - the case no suite currently arranges, and the only one that could have caught this. FIXED 2026-09-01 and MEASURED: with the period filter in place the same second load wrote 1 payment instead of 82, and no second refund at all - 84 rows down to 2. ONE ROW OF RESIDUE REMAINS AND ITS CAUSE IS NAMED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE REDISCOVERED: the overcharge correction re-issues its June bill AFTER this block has run, so that rebill is a June-window invoice whose sample:{invoice_no} key has never been used, and a replay pays it. Measured: confirmation SAMPLE-BL-2607-000049, 16.32, which the allocator placed on the oldest open bill. It is left OPEN at one row because closing it means teaching the block to ignore invoices created after its own first run, which is a change to a money path for a residue of one - worth doing deliberately, not at the end of a session. The other 1 row on a replay is the premises block and belongs to no lane here.

title: THE SEEDED DISPUTED READING WALKS BACKWARDS ON A REPLAY: IT DISPUTES THE MOST RECENT READING THAT IS NOT YET DISPUTED, SO EACH RE-RUN FLAGS ONE MORE MONTH
surface: 06-backend/apps/metering/sample_data.py::_flag_disputed_read, called from seed_sample_next_cycle_reads (and from seed_sample_reads before 2026-09-01)
found_in: 2.114.0, running the documented load a SECOND time on an already-seeded tenant
introduced_in: not a regression - the function has had this shape since spec section 4 case 2 was seeded; only its caller moved
escape_reason: IT ASKS FOR THE WRONG READING AND THE FILTER IS WHAT MAKES IT WRONG. The function resolves the case-2 meter, then takes the most recent reading with disputed_at IS NULL - so on the first run it correctly flags the August reading, and on every run after that the August one is EXCLUDED by that same filter and the next most recent is taken instead. MEASURED, 2026-09-01: after one load the tenant had one disputed reading, W-5007 on 2026-08-14; after a second load it had two, W-5007 on 2026-07-31 as well. A third run would take June's. Nothing caught it because the enclosing block correctly reports 0 rows - the dispute is an UPDATE on a reading that already exists, so the count the panel prints is honest and the change is invisible to it, and no test runs the load twice. It matters beyond tidiness: a disputed reading holds its account out of a bill run (account_held_by_disputed_read), so each replay quietly removes that customer from one more month's billing.
fixed_commit: 6794c673 — _flag_disputed_read asks for the period's own reading (read_at__date) instead of the most recent undisputed one, and returns when that reading is already disputed. A second load now leaves one disputed reading where it used to leave two.
prevention: Ask for the reading the case is ABOUT rather than for the most recent undisputed one: the period's own read date is already in the fixture (PERIODS[-1]['read_on']), so filter on read_at__date and let an already-disputed row match, which makes the second call a no-op instead of a walk. The general shape worth carrying: a seeder step that reports 0 rows can still MUTATE, so 'a replay changes no count' (BR-TEN-063) is not the same claim as 'a replay changes nothing' - and only the second one is what an operator pressing a button twice needs.

reported_by: claude, the CR-051 task 30 / CR-053 task 14 lane
title: A JOB KILLED BY THE HARD TASK TIME LIMIT IS LEFT 'running' FOR EVER AND CANNOT BE RESUMED, AND NOTHING REAPS IT
surface: 06-backend/core/jobs.py start() and run_job(); 06-backend/apps/tenancy/tasks.py run_pending_job; 06-backend/config/settings/base.py CELERY_TASK_TIME_LIMIT
introduced_in: 2026-08-19, when the Celery transport landed with no task time limit at all; surfaced 2026-09-01 when CR-051 task 30's hard limit was added and the question 'what happens after the hard kill' had to be answered
escape_reason: No gate reads a job record's status against the clock, and none can from inside the repo: the condition is a row that has been 'running' for longer than any job takes, which only a live database can show. The soft limit added with this defect makes the hard kill rare, so the hole is a backstop's backstop and was found by reading the code path rather than by anything failing.
prevention: Stated, not built. core.jobs.start() admits queued to running and failed to running only, so a re-delivered message for a hard-killed job raises JobsError and the record keeps saying running; CELERY_TASK_ACKS_LATE re-delivers it exactly once and nothing tries again. The soft limit is what keeps this from happening: it raises inside the task with 300 seconds of headroom, so the ordinary failure path writes the row and the checkpoint survives for a resume. Two ways to close this properly, neither taken here: admit running to running in start() when the record's worker is demonstrably gone, or add a management command that marks a job failed when it has been running longer than the hard limit. Both need a decision about what proves a worker is gone, which is more than a settings change.

title: TWO BILLING CEILINGS TELL THEIR READER THEY ARE DEPLOYMENT OVERRIDES AND NEITHER SETTING EXISTS, SO THE ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE IS READ BY NOBODY
surface: 06-backend/apps/billing/run_jobs.py max_accounts_per_run (BILLING_MAX_ACCOUNTS_PER_RUN); 06-backend/apps/billing/print_set.py max_bills_per_print_set (BILLING_MAX_BILLS_PER_PRINT_SET); 06-backend/config/settings/base.py, which declared neither

Django exposes only what a settings module defines, so an operator putting BILLING_MAX_ACCOUNTS_PER_RUN=5000 in .env changed nothing and was told nothing. The two literals are stated twice because a settings module may not import apps.billing, and tests/test_cr051_task30_time_limit.py asserts each settings default equals its module default so the pair cannot drift the way package.json and pyproject.toml did three times. title: A COMMIT-MESSAGE FILE IN THE SHARED SCRATCHPAD WAS OVERWRITTEN BY ANOTHER LANE BETWEEN BEING WRITTEN AND BEING READ, SO ONE LANE'S COMMIT WENT OUT UNDER ANOTHER LANE'S MESSAGE
surface: the shared scratchpad /tmp/.../scratchpad + 10-scripts/push_paths.sh's <message-file> argument; commit 6794c673 on claude/confirm-app-version-310jd3
introduced_in: not a regression - every lane has always been free to name its message file whatever it likes, and the scratchpad has always been shared
escape_reason: EVERY LAW-11 CHECK PASSES ON IT, BECAUSE THEY ALL READ THE DIFF AND THE DAMAGE IS IN THE LABEL. push_paths.sh reported the sha it created; git diff --numstat against the pinned tip listed exactly the eight paths this lane named and no others; re-reading each file from the tip found every one of this lane's changes present. The commit is correct in every respect except that its MESSAGE describes somebody else's work - 'CR-056 W4 - the browser proof, the findings contract, and DEF-2967' - because a sibling lane wrote its own message to the same generic path (msg6.txt) in the shared scratchpad in the seconds between this lane's 'cat > msg6.txt' and push_paths.sh's 'git commit-tree -F'. The scratchpad holds msg.txt, msg1.txt through msg9.txt and a dozen msg-*.txt files from several lanes; the collision was a matter of time. It cuts BOTH ways: this lane's work is unlabelled, and the sibling's message now points at a commit that contains none of their work.
prevention: Two things, and the first is free. (1) NAME THE MESSAGE FILE FOR THE LANE, never msgN.txt - a subject-specific name (msg-seedverify-reads-order.txt) cannot collide, which is exactly why the msg-cr052/msg-r56g/msg-oq1221 files in that directory never did. Better still, write it inside the lane's own git worktree rather than the shared scratchpad. (2) push_paths.sh could READ THE MESSAGE ONCE, hash it, and print the subject it is about to commit, so a lane sees the wrong title before the push rather than after; today it passes the path straight to git commit-tree and the first sight of the subject is in git log. NOT CORRECTED BY REWRITING: the commit is pushed and this repo does not force-push, so the remedy is this row plus the follow-up commit that states what 6794c673 actually contains.

title: THE ACCOUNTS IMPORT TEMPLATE OFFERS A 'Customer #' COLUMN, AUTO-MAPS IT, REPORTS IT MATCHED AT STAGE 2 AND THEN DROPS IT — SO A UTILITY MIGRATING WITH ITS OWN CUSTOMER NUMBERS LOSES EVERY ONE

title: TWO ACCOUNTS-IMPORT DOORS, AND THE ONE WITH NO SCREEN STILL SERVES THE RULES THE PO REVERSED: POST /accounts/imports ALLOCATES AN ACCOUNT NUMBER FOR A BLANK CELL AND REQUIRES NO CUSTOMER NAME
surface: 06-backend/apps/customers/api.py account_imports + account_import_commit + account_import_template; 06-backend/apps/customers/services.py stage_account_import / commit_account_import / _commit_import_row
found_in: code-review
introduced_in: requirements
escape_reason: A DELETED SCREEN LEAVES ITS ENDPOINTS BEHIND AND NOTHING IN THIS REPO ASKS WHETHER A ROUTE STILL AGREES WITH THE RULES. title: ALLOW_REGISTER_DELETIONS is a GLOBAL waiver, not a per-file one, and it was set to get past a refusal of a legitimate in-place row rewrite - so a stale blob reverted 28 lines of another lane's CR-061 section and the guard that printed them was already switched off
surface: process
found_in: commit ed2fddea (12-governance/11-change-requests.md, 11 insertions / 39 deletions); restored by bff8a67a, whose diff against 7c0622b7 is 1 insertion / 1 deletion - exactly the task-11 row
introduced_in: 2026-09-01, the CR-059 task 11 lane. push_paths.sh refused the first attempt correctly - an in-place task-row rewrite is indistinguishable from a revert to push_register_guard.py. The lane re-derived from the pinned tip and re-applied its row, per law 11, and then the tip MOVED between its git show TIP:path and the push, which pins its own tip: DEF-1706's stale-blob mechanism
escape_reason: The guard DID catch it and printed the CR-061 lines it was about to lose. ALLOW_REGISTER_DELETIONS=1, set to get past the row-rewrite refusal, downgraded that refusal to a notice - and the lane read the printed lines as the deletion it had already declared. Law 11's own post-push checks all pass on it: the file count is right, the lane's own row IS present, and the lost section is not in the diff at all. prevention: FIXED by bff8a67a, verified by subtraction against the sibling's own commit rather than by inspection. Three things for the next lane: (1) ALLOW_REGISTER_DELETIONS is GLOBAL - it waives the guard for every path in the push, not for the deletion you meant. (2) Re-derive AFTER the refusal, not before: push_paths.sh pins its own tip at push time, so a blob derived from a git show taken minutes earlier is already stale by law 11's blob clause. (3) When the guard lists lines, read ALL of them against what you intended to delete, by count - here it was 1 expected and 29 printed. The durable fix is a per-path or per-line waiver on push_register_guard.py so a declared in-place row rewrite does not switch off the check for everything else

title: Every service is declared METERED at signup because provisioning never writes the column - and the column is a BOOLEAN where the product has THREE pricing types
surface: backend
found_in: PO on Settings then Services (SET-03) at v2.123.0: 'you have to align what is meter and what is unmetered here on this screen everything is metered that is not curent even if utility service is not started'
introduced_in: when TenantService rows began being created at signup without naming the metering column, so all ten take the model default
escape_reason: TWO FAULTS, AND THE SECOND IS THE REAL ONE. (1) models.py:992 declares metered = BooleanField(default=True) and services.py:2168 creates all ten TenantService rows at signup naming tenant, service, enabled, primary_uom, alt_uom and the two revenue accounts - and NOT metered. So every service on every tenant is declared metered, including Solar, Battery, Storm water and Sewer, which are not. The screen renders that faithfully, which is why it looks like a display bug and is not. (2) The deeper fault: metered is a BOOLEAN, and services.py:2704 states what the false side means - a service declared unmetered is priced from a COUNT. But the product has THREE pricing types, which the PO named in the same session: meter-based, percentage of another service, and capacity-based. So one boolean is carrying three cases and 'unmetered' silently means 'priced by count'. Sewer is the proof: it is not metered, but it is priced as a share of the water usage charge (BR-RAT-015), NOT by a count - so neither value of the boolean is true for it, and flipping it to unmetered to make the screen honest would tell the engine to price sewer by counting something. No gate could see any of this: nothing asserts that a provisioned tenant's metering declarations match how each service is actually priced.
fixed_commit: 2.125.5 · 5205cdb (billing_basis replaces metered; SERVICE_DEFAULT_UOMS carries all ten with their basis) · 1811991 (the migration split 0030 add / 0031 backfill / 0032 drop, after PostgreSQL refused the single form) · f7fc34b (CR-062: solar is kW, panel never added) · 27563e7 (BR-TEN-1180, the A5 enum, and every document that cited the two-state rule stamped SUPERSEDED). BOTH FAULTS ARE CLOSED. Fault 1, the wrong default: _enable_signup_services created all ten tenant_services rows without naming the measurement column, so every service on every tenant read metered - Sewer, Solar, Battery and Storm water included - and the screen rendered that faithfully, which is why it looked like a display bug. It now NAMES the basis from SERVICE_DEFAULT_UOMS for every row it creates. Fault 2, the vocabulary, which this row called the blocker and said was NOT to be resolved by choosing: it was not chosen, it was RULED. The PO on 2026-09-02: 'Shall we consider Metered, % of service and Capacity based', with a ten-row table approved cell by cell. tenant_services.billing_basis carries metered, share and capacity; TenantService.metered survives as a read-only property so the ~30 readers that ask 'is there a register?' are untouched. Sewer is the case this row named as the proof and it is the case the fix is built around: it reads no register AND is not priced by a count, so the migration sets it to share keyed on the SERVICE CODE rather than on the old boolean, because it was wrong in both directions. Measured on PostgreSQL 16.13 forward, reverse and forward again: sewer -> share, trash -> capacity, water -> metered, and sewer returns to share after a full round trip.
prevention: Provisioning names the column per service instead of inheriting a default, and the catalog carries the declaration so it is one fact in one place. The vocabulary question is the blocker and is NOT to be resolved by choosing: whether metered becomes a three-value declaration matching the three pricing types, or whether pricing model stays on the rate schedule and this column answers only 'is there a meter', is a product decision with a money path behind it. It is raised rather than guessed - a wrong answer here prices sewer by counting carts. RULED 2026-09-02 - the PO answered the vocabulary question this row calls the blocker: 'this says, metered or unmeters, but we agreed, we will have 3 states - meter unmetered and % oaf service' and 'Shall we consider Metered, % of service and Capacity based'. The field is billing_basis with three values metered / share / capacity. BOTH FAULTS ARE ADDRESSED AND BOTH HALVES LANDED THE SAME DAY, IN TWO LANES. Fault (2), the vocabulary: tenancy/0030_br_ten_1180_billing_basis replaces the boolean column, the write payload no longer accepts metered, and the read payload always answers billing_basis. Fault (1), the default: provisioning names the column per service through _default_basis_for, from the same map that names the units, so a service cannot be capacity-based and carry a period as its unit. FRONTEND: SET-03 offers three options, the column heads 'Billing basis' and prints Metered / % of another service / Capacity, and all eleven catalogues carry the copy. A payload with no basis reads 'Not recorded' rather than the old safe default - that state is a GUARD, not a live one, because the server always answers the key. This row is left OPEN for its owning lane to close with a fixed_commit; nothing here claims the closure.

title: --reuse-db against PostgreSQL silently keeps a test database that predates today's migrations, and the failures it produces belong to nobody
surface: Any pytest run using --reuse-db against a real PostgreSQL on a day a sibling lane pushes a migration. Observed 2026-09-01: tests/test_cr008_accounting.py gave 4 failed / 20 passed with --reuse-db and 24 passed / 0 failed on the SAME commit with --create-db, failing on core.errors.ValidationError VAL-005 (settings.lookups.gl_account_unknown), which names neither the migration nor the lane.
found_in: 2026-09-01, by the CR-060 T5/T7c lane. The lane read the four failures as its own chart change (it had just moved the seeded chart from 34 accounts to 48, so a GL-account error was the obvious suspect) and spent a full run proving otherwise. Three migrations had landed from sibling lanes the same day -- ledger/0010_cr060_t8_journal_line_dimension_indexes, customers/0039_def2847_mailing_address_line2_country and customers/0038 -- and the reused test database had none of them. The coordinator's own PostgreSQL run of this branch uses --reuse-db too.
introduced_in: Not a code change. CLAUDE.md hard-won law 14 prescribes 'JOBS_EAGER=false --reuse-db' as the cheapest mitigation for the slow local settings (DEF-567, one lane measured an hour down to four minutes), and states no condition under which reusing is unsafe. On a single-lane repo there is none; on this branch, where six lanes push migrations through one day, there is one every time a migration lands.
escape_reason: Nothing compares the reused test database's django_migrations table against the migrations on disk, and pytest-django reports no warning when it reuses a database that is behind. The failure surfaces as an ordinary application ValidationError in a module nobody touched, so it reads as a real regression by whoever is running the suite -- and it attributes itself to the lane with the most recently changed code, which is the worst possible default. It is the same shape as CLAUDE.md law 12's rewind: a wrong conclusion, not lost work.
prevention: Say it where law 14 says --reuse-db: reuse is safe for a re-run of your own work within one session, and unsafe the moment a sibling pushes a migration. So: when a PostgreSQL run fails in a module you did not touch, re-run that file with --create-db BEFORE reading the failure as yours -- it is two commands and it is the only thing that distinguishes the two cases. A durable fix is a conftest check that compares the reused database's applied-migration set against the migrations on disk and errors with the missing names rather than letting the suite run; that is a check the next lane inherits instead of a paragraph it has to remember.

title: Law 14's PostgreSQL-proof requirement cannot be met for anything needing sample data, because provisioning collapses under the local settings
surface: backend
found_in: the CR-059 W3 door lane, grounded in the run log on disk: 'sample-data block failed for identity / BlockCannotRun: no sample staff user was created: this tenant has no ACTIVE System Admin' with billing and payments collapsing behind it
introduced_in: whenever provisioning under config.settings.local stopped producing an active System Admin owner; DEF-2722 records the same collapse from the signup side on 2026-08-31
escape_reason: THE MECHANISM IS ALREADY FILED AND ITS CONSEQUENCE IS NOT, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE ROW RATHER THAN A DUPLICATE. DEF-2722 (high, open) records that eight sample-plant blocks fail at provisioning and nothing reads the failure. What nobody wrote down is that CLAUDE.md law 14 REQUIRES transaction-sensitive code to be proved on real PostgreSQL because the default suite is in-memory SQLite and cannot show an aborted transaction - and every such proof needs a seeded tenant. So the law and the environment contradict each other: a lane that obeys law 14 cannot get a fixture, and a lane that gives up and uses SQLite has proved nothing about the case the law exists for. Three lanes hit this today. Two correctly reported it as environmental rather than claiming a PostgreSQL result they did not have; that took each of them time to establish from scratch, because the identity block collapses FIRST and billing and payments fail behind it, so the visible failure names the wrong module. Nothing could catch it: no gate asserts that a developer can seed a tenant on the database the law names.
prevention: DELIVERED 2026-09-01, and the mechanism was NOT the one this row predicted. DEF-2722's own fix had already landed, so the CASCADE was gone: on PostgreSQL 16.13 a tenant provisioned through the shared test harness planted 16 of 17 blocks, and only identity failed - billing and payments seeded, because DEF-2722 and DEF-2795 put savepoints in the seeders. What remained was the HEAD of the cascade and it is DEF-566, filed 2026-08-22 and open ever since: tests/test_us_ten_helpers.identity_seam stubbed apps.identity.services.provision_owner with a function returning a bare uuid4 and writing NO users row and NO tenant_memberships row, while the real function had been authored and living at apps/identity/services.py:811. The stub is now a RECORDER that delegates to the real seam; the same run seeds 17 of 17. THE PRODUCT PATH WAS NEVER BROKEN - provisioning through tenancy.services.provision_tenant on a developer database seeded 17 of 17 before any change, which is why this was so hard to see: only the TEST harness produced owner-less tenants, and the test harness is what a law-14 proof needs. A SECOND, INDEPENDENT BLOCKER was found doing this and is filed on its own row: every transaction=True test errors at teardown on PostgreSQL (Django flush truncates only MANAGED model tables; 25 models here are managed=False and carry real FKs), and a law-14 proof NEEDS transaction=True. Fixed in 06-backend/tests/conftest.py. THE GATE THIS ROW ASKED FOR IS BUILT: G68 (10-scripts/gates/g68_plant_on_postgres.py) provisions one tenant and requires all 17 blocks, over 06-backend/tests/test_def2395_sample_plant_on_postgres.py - which is also DEF-2722's own stated prevention, the test it said no suite in this repo made. G68 reports SKIP and never PASS for a run that happened on SQLite, and refuses a PostgreSQL DATABASE_URL carried under config.settings.test, because this row is about a green suite implying coverage it cannot reach. ORIGINAL PREVENTION TEXT, KEPT: Fixing DEF-2722 fixes this. Until it lands, the honest posture is the one two lanes took today - say which database each result came from, and state plainly what SQLite cannot prove, rather than letting a green suite imply coverage of the aborted-transaction case. Worth considering with the fix: a check that provisions one tenant on PostgreSQL, so the day this breaks again it is a red gate rather than three lanes each losing an hour to it.

title: G27's absent-with-fallback ratchet has read 562-565 against a baseline of 558 for at least sixty commits, and no row owns the gap
surface: gate
found_in: measured on 2026-09-01 by the customer-facing-copy lane, from the blobs of the last sixty commits on claude/payments-cr-artifacts-k3s9j2
introduced_in: unknown - the number was already 562 sixty commits back, so it predates the window that was measured
escape_reason: NOTHING IS BLIND HERE - THE GATE REPORTS IT CORRECTLY AND HAS DONE SO FOR SIXTY COMMITS. G27 splits its findings in two: keys with no copy and no fallback FAIL per component, and keys with a fallback are counted as coverage debt against a ratchet baseline of 558, measured 2026-08-28. The live number is 565 and was 562 at every one of the previous sixty commits when this lane recomputed it from the blobs, so the gate has been RED on its ratchet clause continuously and every lane that ran it has read past the line. That is this repo's own recorded failure shape - a gate that has never once passed is a gate nobody reads (DEF-1788 says so about this very gate, and the decision log's 2026-08-27 entry names the family) - and it has a second cost: a lane that genuinely ADDS coverage debt cannot be distinguished from the inherited seven, so the ratchet cannot do the one job a ratchet has.
prevention: Either the seven are paid down to 558 or the baseline is re-measured with a dated note saying who measured it and why it moved - and the rule is that it may only move DOWN, so a re-measure upward needs the same argument a baseline raise always needs. The 565 sit in eight customer-facing wizards (ConnectionDetailPage 107, NewConnectWizard 111, TransferWizard 102, DisconnectWizard 90 and four smaller), so paying them down is a translation lane of its own and not a side effect of anybody's defect fix. Whoever takes it should also decide whether the ratchet belongs per-file rather than as one aggregate: a single number over 223 components cannot say which lane moved it, which is the second half of why it went unread.

title: EVERY pytest transaction=True test errors at teardown on PostgreSQL and leaves the test database dirty, so law 14 proofs cannot be written at all

escape_reason: CLAUDE.md law 14 names the reason in its own words: config/settings/test.py hardcodes in-memory SQLite, and SQLite flushes with DELETE FROM, which has no such restriction. So the entire suite is green on every machine and this appears only on the database law 14 sends you to. It is also invisible to every check in law 11, because nothing is wrong with any commit. THE MECHANISM: transaction=True tears down by FLUSHING, and Django emits one TRUNCATE naming only the tables of MANAGED models. This repo has 25 managed=False models whose tables exist and carry real foreign keys into managed ones, so PostgreSQL refuses: cannot truncate a table referenced in a foreign key constraint / DETAIL: Table transfers references customers. A second one, meter_read_asset_monthly_usage references services, was hit within the hour, so it is not one stray model. THE COST IS NOT THE ONE ERROR: the flush aborts part-done and leaves the test database DIRTY, so the next run inherits the previous run tenants. Measured 2026-09-01: five unrelated red cases in tests/test_us_cus_003_account_race.py, every one refusing with BIZ-STATE (signup.subdomain_taken) over a tenant it never created — the visible failure naming the wrong file, which is DEF-2395 whole complaint one level down. AND IT IS THE HALF OF DEF-2395 THAT MATTERS MOST: a law-14 proof NEEDS transaction=True, because plain django_db wraps the case in one atomic that is rolled back and never reaches the COMMIT semantics an aborted transaction is about.
prevention: FIXED in 06-backend/tests/conftest.py: a session-scoped autouse fixture forces allow_cascade=True on DatabaseOperations.sql_flush, on PostgreSQL ONLY (law 3 — do not change the path that works). That is exactly what PostgreSQL own HINT asks for and what Django already does when TransactionTestCase.available_apps is set, a knob pytest-django does not expose. RED PROOF, law 7: the empty probe above failed with the truncate error before and passes after. TWO THINGS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, said rather than left to be found: (1) the fixture depends on NOTHING — taking django_db_setup would be the obvious way to be sure Django is configured and would drag full database setup into every pure-unit run; connection.vendor is read off the configured ENGINE without opening a connection, and a no-database probe still finishes in 0.47s. (2) A flush also empties migration-seeded PLATFORM reference data (roles, permissions, subscription_plans — the catalog whose absence once made every signup fail with signup.plan_unknown). Django answer to that is serialized_rollback, which is the CALLER decision because it costs a serialize per test; this file does not make it for them and says so in its docstring.

title: The posting service does NOT refuse a closed-period entry_date, and three places say it does
surface: backend
found_in: review
introduced_in: apps/ledger/posting.py — the paragraph went stale when US-LED-015 landed the fiscal-period close
escape_reason: Nothing asserts it because every caller happens to resolve the date itself. apps/ledger/manual_je.py calls close.resolve_entry_date before it posts and apps/ledger/unbilled_accrual.py refuses a closed period outright, so no test has ever handed post() a closed-period date. The three places that state the guarantee are prose: posting.py's own docstring says there is no record of which periods are closed and that entry_date is written exactly as the caller names it (true when it was written, false since FiscalPeriodClose landed); CR-060 section 6 states as fact that post() resolves the entry date to an OPEN fiscal period through close.resolve_entry_date; and BR-LED-006 reads as though the lock is enforced at the writer. Measured on real PostgreSQL 16.13 by removing CR-060 T7's own closed-period refusal in a monkeypatch harness: the accrual posted DATED 31 AUGUST INTO A CLOSED AUGUST — the closed month's trial balance moved, which BR-LED-006 and BR-LED-017 both promise cannot happen. Hard-won law 1: a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee, and here it is on the sole journal writer. CORRECTED BY THE FIXING LANE 2026-09-02, because this reason was too kind to us, and a reason that understates the blast radius is how the next one gets deprioritised. It reads 'every caller happens to resolve the date itself'. NINE call sites reach the posting service and THREE checked anything: manual_je (forwards), unbilled_accrual (refuses) and cost_capture (forwards, and never actually posts - OQ-200). THE OTHER SIX DID NO PERIOD CHECK AT ALL: journal.reverse_and_repost, journal's tax remittance, both deposit_legs postings, both opening_balances postings, and billing/posting_seam, which posts on invoice.service_date - so a bill issued for a month that had closed went straight into it. This was not a latent hole waiting for a caller nobody has written; six live paths could already write into a locked month. AND A FOURTH DOCUMENT WAS WRONG, found while fixing: apps/ledger/manual_je's post path claimed in its own docstring that the date was resolved 'at SAVE as well as at POST' and it was resolved only at save, so a draft written on 20 July posted into a July closed on 5 August - with ManualPostResult.date_note existing and NOTHING anywhere setting it (hard-won law 2, a field nothing writes). WHY NO CHECK CAUGHT ANY OF IT: every gate in this repo reads source text, coverage or document self-consistency, and not one can ask 'does this sentence describe what the code does'. The claims were prose in four different files, each true when written; the fact that decayed (US-LED-015 landing FiscalPeriodClose) moved none of them. Nothing failed because nothing asked.
prevention: The guard is now IN the writer, where CLAUDE.md hard rule 5 puts every journal-line write: posting.post() and posting.post_draft() refuse a closed-period entry_date through close.resolve_entry_date, the one implementation of the fiscal calendar, so a caller written next year inherits the lock without knowing it exists. It REFUSES rather than forwarding, because the two callers that do check want opposite things (BR-TEN-038 forwards a late payment; the CR-060 T7 accrual must never be moved, or August's revenue is recognised in September and reversed in October) and a default that silently picks one would be wrong half the time, in a record hard rule 4 forbids correcting - hard-won law 3, defaults fail closed. tests/test_def3202_closed_period_posting_guard.py holds seven cases, PROVED RED first ('Failed: DID NOT RAISE PostingError' on the closed-July posting; 'assert datetime.date(2026, 7, 20) == datetime.date(2026, 8, 1)' on the draft posted after its month closed) and re-run on real PostgreSQL 16.13 per hard-won law 14. Two of the seven exist only to stop the fix becoming a worse defect: a tenant that has closed nothing, and a tenant with no fiscal calendar at all, must still post - close.period_window refuses by design when a tenant has no fiscal settings, so a naive is_closed_on() would have made every brand-new tenant unpostable, which is why the one implementation with its fast path is reused rather than a second read written. BR-LED-006 is amended, dated, to say WHERE each half lives - the lock is the writer's, the forward is the caller's - because one clause reading as one guarantee is what made three documents wrong at once. NOT CLOSED BY THIS: the six unchecked callers now REFUSE where they used to write silently, which is the safe direction but is not BR-TEN-038's forward; wiring that needs a per-caller decision about where the 'we moved this' note reaches the screen, and it is named in the decision-log row rather than guessed at here.

title: ALLOW_REGISTER_DELETIONS became a habit rather than a decision: a lane overrode the vanished-line guard three times, and the third time the lines were another lane's
surface: process
found_in: Pushing a one-stamp correction to 12-governance/02-decision-log.md at v2.125.5. push_paths.sh step 3b refused it and printed the first four of 62 lines that would vanish, beginning 'No bill generated for Electric + Water + Sewer - the engine bills, and the build is not the difference'. The flag was passed and the push landed as 1 insertion and 75 deletions, publishing a revert of a sibling lane's whole decision entry. Caught by reading the numstat the push helper prints, and repaired in the next commit: the file was re-derived from the commit before, only this lane's own stamp re-applied, and a line-by-line comparison against the tip confirmed nothing was missing.
introduced_in: The same lane had used ALLOW_REGISTER_DELETIONS twice earlier in the same session, correctly both times - the vanished lines were its own rows being replaced - so by the third refusal the flag read as the way past a known-noisy check rather than as a statement about what was being deleted
escape_reason: The guard did its whole job: it refused, it named the lines, and it said in as many words that this is a revert by subtraction every other law-11 check passes on. Nothing downstream could catch it - the file count was right, the lane's own change WAS present, and git show displayed only its own hunks, because deleted lines are not in the diff at all. What failed is that the override is a single environment variable with no argument, so it cannot express WHICH deletion is intended: passing it says 'I have read the list' and nothing verifies that the reader read it. Two correct uses trained the habit and the third carried it into a case where the lines belonged to somebody else.
prevention: Make the override name what it permits instead of permitting everything: ALLOW_REGISTER_DELETIONS should take the count or a marker of the lines expected to go, and refuse when the actual set is larger or different - so an override is a claim that can be wrong rather than a door that is always open. Cheaper and available today: the helper already prints the numstat, and 1 insertion against 75 deletions on a one-stamp edit is arithmetic, not noise (law 11's own 'read the numstat AS ARITHMETIC' clause). A lane that re-derives a shared register should also compare its copy against the tip line by line BEFORE pushing rather than after - that check found the damage in one command and would have prevented it in the same one.

escape_reason: NOTHING READS A COMMIT MESSAGE AGAINST ITS DIFF. Law 11's post-push checks all ask what a commit CONTAINS — the file count, the hunks, re-reading each path from HEAD — and every one of them passes here, because the content is correct and it is only the message that belongs to somebody else. G55 comes closest (it catches a subject claiming a fix for a row that still reads open) and it did not fire, because this subject claims a RECORD rather than a fix. title: G44's ratchet went red the moment the collections-ladder fix landed, and the fall sat unbanked for a day while the register kept both defects open
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g44_display_truth_baseline.txt (COUNT 23 against 22 measured) and the two register rows DEF-2580 and DEF-1122, both reading open over a fix that shipped in 6a333bbf
found_in: 2026-09-02, the lane dispatched to clear the whole red gate suite
introduced_in: 2026-09-01, commit 6a333bbf - Payments > Collections shows the account number, not a raw database id
escape_reason: A RATCHET FAILS ON THE FALL AS WELL AS ON THE RISE, AND ONLY THE RISE FEELS LIKE A DEFECT. G44 clause (c) refuses a count BELOW its banked number for the reason DEF-490 gives - a fall that is not banked is a number nobody reads - so the very commit that removed the last raw uuid from the collections ladder turned the gate red, and it stayed red because the fixing lane had no reason to expect its own good news to block a merge. The commit subject also carries no fix verb, so G55 could not see that DEF-2580's row still read open either: G55 matches closed, fixed, resolved or repaired next to the id, and 6a333bbf says only DEF-2580 followed by an em dash and a description. So two different gates each held half the evidence and neither could state it.
prevention: Bank the fall in the same commit as the fix - the baseline file now records which line left, why, and that DEF-1122 stays open because its returned-mail half is untouched. Wider and cheaper: a gate whose baseline can fall should print the exact one-line edit that banks it, so the fixing lane can paste it rather than work out the arithmetic. G55's blind spot is narrower and is deliberate adjacency, not a bug: the durable answer there is that a commit subject naming a defect id should say what happened to the row.

title: A defect closure was reverted by the very next commit to the register, one minute later, and G55 reported the CLAIM as wrong rather than the revert
surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv, the DEF-3200 row - closed by ad72deb7 at 04:56 and returned to open by 67b91aa1 at 04:56
found_in: 2026-09-02, the lane dispatched to clear the whole red gate suite; G55 was the only thing pointing anywhere near it
introduced_in: 2026-09-02, commit 67b91aa1 - DEF-3201 filed CRITICAL - bills are broken again, and it is ours
escape_reason: LAW 11 MECHANISM TWO, AND THE ONE CHECK THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT IS THE ONE NOBODY READS AS ARITHMETIC. 67b91aa1 appended ONE new row and its register numstat reads 2 insertions, 1 deletion - the deletion being the DEF-3200 line rewritten back to the content its author had read before ad72deb7 landed. A one-row append is 1 insertion and 0 deletions, so the arithmetic was the whole diagnosis and it was sitting in the push output. Every other law 11 check passes: the file count is right, the author's own row IS present, and git show prints only the two hunks the author wrote. Downstream, G55 could see the damage but not describe it - it reports that a COMMIT claims a fix for an OPEN row, which reads as a lane overclaiming, when the truth was the opposite: the fix and the closure were both real and a third commit undid the closure.
prevention: The row is restored with its fixing commit and the reverting commit named in the cell, so the next reader is not left to rediscover this. Mechanically the answer already exists and was not used: push_paths.sh runs a register guard that refuses a push which loses a line, and it counts LINES rather than CHANGED lines - a rewritten row is not a lost one, so it passes. Widen that guard to refuse a register push whose deletions exceed the lines the author actually rewrote, or simplest of all, refuse any register commit that changes a row the author did not name. Wider still and worth stating plainly: closing a defect is a whole-file-risk edit on the busiest shared file in the repo, and file_defect.py deliberately does not offer it, so every closure in this repo is hand-done at exactly the moment law 11 says not to hand-do one.

title: The merge-blocking gate suite has been red in roughly nineteen places with every failure already filed and none owned, so MERGE BLOCKED blocks nothing

A gate suite that says MERGE BLOCKED on every merge has stopped being a gate and become a weather report. Measured on this pass: of nineteen, four were fresh regressions from today fixable at the cause in one session (G12 stale index, G44 unbanked fall, G55 reverted closure, G67 eleven untraced fixes), one was a fresh regression in another lane's fixture (G5, 16 tests, DEF-2392), one is correctly red and must stay red until the PO rules (G53), and the remaining thirteen are backlogs measured in dozens to hundreds of files. title: A migration's 43-line explanation sat below its imports, so it was not a docstring and G7 read the file as having none - a written-up file and a red gate coexisted for six days
surface: 06-backend/apps/tenancy/migrations/0021_cr039_wave_f_commercial_model.py - the string block that ran from line 6 to line 48, after three import statements
found_in: 2026-09-02, the lane clearing the red gate suite, while adding the HUMAN-OWNED marker G7 was asking for
introduced_in: 2026-08-27, commit that added CR-039 wave F - the block was written in the right words and put in the wrong place
escape_reason: A BARE STRING AFTER AN IMPORT IS A NO-OP, AND NOTHING ANYWHERE SAYS SO OUT LOUD. Python only treats a string literal as the module docstring when it is the FIRST statement; put it after the imports and ast.get_docstring returns None while the text still renders perfectly to a human reading the file. So G7, which reads the docstring, reported lacks HUMAN-OWNED marker - which is true and reads as the file having no write-up at all, when the file had 43 lines of one including the rules the database enforces and why three tables are deliberately not tenant-isolated. A lane acting on the gate message alone would have written a SECOND paragraph above the imports and left the first stranded. Nothing catches this class: py_compile, ruff, black, manage.py check and makemigrations --check are all silent, the file reads correctly to a person, and the only reader that can tell is the one asking Python for __doc__.
prevention: The block is moved above the imports, which is the whole fix, and the file now says why in its own words: a marker is only a marker where the reader looks for it. Checkable and worth building: G7 already parses every guarded file with ast, so it can ask the cheap follow-up question - does this file contain the marker text ANYWHERE while its docstring does not - and say lacks HUMAN-OWNED marker (the text is present but is not the docstring, so nothing reads it) instead of a message that sends a lane to write a duplicate. That distinguishes a file with no write-up from a file with an unreachable one, and the two need opposite fixes.

escape_reason: no gate runs the push helpers, and the guard's own self-checks compare a tip against a file rather than against a tree it was told to use. prevention: make the tree explicit: have push_paths.sh pass its own cwd to push_register_guard.py (an argument or GIT_WORK_TREE), and have the guard refuse rather than guess when the path it is asked about is not under the tree it resolved. title: A re-apply script's idempotence guard never matched its own row, so one human-review-ledger row was written FOUR times and two copies reached the branch
surface: 12-governance/09-human-review-ledger.md — the CR-060 C4 opening/closing row, four byte-identical copies (two of them pushed in 816b7dd)

introduced_in: the same lane, 2026-09-02 — the law-11 re-derivation helper re-applies every lane edit after taking the pinned tip's bytes, and each patch script guards itself by searching the file for a string from its own row
escape_reason: THE GUARD STRING WAS NOT A SUBSTRING OF THE ROW IT GUARDED. The row reads (**NEW** then the backticked function name, and the guard searched for NEW followed directly by that backticked name — the markdown bold markers sit between the two halves, so the test was false every time and the script appended on every run. It is the shape a check cannot fail in reverse: a guard that never fires reads exactly like a guard that has nothing to do. Nothing downstream could see it either — G7 counts rows awaiting sign-off and PASSES on four identical ones, because four pending rows is a legitimate state of that register
prevention: An idempotence guard must be derived from the text being written, never retyped beside it. Take the guard string OUT of the row variable itself (row[:80], or a stable id the row already carries) so the two cannot drift by a formatting character. And after a re-derive, grep the register for the row you just wrote and count it — one is the answer, and it is the same glance law 11 already asks for on the numstat

title: A tree-resync that exempted this lane's own files pushed a revert by subtraction across fourteen shared files
surface: 45a1bc4f — 12-governance/02-decision-log.md lost 166 lines, the eleven locale catalogues 31 lines each, 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv two rows and 11-change-requests.md seven rows

DEF-2100 says the stale half is safe to restore precisely because nobody has touched it, and that the live half must not be moved - correct, and it does not say what to do when a file is BOTH: stale content with this lane's edits on top. Read numstat as arithmetic on the exempted files SPECIFICALLY, where a sweep replacing ten values cannot be 15 insertions and 41 deletions, and a one-row append cannot be 1 insertion and 166 deletions. title: A re-derive script piped through head lost its pipe, and nine catalogues were pushed from a two-commit-old tip
surface: 07-frontend/src/i18n/locales — es, es-MX, fr-FR, hi, id-ID, it-IT, ja-JP, ko-KR, pt-BR (90 values)
found_in: 2.128.2, CR-059 task 25 push (34ad19ba)
introduced_in: 2.128.2, the same push
escape_reason: Every law-11 push check passed. push_paths.sh compares each named path between the base and the tip and none had MOVED, because the re-derive had just re-read them; the paths were this lane's own and so were the hunks. What no check asks is HOW OLD the bytes going into the tree are, which is the blob-staleness mechanism law 11 already names. The cause was a shell pipe: the re-derive prints one line per file AFTER writing it, its output was piped through 'head -2', and the third print raised BrokenPipeError and killed the script with two of eleven catalogues written from the new tip and nine still holding content built from a tip two commits older. Ten values per file — the CR-060 C11 rule-34 vocabulary sweep — were overwritten with this lane's earlier wording.
prevention: Reading the push's own numstat AS ARITHMETIC is what caught it and is the only thing that could have: nine files reported 44 insertions and 15 deletions in the same push where two reported 3 and 0, and those cannot both be right for one edit. THE RULE: never pipe a script that WRITES FILES through head, or through anything that can close the pipe early — redirect to a file and read that. A script that builds every file before writing any (which this one does for CONTENT) must do the same for its LOOP, or make its progress reporting unable to kill it.

escape_reason: The wire path was never broken, which is why every test passed: the query fired, the rows came back and the options landed in the select. What was missing was every state around it. The select renders its placeholder while searching, when nothing matched, when the search failed AND on success, so all four look identical to a clerk and there is no way to tell a broken search from an empty one. The mechanical half is provable and nothing checked it: enabled read accountQuery.trim().length >= 2 while the request sent q: accountQuery, so a number pasted out of a spreadsheet took its whitespace to the server and matched nothing. tsc cannot see a mismatch between two expressions that are both valid, and the screen's tests asserted the select RENDERS - which it did. The product's two other account searches, customers/accountFinder.tsx and metering/OwnerAccount.tsx, both send the trimmed term and both draw the three states; payments was the odd one out and no gate compares one screen's search with another's.

The durable half is the shared hook - useAccountSearch in paymentsShared.tsx owns the trim, the gate and the three states in one place, so the two payment pickers cannot drift apart again.

title: The Batch cell on S33 would print a raw uuid at a clerk the moment the server stops sending null — a B14 rule 31 violation that no test can fire today
surface: S33 Record payments and the S21 account Payments tab, the Batch column cell
introduced_in: the S33 cell set, written against a column documented as always null
escape_reason: The cell has two branches and only one of them can run. The server hardcodes the value to null, so the non-null branch — which renders the uuid as the visible value of the field — is unreachable, and every fixture in the suite carries null because the type says the column is always null. B14 rule 31 (no database id is ever the visible value of a field) is ratified and UNENFORCED: no gate in this repo reads rendered output, and the two gates nearest to it read source shapes rather than what a branch would print. So the violation is invisible to tsc, to eslint, to every assertion, and to a person clicking the screen — until the day the other half of DEF-2353 lands in a different lane and the branch starts running.
prevention: The cell now refuses to print an id at all: it renders the stated absence until the read serves a batch CODE, and it says so in its own comment so the next lane wires the code rather than un-commenting the uuid. The general lesson is that a two-branch cell written against a column documented as constant has one branch nothing can test, and that branch is where a rule goes to hide — when the constant is the reason a branch is unreachable, the branch should render the rule-abiding thing, not the convenient one.
