title: file_defect.py allocates the id against the remote and writes it into whatever tree it is standing in, so a correct id lands in a stale file
surface: tooling
found_in: 10-scripts/file_defect.py
introduced_in: by design, since the tool was written
escape_reason: The tool's own docstring states the guarantee that is missing. Its allocator FETCHES and reads the working tree, HEAD, the upstream tracking ref and every refs/remotes/origin ref, so the id it hands out is correct against the pushed world. The append is then made to the working-tree copy of the register, whose freshness nothing checks. In a lane whose worktree is behind the branch those two facts combine into a file that is correct in its newest row and missing every row pushed since that tree was made. Measured live 2026-09-03: this lane's worktree held 1526 defect rows and the branch tip held 1543, so appending here and committing that one path would have deleted 17 rows siblings had pushed. Every check CLAUDE.md law 11 prescribes passes on it - the file count is one, the lane's own row IS present, and git show prints only that hunk, because the deleted rows are not in the diff at all. And guarantee 2 of the docstring reads as though it covered this: 'no other lane's row can be carried, altered, or reverted'. That is true of the WRITE and false of the FILE, which is hard-won law 1 with the tool as the culprit. NOTE ON THE FIGURE, because two numbers exist: this lane first reported the loss as 34 rows, which is wrong. It compared the id count of one file against the line count of the other. Counted the same way both times it is 17 rows and 17 lines. Commit 2f49ceae's message carries the wrong number and cannot be amended; this row is the correction.
prevention: The tool now measures its own staleness at the moment it allocates and says so loudly with the figure: it compares the ids in the working-tree register against the ids on the branch's own remote ref and prints how many rows the copy it is about to append to is missing, and what to do about it. It does NOT refuse, because nothing may stop a lane filing a defect - the same reason the fetch is best-effort. It also does NOT re-derive the file from the tip before appending, and that is a decision rather than an omission: overwriting the working copy would delete a sibling's UNPUSHED rows in a shared tree, which is this same defect running backwards. The hard stop stays at push time in push_register_guard.py, which compares the tip's lines against what is about to be pushed and refuses. What this closes is the two gaps that guard leaves: a lane committing with an ordinary pathspec commit never reaches it, and a lane that does reach it learns only after the work is done.

title: G40, the gate that enforces built-is-not-wired, reads git ls-files — so a NEW component file is invisible to it and a lane that runs gates before staging sees a false green
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g40*.py — the unmounted-components gate; found while proving a RED for CR-060's Refunds panel (RefundsQueuePanel.tsx)

A brand-new component that has never been staged is not in that list, so G40 has nothing to check and reports PASS. Hard-won law 2 exists because a component nothing renders is dead UI that passes every test, and four such defects reached a running product in one day; G40 is the check written to stop exactly that, and this is the one shape of the defect it cannot see. The lane that found it only saw it because law 7 made it prove the gate RED first: the proof would not fire until it ran git add -N in its own private index. A lane that writes a new component, never mounts it, and pushes it in one go IS caught, so the hole is narrow and it is precisely the workflow law 7 prescribes - run your gates before you stage - that walks into it.
prevention: G40 should enumerate from the working tree (or union git ls-files with untracked, non-ignored files) rather than from the index, so an unstaged new component is checked like any other. Until then the gate's own output should say which files it did NOT consider.

title: A front-end lane dispatched into a git worktree usually has NO node_modules there, so it cannot run tsc or vitest and pushes unverified UI — 36 of 52 lane worktrees are in that state right now
surface: the worktree dispatch mechanism; observed on the CR-016/screen-badge lane, which pushed 3dcc6774 with two of its own rewritten test cases RED
found_in: 2.128.2, branch claude/payments-cr-artifacts-k3s9j2 at 3dcc6774. The lane reported honestly that 07-frontend/node_modules was absent and that its three rewritten cases had not been executed by anything; run in the main tree they came back 2 failed, 16 passed of 18.
introduced_in: whenever lane dispatch into git worktrees began; the worktree is created from the repo but node_modules is git-ignored and is not installed into it
escape_reason: NOTHING READS WHETHER A LANE COULD RUN THE SUITE IT REPORTS ON. Every gate in this repo reads files and commits; none asks whether the toolchain that would have caught a defect was present. So a lane with no node_modules has exactly two honest options - notice and say so, or not notice - and BOTH end with unverified UI on the branch. The lane that hit this did the right thing and said so in plain terms, and the work still landed red, because a truthful disclaimer in a report is not a gate. This is hard-won law 1 in a new place: a lane SAYING it could not verify is not the verification, just as a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee. Measured at the time of filing: 36 of 52 agent worktrees have no 07-frontend/node_modules.
prevention: Either install frontend dependencies as part of worktree creation, or have the frontend gates FAIL LOUDLY when node_modules is absent instead of being skipped - a skipped check reads as a passing one. The second is cheaper and is the one that generalises: a check that cannot run must not be silent. Until then, a dispatch brief for front-end work should say to run npm ci in the worktree first, and the integrator should re-run tsc and the touched suites in the main tree before trusting any front-end lane report.

BEFORE at tip 5da4c02c: 969 tests, 497 failed, of which 471 were this defect across 47 files. AFTER at e1b0fa5d: 90 failed across 23 files and ZERO of them are identity. escape_reason: THE PATTERN IS THE FINDING AND IT IS NOT ABOUT ANY ONE FILE. Five lanes filed seven rows for one defect between 2026-09-01 and 2026-09-03 - DEF-2585 counted 3, DEF-2398 counted 2, DEF-3157 counted 2, DEF-3220 counted 17, DEF-2392 counted 16, DEF-3343 counted 12, DEF-2343 counted 17 - and every one was filed honestly: each lane ran the file in front of it, measured what it saw, and wrote down a number true of that file. Nobody was in a position to add them up and nothing in this repository would have done it for them, because no gate and no script enumerates the suites that construct an account. So the count grew one discovery at a time, the total was never 66 and was never stated, and the real figure is 471. THE COST IS NOT THE RED TESTS, IT IS THAT EACH ROW LOOKED SMALL: two tests is a tidy-up, 471 is a blocked branch, and filed one file at a time a branch-blocking defect presented seven times as somebody else's small chore. Two of the rows then deferred to each other in writing - DEF-2343 says it is filed and not fixed because DEF-2392 is settling the canonical shape, and DEF-2392 was left open on exactly that question - so the defect sat three days with five people knowing about it and no owner. An aggregate nobody owns does not exist. SECOND ESCAPE, AND IT IS THE STRUCTURAL ONE: a rule that changes what a WRITE requires lands with no sweep of the callers that build that object, and nothing type-checks a fixture
prevention: ONE SHAPE IN ONE FILE THAT EVERY FIXTURE CALLS: 06-backend/tests/identity_fixtures.py, copied from apps/customers/sample_data._customer_block rather than invented - a person by a 555- phone, a company by 99-0001234. escape_reason: A TEST THAT DIES IN SETUP REPORTS THE FIRST EXCEPTION AND NOTHING ELSE, so for three days 471 identity refusals stood in front of whatever those cases would have said next. The deposit_interest_accrued break is the sharp example: fifteen tests would have caught it on the commit that caused it, this morning, and every one of them was already red for an unrelated reason. So the cost of leaving a fixture wall standing is not the wall - it is that the suite behind it stops being a suite, silently, and the next real regression lands into a green-looking absence of information

Each cause belongs to the lane that owns its module and none is a fixture question: the transfers caller needs an as_of value, and WHICH date that is is a money judgment on a deposit, not something a fixture sweep may choose. test_cr030_w0_customer_no.py is a third kind and is named separately: its seven cases assert that link_customer mints C-00001 from a display name and a legacy reference, which BR-CUS-1023 stopped being true - a test asserting a superseded rule, so it is reported rather than rewritten and the rule's owner re-states it. title: The portal address QR code renders as a broken image: segno's inline SVG carries no xmlns, so a standalone image/svg+xml document is not SVG
surface: Settings > Configure > Customer portal > Overview (CWP-069), the QR panel

escape_reason: The backend test asserts 200, content_type image/svg+xml, and that the body contains the address; all three are true of the broken body. segno.svg_inline() is built for pasting INTO an HTML document, where the surrounding HTML parser supplies the SVG namespace, so it emits no xmlns and no XML declaration. title: The ConfirmDialog census reads the WRONG TIER when a trailing comment follows the prop, and calls it 'primary'
surface: 07-frontend/src/components/ConfirmDialogTier.dom.test.tsx — the B14 rule 6 audit for all 32 call sites
introduced_in: 2026-08-26 (the census, DEF-718)
escape_reason: The scanner's pattern anchored on `\\s*$`, so `confirmVariant="danger" // B14 rule 6` did not match — and the no-match branch recorded 'primary', because `null` had been made to mean 'the prop is absent'. It cannot mean only that: it also means 'a prop is here and I could not read it', and those two want OPPOSITE answers. SettingsServiceCentres declared danger, in the very words of the rule it was obeying, and the census read primary. ⚠ WORSE THAN A RED TEST: a lane trusting the scanner would have written ["primary"] into the audit to make the suite pass, and the census — whose whole job is to BE the record of what was audited — would then have pinned the wrong tier on a destructive action, permanently, with a green suite. Same shape as DEF-182: a check whose output cannot tell pass from fail is worse than no check, because it is trusted. It was found only because the correct classification was entered and the test still failed; the lane that hit it first worked around it by deleting the trailing comment, which fixes one call site and leaves the scanner.
prevention: Two changes, and the second is the one that matters. (1) A trailing `// comment` after the value is now read. (2) ABSENT and UNREADABLE are separated: an absent prop is primary by the prop's own contract, and a prop that is PRESENT but unparseable THROWS by name — because the honest answer to 'which tier is this?' is sometimes 'I cannot tell', and that must never be spelled 'primary'. Proved RED with `confirmVariant="Danger"`, which the pattern genuinely cannot read: 'a <ConfirmDialog> declares confirmVariant in a form this census cannot read'.

title: G85 and G87 passed standalone and CRASHED in the gate suite — both were missing run()
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g85_one_address_home.py · g87_declared_dependencies.py
introduced_in: the commits that added each gate, 2026-09-04
escape_reason: run_gates calls `module.run()`; both gates exposed only `main()` and `__main__`. Running `python3 g85_one_address_home.py` exercises the path a person uses by hand and NEVER the path the suite uses, so both were announced green on a proof that could not see the failure — 'gate crashed: AttributeError: module has no attribute run', twice, among 28 failures where a new one is easy to miss. Hard-won law 7 says prove a guard RED before trusting it green; this is its other half, and it was not written down: a guard must also be proved IN THE HARNESS THAT WILL RUN IT. Nothing else could have caught it — no gate checks the gates' own interface, which is why the crash surfaced only when somebody ran the whole suite.
prevention: Both now expose `run() -> (status, detail)` and were exercised through it, not through __main__. G87's wrong-interpreter case is deliberately SKIP inside the suite and FAIL standalone: by hand, being in the wrong environment is the user's mistake and should stop them; inside the suite it would put a red gate in front of every lane for a condition none of them caused, and SKIP says 'I could not look' without ever saying 'everything is fine'. The durable fix is a gate over the gates — run_gates' own registry check should assert every registered module exposes a callable `run`, which is one line and would have gone red on both of these before they were pushed. Filed alongside DEF-GOV-3654's duplicate-number check, which belongs in the same place.

title: POST /public/reports 500s on the branch: services.report_a_problem was renamed behind raise_service_request and guest_api.reports still calls the old name

Wave B added report_a_problem and called it from guest_api.reports; wave C folded three shapes behind one write-point function raise_service_request(shape=...) — which is CORRECT, because G81 requires exactly one public function per declared write point and wave C needed three shapes on one — renaming wave B's function to _report and updating its OWN two callers, not wave B's. title: The customer portal renders with NO brand colour at all — the utility's own hexes are fetched, set as CSS variables, and read by nothing
surface: Every guest screen. Seen on CWP-001 at smartbillhub.bynry.com/silver-creek-water1/portal
introduced_in: 2.133.0 (portal wave A)
escape_reason: Four measured facts. (1) src/portal writes ZERO brand-colour classes — not wrong ones, none: a grep for (bg|text|border)-(accent|brand|primary)* across the whole directory returns nothing. (2) The API DOES serve the colours — GET /portal/public/front carries brand_primary_hex and brand_accent_hex, #EC3013 on the sample utility. (3) The frontend DOES set them — GuestFrame.brandStyle() writes them onto the frame as --brand and --accent. (4) NOTHING READS EITHER: a grep for var(--brand) and var(--accent) across every stylesheet returns nothing, because the theme's variable is spelled --color-accent and r10's own CSS reads var(--color-accent) in twenty places. So the colour is fetched, threaded through three components, written to the DOM and lands nowhere — hard-won law 2 exactly. GuestFrame's docstring even describes behaviour that does not happen ('every var(--brand) falls back to the ink it sits in') of a var(--brand) that appears nowhere in the repo — law 1. Every test passes because the fixtures set the hex and the tests assert the style attribute is PRESENT; none asks whether a rule consumes it, and no gate reads rendered output (law 6). G86 refuses a hand-rolled button and a wireframe style; it does not ask whether a screen is the right colour. The PO found it by opening the page, which is the only thing that could have.
prevention: Two parts. (1) The portal composes r10's own classes so var(--color-accent) reaches it, and the tenant's hex OVERRIDES --color-accent on the frame rather than inventing a parallel --brand nobody reads — one variable, the one the stylesheets already use. (2) A gate is owed and is mechanically catchable where the visual rules are not: fail a CSS custom property that is SET and never READ. Both halves of that are greppable — the style objects a component writes, and every var() in every stylesheet — and it would have gone red on the day GuestFrame landed. It generalises past colour: any --foo set and never consumed is dead wiring.

title: A utility can set a SECOND brand colour that nothing in the product reads
surface: Settings > Company > Branding (accent colour) and every guest screen
introduced_in: 2026-08 (the field has existed since tenancy/0001)
escape_reason: Found only by measuring the fix for DEF-CWP-3736 in a browser. `brand_accent_hex` is a stored column, is validated and edited on Settings > Company, is echoed on Settings > Customer portal, and is served by `GET /portal/public/front` -- and the whole product contains ZERO readers of a second accent: `--color-accent-2` is declared twice (tokens.css and tailwind.css `@theme`) and consumed nowhere, and a grep for `accent-2` outside those two declaration blocks returns nothing. GuestFrame wrote it to the DOM as `--accent`, which nothing read either, so the field looked wired from every direction: the form saves, the API serves, the frame sets an attribute, and the tests assert the attribute is PRESENT. No gate reads rendered output (law 6) and, until G89, no gate asked whether a property a component writes is ever read. The primary colour hid it: on the sample utility both hexes are set, so nobody looking at a fixture could tell that only one of them could possibly have an effect.
prevention: Decided here rather than put to the PO (law 13): the fix for DEF-CWP-3736 honours `brand_primary_hex` only, because inventing a rule about where a second colour appears would be inventing law that neither r10's UI-RULES.md nor B14 states. Setting `--color-accent-2` from it would move the dead wiring one variable along, and G90 -- written in the same commit -- would refuse it by name, which is the check working. So the field is honestly unread until a signed rule says what a second accent is FOR; the Branding screen must not describe it as reaching the portal until then. MEASURED AND CLOSED 2026-09-05 (0ad3a6bc): in a real Chromium, with brand_accent_hex #B45309 set on the fixture, --color-accent-2 computes to #e15b47 on every guest screen -- the utility's second colour reaches nothing, which is the decision above holding rather than drifting. What was WRONG was the SCREEN: Settings > Customer portal > Branding showed the accent under the heading 'How the portal looks to your customers' with the sentence 'These four are edited once ... and used by the bill, the letterhead and the portal' -- true of three of the four and false of this one, so a clerk reading it would set a colour expecting the portal to change. All eleven catalogues now say which of the four goes where, each written in its own language (B14 rule 35) rather than translated from the English. The field is honestly labelled, not wired: G90 still refuses any attempt to set a property nothing reads.

reported_by: CR-069 wave E build lane, from its own pre-push arithmetic
title: Resolving a register conflict in TEXT mode silently rewrote five of other lanes' rows — Python's universal newlines turned an embedded CR into a newline and wrote it back changed
surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv (and any register a lane resolves by script)
found_in: unreleased — caught before the push
introduced_in: 2026-09-04, this lane's own conflict resolution during a cherry-pick onto a moved tip
escape_reason: CAUGHT BY THE ONE CHECK LAW 11 PRESCRIBES AND BY NOTHING ELSE: `git diff --numstat <tip> <commit>` read as ARITHMETIC rather than as a glance. A one-row append must be `1 0`; it read `6 5`. Reading the diff itself was NOT enough — the four rewritten rows are visually IDENTICAL at any sane column width, because the only difference is a CR inside a quoted field, and `git show` prints them as an ordinary -/+ pair in a 1,663-row register. Every other law-11 check passes on it: the file count is right, my own row IS present, `git status` is clean, and no test reads this file's bytes. THE MECHANISM IS NEW AND IS NOT ON LAW 11's LIST: `io.open(p, encoding='utf-8').read()` applies UNIVERSAL NEWLINES, so every CRLF and lone CR becomes LF on the way in and is written back as LF — the script never touched those rows and changed them anyway. It is law 11's revert-by-subtraction with a character instead of a hunk.
prevention: The resolution was redone from the tip's BYTES — `git show <tip>:<path>` into `bytes`, my row appended as bytes, written with `open(path, 'wb')` — and the numstat then read `1 0` with all five CR-bearing rows byte-identical. THE RULE THIS GENERALISES TO, and it belongs beside law 11's re-derivation clause: A SHARED REGISTER IS BYTES, NOT TEXT. Any script that appends to or resolves one must read and write in binary, or at minimum `newline=''`. The check that found it is already law 11's and needs no change — but it only works if the arithmetic is read as arithmetic, which is the second half of what DEF-1706 said and is now the second time that clause has paid for itself.

prevention: TWO fixes and ONE thing NAMED AND NOT BUILT, and the third is the important one. (1) The 27 keys are re-applied in all eleven catalogues, each in its own language, and the screenshots re-taken — the tab strip reads Overview · Units · Common areas · Assets · Build · Work orders · Audit log. (2) `10-scripts/render-checks/cr070-o-one-destination.mjs` gained a `raw catalogue key` pattern to its clerk-copy forbidden list, so a dotted lowercase key reaching a screen now FAILS the walkthrough rather than being noticed by a person looking at a picture — this wave's own screens are covered. (3) ⚠ **THE GENERAL GUARD IS OWED AND IS NOT BUILT HERE, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT (law 1).** `G15` compares the eleven catalogues WITH EACH OTHER and cannot see a key that none of them has; `G27` resolves every LITERAL translation key against `en.json` and cannot resolve a TEMPLATE one — and `premisesTabs` asks for `metering.premises.tab.${id}` over a declared tuple, which is exactly the shape that got through. The gate that would have caught this expands a template key over its own declared id list and resolves each result; it belongs beside `G27` and is named here so the next lane meets a decision rather than an absence. The lane-local worktree-sync helper that caused it now refuses to overwrite any file whose content matches NEITHER the base NOR the tip — a named 'these are mine' list is written when the sync is CALLED and says nothing about what has been edited since — but that helper is this lane's own scratch tooling and is deliberately NOT pushed: it hardcodes one worktree path, and shipping a script nobody else can run would be dead code (law 2). The rule it encodes is what generalises: **before writing a tip's bytes over a file, hash the working copy — a file matching neither end has local work in it, whoever's it is.** ⚠ **AND THE FIRST FIX FOR THIS DEFECT COMMITTED THE DEFECT AGAIN, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH READING.** Re-applying the 27 keys was done from the lane's OWN working copies — the very copies the sync had already rewound — instead of from the pinned tip, so the commit that repaired two tab labels **deleted 118 sibling keys from all eleven catalogues and reverted two changed values**. `G15` was GREEN on it, again symmetrically, and it was green for a worse reason the second time: the tip's own `G15` is RED on five untranslated `portal.*` values a sibling lane added, and deleting those keys made the gate pass. **What caught it was `git diff --numstat <tip> <commit>` READ AS ARITHMETIC** — `29 insertions, 120 deletions` on a change that adds 27 keys and removes none — which is CLAUDE.md law 11's own instruction, word for word, and the only check in this repository that could have. Corrected in the next commit by rebuilding every catalogue from `git show <tip>:<path>` and adding the 27 to THAT. ⚠ A second near-miss in the same commit, same cause, no damage: the defect register was rewritten through `csv.writer`, which re-quoted 1,649 sibling rows — every record identical, no row lost, and a diff so large that a real subtraction inside it could not have been seen. It is now `git show <tip>:<path>` bytes plus five appended lines, and read in BINARY: `subprocess(text=True)` turns on universal newlines and silently normalises a stray CR inside a quoted cell, which re-diffs the whole file on its own.

title: The portal demo fixture read ANOTHER TENANT'S rows: two unscoped querysets in _fixture_owner, invisible under RLS and fatal on a realistic database
surface: seed_portal_demo — the first command of every customer-portal browser walkthrough
introduced_in: 2.133.0 (portal wave A, apps/portal/sample_data.py)
escape_reason: CLAUDE.md hard rule 1 says no cross-tenant queryset, and these were two: `PremisesOwner.objects.filter(name=FIXTURE_OWNER_NAME)` and `PremisesOwnerCategory.objects.filter(code__iexact='landlord')`, neither scoped by tenant. RLS would normally make that harmless — but seeding runs as a role with rolsuper=t, which the process WARNS about on every start ('RLS IS NOT ENFORCED on this connection'), so every policy is skipped and the filters see every tenant. ⚠ THE DIRECTION IS THE WORST PART: on an EMPTY database both were right by accident, because one tenant existed. They only fail on a database that already holds a realistic utility — which is exactly what a proof-db template IS. So the more realistic the data, the more certainly it broke. And the failure named the wrong subject: `VAL-005 (metering.premises_owner.category_unknown)`, raised by the validator that IS scoped, reads as a missing lookup rather than as one tenant's id handed to another. The second query was never even reached: seeding the SECOND utility would have found the FIRST one's owner by name and returned somebody else's id. No test covers it — the suite runs on SQLite with one tenant per test, which is the empty-database case where both queries are right.
prevention: Both scoped to `core.tenancy.current_tenant_id()`, with the traceback quoted in the comment so the next reader meets the explanation rather than the symptom. PROVED by the thing that failed: `seed_portal_demo` now completes and seeds BOTH utilities — 'portal fixture seeded: pine-hill (live), oak-ridge (live)' — which is the two-tenant case the second query would have broken and which had never run to completion before. ⚠ A GATE IS OWED AND IS MECHANICALLY EASY: fail an unscoped `.objects.filter(` on a tenant-owned model inside any seeding or fixture path, where RLS is deliberately bypassed and is therefore not the safety net it is everywhere else. That is a greppable pattern over a known list of tenant models, and it would have gone red the day this file landed.

title: Two maintenance commands acted on THEMSELVES: the tree sync overwrote the shell script it was running, and pkill -f matched its own shell
surface: 10-scripts/proof-db.sh (a 322s build killed on its last lines) and any pkill -f in a lane's own session
introduced_in: the sync procedure in CLAUDE.md law 12, and every ad-hoc pkill
escape_reason: ONE SHAPE, TWO INSTANCES, TEN MINUTES APART. (1) Law 12's restore writes the tip's bytes over every differing path. `proof-db.sh build` was STILL EXECUTING from one of those paths. Bash reads a script incrementally by byte offset, so replacing it under a running invocation garbles whatever it has not read yet: the build finished its work (322s, template stamped and usable) and then died on `syntax error near unexpected token '('` at a line that is syntactically fine — `bash -n` on the same file returns clean. A syntax error that cannot be reproduced from the file is the signature. (2) `pkill -f "run-walkthrough"` matched the shell whose own command line contained that string, killing the command that issued it — exit 144. The style lane hit the identical self-match twice earlier the same night on its polling loops, so this is the third and fourth occurrence across three different agents. Nothing catches either: both commands did exactly what they were told.
prevention: The rule is one sentence: A COMMAND THAT ACTS ON A PATTERN OR A PATH MUST FIRST ASK WHETHER IT IS ACTING ON ITSELF. Concretely — (a) before a law-12 sync, check whether any process is executing from the tree (`pgrep -f '10-scripts/'`) and wait, or copy the script to a temp path and run THAT; the restore is the one maintenance step that rewrites files other running work is reading. (b) Never `pkill -f <substring>` from a shell whose own command line can contain that substring: match on a pidfile, or exclude self with `pgrep -f <pat> | grep -v $$`. Worth a gate only for (b) — a `pkill -f` in a committed script is greppable; (a) is a procedure hazard and belongs in CLAUDE.md law 12 beside the restore it complicates.

reported_by: the CR-070 wave O build lane (claude)
title: TWO WAVES CLAIMED `2.141.0` ON THE SAME DAY — a version is a shared allocation, and this lane re-derived its defect ids and its gate number at push time but not its version
surface: governance (07-frontend/package.json, package-lock.json, 06-backend/pyproject.toml, CHANGELOG.md)
introduced_in: the version step of CR-070 wave O
escape_reason: `G35` CHECKS THAT THE FOUR LITERALS AGREE WITH EACH OTHER AND THAT THE CURRENT ONE HAS A CHANGELOG ENTRY. It cannot see a SECOND entry for the same number, and it was GREEN on this lane's tree at the moment of the push — all four literals read `2.141.0` and `2.141.0` had an entry. What it could not say is that the entry it found was one of TWO: `CR-068` wave E had already written `## [2.141.0] — Your customers can sign in` into the CHANGELOG at the pinned tip and had bumped `package.json` to match, leaving only its lockfile behind. This lane read *the next free change number* from a CHANGELOG it had synced earlier rather than from the tip it was about to push onto, took `2.141.0`, and inserted its own entry above theirs. It is exactly the shape of `DEF-CWP-3734` (three lanes, three correct computations, one gate number) and of the defect-id collision this same lane caught an hour earlier with its own re-derivation step — **the lane re-derived its defect ids and its gate number from the pinned tip and did not think of the version as the same kind of number.** Resolved on the branch without data loss: the sibling's entry is renumbered `2.143.0` and both stand.
prevention: THE RULE, AND IT IS ONE THIS REPOSITORY ALREADY WRITES DOWN TWICE: a version is an ALLOCATION FROM A SHARED REGISTER, like a defect id, a gate number and a screen id — and every one of those is re-read from the PINNED TIP at push time, never from a copy the lane was holding. Concretely: `git show <tip>:CHANGELOG.md | grep -m1 '^## \['` immediately before the push, and take the next number from THAT. ⚠ The durable half is a gate and it is NAMED AND NOT BUILT: `G35` should also refuse a CHANGELOG carrying two entries for one version — one line over the headings it already parses — and it belongs with whoever owns `G35`. Named here rather than added by a passing lane, because widening a version gate in the middle of a collision is how the collision gets baselined.

reported_by: the CR-070 wave O build lane (claude)
title: THE COMMITTED OPENAPI SNAPSHOT WAS TEN VERSIONS AND FOUR WAVES STALE — 46 routes the product serves were not in the contract the typed front end is built against, and `test_be11_tc05` had been RED for all of them
surface: backend (06-backend/openapi/schema.json)
introduced_in: between 2.133.0 and 2.143.0 — the export was last run at `f1f1f9a3` (CR-068 wave A)
escape_reason: THE CHECK EXISTS, IS CORRECT, AND WAS SIMPLY LEFT RED. `tests/test_be11_openapi.py::test_be11_tc05` compares the committed snapshot with what the code exports and says in its own failure message *"Run: python manage.py export_openapi"* — so this is not a missing guard, it is a guard whose failure four consecutive waves stepped over. The snapshot held 467 paths and the code serves 513: every route of `CR-070` waves A, B and C (`/work-orders`, `/work-orders/awaiting-approval`, `/work/parts`), of `CR-068`'s portal, of `CR-069`'s integrations and of `CR-072` was absent. ⚠ **AND WAVE A'S LIFECYCLE TRAILER CLAIMS THE OPPOSITE IN AS MANY WORDS** — `apps/work/api.py` reads *"gates: … openapi export re-run (one new path)"* — which is hard-won law 1 exactly (a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee) and the same shape as `DEF-CWP-3743`, a citation pointing at a proof that was never made. Fixed by a passing lane rather than reported, because this file is a DERIVED artifact — regenerating it is the whole of the fix, the test names the command, and leaving it red would have made this lane's own five routes the fifth wave to step over the same failure. ⚠ Two things it does NOT fix, both stated rather than absorbed: `test_be11_tc02` (the schema declaring the session cookie it uses) is a DIFFERENT assertion and is red at the branch base too — not staleness, and not this lane's; and the export is still a thing somebody has to remember, so the durable fix is a CI step or a gate that runs it, which `base.py:220` already describes as existing and which nothing in `10-scripts/gates/` implements. reported_by: coordinator, closing wave E's last verify row
title: US-CWP-024 TC-6 compared two error bodies BYTE FOR BYTE and could never pass — every envelope carries a per-request random trace_id
surface: 06-backend/tests/test_us_cwp_024_balance.py — the BR-CWP-010 indistinguishability case
escape_reason: `core/errors.py` sets `trace_id = uuid.uuid4().hex` on every refusal, a fresh 32-hex string PER REQUEST, so two 404 bodies are byte-identical only when the same request is compared with itself. The wave recorded this case as UNPROVED and attributed the failures to machine load; three reruns starved and a fourth would have failed the same way. ⚠ UNPROVED AND UNPROVABLE ARE DIFFERENT CATEGORIES AND THE SECOND IS WORSE: an unproved case invites a rerun and eventually yields; an unprovable one absorbs reruns forever and never does. Nothing catches it — the assertion is well-formed, the property it names is real, and the only symptom is a failure that looks like flakiness. It was found by reading the diff of the two bodies rather than the summary line, which showed them differing in exactly one field and that field random by design.
prevention: The test now asserts what BR-CWP-010 actually wants — INDISTINGUISHABILITY, not byte-equality — and byte-equality was always the stronger claim. Three assertions replace one: both bodies carry a trace id OF THE SAME SHAPE (a refusal whose trace id merely looks different is as much a tell as one that is absent); the two ids DIFFER from each other (a reused id would correlate the two requests rather than separate them); and with that field set aside the bodies are identical. ⚠ The general lesson is worth more than the fix: when a test compares whole payloads, every field that is random, timestamped or per-request must be named and excluded DELIBERATELY, because such a field turns a security assertion into one that cannot hold. Wave E's enrolment test does compare `response.content` directly and is correct to — that response carries no trace id — so the technique is not wrong, only its reach.

reported_by: CR-069 wave E build lane, from its own browser walkthrough
title: Replacing a mail password leaves the card reading Working on a test taken against the password that was just replaced
surface: Settings > Integrations (the card) and S142 (the state word)
found_in: unreleased — found in the browser before the wave was signed off
introduced_in: 2026-09-03, wave B's rotate_credential
escape_reason: FOUND BY CLICKING IT AND BY NOTHING ELSE (hard-won law 6). `rotate_credential` queues a test only when the provider has an operation that needs no typed address; `email_smtp`'s test sends a real message, so it declares `test_needs_recipient` and NOTHING is queued — deliberately, because nothing should be sent blind. But the connection keeps `status`, `last_test_ok` and `last_test_text` from the PREVIOUS password, so the card goes on saying Working, and the sentence underneath it goes on being the old one. That is hard-won law 1 exactly: a claim that WAS true and is no longer known to be. Every backend test passes because they assert the credential rows, which are correct; no test asserted the connection's WORD after a rotation, and no gate reads rendered output. `rollback_credential` in the same commit already resets to `untested` for this very reason and says so in its docstring — the two halves of one story disagreed.
prevention: `rotate_credential` now clears `last_test_ok`/`last_test_text` and sets `untested` whenever it does NOT queue a test — the same three lines and the same reasoning as `rollback_credential`. *Not tested yet* is the honest word for a password nobody has tried. The standing prevention is the one this defect demonstrates rather than a new gate: a walkthrough that clicks the screen is the only thing in this repository that can see a stale word, and `US-INT-024` TC-1's *`test()` re-runs* was read as a promise the runtime cannot keep for a provider that needs an address.

reported_by: coordinator, recording the CR-069 and CR-070 rulings
title: G8 clause D knew three of the register's four lifecycle states — ROUTED was missing
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g08_stub_honesty.py KNOWN_OQ_STATES
introduced_in: 2026-08-15, when clause D was written
escape_reason: The register's own header has said "Lifecycle: OPEN → ROUTED → ANSWERED → CLOSED" since the file was created, and the gate that validates its status cells carries its OWN copy of that vocabulary with ROUTED absent. Nothing caught it for three weeks because NOTHING HAD EVER USED THE STATE: every question so far was answered by the PO or by us, and ROUTED means routed OUTSIDE this team. The first one to need it — OQ-INT-1477, sent to the card processor by PO instruction (⚑ Ask the processor) — failed the gate for spelling its own lifecycle correctly, which reads as the ROW being wrong rather than the gate. ⚠ THE GENERAL FORM IS THE FINDING: a gate holding a private copy of a vocabulary the document also declares drifts from it silently, and the drift is invisible until somebody uses the part that was dropped. Clause D is otherwise doing its job — it is red at HEAD on 87 legacy narrative status cells, which is a separate standing item and not this defect.
prevention: ROUTED added to KNOWN_OQ_STATES with the register's own lifecycle line quoted beside it, so the next reader sees where the list came from. The durable fix — deriving the set FROM the register's header rather than restating it — is not made here because the header is prose and parsing it would be a second guess at the same vocabulary; the comment naming the source is the mitigation a reader can act on.

title: A one-row CSV append reported "6 insertions, 5 deletions" — pathlib text mode had silently stripped five carriage returns
surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv (the append) and every helper that edits a register with read_text/write_text
introduced_in: long-standing; any lane using pathlib text mode on a register
escape_reason:
NOTHING WAS LOST — the five deleted lines were the same five rows re-added without their . But hard-won law 11 says to read `git diff --numstat` AS ARITHMETIC, because on a two-row append "2 insertions, 1 deletion" is a destroyed row; a one-row append reporting five deletions is exactly the signal that law exists to catch. ⚠ THE HAZARD IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE USUAL ONE: this is a check crying wolf, and a check that raises a false alarm is dangerous in a specific way — DEF-174 records a lane acting on a wrong numstat with `git checkout HEAD~ --` over six shared files. A lane that learns the arithmetic is noisy stops reading it, and then the real destroyed row goes through. CAUSE: `pathlib.Path.read_text()` opens in TEXT mode, so universal newlines turn every 
 into 
, and `write_text()` writes 
 back. The five rows carrying CRLF came from an earlier lane and had been invisible until something rewrote the whole file. Nothing catches it: the diff is correct, the content is correct, and only the COUNTS look wrong.
prevention: Verified by subtraction rather than by inspection, which is what settled it in one command: compare the two blobs with \r\n and \r normalised, then assert that no row present before is missing after and exactly one row is new. That check distinguishes a line-ending rewrite from a destroyed row, which numstat alone cannot. ⚠ The standing advice for the next lane: when a register append reports more deletions than you made, normalise and diff the ROWS before believing either reading — and never remediate on numstat alone (DEF-174). For a register that must not be reflowed at all, read and write BYTES.

reported_by: CR-068 wave F build lane, reading the model behind a shipped field
title: The portal decided *is this a master account* from the SHAPE of the row rather than from `accounts.kind`, and was right only by coincidence
surface: 06-backend/apps/portal/api.py `_account_rows` (the signed-in switcher's `is_master`)
escape_reason: Wave E wrote `unit_id is None and premises_id is not None`, which is what BR-CUS-068's ORIGINAL anchoring implied — "attached to the premises' common-area units". That clause was SUPERSEDED on 2026-09-01 (CR-056 W1, BR-CUS-1010): a master now writes `premises_id` and leaves `unit_id` NULL. So the proxy agreed with the truth by accident, and only for rows created after migration customers/0036; the same ruling says accounts created before it "keep the anchor they were created with", and such a master HAS a unit — the switcher would label a landlord's common-areas account Tenant billed. NOTHING COULD CATCH IT: no test seeds a kind=master account, and both readings agree on every row the fixtures create, so a test written today passes either way. It was found by reading customers/models.py to check what a new fixture should set — not by any check. AND THE FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: the shape was read as plainly broken until create_master_account's own docstring showed the anchoring had moved. Verifying before reporting is what kept a false claim out of the record.

The constant is RE-EXPORTED through the seam so the portal names one spelling, and test_us_cwp_026_my_accounts.py asserts the seam and apps.customers.services agree — because a re-exported constant is a second copy until something compares them. The standing lesson is the general one: when a model has an exact column for a fact, read the column. A shape that implies it is a rule in disguise, and rules move.

reported_by: CR-068 wave F build lane, going to read the test a file said it had
title: `portal/home/Home.tsx` cited `Home.test.tsx` from the day the balance tile shipped, and that file has never existed — the SECOND occurrence of DEF-CWP-3743's shape in one day
surface: 07-frontend/src/portal/home/Home.tsx (the Trace `Tests:` line) — and 149 more citations across the repo
escape_reason: A `Tests:` line is the most load-bearing comment in this repo: it is how a reviewer decides a file is covered and how the next lane finds the case it must not break. A citation to a test nobody wrote reads EXACTLY like a citation to one that passes, which is hard-won law 1 in its purest form. Nothing caught it: no gate read Trace headers, `tsc` and every suite are green whether or not the named file exists, and the wave that wrote the line was honest — it intended the test and ran out of wave. Found by opening the file to copy its mocking pattern and finding no file. MEASURED at that moment: 120 broken citations of 1,004 across the backend and front end, 150 once 10-scripts was scanned too. Two occurrences in one day (DEF-CWP-3743 was the first) is a missing gate rather than a discipline problem.
prevention: G95 (`g95_trace_tests_exist.py`) reads every Trace `Tests:` line and its continuations and refuses a citation that resolves against none of the four roots citations are actually written against. A RATCHET, not a cliff: the 149 standing gaps are parked in `trace_tests_known_gaps.txt`, a NEW broken citation fails outright, and a parked row that starts resolving ALSO fails until its line is deleted in the same diff — so the file can only shrink and the debt cannot quietly re-grow. Proved red in both directions by `selftest()`, which is the same entry point `run_gates` uses (law 7's second half, DEF-GOV-3733). The first row was paid off in this same commit: `Home.dom.test.tsx` now exists with eight cases over the balance tile, and the baseline is 149. The gate deliberately does NOT claim the cited test COVERS anything — that needs semantic knowledge, and a gate claiming coverage would be the same lie one level up.

reported_by: CR-068 wave F build lane, building the panel the story asked for
title: US-CWP-031 asks for a move history read from a `MoveRecord` table that has never existed, and the relationship that would replace it is documented as not built
surface: 04-docs/05-modules/15-portal/06-epics/EP-CWP-06-shell-and-access.md §5 (US-CWP-031) — and the CWP-065 panel it specifies
introduced_in: the day US-CWP-031 was written
escape_reason: §5 maps *Move history* to `MoveRecord`. There is no such model anywhere in this product. A move IS recorded — as a `service_requests` row carrying outcome=move_in — but that row has NO account_id: the link runs the other way through `outcome_ref`, which is free text, and the matching `origin_service_request_id` on the child is described in the model's own comment as "it does not exist yet". So an account cannot be walked back to the move that opened it. ⚠ NOTHING CAUGHT IT BECAUSE NOTHING CHECKS A STORY AGAINST THE SCHEMA: §5 is a table in a markdown file, and the feasibility review reads field maps rather than each story's data-mapping rows. What found it was Django refusing the query — `FieldError: Cannot resolve keyword 'account_id'` — which is the database saying the relationship the story assumes is not modelled. ⚠ AND THE TEMPTING FIX IS THE DANGEROUS ONE: `outcome_ref` is text, so a lane could match strings and get a plausible answer most of the time. That is a join on prose, on a screen that tells a customer what happened to their account.
prevention: The panel ships with what the schema can honestly answer — `accounts.opened_at`, *this account opened on 4 March 2021* — and the move that caused it is left out. The absence is written in three places so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight: the seam (where the read would have gone, with the FieldError quoted), the selector (where the key would have been), and the screen (where the sentence would have been). ⚠ The standing lesson: a story's §5 data map names DB targets and nothing verifies them, so the first lane to build a panel is the first check the mapping ever gets — which means a build lane finding a phantom table is the system working, not the lane going slowly.

reported_by: CR-068 wave G build lane, writing up the OQ-CWP-1562 ruling
title: BR-CWP-001 said the portal writes FOUR kinds of row and the blueprint it was extracted from specified FIVE — BR-CWP-009's customer-to-account link was never counted, so US-CWP-027 (add another account) sat blocked on a question the blueprint had already answered
surface: 04-docs/05-modules/15-portal/02-business-rules.md · 06-backend/apps/portal/write_points.py · 10-scripts/gates/g81_portal_write_points.py
found_in: 2026-09-04, closing OQ-CWP-1562 — the ruling covered the contact detail, and writing up the second half found it needed no ruling at all

reported_by: CR-068 wave H build lane, moving the home tile onto the stored months
title: The portal home page's usage tile printed the STORED precision — `4820.000000 gal` where the ratified display is `4820 gal`
surface: 07-frontend/src/portal/home/Home.tsx (the `data-home-usage` tile) · apps/portal/seams/billing_seam.py `usage_series`
escape_reason: THE TEST HANDED THE COMPONENT A NUMBER NO SERVER HAS EVER SENT. `Home.dom.test.tsx` TC-7 built its fixture row by hand as `quantity: "4820"` and asserted the tile contained `4820` and `gal` — both true of the fixture and neither true of the product. The wire value comes from `invoice_lines.quantity`, which is `NUMERIC(18,6)`, so `str(Decimal)` serves `4820.000000` and the tile rendered it verbatim. NOTHING ELSE COULD HAVE CAUGHT IT: `tsc` sees a string either way, the backend test asserted `Decimal(row["quantity"]) == 4820` which is TRUE of `4820.000000`, and no gate in this repo reads rendered output (hard-won law 6). It is `DEF-646` one screen over — the staff reads list printed `1008.000000` for the same reason and `BR-MET-144` was ruled for it on 2026-08-27, three days before this tile was written.
prevention: The DISPLAY string is composed by the SERVER and the screen renders that: `selectors._home_usage_series` serves `quantity_display` through `metering.quantity_display.quantity_text` — `BR-MET-144`'s two decimals with trailing zeros trimmed, the same function every staff quantity already goes through — beside the stored `quantity`, which keeps its six places for anything that computes. `Home.dom.test.tsx` TC-7 now feeds the row the shape the read really serves (`quantity: "4820.000000"`, `quantity_display: "4820"`) and asserts the tile does NOT contain `4820.000000`. THE STANDING LESSON IS ABOUT THE FIXTURE, NOT THE FORMATTER: a hand-typed test value that is tidier than the wire value is a test of the fixture, and it passes while the product is wrong. Copy the shape from the read, not from what looks right.

title: The portal front door's utility name renders at body size — `text-xl` is a class no stylesheet declares
surface: CWP-015 · portal/signin/FrontDoor.tsx
escape_reason: Nothing that runs on a merge reads rendered output. `tsc`, eslint and every `toContain` assertion pass on it because the class IS in the DOM — DEF-974's exact trap, and the theme clears Tailwind's stock type scale so `text-xl` compiles to no rule at all. `routeBUtilities.test.ts` DOES catch it and is not in `run_gates`, so it only fails for a lane that happens to run it; this one did, while checking its own classes.
prevention: The check exists and is correct — what is missing is that it runs. Either register `src/styles/routeBUtilities.test.ts` in the frontend test job the merge gate reads, or have G31 refuse a Route-B file's orphan tokens directly rather than skipping those files entirely. PREVENTION DELIVERED 2026-09-05 (0ad3a6bc). Of this row's two options the first is not available: every workflow in .github/workflows/ is .disabled, so there is no frontend test job for routeBUtilities.test.ts to be registered in, and run_gates.py IS the merge gate. So the second was taken -- G31 now refuses a Route-B file's orphan named tokens directly. A cleared namespace does not need the Tailwind compiler: `--text-*: initial` deletes Tailwind's own scale outright, so the only surviving sizes are the ones the token files re-declare, and that set is readable in Python. G31 therefore reads EVERY file, all 280 Route B ones included. Proved red through module.run() -- the path run_gates uses, not __main__ (DEF-GOV-3733) -- by restoring text-xl here, and it named 'text-xl (asked for by portal/signin/FrontDoor.tsx)'. It also found a LIVE orphan nobody had reported, text-danger on the field-work refusal, which a work lane fixed independently the same hour as DEF-WRK-4005.

title: A law-11 re-derivation deleted this lane's OWN function by subtraction: level_pay_position vanished from portal/seams/billing_seam.py while selectors.py went on calling it, so GET /portal/level-pay would have raised AttributeError on the branch
surface: backend
found_in: code
introduced_in: 2026-09-04, CR-068 wave H (commit 4d94ee85)
escape_reason: EVERY CHECK IN HARD-WON LAW 11 PASSED ON IT, AND THE BASELINE IS WHY. A sibling pushed between this lane's commit and its push, so the file was rebuilt as `the pinned tip + my own append` exactly as the law prescribes — and the script re-applied only `invoice_numbers`, the block its author had in front of them. `level_pay_position` had been appended to the same file forty minutes earlier and was in no script. Then: `git diff --numstat <tip> <commit>` showed ZERO deletions, which was TRUE because the tip never held the function; `git show <commit>` showed only this lane's own hunks, also true; the file count was right; ruff passed; and the suite that was run (documents) does not import the level-pay path. THE SUBTRACTION WAS MEASURED AGAINST THE WRONG BASELINE. Law 11's `git diff --numstat <pinned-tip> <commit>` protects SIBLINGS and says nothing about protecting a lane's own earlier commit from its own re-derivation, which is the gap this sits in. Found by grepping for the function while making an unrelated correction to it.
prevention: Restored from 590c398f — the commit that held it — rather than retyped. THE CHECK THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT, and it is one command law 11 does not currently name: after a rebase or a commit-tree re-derivation, run `git diff <your own previous commit> <the rebased one>` and read it as arithmetic. It must show the SIBLING's additions and nothing of yours missing. Verifying only against the tip cannot see this class, because the tip is exactly the baseline your own work is absent from. Proposed for law 11's re-derivation paragraph; REPORTED rather than edited into CLAUDE.md by this lane, since amending a hard-won law mid-wave is a process event.

title: Fifteen portal read chains over another module's table name no tenant and rely on RLS FORCE alone — BR-CWP-010 says the tenant is intersected IN THE QUERY, and the SQLite test suite can never see the difference
surface: 06-backend/apps/portal/seams/billing_seam.py (5) · seams/customers_seam.py (3) · seams/payments_seam.py (2) · credentials.py (2) · selectors.py (2) · seams/tenancy_seam.py (1, a false positive — see prevention)

introduced_in: spread across three weeks and four lanes — the oldest is wave E's credentials matcher, the newest wave G's bills_for; every one of them written by a different lane, each correct-looking on its own
escape_reason: NOT A LIVE EXPOSURE — row-level security is FORCEd and does enforce the tenant. What no check could see is that the SECOND half of a belt-and-braces rule had quietly gone. config/settings/test.py hardcodes in-memory SQLite, which has no RLS at all (hard-won law 14), so a portal read that omits the tenant passes every test in this repository on every machine — forever, and identically to one that does not. No gate read portal queries for scope, and BR-CWP-010's wording (*in the query*) was satisfied by half the lanes and not the other half with nothing to tell them apart.
prevention: G96 (g96_portal_reads_name_the_tenant.py) walks each queryset CHAIN with ast and fails a portal read over another module's model that names no tenant. Ten of the fifteen fixed the same hour; the other five sit in two files two live lanes were editing, so they are held in portal_tenantless_reads.txt — a ratchet that may only SHRINK, and which also fails on a row that has since been fixed, so it cannot rot into a permanent pardon. TWO THINGS THE GATE HAD TO GET RIGHT AND THE FIRST DRAFT DID NOT: it reads the CHAIN, not the call, or filter(tenant_id=...).exclude(...) reports as a violation — which would have filed this defect against session.py's account set, the single most carefully scoped query in the portal; and the tenants table is exempt when filtered by pk, because there tenant_id IS the primary key and tenancy_seam.branding was already correct. Proved RED through run_gates' registry rather than __main__ (DEF-GOV-3733), on the real defect and on a stale ratchet row.

reported_by: the CR-068 lead lane, self-reported — I wrote the gate, believed it, and broke seven tests with it
title: G96 reported customers_seam's residential-account-type read as unscoped and it was WRONG: AccountType is platform-seeded and has no tenant column at all. Adding tenant_id raised FieldError: Cannot resolve keyword 'tenant_id' into field and took seven wave-B and wave-C tests red
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g96_portal_reads_name_the_tenant.py · 06-backend/apps/portal/seams/customers_seam.py
found_in: 2026-09-04, running the whole portal backend suite after closing the last three ratchet rows — 7 failed, 326 passed
introduced_in: 2026-09-04, the same hour G96 landed (commit ae642aab)
escape_reason: THE GATE'S OWN SELF-TEST PASSED, AND SO DID EVERY CHECK AROUND IT. G96 proves it can tell a tenant-less read from a scoped one, and it can. What it could not do is tell a tenant-less read from a table that HAS NO TENANT — it inferred 'this model belongs to another module, therefore it is tenant-scoped', which is true of 153 models and false of AccountType, whose own docstring says so in as many words: 'platform-seeded, identical for every tenant, so NO tenant_id and NO RLS'. I had ALREADY hit this class of error once in the same file — the tenants table, exempted by hand — and generalised from the instance instead of from the cause. ⚠ AND THE SEQUENCE IS THE POINT: I ran the targeted suites for the files I changed (28 tests, green) and only ran the WHOLE portal suite afterwards. The seven that broke were wave B and wave C — code I had not touched, reached through a seam function I had. A gate that reports a fix which breaks the product is worse than no gate, because it is trusted; this one was obeyed within the hour, by its author.
prevention: G96 now READS THE SCHEMA rather than assuming it: tenant_scoped_models() parses every apps/*/models.py with ast and collects the 153 model classes that actually declare a tenant column; a chain over anything else is skipped, because there is no keyword to add. The hand-written Tenant-by-pk exemption is subsumed by it. selftest() gains UNSCOPED_MODEL — the exact AccountType read that cost the seven — and returns False if the gate reports it, so this cannot regress. THE PROCESS FIX IS THE BIGGER ONE: when a gate's finding causes an edit to a SHARED seam function, the targeted suite for the file changed is not enough — run every suite that reaches that function. customers_seam.residential_account_type_id is called by two waves I had no reason to think about.

reported_by: the CR-068 lead lane, asked by the Product Owner why 24 hours produced 31 screens
title: `--reuse-db` has been a NO-OP for the entire project: Django's SQLite backend builds its test database IN MEMORY unless TEST['NAME'] is set, so every pytest run re-applied all 278 migrations from scratch — 133s of fixed cost on every invocation by every lane
surface: 06-backend/config/settings/test.py
found_in: 2026-09-04, profiling a 146s run of an 8-test file: `--durations` put 137s in the FIRST test's setup and 0.8s in every other, which is where pytest attributes session database creation
introduced_in: the original test settings, unchanged since the suite existed — `NAME: ':memory:'` with no TEST key, which is the documented Django default for SQLite and reads as deliberate
escape_reason: NOTHING WAS EVER WRONG, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVED. Every test passed, every lane passed `--reuse-db` exactly as CLAUDE.md instructs, and the flag is silently ignored rather than refused — there is no warning, no error and no output difference between a reuse that works and one that cannot. The only symptom is a wall-clock number nobody was measuring, on a suite everybody had learned to treat as slow. CLAUDE.md even records a FASTER measurement from a different suite family (DEF-567: an hour to four minutes with JOBS_EAGER=false), which made the remaining slowness look like the known, already-mitigated cost. ⚠ AND THE PROJECT PAID IT ON EVERY RUN FOR MONTHS: four parallel lanes on 2026-09-04 ran pytest roughly 25 times each, which is about 4½ hours of pure waiting inside a 24-hour push.
prevention: TEST['NAME'] now points at a file whose name carries a SHA-256 digest of all 278 migration files plus the checkout path. Measured on tests/test_us_cwp_032_bills.py: 133s → 9s (15x). Whole portal suite: 12m30s → 6m15s. THE DIGEST IS THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR SAFETY: a stale reused schema would be far worse than a slow one, so the reuse invalidates ITSELF — add or edit a migration and the digest changes, the file is not found, and the schema is rebuilt once. Nobody has to remember `--create-db`, which is exactly the kind of step CLAUDE.md's own change process says is 'many times not followed correctly'. The checkout path is in the digest so two worktrees do not share one file. ⚠ HARD-WON LAW 14 IS UNTOUCHED: same engine, same SQLite, so there is still no RLS here and transaction-sensitive code still has to be proved under config.settings.local. Only the database's LOCATION changed.

title: `seed_portal_demo` enqueued the sample-data plant for a Celery worker that never runs beside it, so the demo utility had premises and prices and NO accounts, meters, reads, bills, payments or documents — every portal screen built on them opened honestly empty
surface: 06-backend/apps/portal/management/commands/seed_portal_demo.py

introduced_in: CR-068 wave A, when the command was written
escape_reason: THE COMMAND REPORTED SUCCESS AND THE FAILURE WAS ONE INFO LINE IN THE MIDDLE OF IT: 'celery: could not dispatch job (tenancy.sample_data_plant) — the record stays queued and is picked up by the next worker that sees it, or by `manage.py run_pending_jobs`'. BOTH HALVES OF THAT SENTENCE WERE FALSE HERE: no worker runs beside a management command, and `run_pending_jobs` DOES NOT EXIST IN THIS REPOSITORY — the message names a recovery nobody built, which is hard-won law 1 exactly (a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee). MEASURED on a fresh database: 145 accounts, 99 customers, 200 meters, 604 meter reads, 100 invoices with 423 lines, 83 payments and 353 outbound messages, where there had been none.

title: `allocate.py --lane` silently RESHUFFLED every lane's block when a lane was asked for that was not in the roster: it appended the name, re-sorted, and handed out different windows to lanes already building
surface: 10-scripts/allocate.py
found_in: 2026-09-04, the orchestrator asking for its own block against a roster of the six lanes already running
introduced_in: 2026-09-04, the same hour --lane was written
escape_reason: THE TOOL WAS BUILT TO PREVENT COLLISIONS AND ITS FIRST REAL USE PRODUCED ONE. Blocks are stable only while the roster is; the code hid that by quietly adding the missing lane, so a seventh lane asking for a block moved the six. It printed a correct-looking answer — 3880-3899, already held by the `requests` lane — and nothing in the output said the roster had changed. The orchestrator took ids above every block by hand instead. The general form is the one this repo keeps meeting: a tool that silently repairs its caller's mistake hides the precondition that made it a mistake.

title: The faster test database put every run in one checkout on ONE file, so two concurrent `pytest` runs collided: the second failed 8 tests with sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked. A 60-second busy timeout was tried as the fix and did NOT work
surface: 06-backend/config/settings/test.py

escape_reason: THE SPEED-UP TRADED A PROPERTY NOBODY HAD NOTICED THEY RELIED ON. The in-memory database it replaced was private to each process, so overlapping runs could never meet — a guarantee that came free and was written down nowhere. Each slot is a file plus an flock held for the process's life; a run claims the lowest free one, falling back to a private per-pid file beyond 8 concurrent runs — slow and correct, the right way round. MEASURED: two concurrent runs now pass with 0 lock errors where the second failed 8, and a sequential run still reuses slot 0 in 17s rather than 133s, so the speed-up is intact. A lane in its own worktree was never affected either way, because BASE_DIR is in the digest. DEF-CWP-3904 is closed by this.

title: The tenant regional date format and TIME ZONE are saved, read by the shell, and never applied — 83 screens render every date in MM/DD/YYYY and every time in UTC
surface: 07-frontend/src/components/ShellWithSession.tsx · src/features/metering/meteringShared.tsx regionalOf

escape_reason: HARD-WON LAW 2 WITH A FALLBACK ON TOP, WHICH IS WHY IT IS SILENT. The chain is four links and every one of them looks correct alone. (1) The settings screen saves date_format and time_zone, and previews them correctly, because it reads its own draft directly. (2) ShellWithSession — the ONE place that fetches the regional settings for the whole app — reads regionalQuery.data?.language and nothing else. (3) So props.dateFormat and props.timeZone, which are OPTIONAL, are undefined on every routed screen. (4) regionalOf returns props.dateFormat ?? SEED_DATE_FORMAT and props.timeZone ?? SEED_TIME_ZONE, so every screen falls back to the hardcoded seed. THE FALLBACK IS THE REASON NOBODY SAW IT: there is no crash, no blank, no raw key — just a plausible date in the wrong format, forever. Every test passes because every test that renders a date passes the format it then asserts. Only 3 files in the whole product originate the value from the server and two of them are integrations screens; 160 call sites pass props.dateFormat down from a root that never sets it. AND IT IS EXACTLY WHY LANGUAGE WORKS: the shell applies language to i18next GLOBALLY, so that one setting needs no prop and reaches every screen. The two settings sit side by side on one page and only one of them was ever wired.
fixed_commit: 9906cfd2 — ShellWithSession applies the tenant date format and time zone and no screen renders before they are known; regionalOf rewritten
prevention: THE TIME ZONE IS THE WORSE HALF AND WAS NOT REPORTED: SEED_TIME_ZONE is UTC, so a Texas utility reads every timestamp five or six hours out — a payment taken at 7pm local shows as the next day. SEED_DATE_FORMAT is MM/DD/YYYY. 83 screens render a date. THE FIX IS AT THE ROOT, NOT AT THE 160 CALL SITES: the shell already fetches the settings, so it should publish them through a context (there is none today — this is prop-drilled), and regionalOf should fall back to the CONTEXT rather than to a constant. Every existing props.dateFormat keeps working where it is genuinely supplied. DELETE THE CONSTANTS FROM THE FALLBACK PATH ENTIRELY — a default that silently substitutes a plausible wrong answer is the defect, not the missing wire; if the settings have not loaded the screens should wait or say so, not invent a format. Hard rule: defaults fail closed (law 3).

title: A customer's bill shows raw engine values: rates as bare numbers with no currency or unit, line descriptions as internal codes including storm_water, and a reading timestamp as a full ISO string
surface: 07-frontend/src/portal/bills/BillDetail.tsx line 314 · the bill-line description and rate the billing engine writes
found_in: the PO opening a real bill on the live portal and pointing at the readings timestamp
introduced_in: the bill detail screen, which renders what the engine serves without translating any of it for a reader
escape_reason: NO GATE READS RENDERED OUTPUT (law 6) AND NO TEST COMPARES A BILL SCREEN WITH ITS SPEC, so a screen showing correct figures in machine form passes everything. FIVE FAULTS, ALL ON ONE MONEY DOCUMENT, and every one is the same mistake — the engine's own value went to a customer untranslated. (1) RATES ARE BARE NUMBERS: the water tier reads 4.2400, electric 0.1100, trash 15.0000, the sewer share 0.4000 and the local tax 0.0200. No currency, no unit, no percent sign. The spec's version reads .90 / 1,000 gal and 4.25%. A customer cannot tell whether 4.2400 is four dollars or four cents, or per what. (2) LINE DESCRIPTIONS ARE ENGINE STRINGS: storm_water usage and storm_water base charge put a snake_case identifier on a bill; electric usage tier 1 (0-500 kWh) and sewer usage - 40.00% of water usage charges are rule descriptions, where the spec has Monthly service charge, Usage - first 2,000 gal and Sewer - share of water used. (3) THE READING TIMESTAMP IS RAW: BillDetail.tsx line 314 is taken: row.read_at ?? '-' — the value never touches a date formatter at all, so 2026-07-31T00:00:00+00:00 reaches the screen verbatim. This is NOT DEF-SHL-3964, which produces a plausible wrong FORMAT; this is no formatting whatsoever, and it is the only place in the portal doing it. (4) THE METER IS ITS SERIAL: W-5026 and E-5026 where the spec shows 'Water - front'. (5) SERVICES WITH NOTHING TO CHARGE ARE DRAWN ANYWAY: FIRE 0 connection /bin/bash.00 and TRASH 0 cart /bin/bash.00 occupy two full blocks of a bill.
prevention: SPLIT THE FIX BY WHERE THE STRING IS BORN, because these are not all the same lane's work. THE RATE FORMATTING AND THE TIMESTAMP ARE THE SCREEN'S: the rate column needs the currency and the per-unit the spec shows, a percentage rate needs a percent sign, and line 314 needs the same date treatment every other portal date gets. THE LINE DESCRIPTIONS ARE THE ENGINE'S: a bill line's wording is written when the bill is priced, so 'storm_water usage' is a backend copy fault on a financial record — and financial immutability means bills already issued keep the wording they were given, so this fixes forward only and the old bills must not be rewritten. THAT CONSTRAINT IS THE REASON TO DO IT SOON RATHER THAN LATER: every bill issued between now and the fix carries the wrong words permanently. Check whether the engine has the service NAME available where it currently uses the CODE — most services hide this because their code and name look alike, and storm_water is the one that exposes it. Also worth deciding deliberately: whether a service with no charge belongs on the bill at all; the spec shows only what was charged.

escape_reason: The convention it follows is real and is documented three modules away: integrations/0001_initial.py says to double every % because schema_editor.execute(sql) defaults to params=() and psycopg then substitutes, so %% arrives as one %. That is TRUE for that path and FALSE for this one - RunSQL passes params=None, psycopg substitutes nothing, and %% reaches PostgreSQL verbatim. PL/pgSQL reads %% as a literal percent with no placeholder behind it, so RAISE had two arguments and nowhere to put them. Mechanically: a gate that parses PL/pgSQL RAISE statements in migrations and compares placeholder count to argument count would catch both directions, and it is cheap because the two numbers are on the same statement

title: THE HEADLINE LAW-14 TEST COULD NOT FAIL: IT PROVED THE CHEAP READ AND NEVER THE SAVEPOINT. tests/test_us_wrk_044_sync_pg.py::test_tc3_044_a_duplicate_key_inside_a_batch_does_not_poison_the_rest is the case wave L exists to write - a refused item inside a batch must not take the other nineteen down with it on PostgreSQL. The case therefore passed with the savepoint DELETED, on real PostgreSQL, which is precisely the configuration it was written to be conclusive in.

escape_reason: A GUARD BEHIND A FAST PATH IS NOT TESTED BY A CASE THAT ONLY EVER TAKES THE FAST PATH, AND BREAKING THE GUARD IS THE ONLY WAY TO LEARN WHICH PATH YOUR TEST TOOK. That is the lesson, and it generalises well past this bug. sync_batch answers 'have I seen this key' TWICE: a cheap SELECT first (the fast path, for the ordinary case of a phone re-sending a queue it already delivered) and the unique constraint second (the guarantee, for the race the SELECT cannot see). THE SAVEPOINT PROTECTS ONLY THE SECOND. The test staged its duplicate in a SEPARATE call, so the key was already in the receipts table when the batch arrived, the SELECT answered 'duplicate' and returned, and no IntegrityError was ever raised - so the savepoint was never exercised and the case passed with it DELETED, on real PostgreSQL, in the one configuration it was written to be conclusive in. Green with correct code and green with broken code. NOTHING ELSE COULD HAVE FOUND IT: reading the test does not tell you which branch it took, no gate reads a per-file suite result, and the whole file was green. Only the law-7 sabotage did, and only because it was aimed at the exact mechanism - remove the nested atomic, change nothing else. This is the fourth occurrence in this repository of an assertion passing for a reason other than the one it names (toContain('disabled') matching a Tailwind variant class; not.toContain('<p') matching '<path>'; --stat answering 'is every change inside these files mine'), and the FIRST where the wrong reason was a different CODE PATH rather than a looser string match - which is why the earlier three were all findable by re-reading the assertion and this one was not.

THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is the one worth carrying: when a guard protects a SECOND path behind a fast path, the test must be written to take the second path, and the way to find out which one it took is to break the guard rather than to read the code. title: cr068-e-getting-in.mjs's resolveChromium() has a FALLBACK THAT CAN NEVER FIRE. escape_reason: IT IS A FALLBACK, SO IT ONLY RUNS ON THE DAY IT IS NEEDED - and on the day it was written the revisions matched, so the happy path was taken and the recovery was never exercised. escape_reason: THE MODULE READS AS THOUGH THE DISTINCTION IS MADE, AND EVERY TEST SENDS A SETTLEMENT. `CHARGE_SETTLED = "charge.settled"` is declared as a named constant; `_deliver` stores `event_type=str(body.get("type") or "")` on the delivery row; and `_amount` refuses a negative figure with the words "a refund or a chargeback is a different event and a different path (BR-PAY-013 / BR-PAY-014)" — a sentence that PRESUPPOSES this path separates them. It does not: the constant is used only as a `setdefault` for the in-process settle_charge call, and no inbound branch ever compares `body["type"]` to anything. All 15 C21 cases and the wave-P walkthrough fixtures post a settlement, so the type is never varied and the missing branch is never exercised; the negative-amount guard is what everyone reads as the reversal guard, and it only catches a reversal that also happens to carry a negative number. Nothing else can see it either: the delivery is signed, so no security check fires; the amount is positive and parses, so BR-PAY-002 is satisfied; the account exists, so the payment rule passes; and the resulting row is an ordinary, well-formed, correctly-allocated payment that the ledger balances. THE COST IS THE CUSTOMER-FACING ONE: money the processor is taking BACK is recorded as money arriving, so the bill it is allocated against reads as paid and the allocation engine spends it on the next bill — the exact outcome the C21 decision-log entry names for a duplicate ("money the customer did not pay, sitting on their account ... and nobody looks at it again"), reached by a different door. It matters now rather than later because PO ruling 2026-09-05 names FIVE payment providers to be adapted (invoiceCloud, Worldpay, US payments, Global Payments, spruse) and a real processor sends its whole event stream to one callback URL, not settlements only.
prevention: REFUSE BY DEFAULT ON THE INBOUND PATH AND ACCEPT A NAMED SET, never the reverse: an allow-list of event types that mean money arrived, and every other type recorded on its delivery row with a new refusal code (`event_type_not_a_settlement`) and NO payment. That is the same fail-closed shape as the empty-secret default and for the same reason — an unknown event from a provider we have not adapted yet must not be guessed at. Keep the delivery row: the whole point of payment_webhook_events is that a delivery producing no payment is still findable, and a support engineer needs to see the reversal arrive even while nothing acts on it. The reversal HANDLING itself is a separate and larger question (BR-PAY-013/014, CR-069 R-8, and OQ-INT-1477 is already ROUTED to the processor on how chargebacks are broken out) and this defect does not pre-empt it — refusing an unhandled type is not a decision about how reversals will eventually be recorded, it is the absence of one. Test it by VARYING THE TYPE, which no existing case does: one settlement accepted, one non-settlement refused by name, both signed identically, so the assertion is about the type and not about the signature. ⚠ AND NOTE WHAT THE EXECUTION PLAN SAYS: wave P demo-script step 6 asks for a reversal to produce "two rows, the payment and the reversal above it — not mistaken for a duplicate". It is not mistaken for a duplicate; it is mistaken for a PAYMENT, which is worse, and the AS BUILT stamp is amended in the same commit to say so rather than leaving the table reading as though step 6 worked.

title: The wave P walkthrough's BR-CWP-057 wire check counts digits inside a UUIDv7 ref, so it fails or passes according to the clock
surface: 10-scripts/render-checks/cr068-p-rails-and-webhook.mjs:290 (the served-body arm of the 5+ digit run check)
found_in: re-running the wave P walkthrough during the rescue of that lane's own close-the-record work, on a freshly seeded clone
introduced_in: the wave P walkthrough itself, landed 03edc131, and the assertion has never been wrong about the product
escape_reason: THE CHECK IS RIGHT ABOUT ITS SUBJECT AND WRONG ABOUT ITS SCOPE. BR-CWP-057 says no column holds more than four digits of a card, and the walkthrough checks it the only way an outsider can: look for any run of 5+ digits in the DOM and in the served body. The DOM arm is sound. The WIRE arm stringifies the whole response, which carries each instrument's `ref` -- a UUIDv7 whose leading hex is a TIMESTAMP. On this run both instruments were minted in the same millisecond window and both refs began 01a07512-, so the 5-or-more-digits pattern found 07512 twice and the run reported FAIL over a body containing no card digits at all. Nothing is wrong with the product. It is the clock: the same fixture, the same code and the same assertions pass or fail according to what time the fixture ran, which is why the lane recorded this walkthrough GREEN at 33 assertions and it is red at 33 assertions now.
prevention: EXCLUDE THE ref BEFORE COUNTING DIGITS, or count digits per VALUE rather than over the stringified envelope -- the rule is about card digits in a column, and a UUID is not a column of card digits. The DOM arm needs no change. NOT TAKEN HERE: this is the wave P lane's own file and this rescue landed its work unaltered; changing an author's assertion while rescuing their work substitutes a fourth lane's judgment for theirs, which is DEF-CWP-4205's own reasoning one file along. THE TRANSFERABLE PART: a negative assertion over a JSON envelope inherits every id the envelope happens to carry, so it is only as stable as the id format -- and a UUIDv7 prefix is a clock, which makes such a check intermittently red for reasons that have nothing to do with what it guards. It is also why a walkthrough recorded GREEN once is not thereby proved repeatable.
