title: proof-db.sh clone picks the newest template by NAME, so a hand-named one outsorts every commit-sha template forever
surface: tooling
introduced_in: 10-scripts/proof-db.sh clone fallback
category: check looks at the wrong thing
escape_reason: Nothing compares a template's build time with any other's. When sbh_tpl_<short_sha> does not exist, clone falls back to 'select datname ... order by datname desc limit 1' — a LEXICOGRAPHIC sort of database names. A template built minutes ago as sbh_tpl_a8df233d loses to sbh_tpl_waveo, because w sorts above a, so every lane is sent to the older one and then correctly refused for being behind. The refusal names the right remedy (build --force) and the remedy does not help: the new template IS built, and the fallback still picks the old one. A lane that ran build --force twice would conclude the builder was broken; this lane lost six minutes and got past it only with --template.
prevention: Order by the stamp table's built_at (proof_db_stamp already records it) rather than by datname, and PRINT which template was chosen and how old it is on every clone. A fallback that cannot state its own basis is indistinguishable from one that has none.

title: net_pair picks the newest read head with order_by('-id'), and uuid7 is only time-ordered to the millisecond
surface: backend
escape_reason: apps/metering/selectors.py lines 2535-2536 pick the consumption and export halves of a net-meter pair with .order_by('-id').first(). core/dbfields.uuid7 is RFC 9562: a 48-bit unix-millisecond prefix followed by 12 RANDOM bits and 62 more, so two rows written inside one millisecond order at RANDOM and the greatest id is not the newest. An importer writing two heads for one asset, read_at and channel in the same millisecond would show a clerk the wrong half of the pair on S29, with nothing to notice. Nothing caught it because no test writes two rows fast enough, and the idiom reads as obviously correct. Found while writing the runbooks catalogue, where the same idiom returned the second of three runs and its own test caught it.
prevention: Order on created_at first and id second: created_at is auto_now_add at microsecond resolution and id is the deterministic tiebreak underneath it. The general rule worth writing down once: uuid7 is time-ordered to the MILLISECOND and no finer, so Max(id) and order_by('-id') are wrong for 'the latest' wherever two rows can be written in one millisecond.

title: on PostgreSQL 16 the isolation probe role can be created and cannot be entered, so the whole tier ERRORS instead of proving anything
surface: backend
escape_reason: PostgreSQL 16 split role membership into ADMIN, INHERIT and SET options, and SET ROLE needs the SET option specifically. When a CREATEROLE role creates another role, PG16 grants it membership WITH ADMIN TRUE, INHERIT FALSE, SET FALSE - so tests/isolation_helpers.py creates sbh_rls_probe successfully, pg_auth_members shows the membership, and every SET ROLE sbh_rls_probe is refused with InsufficientPrivilege. The fixture's own docstring promises it SKIPS with a reason when the probe role cannot be created; it CAN be created, so that branch never runs and the tier errors at setup and again at teardown instead. That is law 7's incapable-of-passing shape inside the harness whose entire job is to prove tenant isolation. Measured 2026-09-06 on PostgreSQL 16.13: set_option was f for smartbillhub on sbh_rls_probe, and six isolation cases went from 4 errors to 6 passed after GRANT sbh_rls_probe TO smartbillhub WITH SET TRUE.
prevention: rls_probe_role should issue the GRANT explicitly with WITH SET TRUE after CREATE ROLE rather than relying on what creation implies, and assert_is_a_real_proof should also assert the role can be ENTERED - a proof that cannot start is worth exactly as much as one that cannot fail. title: push_paths.sh publishes a register row a sibling appended between the re-derivation and the push - its guard looks only for VANISHED lines, never for extra ones
surface: 10-scripts/push_paths.sh step 3; 10-scripts/push_register_guard.py; 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv
found_in: CR-075 wave E task E4, by reading the push output as arithmetic: the register grew by 4 lines where the lane had appended 3

escape_reason: The tool does everything law 11 asks and still carries a stranger's row. The lane re-derived the register from the pinned tip, appended its own three rows, proved the prefix byte-identical, and ran the push. Between the copy and the push a sibling in the same shared tree filed one more defect, and step 3 hashes the WORKING TREE at push time - correctly, that is what a pathspec push means. The register guard then reported nothing vanished, which was true. This is DEF-168 mechanism five surviving inside the tool written to prevent mechanism two: it refuses a path that MOVED at the remote and a line that DISAPPEARED locally, and has no opinion about a line that APPEARED locally. title: git checkout-index -f is not on law 11's banned list and does exactly what the banned commands do - it reverted three of a sibling's register rows in a shared tree
surface: CLAUDE.md hard-won law 11, the sentence naming git stash / git checkout -- / git restore / git reset --hard / git clean; 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv
found_in: CR-075 wave E task E6, self-reported: a lane clearing a blocker before a fast-forward reached for the one restore verb the ban does not name
introduced_in: the wording of law 11's ban, which enumerates commands rather than describing the act
escape_reason: Law 11 already diagnosed this once and the fix did not generalise. DEF-172's own lesson is that the ban reads as being about stashing YOUR work while the dangerous use is a throwaway diagnostic, and the wording was widened to any command that makes the working tree momentarily not-what-it-was - but the LIST beside it is still five names, and a list is what a reader checks against. git checkout-index -f is not on it, sounds like an index operation rather than a working-tree one, and overwrites the working copy from the index without a word. It reverted three register rows a sibling had appended (two runbooks findings and a metering docstring defect). Nothing was lost, because all three had already been pushed and the tip was a superset - which is luck, not a check, and is the same reason the first two occurrences of law 11 stayed invisible.
prevention: Restore by WRITING the bytes you want, never by asking git to restore for you: git show <tip>:<path> > <path> is the form law 12 already prescribes and it names the version explicitly. The durable fix is in the law's wording: the test is not whether a command is on a list of five, it is whether the command can change a file you did not author - which also covers git checkout-index, git worktree add --force, git sparse-checkout and git read-tree -u. And before any fast-forward in a shared tree, compare each blocking path with the tip: a path byte-identical to the tip is safe to move aside, and one that differs is a sibling mid-edit and the ff does not happen at all.

title: A blanket regex renumbered SEVEN other lanes' defect citations in one file — the id-renumbering step of a push helper had no scope
surface: 06-backend/apps/runbooks/selectors.py at 042a86ab — DEF-RBS-4291 (x2), DEF-RBS-4285 (x2), DEF-RBS-4338, DEF-RBS-4292 and DEF-RBS-4284 all rewritten to this lane's own new id

escape_reason: Every check CLAUDE.md law 11 prescribes PASSED. The file count was right (one path named). The author's own change was present. push_paths.sh's staleness check was satisfied because the file had been re-derived from the pinned tip seconds earlier. The register guard watches the REGISTER, not source files. And git diff --numstat printed 27/10 — which is not obviously wrong on a 1,300-line file, because a rename hunk legitimately deletes lines. What found it was reading the DELETIONS one by one instead of reading the count, which is law 11's own instruction and the only thing that could have. Nothing was lost — a citation still resolves, to the WRONG defect, which is DEF-2804's shape on a governance path rather than a money one.
prevention: An id-renumbering step is scoped to the hunks the lane authored, never to a file: renumber the string INSIDE the replacement text before it is inserted, so the rest of the file is never a candidate. The general rule this is an instance of, and it is worth more than the fix: a re-derivation script may only ever write text it can name — 'the tip's bytes plus these N literals'. A regex over a whole file cannot name what it changed, so the operator cannot check it, and law 11's read-the-hunks check is exactly the check a whole-file regex makes impossible to perform.

reported_by: the CR-075 wave S build lane
title: A GUARDED RECORD WAS INVISIBLE TO HALF OF TWO CHECKS AND COUNTED BY THE OTHER HALF, SO ONE DREW A DISCONNECT VERDICT AND THE OTHER +339.04 OF REVENUE OVER RECORDS THEY HAD REFUSED TO LOOK AT
surface: backend
found_in: 2026-09-07, CR-075 wave S, by running both runbooks on the seeded utility rather than by any test: runbook 12 reported '2 letters served, notice period passed on both' with an empty table, and runbook 16 reported '47 bills up 5-15%, revenue +339.04' with an empty table
introduced_in: the same wave, in the first build of apps/runbooks/definitions/disconnect_eligibility.py and apps/runbooks/definitions/rate_change_preview.py
escape_reason: BR-RBS-012 says a guard is evaluated before any step and a guarded record is seen by NONE of them. Guards run BETWEEN resolve() and the first step, so anything a set step reads out of a cached whole-estate read - or anything resolve() itself computes - covers records the runbook has been told not to look at. In runbook 12 steps 2, 3 and 4 walked the whole board of cases at the last tier; in runbook 16 the whole re-price happened in resolve() and the sums walked the whole cycle. Every mocked test passed because no fixture had a guarded row in it, and the two halves of each run were internally consistent. Only the seeded utility showed it, because 72 of its 78 accounts are sample records, so the guard removed nearly the whole scope and the disagreement became visible as a verdict with counts over a table with nothing in it.
prevention: Every set step reads the SUBJECTS the executor hands it, never a cached whole-estate read, and nothing is priced in resolve(). The executor decides who was walked and no step gets to decide it a second time. Both runbooks now report the number a guard took out beside the number checked, and a regression case in each puts a guarded row in the fixture and asserts every step counts one rather than two - proved red by restoring the old expression.

title: GET THE NAME OF ANY ACCOUNT A RUNBOOK PARAMETER POINTS AT AND THE REQUEST RAISES ON POSTGRESQL - account_labels HAS NEVER WORKED ON A REAL DATABASE

Django refuses the combination outright: 'Field Account.status cannot be both deferred and traversed using select_related at the same time.' title: A lane reset the shared defect register to the tip with cp, discarding about thirteen unpushed rows and two closures belonging to three running lanes
surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv in the shared working tree; three lanes running at the time

introduced_in: my own command, minutes earlier: cp of the tip's register over the shared working copy to strip siblings' in-flight rows out of my commit
escape_reason: CLAUDE.md law 11 already forbids this in two clauses - never round-trip a shared register, and never make the working tree momentarily not-what-it-was - and I had quoted the second to a lane earlier the same day. Not ignorance: the INTENT was correct (do not publish siblings unpushed rows) and only the METHOD was wrong, which is the exact shape law 11 records for git stash - the forbidden operation felt incidental to a legitimate goal, so the rule never came to mind. No check could catch it either: push_paths.sh refuses a line VANISHING from a shared register measured AGAINST THE TIP, and an unpushed row is invisible to that comparison by construction. Each lane would have pushed a register lacking its own row, with a correct file count and its other work intact.
prevention: The intent was right and there is a correct way to reach it: rebuild the file as the tips bytes PLUS ONLY YOUR OWN HUNK using the tool that owns it, and never write over the working copy other lanes are appending to. A stronger fix worth building: file_defect.py and close_defect.py could refuse a register whose byte length is SMALLER than the tips, which is the signature of exactly this accident and costs one stat call.

title: A closed question reads as OPEN to every gate when its status cell starts with a tick: oq_is_closed() is False for 25 CLOSED rows
surface: 10-scripts/gates/common.py _OQ_STATE_RE and oq_is_closed(); 12-governance/01-open-questions.md status column; G8 clauses A, C and D
found_in: the gate-triage lane of 2026-09-07, measuring why G8 reported 77 problems
introduced_in: the register's ✅/⏳/⚠ status convention, in use since 2026-08-24 (OQ-351); _OQ_STATE_RE has never skipped a leading symbol
escape_reason: The regex reads the state token as ^\**\s*([A-Za-z]...), so a cell beginning '✅ **CLOSED 2026-09-06 - ...' returns the EMPTY state. oq_is_closed() then answers False for 25 questions the PO has actually ruled. G8's clause D DOES report the unreadable cell, so the symptom was visible - but it was visible as 35 lines of formatting nitpick inside a 77-problem gate that has been red for weeks, and nobody read the CONSEQUENCE: clause A (a stub citing a CLOSED question is a stale stub) and clause C (a story still blocked_by a CLOSED question) are both switched OFF for every one of those 25. That is the DEF-WRK-4030 failure with a machine cause instead of a human one.
prevention: oq_state() now skips leading non-alphanumeric decoration, so a tick, an hourglass or a warning sign cannot hide a state; DIGITS are deliberately not skipped, so a date-first cell stays unparseable and stays reported - skip decoration, never content. self_test() carries the emoji-prefixed CLOSED cell, the CLOSED IN PART cell and the date-first cell as named cases, so the parser cannot silently narrow OR widen again. The general shape is law 7's 'reporting zero over a scope it silently excludes' inside a shared helper: a parser that returns '' rather than raising turns every caller into a false negative at once.

title: G8 counts a docstring as a stub: 20 of the 32 'OQ-cited stubs' it reports are prose describing a stub that was REMOVED
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g08_stub_honesty.py _oq_citations_in_stubs(); 06-backend/apps/work/edit.py:477, apps/portal/api.py:1536, apps/metering/premises_owners.py:820 and 17 more
found_in: the gate-triage lane of 2026-09-07, while proving the DEF-GOV-4384 parser fix could not fire wrongly
introduced_in: the clause-A line scanner, which skips a line beginning # // or * and nothing else
escape_reason: This repo writes long docstrings that QUOTE the stub they replaced - 'THIS RAISED NotImplementedError(OQ-790) UNTIL 2026-09-01'. Those lines start with a warning sign or a back-tick, not with a comment marker, so the line scanner charged them as live stubs. The gate reported 32 stubs where 12 exist, and its PASS line ('32 OQ-cited stub(s) all open') overstated its own coverage by 167 per cent. It was invisible because over-reporting a guard's reach never turns anything red - and it became load-bearing the moment the parser above was fixed, because the three loudest prose matches are docstrings saying the question CLOSED, which would have arrived as three brand-new FALSE failures naming correct code.
prevention: Clause A now asks Python's own tokenizer where the string literals are and refuses to charge a NotImplementedError( that sits inside one, COLUMN-aware so a one-line raise with its message on the same line still counts - a line-scoped skip would have thrown away every real stub in the repository.
