title: G15 has been failing on 493 untranslated values beyond its baseline and nobody has acted; the baseline itself grandfathers 5,906
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g15_i18n_parity.py + g15_untranslated_baseline.txt; 07-frontend/src/i18n/locales/*.json
introduced_in: accumulated since 8e7a34fca (2026-09-11), the last time the baseline was re-pinned
escape_reason: THE GATE IS NOT BLIND AND THAT IS THE POINT -- it already asserts what a coordinating session twice claimed it did not. G15's own docstring states assertion 2: 'a value byte-identical to English in a non-English catalogue is a paste-in that was never translated'. Measured today it reports FAIL: 493 NEW value(s) pasted in English rather than translated, against a baseline of 5,906, with 5,770 still identical to English and 0 missing / 0 extra keys -- so KEY PARITY is perfect and VALUE translation is not, which is exactly the distinction the gate was built to draw. Two things let it pass unnoticed anyway. (1) NOBODY READ THE RED: this repo runs no CI (all seven workflows are .disabled), so a gate result exists only when a person runs the suite and reads the output, and G15 sits among ~51 failing gates where one more is invisible. (2) THE BASELINE IS A RATCHET OVER 5,906 GRANDFATHERED VALUES, last re-pinned 2026-09-11, so the gate can only ever report drift beyond a number that is itself most of the debt -- and when that drift arrived (493) it was still not acted on. Sample offenders are in assets and billing (de :: assets.exportCapacityKw, de :: billing.bill.field.post, de :: billing.print.tile.about), so not all of it is recent work. THIS IS THE THIRD RED-AND-UNREAD FINDING OF 2026-09-17/18, after DEF-SHL-5695 (the silent-timezone-fallback guard, red since 09-13 with five screens having reintroduced the defect) and DEF-RAT-5713 (sixteen rating tests red since 09-08). One a day is a pattern, not an accident.
prevention: Clear the 493 rather than re-pin the baseline -- re-pinning is how 5,906 got there. Then decide what the baseline is FOR: a ratchet that grandfathers a third of the catalogue reports drift and never debt, and a reader cannot tell a product that is 3% untranslated from one that is 60%. Measured for scale: per-locale identical-to-English runs 6.7% (id-ID) down to 0.7% (pt-BR), and only 75 of 18,325 keys are English in ALL ten languages -- so the debt is CONCENTRATED in hot spots, not spread, and a per-AREA report would name the screens that need work instead of one product-wide number. Separately and more durably: a red that only exists when somebody runs the suite by hand is not a check, and three findings in two days say so.

title: A lane ran pkill -f over a pattern that matches sibling lanes' command lines in the shared container
surface: the pagination lane's own shell, 2026-09-18 ~21:06 UTC: pkill -f config.settings.pgtest and pkill -f a pytest file list, run to free machine load

introduced_in: no commit - a shell command, which is why nothing in the repo can see it
escape_reason: NOTHING IN THIS REPO CAN CATCH IT. Every guard in laws 11 and 12 reads COMMITS - the file count, the hunks, the numstat, the register prefix. The lane had also just read CLAUDE.md law 11 in full, which is about git and says nothing about signals, so the rule it was breaking was one it had not been told.
prevention: Never pass pkill a pattern that is not unique to your own process, and prefer killing by the PID your own tooling reported. Two concrete facts from this occurrence: (a) the lane's own PostgreSQL run had ALREADY FINISHED one minute earlier, so the command could only have harmed others and could not have helped the lane at all; (b) the pattern matched the lane's own bash -c wrapper, so pkill killed the shell it was typed into and returned 144 with no output - meaning the lane could not even see what it had signalled. Evidence gathered afterwards: one sibling PostgreSQL benchmark was running across that moment and completed intact at 21:08 with its final stage present, which is the strongest single indication nothing was lost; one 0-byte output file from 20:52 is abandoned and cannot be attributed either way.

title: Django's 2.5 MB DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE default was the real import ceiling at ~25,000 rows, and no cap we wrote could move it
surface: An import file arrives as a JSON string field, so it is a request BODY. config/settings/base.py never set DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE, so Django's 2.5 MB default refused it before one line of application code ran. reported_by: the Product Owner in the beta, 2026-09-19
title: The Applied column on plan step 4 writes a value the billing engine never reads, and 'On an event' names an event that is stored nowhere
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/rating/PlanWizard.tsx RECURRENCES = [once, recurring, event] at :543, rendered as the APPLIED column of step 4's table — over 06-backend/apps/rating/models.py:1576 PlanChargeRule.recurrence = TextField(default='event'). S12 plan wizard step 4, every plan
found_in: the Product Owner in the beta, 2026-09-19, asking the question that found it: 'what does on event means here ? how do you decide the event?'
introduced_in: r5 #9 gave PlanChargeRule a recurrence column and the wizard a control for it. BR-RAT-730 (2026-08-28) then made R4's recurrence test read charges.charge_type AND charges.auto_apply — the CHARGE CODE's two columns, never the plan rule's — and nothing removed the plan-side control
escape_reason: THE COLUMN IS WRITTEN, VALIDATED, STORED, SERVED AND RENDERED, SO EVERY CHECK ALONG THAT PATH PASSES. It appears in PLAN_CHARGE_RULE_FIELDS (services.py:658), is validated against RECURRENCES (:1071), is written (:1406) and is served back to the screen (selectors.py:740) — a complete round trip with tests at each hop. What no test asks is whether apps/billing READS it, and it does not: grepped across every backend app, the only hits outside rating are two fixtures writing it and one comment. R4's four conjunctive conditions gate on the code's service, its customer classes, whether it rides a periodic bill (charge_type + auto_apply) and its amount. The plan rule's recurrence is in none of them. Hard-won law 2 in the direction G13 cannot see: not a prop nobody passes, but a value everybody passes and nobody consumes. AND THE PRODUCT ALREADY SAID SO IN ITS OWN WORDS ON A DIFFERENT SCREEN — the charge code wizard renders 'The event that raises this charge, the grace period before it does, and the cap on how many times it can be raised in one cycle are not stored...' — so one screen states the absence while another offers the control. Nobody compared them.
prevention: Assert the CONSUMER, not the round trip: a test that sets recurrence to each of the three values on one attached code and asserts the resulting bill lines DIFFER. It fails today for all three, which is the proof. More generally, a control whose value no engine reads is invisible to every gate here — when a field is added to a writable-field list, the same commit should name what reads it or state that nothing does yet.

title: The plan builder's SAVE read a different draft from the one the screen was drawing
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/rating/PlanWizard.tsx — the save mutation
found_in: an AI lane wiring DEF-RAT-5765's correction door, 2026-09-19
introduced_in: 8e7a34fca, 2026-09-11 (CR-085 step 1 lane 7) — the line 'const current = draft ?? emptyPlanDraft();' inside the save mutation
escape_reason: Two derivations of one value, 90 lines apart, and only the SCREEN's was ever asserted. The save mutation kept a private 'draft ?? emptyPlanDraft()' while the screen rendered 'draftFromPlan(plan)'. Until an operator touches a field 'draft' is null, so an open-and-save sent the EMPTY draft for a plan that has a name, a code and services. Every rendering test passed because the rendering was correct; no test asserted the REQUEST a save makes, which is the only place the two derivations differ. Found only by a request-asserting test written for another defect: the correction door reached POST /plans/{id}/corrections in the DOM harness and took PATCH /plans/{id} in the browser, and the difference was which draft the mutation read.
prevention: Name the derivation once and call it from both places — planDraftFor(plan, draft, entryIntent). The durable check is a test that asserts the REQUEST a commit makes rather than the markup it renders; DEF-RAT-5765's own row already demanded one and it is what caught this. Tests that assert rendering cannot see a second copy of a value that renders identically.

title: Two lanes write the same unprefixed filename in the shared scratchpad and the second silently wins
surface: /tmp/claude-0/<session>/scratchpad - every lane in a session shares one directory. This lane wrote decision_row.md and msg1.txt there; a sibling wrote its own decision_row.md and msg1.txt over them. Found only because the file was re-read before use.
found_in: DEF-NOT-5750 lane, 2026-09-19, re-reading its own draft before splicing it into the decision log
introduced_in: no commit - it is the shape of the environment, and law 11 names the same mechanism one directory over (a shared index, a shared working tree) without naming this one
escape_reason: Law 11 is written about the shared GIT TREE - the index, the working tree, a register's bytes - and every check it prescribes reads commits. A scratchpad file is in none of them: it is untracked, outside the repo, and no gate, no numstat and no git status can see it change. A lane that drafts a governance row, works for twenty minutes and then splices it in is splicing whatever the last writer left, and the row reads as a perfectly good row.
prevention: Give each lane its own SUBDIRECTORY of the scratchpad - scratchpad/<defect-or-cr-id>/ - and never write an unprefixed name at its root. It costs one mkdir. The general form is law 11's own: before writing to any shared surface, ask who else writes there, and re-read what you wrote immediately before you use it.

title: The live billing path does not receive the rate schedule's base-charge binding, so a two-base-code catalogue still refuses
surface: backend
found_in: branch
introduced_in: CR-120-BRC06
escape_reason: Nothing asked the question. BR-RAT-1017 was built into the R1-R7 chain (resolution.resolve_base_charge) and into rating's live read (selectors.base_charge_from_charge_code gained a named_code parameter), but the caller that actually bills -- billing/gather._base_charge_code_for -- calls that seam by name with three keyword arguments and passes no binding. No gate compares what the ruled chain honours against what the live path honours, and the two agree on every tenant that exists today, so a check would have reported green.
prevention: A test that asserts the two paths resolve the SAME code for a schedule that NAMES one, run on the configuration where they can differ -- two is_base codes for one service, both reaching one account. Today the chain returns the named code and the live path refuses the bill (DEF-468), so the binding unblocks that catalogue on the chain and not yet on the path that bills. It cannot produce a WRONG figure: the live path refuses rather than choosing, which is visible. The fix is four lines in billing/gather to pass the version's bound code down, and it was not taken here because that file belongs to another module and another lane.

title: BR-RAT-1017 was taken by hand without checking and pushed in 45 citations on a money path; the number was already a sibling's rule minted the day before
surface: governance
found_in: branch
introduced_in: CR-120-BRC06
escape_reason: BR- has no allocator. CLAUDE.md says so in as many words -- allocate.py covers defect, gate, oq, cr and version and nothing else -- and 14-id-reservations.md's own account-types row, written by THIS branch two days earlier, records the same hazard for BR-CUS-1079. The number was read as max+1 from a grep of this checkout that was run AFTER the code was written and cited, not before. Nothing downstream can see it: a duplicate BR- id reads as a rule citation, G17 fails a duplicate CR number and has never asked the same of a business rule, and both rules are real, so every id-existence check passes over it. It was found only because the business-rule ROW was being written last and the grep for the watermark returned 48 hits at 1017 -- all of them this lane's own, which is what made it look free.
prevention: Verify a BR- number across every refs/remotes/origin ref BEFORE citing it in the first file, not before writing the register row. git grep -lE 'BR-RAT-<n>' over every ref answers it in one command and the whole 55-ref scan takes under two minutes. Then STEP CLEAR OF THE FRONTIER rather than taking max+1: BR-RAT-1017 was minted 2026-09-18, one day before, so max+1 is exactly where a sibling lands. This renumber took BR-RAT-1025 with 1018-1022 left free, which is the practice 14-id-reservations.md already records for BR-CUS-1070 and BR-CUS-1075 and the reasoning it gives for both.

reported_by: an AI lane (money-path review of billable_charge_codes against BR-RAT-117's words)
title: A CHARGE CODE A PLAN NAMES RIDES EVERY ORDINARY BILL WHATEVER ITS OWN TRIGGER — a $250.00 tamper fee billed twelve times a year, $955.00 a month across ten units
surface: 06-backend/apps/rating/selectors.py :: billable_charge_codes (route 2, the plan_charge_rules union arm) -> apps/billing/gather.py :: _charge_fees_for
introduced_in: DEF-561's fix, 2026-08-22 — the route that gave plan_charge_rules its first billing reader
escape_reason: THE SUITE ASSERTED THE DEFECT AS CORRECT. test_br_rat_117_auto_apply_charges.py::test_a_plan_named_code_lands_even_without_the_flags created a one_time code, had a plan name it, and asserted it BILLS -- 'the route DEF-561 found dead: the plan names it, so it bills.' So DEF-561's over-implementation was written down as an expectation and every green run confirmed it. Nothing else could see it either: R4's rides_a_periodic_bill (BR-RAT-730, 2026-08-28) fixed the identical fault in resolution.resolve_charge_codes and nobody asked whether the OTHER reader over the same table had it too -- the two narrowings are deliberately independent so the pricing shadow can compare them, and there was no test asserting they AGREE. The class and service gates could not narrow these codes because all five are account-level and class-unrestricted, and the per-size refusal could not fire because none carries a charge_code_amounts row. A query-count check would also have passed: the old path was a single statement returning everything, so the cost lived in ROWS and never in STATEMENTS.

More generally: when a rule is fixed in one reader, grep for the OTHER readers of the same columns -- BR-RAT-730 fixed R4 on 2026-08-28 and this reader sat wrong for 28 days beside it.

title: G105's furniture check reads ONE spelling of a search box and matches the drawing's phrases against hand-WRAPPED text, so it reported two screens for controls that are on them
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g105_screen_matches_its_drawing.py — list_call_sites() tested `search= in text`, and furniture() tested `no footer in body` over raw wrapped prose. Findings: CWP-041 search (false since DEF-CWP-4879 moved that box out of the table on 2026-09-11) and CWP-037 footer (false because 08-screen-layouts.md wraps between 'no' and 'footer')
found_in: the DEF-CWP-5747 lane, 2026-09-19, reading a gate that went red on its own change rather than scrolling past it; both findings DATED by running furniture() at the branch tip
introduced_in: G105 as written; the CWP-041 half became false on 2026-09-11 when DEF-CWP-4879 moved that screen's search box above the width split
escape_reason: The gate was not silent — it was WRONG, and a wrong finding on a branch that expects ~50 pre-existing failures is indistinguishable from a known one. Nothing re-asks whether a gate's PROXY still means what it meant: 'search=' was the whole truth the day it was written and stopped being so the day a screen drew its own box, and a substring test cannot see a phrase its own source file wrapped. Hard-won law 7's 'reporting zero over a scope it silently excludes', in the other direction.
prevention: SEARCH_IDIOMS names the three spellings and the self-test proves each is SEEN and that a file with none of them is still reported; the phrase tests run over unwrapped text and the self-test proves a wrapped 'no footer' is read AND that unwrapping did not turn the footer check off. A widening that only ever answers yes is a check that cannot fail.

title: The charge code wizard's three steps carry 47 strings over B14 rule 33's caps, and five blocks are the wrong KIND of text entirely
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/rating/ChargeCodeWizard.tsx (S12 / CHG-02, steps 1-3) and the eleven locale catalogues - measured at the call site against the pinned tip: 145 strings rendered, 47 over the per-sentence cap, longest 33 words, 24 of two or more sentences
found_in: 2026-09-19, Product Owner walking CHG-02 in the beta: 'too much text on step 1', 'step 2 too much text', 'step 3 too much text'
introduced_in: CR-013 P2 and CR-087, which built the screen before B14 rule 33 was ratified (2026-08-30) and were never re-measured against it
escape_reason: G33 enforces rule 33's cap for REFUSAL copy ONLY - B14's own status column reads 'NOT ENFORCED for these five kinds', so a label, a fact, an instruction, a consequence and the ZERO-word RATIONALE kind have no gate at all. And the obvious instrument under-reports: a scan of t() call sites cannot see keys passed as PROPS (StepHead's headingKey/hintKey) or keys written as bare literals in a ternary - eleven strings, nine over cap, including a 19-word hint directly under STEP 2 OF 3. tsc, 51 test files and every gate were green over all of them; the browser found them (law 6)
prevention: A gate over the four numbered kinds is buildable exactly as G33's baseline works - count words per sentence per key, bucket by key suffix, baseline what exists and let it only shrink. Until then the walkthrough added with this fix reads all three steps as RENDERED text. And any copy-measuring script must take every quoted catalogue key in the file, never only t() call sites: a narrow extractor reports zero over a scope it silently excludes (law 7)

title: A lane freed memory with pkill -f on a shared box and may have killed sibling lanes' dev servers and walkthroughs
surface: Not a repo file - the container. 'pkill -9 -f server.mjs', 'pkill -9 -f vitest' and 'pkill -9 -f manage.py runserver', run to recover from two OOM kills (exit 137), match EVERY lane's processes and not just the running lane's. Afterwards the box showed three server.mjs and a sibling's scratchpad walkthrough (lane-discount-rl0uzt/walk.mjs) running
found_in: 2026-09-19, self-reported by the lane that did it, on noticing other lanes' process names in ps output afterwards
introduced_in: This lane, recovering from OOM after running a vitest suite, a vite build, a browser walkthrough, a Django server and two git worktrees at once on a 16 GB box
escape_reason: CLAUDE.md law 11 forbids the commands that make the shared WORKING TREE momentarily not-what-it-was - git stash, git checkout --, git reset --hard - and names them individually. It says nothing about the shared PROCESS TABLE, which is the same hazard one layer out: a pattern kill is indistinguishable from a targeted one in the command, and the blast radius is invisible until afterwards. Nothing in the repo can see it and no gate ever will
prevention: Kill by PID, from the pid recorded when this lane started the process, never by pattern - and prefer letting a background job time out over reaping anything. The general rule is law 11's seventh clause generalised beyond git: ANY command whose effect is scoped by a pattern rather than by ownership will hit siblings in a shared container, whatever it was wanted for. Also: run one heavy job at a time here; two OOM kills (tsc and vitest, both exit 137) are what prompted the reach for pkill in the first place

title: DIS-02 discount wizard: 1,096 words of on-screen copy, 75 strings over B14 rule 33's caps

title: DIS-02 shows stored precision: value 1.500000, floor 0.000000, budget cap 2383.000000, review row '1.500000 as typed'
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/rating/DiscountWizard.tsx - its private MoneyField, the value box, reviewValueLine and valueReadBack

escape_reason: DEF-2361 is this same defect and this same PO complaint ('decimal', 2026-09-03) on the charge-code and rate-schedule wizards. title: B14 rule 33's prose says TWELVE words for instruction and consequence; its own status table says six per sentence
surface: 04-docs/02-decisions/14-ui-conventions.md 'WHY THE VARIATION' + 10-scripts/i18n_fanin.py docstring
introduced_in: 2026-08-30, the day the PO tightened the cap from twelve to six
escape_reason: The cap was tightened in the same breath as rule 33 was minted. title: A push script's global sed of DEF-PAY-nnnn over apps/payments/api.py rewrote an UNRELATED, correct citation: DEF-PAY-5128 became DEF-PAY-5875

prevention: Never sed an ID FAMILY over a shared file. Stamp a placeholder unique to the lane (e.g. __MY_DEFECT_ID__) at authoring time and substitute THAT at push time, so the pattern cannot match anybody else's citation; then diff the file against the tip and read every hunk before pushing.

title: Seven lanes sat blocked for up to ten hours on background jobs that had hung, and nothing anywhere noticed
surface: 10-scripts walkthrough and typecheck runners, and the lane dispatch pattern
introduced_in: unknown
escape_reason: Nothing in this repo puts a deadline on a background job or watches one. A lane that starts a tsc run, a pytest run or a Playwright walk in the background and then waits for it has no upper bound on that wait, and the wait is indistinguishable from slow work: the process is alive, it holds its memory, and the lane is politely blocked. No gate reads process age or elapsed wall clock, and the lane's own report never arrives -- so the silence that would be the signal is exactly what the hang produces. Measured 2026-09-19: 45 orphaned processes holding 2932MB, including two vite servers alive 7.5h, eight Django dev servers, and a 13-process headless Chromium tree alive 4.2h from a walk that never ended. Seven agents were blocked behind them, two for nine and ten hours, and all seven reported complete within one minute of those processes being terminated. The same leak caused a real failure earlier that day, reported by the fee-posting lane as the container running out of memory and killing several test runs mid-flight.
prevention: Put a hard timeout on every background job a lane waits on -- timeout(1) around tsc, pytest and node walkthroughs -- and an explicit browser.close() in a finally block in every .mjs walkthrough in 10-scripts. Then add a check that fails when any node, python or chrome process owned by this checkout is older than a stated bound, so a hang is reported as a hang instead of as a slow lane.

title: A wait loop that polls for a process by name matches ITSELF, so it can never exit - nine sat for 82 minutes
surface: lane-authored Bash waiters: until ! pgrep -f <script-name>; do sleep N; done
found_in: PO screenshot of the background-task list, 2026-09-19: nine Bash tasks named Wait for the walk... running 1h01m to 1h22m
introduced_in: a lane backgrounding a browser walk and polling for its exit by script name
escape_reason: pgrep -f searches the FULL command line, and the waiter's own command line contains the name it is searching for - so the loop matches itself and its siblings and can never reach zero. The walk had finished over an hour earlier. Nothing times out a background Bash task and nothing reports one that outlives its subject, so the only reason it was found is that a human looked at the task list. This is the second occurrence today: DEF-GOV-5877 was seven lanes blocked up to ten hours on hung jobs.
prevention: A wait must be anchored to something that cannot match the waiter: a PID captured at launch (kill -0), a sentinel file the job writes on exit, or pgrep --exact on the interpreter. Never poll by a name string that appears in the polling command. Confirmed live while clearing it - the reaping command itself contained the same literal and killed its own shell on the first attempt, exit 144.

title: The move-out shortfall decision can never be recorded: POST /settle-shortfall takes no final-bill figure while GET /close-impact does, so it refuses no_shortfall on every account

found_in: walking the move-out wizard in a real browser on AC-2026-00031, 2026-09-19, then probing the two endpoints directly with a signed-in session

escape_reason: Measured on one account in one sitting. GET /close-impact?final_bill=789.42&as_of=2026-09-30 answers landing short with gaps [], and the wizard draws Short by $1,591.85. GET /close-impact with no figure answers landing null, gaps [final_bill_not_stated] — and that is what the POST recomputes, because its body is {path} and nothing else. So POST /accounts/{id}/settle-shortfall returns 409 BIZ-STATE, message_key customers.move_out.no_shortfall, params {landing: null, gaps: [final_bill_not_stated]}, br_ref BR-CUS-082, on every account and every path. MoveOutWizard.tsx's own docstring describes this exact state as the OLD behaviour that the preview fixed — hard-won law 1, a comment claiming a guarantee is not the guarantee. escape_reason: The head renders '10 tabs · Move-outs' where four blueprint frames draw a third fragment ('1 still open' p117 and p131, '3 open' p48, '4 open, 1 past due' p41). title: resolution_shadow._multiplier_for asks the seam for the LATEST billable head, not the factor on the row being priced
surface: 06-backend/apps/billing/resolution_shadow.py _multiplier_for and _chain_inputs, against apps/metering/selectors.py billing_multiplier_for and billing_reads_for_unit's multiplier key
found_in: reading the seam's own docstring while building DEF-CUS-5931's provisional-read path (2026-09-20)
introduced_in: BR-MET-500 (DEF-1812, 2026-08-27) published the factor on the reading row and the chain adapter went on resolving it by name
escape_reason: billing_reads_for_unit's own docstring already says the row's key IS the authoritative answer and that billing_multiplier_for is for a caller with no row in hand — and _chain_inputs HAS the row in hand, in the same loop. Nothing compares a docstring with its caller, and the two answers are the same number on every account whose latest billable head is the read being priced, which is nearly all of them: the difference appears only on a CLOSED period, where the seam answers from a LATER read. So a wrong factor here is invisible on every test this repo has and would land on a back-bill or a correction.
prevention: Prefer ServiceReading.multiplier on EVERY row and fall back to the seam only where the row carries none, which is what billing_reads_for_unit's docstring already prescribes. Not taken in DEF-CUS-5931's commit because it moves the factor on live bills and that is money: the commit takes the row's factor only where the row is PROVISIONAL and the seam CANNOT answer, which can unblock and can never change an existing figure. And the general form: when a seam's docstring names the caller it is for, a gate can check that the other callers do not use it.

title: the commit message of 9e7650a8a names v2.314.1 and the commit ships 2.314.3
surface: git commit 9e7650a8a on claude/kind-wozniak-rl0uzt; 07-frontend/package.json, package-lock.json, 06-backend/pyproject.toml and CHANGELOG.md all read 2.314.3

introduced_in: the push helper re-allocated the version from the pinned tip at push time, three tips after the message was written
escape_reason: The version is allocated from the REMOTE and the commit message is written by hand, and on a branch taking a commit every few minutes those two facts are minutes apart: this lane was refused four times by the moved-path guard and each retry re-allocated the version (2.313.3 to 2.314.1 to 2.314.3) while the message kept the number it was drafted with. surface: 06-backend/apps/customers/selectors.primary_contact_name (and _primary_contact_names), reached by selectors.account_row 'name' (the Accounts list, beside its own 'customer_no'), selectors.active_account_for_unit 'customer_name' -> assets.selectors.asset_detail billing_chain.account (S50's header) and metering.selectors.unit_list_dict 'occupant' (S15's Occupant column), and selectors 'payer_name'

introduced_in: BR-CUS-1030, d1066469e, 2026-09-01 — the ruling that made a transfer reassign the CUSTOMER of an existing account. Before it a transfer opened a NEW account with its own contact, so no surface could disagree with itself; reassignment moved customer_accounts and left contacts where it was, and nothing re-read the name-bearing consumers.
escape_reason: THE NAME AND THE CUSTOMER COME FROM TWO DIFFERENT TABLES AND ONLY ONE OF THEM MOVES. reassign_account rewrites customer_accounts, correctly and by design; every display name in the product is primary_contact_name, which reads contacts.full_name, which a sale does not touch. So selectors.account_row serves customer_no (the buyer's, right) and name (the seller's, stale) on ONE ROW - one product giving two answers to 'whose account is this'. No check can see it: 42 call sites read the contact name and every one of them returns a real string, so there is no null, no exception and no absence for a gate to catch, and hard rule 8's closing lesson applies exactly - an absence is invisible to every check this repo has, and a WRONG-BUT-PRESENT value is worse. The blueprint's own step-5 note covers CONTACT DETAILS - 'the bill email is still the seller's, and autopay is still running on the seller's bank instruction' - and says nothing about the displayed NAME, so the drawing neither sanctions nor forbids this; it was simply never asked.
fixed_commit: v2.319.5 a23fb87f7 (the three name surfaces; B2 r9 #1's contacts re-home is NOT done and is the Eng-Lead disposition)
prevention: FILED, NOT DECIDED - the disposition is a ruling and not a lane's to pick. Three readings exist and they differ in what a clerk sees: (a) the sale writes a new primary contact for the buyer, which changes where the bill goes and collides with the drawn note; (b) the name-bearing selectors read the LINKED CUSTOMER's display_name and fall back to the contact, which fixes every surface at once and leaves the bill email alone; (c) the drawing is right and the seller's name is meant to persist, in which case four screens need a word saying whose name it is. Option (b) is the one that costs nothing a clerk can see and it is still a ruling. What is NOT in doubt is the measurement: one row, two parties, today.

title: SELLING A PROPERTY TO THE PERSON WHO ALREADY OWNS IT IS NOT REFUSED — the guard cannot fire for a phone-identified buyer, and the sale mints them a SECOND customer number and deletes the first one's link
surface: 06-backend/apps/customers/transfers.py reassign_account, the REFUSAL_BUYER_IS_THE_SELLER guard (it compares link_customer's returned id against transfer.customer_id); reached by POST /transfers/commit and by the wizard's step 2, whose own help text reads 'A phone identifies a person here'
found_in: the PO's property-sale end-to-end walk, 2026-09-20 — 06-backend/tests/test_transfer_scenarios.py row RF2 on real PostgreSQL: the buyer block carries the seller's own name and the seller's own phone, and the sale COMMITS with second_customer_created true and no refusal raised
introduced_in: CR-058 task 14, d1066469e, 2026-09-01 — the guard was written with the reassignment. It has never been able to fire on a phone: identity_match.REUSE_ID_FIELDS has always been (ssn, driving_licence) for a person and (tax_id) for a company, and reuse_candidate says so in as many words — 'A PHONE CANNOT REUSE, THOUGH IT CAN CREATE.'
escape_reason: A GUARD IN PRODUCTION CODE THAT IS STRUCTURALLY INCAPABLE OF FIRING - hard-won law 7's shape, outside a test. The guard asks whether the RESOLVED customer id equals the seller's, and link_customer can only return the seller when the buyer presents a GOVERNMENT-GRADE identifier that matches: an SSN, a driving licence or a Tax ID. A phone creates a new customer instead, by deliberate design and for a good reason that is written down - 'minting a spare row on a shared household line costs a merge; reusing one hands a stranger an existing customer's file'. So with the one identifier the step's own help text offers, the ids always differ, the guard always passes, the seller's customer_accounts link is deleted and the account is handed to a second number for the same person - whose history hangs off the number just unlinked. Nothing catches it: the refusal constant exists, is exported and is cited, which is exactly what transfers.py's own docstring warns about in another place - 'an unused refusal constant reads as a check that exists'. The COMPANY path is measured GREEN in the same suite (SL2 matches on its Tax ID and mints no second number), so this is not the reuse rule being broken; it is a guard that depends on reuse standing over a door that does not require it.
prevention: Do not compare resolved ids - ask the question the guard is for, before resolving anything: does the buyer's evidence match the SELLER's own stored identity, on any fact including the phone? identity_match already computes that comparison for the recognise path. Then RF2 in tests/test_transfer_scenarios.py turns green and stays a guard. The general habit: a guard whose condition is computed by somebody else's matching rule inherits that rule's limits, so write the case that MUST be refused as a test in the same commit as the guard - this one has existed for nineteen days and no case ever asked it to fire.

title: THE TRANSFERS TAB'S SALE-DATE SORT ORDERS BY from_account__closed_at, WHICH BR-CUS-1030 MADE NULL ON EVERY LIVE ROW
surface: 06-backend/apps/customers/transfer_reads.py SORTS['out_date'] = ('from_account__closed_at','id') and SORTS['in_date'] = ('to_account__opened_at','id'); consumed by 07-frontend/src/features/customers/TransfersTab.tsx (S89, the Sale date column)

A date header that reorders rows by a column that is NULL everywhere falls through to the id tiebreak and looks to a clerk like an arbitrary shuffle, which reports as 'the sort is odd' rather than as a fault.

The general form: when a ruling deletes a lifecycle event, grep for every ORDER BY, filter and index that named it - a sort term is a consumer of a fact exactly as a screen line is (DEF-CUS-3653).

title: THE TRANSFERS SEARCH PROMPT OFFERS 'EITHER ADDRESS' ON A FLOW WITH ONE ADDRESS, AND DOES NOT OFFER THE REFERENCE IT CAN ACTUALLY MATCH
surface: 06-backend/apps/customers/transfer_reads.py SEARCH_HINT = 'Customer, account #, or either address…' and the catalogue key customers.transfers.list.searchPlaceholder that mirrors it; drawn on p131 as 'Search by reference, account, address or name'

title: A RENUMBER HELPER REPLACED IDS SEQUENTIALLY AND CASCADED - SIX DEFECT ROWS ARE PUBLISHED CARRYING TWO IDS, THREE TIMES EACH, AND FIFTEEN CITATIONS POINT AT THEM
surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv rows DEF-CUS-5979 and DEF-CUS-5980, three rows each, published in 39174783a; cited from 07-frontend/src/features/customers/TransfersTab.tsx, its test and the 2026-09-20 decision-log section
escape_reason: THE HELPER CHECKED THE RIGHT THING AND NOT ENOUGH THINGS. Sibling lanes took this lane's defect ids twice while it worked, so its re-derivation helper was taught to renumber on every pass. It replaced old with new ONE PAIR AT A TIME - 5973 to 5975, then 5975 to 5977 - so each rule rewrote the id the previous rule had just created, and the six collapsed pairwise onto the last two. Every check the helper ran PASSED and every one was true: the new ids were free at the tip, both registers were byte-identical prefixes of the tip, the numstat showed additions only, and every hunk in the commit was this lane's. NOT ONE OF THEM ASKS WHETHER SIX IDS ARE STILL SIX. It was found by law 11's last step done literally - reading each marker back out of HEAD, where one cited id returned a count of zero.
prevention: ⚠ THE REPAIR IS PREPARED AND NOT APPLIED. Correcting an id means the old line VANISHES from the register, which push_register_guard.py refuses by design - its allowance is per-ID and the id is the field that must change. The repair is a splice that leaves the file the same length with exactly six lines differing and all 3,482 other rows byte-identical, and it was proved that way; it needs ALLOW_REGISTER_DELETIONS=1, which this lane could not run. A lane that can should rewrite the six id fields to a fresh distinct block and re-point the fifteen citations BY READING WHAT EACH SENTENCE IS ABOUT, because the cascade destroyed the mapping and no mechanical rule recovers it. THE DURABLE FIX is in how a renumber is written: one single-pass mapping (a regex with a callback), never a loop of sequential replaces whose later rules can match its own earlier output - and assert the INVARIANT, distinct ids == rows, rather than checking the inputs. G17 fails a duplicate id and would have caught this; the lane pushed before running it.

title: days served are clamped to the cycle length, so an account with a 43-day unbilled closing window is charged ONE month's base charge
surface: 06-backend/apps/billing/gather.py _service_days - 'return max(0, min(cycle_days, days))'; every bill type that reaches it, measured on the final bill
found_in: measuring the beta before and after the final-bill proration, 2026-09-20 - read off brazosbend accounts AC-2026-00001, 00002 and 00003
introduced_in: PRE-EXISTING and untouched by the proration commit - the clamp is older than it and the figure is identical on both sides
escape_reason: B4.3's factor is service_days / cycle_days and the clamp holds it at 1, so a window LONGER than one cycle is billed as exactly one cycle. Measured on the beta 2026-09-20: every brazosbend account's closing window is 1 Aug to 12 Sep - 43 days against a 31-day cycle - and each is charged 2.00 electric and .00 water base, one month's worth, for six weeks of service. Nothing could catch it because there is no signed rule to check it against: B4.3 is written for a PARTIAL period and says nothing about an over-long one, and every fixture in the repo bills a window inside one cycle. It is not a regression and may well be deliberate (a bill covering more than a cycle is arguably a back-bill's job, BR-BIL-018, which DOES weight day by day across segments). It is filed because it is a real money figure on live data that no document states either way.
prevention: Put the question to the PO with the beta's own figure rather than reading a rule that does not cover the case: does a final bill covering 43 days carry one base charge or one-point-four? If the answer is the second, the shape already exists - backbill.price_day_weighted makes one pricing call per proration factor for exactly this reason (OQ-155) - and the final bill would use it rather than a second clamp. Either way, _service_days's docstring should say what the clamp is FOR; today it explains the max(0, ...) half and not the min(cycle_days, ...) half.

title: a push replaced another lane's register row with one carrying the SAME id, and push_register_guard passed because the id survived
surface: 10-scripts/push_register_guard.py vanished/lost_lines - the id-survives allowance; 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv row DEF-GOV-5985; commit 3a8692a42 on claude/kind-wozniak-rl0uzt
found_in: the post-push subtraction check on commit 3a8692a42, 2026-09-20 - git diff --numstat read AS ARITHMETIC showed '4 insertions, 1 deletion' on an append-only register
introduced_in: the guard's deliberate allowance, which predates this - the collision itself is 2026-09-20
escape_reason: Two lanes allocated DEF-GOV-5985 minutes apart, both correctly: allocate.py asks the REMOTE, and the transfer-record lane's row was not pushed yet when this lane read the maximum. That is law 11's known collision and it is not the finding. The finding is that push_register_guard.py did NOT refuse the push. Its rule is that a row's BYTES may change as long as the ID SURVIVES - deliberately, so that close_defect.py marking a row fixed is not read as a deletion - and here the id survived because the replacing row carried the same id. So the one guard standing between a shared register and a silent revert is blind to exactly the collision the allocator warns about. Every other check in law 11 passed too: the file count was right, this lane's own rows WERE present, and git show's hunks were all its own. The numstat's single deletion is the only thing that showed, and only because it was read as arithmetic rather than glanced at.
prevention: Restored in the next commit - the transfer-record lane's row is back byte-for-byte from e0eab74ca and this lane's row is renumbered DEF-GOV-5989. The guard needs one more rule beside the id-survives allowance: if a row's id survives but its SECOND field (the reporter) or its date changes, that is not an edit to a row, it is a different row wearing its number - refuse and name both. That is cheap, it cannot fire on close_defect.py (which rewrites status and fixed_commit, never the reporter), and it turns the collision the allocator can only warn about into one the push refuses.

title: M4 asserted a 2-decimal SCREEN string against a 4-decimal wire payload, so the row would have stayed red over the right number
surface: 06-backend/tests/test_move_in_nineteen_scenarios.py scenario M4, move_record.still_to_collect
found_in: fixing DEF-CUS-5909, 2026-09-20 - the arithmetic went right and the row stayed red on the format alone
introduced_in: the suite's own landing 2026-09-19 - written against blueprint p075's drawn $0.00, which is a SCREEN figure
escape_reason: Money travels this API as a string at FOUR decimals and the screen renders two - hard rule 2 (round only at finalization/display), BR-TEN-080 (exactly 2 dp on screen) and components/MoneyCell.formatMoney, which trims 8.2985 to $8.30 for that reason. title: The move record prints money straight from the payload, so a clerk reads 125.0000 where the rule says two decimals
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/customers/MoveRecordPage.tsx - money_taken required, taken and still_to_collect render the raw value
found_in: fixing DEF-CUS-5909, 2026-09-20 - the served figure is correct and the screen does not round it

escape_reason: Hard rule 2 and BR-TEN-080 both say exactly two decimals on screen, and components/MoneyCell.formatMoney exists to do it - it pads 148.6 to $148.60 and trims 8.2985 to $8.30. title: A number-series catalogue count has been RED for four days: the test says 29 and core/numbering.py holds 30
surface: 06-backend/tests/test_cr039_wd_transfer_and_case_numbers.py::test_both_the_transfer_and_the_disconnect_series_are_catalogued, the line 'assert len(catalogued) == 29'; the catalogue itself is 06-backend/core/numbering.py SERIES_CATALOG / KNOWN_SERIES
found_in: the transfer backend lane running the five transfer suites on real PostgreSQL before touching them, 2026-09-20: 1 failed, 82 passed. AssertionError: assert 30 == 29. KNOWN_SERIES holds 30 names; the test pins 29.
introduced_in: fe08a6c3c, 2026-09-16, DEF-MET-5446 — that commit added the 30th series (interruption_report) to core/numbering.py and did not move the count the test pins. The test file has not been touched since c7485bebc, 2026-09-08.
escape_reason: NOBODY READ A FAILURE THEY DID NOT CAUSE. The assertion is deliberately a canary — its own comment says 'this count is here only so a fifth row cannot arrive unnoticed' — so it did exactly what it was written to do, four days ago, and then sat red while lanes ran the customers suites past it. CLAUDE.md hard-won law 7's first shape, verbatim: 'PROVED RED, THEN NEVER READ ... a guard is a claim only while somebody reads its output.' It was dated with git log -S rather than called pre-existing, which is the habit DEF-CWP-4187 added.
prevention: The catalogue gained a row and four sibling assertions did not move; the canary names all of them in its own failure message. Whoever adds a series updates the count in the same commit, which is what the message asks for. The general habit is the one that found it: before pushing, read every red line in the suite and ask WAS THIS RED BEFORE I STARTED, and answer it with git log -S rather than from memory.

title: RF2 declares that the occupant is NOT the buyer, and in RF2 the buyer's name IS the seller's name — the row asserts a distinction it removed
surface: 06-backend/tests/test_transfer_scenarios.py row RF2: steps=Steps(buyer={display_name: SELLER_NAME ...}) against _refused()'s assets_seen(names_buyer=False) and occupancy_seen(names_buyer=False)
found_in: the transfer backend lane, 2026-09-20, on real PostgreSQL. RF2 is red on exactly two checks BOTH BEFORE AND AFTER the contacts-seam fix, byte-identical in the two reports: 'assets_and_account: names_the_buyer: want False, saw True' and 'occupancy_at_unit: occupant_names_the_buyer: want False, saw True'.
introduced_in: the suite itself, 2026-09-20, in the commit that wrote the twenty-five rows. RF2 is the row where the buyer and the seller are THE SAME PERSON, so it passes SELLER_NAME as the buyer's display_name — and the observation computes names_the_buyer as (occupant == buyer_name) and names_the_seller as (occupant == SELLER_NAME), which on this one row are the same comparison.
escape_reason: A CHECK THAT IS INCAPABLE OF PASSING — hard-won law 7's third shape, in a test rather than in a product. On every other row the two keys are genuinely different questions; on RF2 they are one, and the row declares them opposite, so no product state can satisfy it. It hid because RF2 had five other red checks in front of it: the sale COMMITTED instead of being refused, so a reader attributed the pair to the missing refusal. Fixing the refusal (DEF-CUS-5972) left them standing, which is what exposed them.
prevention: Do not weaken the row — the suite's own instruction. Either give RF2's buyer a display_name that differs from the seller's while keeping the seller's identifier (which is the realistic clerk case: the same person, typed slightly differently), or declare those two keys Silent on this row with the reason written out. The general habit: when a row's fixture makes two observed keys the same expression, the row cannot assert them apart, and only running it once green everywhere else reveals that.

title: PR2 sells a unit with NO METER and asserts that every asset names the buyer — with no assets the check can never be true
surface: 06-backend/tests/test_transfer_scenarios.py row PR2 against assets_seen()'s names_the_buyer, observed as bool(customers_named) and all(...); the observation already carries vacuously_true_because_there_are_no_assets and the declaration does not read it
found_in: the transfer backend lane, 2026-09-20, on real PostgreSQL. PR2 is red on 'assets_and_account: names_the_buyer: want True, saw False' BOTH BEFORE AND AFTER the contacts-seam fix, byte-identical in the two reports, while PR2's occupancy half went green with that fix.
introduced_in: the suite itself, 2026-09-20. PR2 is the row whose whole point is a unit with nothing on it, and it inherits _ordinary's assets declaration, where names_the_buyer is guarded by bool(customers_named) — an empty list is False, so the key is False whatever the product does.
escape_reason: A CHECK INCAPABLE OF PASSING, and it hid behind a real one. Until the contacts seam was fixed this row was red for the same reason seventeen others were, so the failure read as the known defect; the observation's own vacuously_true_because_there_are_no_assets key exists precisely because somebody saw this coming and no declaration consults it. Hard-won law 7's second habit — ask what would make this check pass WRONGLY — has a mirror this repo meets less often: ask what would make it FAIL wrongly.
prevention: PR2 should declare names_the_buyer through the vacuous key the observation already computes, or declare it Silent with the reason. The general shape: a dimension written for the ordinary case needs its own answer for the EMPTY case, and a zero-length collection is where a universal quantifier and an existential one stop agreeing.

title: A clerk can verify and reject a service-request document but cannot open one — three screens, one live download route, no caller
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/customers/ServiceRequestDetailPage.tsx DocumentsTab (Verify + Reject row actions, no Open) and 07-frontend/src/features/customers/moveInRequestBlocks.tsx RequestDocuments (file name, what it proves, state — zero clickable controls), over GET /service-requests/{id}/documents/{docId}/download, live since 2026-09-19
escape_reason: Nothing in this repository asks whether a live endpoint has a caller. G13 asks the opposite question — whether a component's prop is passed — so a screen that simply never offers a control is invisible to it, and G32 only asks whether a refusal RESOLVES, not whether an absence is justified. Each of the three surfaces was built by its own wave, each tested its own screen at its own address, and the question 'can a clerk read the file this row is about' belonged to nobody. The detail tab makes it visible: it offers Verify and Reject on a document it gives no way to read. The capture step carried a written reason for the absence — p078 draws the file as text, and the dev store mints file:// URLs a browser cannot follow — which was true when written and outlived the wrapper's absence.
prevention: components/documents/openStoredDocument.ts is the wrapper all three were missing: it takes the host's own download path, checks the URL scheme and refuses an unfollowable link BY NAME so the control is never silently dead. ServiceRequestCapturePage now passes onOpen and DocumentTable draws Open the file over file_present rows only. The two surfaces above are other lanes' files; DocumentCapture.dom.test.tsx records which hosts import the kit and goes RED naming the file the day one more adopts it, so the adoption is somebody's rather than nobody's.

title: TWO OF THE FIVE CUT REASONS CAN NEVER COMMIT — the screen sends 'tampering' and 'abandoned', the server and a CHECK constraint require 'tampering_or_theft' and 'premises_abandoned'
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/customers/transferDisconnectShared.tsx CUT_REASONS (the five buttons on the disconnect wizard's step 1) against 06-backend/apps/customers/disconnects.py CUT_REASONS and the disconnect_cases check constraint; reached by POST /disconnects/schedule, where the reason check runs FIRST
found_in: the disconnect wizard action census, 2026-09-21, driving the real service code against real PostgreSQL inside rolled-back transactions. A lawful final-tier case with every other precondition satisfied is refused on the reason alone
introduced_in: the wizard's reason picker, when the five buttons were written with abbreviated codes that were never compared against the server's own tuple or the database's CHECK constraint
escape_reason: NOTHING COMPARED THE TWO LISTS, AND A FRONT-END TEST PINS THE WRONG SPELLING IN PLACE. The front end holds its own copy of the five reason codes and asserts its own copy back, so the test is a mirror rather than a check -- it would pass for any five strings. No gate reads both sides, and the wizard's own test suite never commits, so the refusal that would have exposed it is never reached. It is also HIDDEN BY A SECOND DEFECT: all twelve distinct server refusals reach the clerk as the same eleven words, so pressing Tampering or theft and being refused looks identical to being two notices too early
prevention: One shared source for an enum a screen posts to a server, or a gate that reads both sides and fails when they differ -- this is the third family in this repo where a front-end constant duplicates a back-end tuple. Narrower and cheaper: a test that posts EACH offered reason and asserts the server accepts it, which is the check the mirror-test pretends to be. The general habit: a test asserting a constant against itself passes for every possible value of that constant

title: The transfer wizard's buyer step captures no DOCUMENT, so a buyer's identity papers cannot be filed at the moment of sale
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/customers/TransferWizard.tsx step 2 'The buyer' (the ApplicantCaptureFields block)
found_in: Chromium against a live Django+PostgreSQL+built SPA on tenant brazosbend at dcec7af91, walking a real sale of AC-2026-00012 with 10-scripts/po20260921_transfer_web_walk.mjs. Step 2 renders ZERO input[type=file] and its text mentions no document, upload, attachment, ID proof or KYC. Measured on the rendered step, not in source. The buyer's own details ARE captured - name, date of birth, driving licence, Social Security number, email, telephone, co-applicant and a separate billing address, all eight offered and every one keeping what is typed into it. Only the papers are missing. The door exists on the server: BR-CUS-1081's own table routes a buyer's KYC document to account_documents doc_type='kyc' through POST /accounts/{id}/documents, the endpoint is served (measured: upload 3 rows, DELETE 204), the account id is in hand at step 2 because a sale reassigns an account that already exists, and 07-frontend/src/components/documents/ landed on this branch at da35d25f as a shared component that ServiceRequestCapturePage - the move-in request the PO named as the benchmark - already uses.
introduced_in: the step as first written; git log -S 'input type=file' over TransferWizard.tsx returns nothing. The PO's ruling of 2026-09-20 ('step 2 dont allow to take kYC documents - DOB, all detaisl we need to create account - Similar to Move in request') was built as ApplicantCaptureFields, which carries the DETAILS half and no file control.
escape_reason: No test asserts the ABSENCE of a control, and an absence is invisible to every check this repo has - the wizard's 39 green cases and a clean tsc all pass over it, G13 asks whether a prop is passed rather than whether a required control exists, and no gate reads rendered output. BR-CUS-1081's table names the document row beside four that were built, so a reader of the rule would assume all five landed; only pressing the step in a browser shows that one did not.
prevention: Where a signed rule lists the places a captured fact lands, assert the SET on the rendered step and not each member - a test that counts the rule's rows against the step's controls goes red when one is missing rather than staying silent. Cheaper and generalisable: for any capture step built from a rule with a 'where it lands' table, one DOM case per row.

title: A completed property sale queues NO message at all - neither the buyer nor the seller is told
surface: 06-backend/apps/customers/transfers.py commit_transfer; the outbound queue (outbound_messages) and the review step's 'Telling them' panel in 07-frontend/src/features/customers/TransferWizard.tsx
found_in: Chromium against a live Django+PostgreSQL stack on brazosbend at dcec7af91, completing a real sale of AC-2026-00012 through the wizard's own 'Complete the sale' control. The outbound queue held 373 messages before the sale and 373 after it: the sale queued ZERO. Separately and more widely, 0 of those 373 have ever been sent - sent_at is null on every row on the tenant - so even a queued message would not have reached anybody. The three newest are staff_bulk_summary (in_app), sms_payment_received (sms) and email_payment_receipt (email), all status 'queued'. The PO asked for this by name on 2026-09-20: 'email, communcation is send'.
introduced_in: commit_transfer as first written for CR-030 W7 and unchanged by the BR-CUS-1030 rebuild of 2026-09-01; the conformance file 12-governance/26-the-transfer-does-not-transfer.md already records transfer_message_kind as one of its five keystones, with 81 checks behind it, and records the 'not one message has ever been sent' figure too.
escape_reason: The screen is HONEST about it - the review step reads 'Nobody is told about this sale. Tell the buyer and seller yourself.' - so a clerk walking the wizard sees a stated absence rather than a broken promise, and nothing reads that sentence and asks whether it should still be true. The scenario suite names the gap but drives services rather than a browser, and no front-end check can see a queue row. A stated absence is exactly the shape that survives every gate in this repository.
prevention: When a flow states an absence on screen ('nobody is told'), write the test that fires when the absence ends, in the same commit - assert the queue count does NOT move and name the rule, so the day a message is queued the suite goes red and somebody reads the sentence again. That is hard-won law 2's mirror applied to copy rather than to a control.

title: The four transfer walkthrough scripts hardcode /home/user/SMARTBillHub, so a lane running one from its own worktree drives ITS bundle and then reads ANOTHER BRANCH's Django to say what happened
surface: 10-scripts/po20260920_transfer_walkthrough.mjs (ROOT and createRequire), and the same shape in po20260920_transfer_record_walkthrough.mjs, po20260920_transfers_tab_walkthrough.mjs and def_cus_5934_transfer_wizard_walkthrough.mjs
found_in: Reading the four scripts while running one of them from /tmp/claude-0/wt-walk, a git worktree on claude/kind-wozniak-rl0uzt. po20260920_transfer_walkthrough.mjs opens with const ROOT = '/home/user/SMARTBillHub' and createRequire('/home/user/SMARTBillHub/07-frontend/package.json'), and every backend read, the purge invocation and the planted-state file it writes are built from that ROOT. The browser half is driven through TW_BASE, which a lane points at its OWN server.mjs. So the wizard under test is one branch's build and 'what the database says happened' is answered by another branch's ORM, models and selectors - and nothing in the output says which tree either half came from. CLAUDE.md law 11 tells every lane to work in its own worktree, so the hazard is the normal case rather than an edge one.
introduced_in: the scripts as first written on 2026-09-20; the shared checkout was the only tree any of them had been run from, so the constant was true on the day and silently false the first time a lane obeyed law 11.
escape_reason: Nothing goes red. The reads succeed, the JSON parses and the figures look right, because the two branches share one database and most of the schema - the divergence only shows where the branches differ, which is exactly the code a lane is there to test. It is law 7's 'looking at the wrong thing' with the added trap that the WRONG THING IS USUALLY RIGHT. No gate runs these scripts, so nothing has ever executed their preconditions.
prevention: Derive the root from the script's own location - path.resolve(path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..') - and PRINT it in the header alongside the interpreter, as 10-scripts/po20260921_transfer_web_walk.mjs now does. Generalisable: any script in 10-scripts/ that names an absolute repo path is making a claim about which checkout it is in, and the claim is false the moment a lane opens a worktree. A grep for the literal path across 10-scripts/ is a cheap one-off check.

title: --reuse-db on PostgreSQL reuses the test database by a PER-CHECKOUT name, not a migration digest, so a new migration is silently NOT applied and the code hits columns that do not exist
surface: 06-backend/config/settings/pgtest.py and base.py's TEST[NAME] derivation; reached by any pytest run with --ds=config.settings.pgtest --reuse-db, which is what 10-scripts/transfer_scenarios.sh and the move-out and move-in runners all use
found_in: the transfer seller-link lane, 2026-09-21. After adding customers/0060 and renaming one of its columns, two full suite runs reported 20 failed then 25 failed with 24 errors; the real error was 'current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block', which is hard-won law 14's signature and reads exactly like a code fault. The test database still carried the PREVIOUS name of the column. Confirmed by querying information_schema on the test database directly and by the wall clock: 78 seconds against a 304-second full rebuild
introduced_in: base.py's per-checkout TEST[NAME] derivation, which exists for a good reason -- it stops a git worktree colliding with the main tree on one shared database (DEF-054). The digest is of the CHECKOUT, not of the migration set
escape_reason: CLAUDE.md's own law 14 says the test database 'is now a file named for a digest of the migrations, so it rebuilds itself when they change' -- TRUE OF SQLITE and not of the PostgreSQL path, and the line does not say which. So a lane reading the law believes a migration change rebuilds the database, and nothing contradicts it: --reuse-db does not warn, does not error, and reports a normal-looking failure. The wall clock is the only signal and it is the thing a lane has stopped noticing, which is the same lesson DEF-GOV-3778 already recorded about --reuse-db doing nothing at all for a month
prevention: Either derive the PostgreSQL TEST[NAME] from the checkout AND a migration digest, so it rebuilds itself exactly as the SQLite path does, or make the pgtest runner refuse when the test database's applied-migration set differs from the tree's. Cheapest immediate step: amend law 14's sentence to say WHICH backend it is true of, because the law as written actively misleads. The general habit this repo already knows: a flag that is silently ignored is worse than one that errors

title: The Disconnects filter offers an On hold state that can never match a row
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/customers/DisconnectsTab.tsx (the + Filter panel) · 06-backend/apps/customers/disconnect_reads.py DISCONNECT_FILTER_STATES
escape_reason: The option list is derived on the server by subtracting the two states that take a row OFF this list - correct arithmetic over a vocabulary nobody measured against reality. disconnects.STATE_ON_HOLD is declared, is in migration 0022's CHECK vocabulary, and is assigned by NOTHING (the hold is derived from account_protections), so f.state=on_hold returns zero rows every time, on a list that shows held rows every day. No gate reads rendered output and no test asked whether an offered option can ever match, so the panel has offered a dead choice since CR-045 wave D. It also stops p142's On hold chip being buildable.
prevention: A filter option list is proved against the data it filters, not only against the enum it was derived from: for every option the server offers, assert that some reachable row can hold that value. The general shape is hard-won law 7's INCAPABLE OF PASSING - a control that looks live, answers nothing, and leaves tsc and every test green.

title: Scheduling a disconnection was TWO unwrapped writes, so a failed audit row left a household scheduled with nobody named
surface: POST /disconnects/schedule (S90 · DSC-02.5)
found_in: CR-125-BRC07, driving the completion path against real PostgreSQL, 2026-09-20
introduced_in: apps/customers/disconnects.schedule_cut, since the ladder shipped 2026-08-25
escape_reason: No check reads a comment. The route's docstring in transfer_disconnect_api.py CLAIMED 'one payload, one address, one transaction' and satisfied BR-SHL-019 on the first two; the guarantee lived in a DIFFERENT FILE from the two writes it described, so a reader of either found nothing wrong (hard-won law 1). ATOMIC_REQUESTS is off and no gate asks whether a service that writes a row and then an audit row wraps them. Every happy-path test passes on the broken version - only a test that MAKES the audit write fail can see it, and none did.
prevention: transaction.atomic() around the case write and its audit row, at the ACT and not at the route (a route-level wrapper would be ATOMIC_REQUESTS on one lane's authority). stop_by_hand had the identical shape and is wrapped in the same commit. Both proved by a test that explodes _audit and asserts the case row did not move - tests/test_disconnect_wizard_cr125_brc07.py.

title: A disconnection was accepted and recorded for a service this utility does not sell - the cut for 'unicorn' was stored
surface: POST /disconnects/schedule (S90 · DSC-02.1's per-service table)
found_in: CR-125-BRC07, driving the completion path against real PostgreSQL, 2026-09-20

title: TWO DEFECTS CAN SHARE A NUMBER WHILE THEIR IDS DIFFER, AND NOTHING COUNTS IT. The PO's 2026-09-03 ruling is ONE RUNNING NUMBER across the whole register - 'register max + 1, so ids stay unique' - with the module code as a prefix and nothing renumbered. On the branch today that is broken three times: DEF-CUS-6050 and DEF-SHL-6050, DEF-GOV-6056 and DEF-MET-6056, DEF-CUS-6057 and DEF-MET-6057. G17 passes over all three because it keys on the full STRING, and the strings are unique; its only complaint is the same-string triples DEF-GOV-6056 already covers. CLAUDE.md states this hazard for CHANGE REQUESTS in as many words - 'the STRING is unique and the NUMBER is not, and a number is what a person says out loud and cites from a business rule' - and says G17 is the layer that ensures it. It ensures it for CRs and not for defects. Lane NCD-1 hit it live: file_defect.py printed 'allocated DEF-6056' and 'allocated DEF-6057', both correct against what that lane could see, and both numbers had been taken by siblings in other modules minutes earlier. Those two rows were renumbered to DEF-MET-6058 and DEF-MET-6059 before this was filed; DEF-CUS-6050 and DEF-SHL-6050 are left, because renumbering somebody else's row is how a citation dangles.
surface: 10-scripts/gates/g17_duplicate_ids.py (keys on the full id string) and 10-scripts/file_defect.py / allocate.py, which allocate a NUMBER and cannot see a sibling's unpushed row
found_in: lane NCD-1 (CR-126-BRC07) re-verifying its own allocated ids against the tip at push time, as CLAUDE.md law 11 requires, 2026-09-21
introduced_in: the 2026-09-03 module-prefix ruling: from that day two lanes in different modules can compute the same maximum and both be right, and no check compares numbers across prefixes
escape_reason: THE CHECK IS TRUE OVER THE SCOPE IT LOOKS AT AND THAT SCOPE IS THE WRONG ONE - law 7's fifth shape. G17 asks whether an ID is defined twice and the answer is honestly no; the question the ruling actually asks is whether a NUMBER is issued twice, and nothing asks it. It is also invisible at allocation time by construction: allocate.py reads the remote plus this checkout, and a sibling in its own worktree has its row in NEITHER until it pushes, so both lanes compute max+1 correctly and get the same answer. The register reads as a register - a duplicate number in 3,571 rows looks like nothing at all.
prevention: Have G17 compare the NUMBER as well as the string for the OQ and DEF families, exactly as it already does for CR - one regex change, and it fails a duplicate number even when the prefixes differ. Cheaper and complementary: have allocate.py print the colliding row when the number it hands out is already taken under another prefix, so a lane sees it at the moment it can still renumber for free. The durable form is CLAUDE.md's own answer for CRs - a disjoint number block per branch, recorded in 14-id-reservations.md before that branch starts.

The number it should be weighed against is 06-backend/apps/billing/payments_seam.py::credit_position_for_account, which BR-BIL-160 already uses one module over. NOT the allocation engine and NOT the seed.

The gap is that BR-BIL-160 taught BILLING to weigh the credit position against a migrated opening balance on 2026-08-27 and nothing taught the DISCONNECT gate. It could not be seen before 2026-09-20 because before then no cut had ever committed.
escape_reason: Both halves are individually correct and individually tested. The allocation engine does what BR-PAY-001 and BR-PAY-012 say - a payment meets an INVOICE and the remainder becomes account credit - and OQ-570 is already registered for the half that is inferred rather than recorded. The gate does what BR-PAY-036 and BR-CUS-104 say. Nothing tests the two TOGETHER, because no cut had ever committed until today. It is invisible on screen too: the record shows 'To clear $1,354.50' beside 'Owes now $1,204.50', both true, with nothing saying the account has already paid $2,409.00. AND THE WALK THAT FOUND IT NEARLY MISSED IT THE SAME WAY: its first run asserted the payment's HTTP 201 when the thing under test was the BALANCE, so it reported success over a gate that had not moved - a check that asserts the call succeeded when the NUMBER is the subject is the shape that hides this whole class.
prevention: THE DECISION, AND IT IS OURS TO MAKE AND WRITE DOWN RATHER THAN THE PO'S: what does 'what this account owes' mean on the disconnect path - the ledger receivable alone, or BR-BIL-160's pair? Billing has already answered it for the bill, and the two answers must not stay different, because they are the same sentence to a customer. Whoever takes it: it is a money path and a 4-decimal one, BR-PAY-041 says a negative position is a real debt and must not be floored, and weighing a ledger receivable against a ledger liability is an accounting judgment that belongs in the decision log with its worked figure. DO NOT make one number agree with the other by changing the seed - the seed is right. THE TEST THAT WOULD CATCH IT: take a real payment for the full arrears of an account whose balance arrived as an opening bucket, and assert the figure the GATE reads becomes 0.00 - not that the call returned 201.

surface: 07-frontend/src/features/customers/newConnectDraft.ts commitPlanOf pushes a meters row only where takesAMeter(service) is true, and CommitPlan has no unit_services member - so trash, fire, storm water, broadband and thermal heat are mapped to units by step 4's grid in the browser and travel on no key of the payload. 06-backend/apps/metering/connections.py commit_connection step 2b therefore writes a connection_services row for the METERED services only, and the build record's unit count, service tags and service-point tile are short by the rest.

title: THE VERSION BUMP IS FOUR HAND-TYPED LITERALS IN THREE FILES AND ONE FILE CARRIES IT TWICE, SO A CORRECT sed BUMPS HALF OF IT
surface: 07-frontend/package-lock.json carries the version on line 3 (the lockfile's own) AND line 9 (packages."" mirroring package.json). The bump to 2.322.0 was applied with sed -i '0,/2\.321\.0/s//2.322.0/', which by construction replaces ONE match, so line 3 moved and line 9 stayed at 2.321.0. 10-scripts/allocate.py version --bump PRINTS the next number and writes nothing - the four literals are typed by hand at the last moment of a lane's work
found_in: 2.322.0, on 2026-09-21 - G35 reported 'package.json 2.322.0 vs package-lock.json 2.321.0' to a lane running the suite for unrelated work. The bump had been pushed to claude/laughing-thompson-kpmwih, so the branch sat with its own version gate red until the lane read the failure it had not caused
introduced_in: with the bump itself, in this session
escape_reason: G35 CAUGHT IT - this is the gate working, and the escape is upstream of it. Nothing runs G35 at the moment of a bump; it runs when someone next runs the suite, which was a sibling lane doing something else. The deeper gap is that allocate.py owns the NUMBER and not the WRITING: it prints 2.322.0 and leaves a human to place it in four spots across three files in two languages, which is exactly the shape 13-change-process.md step 7 says is 'many times not followed correctly'. A step that depends on someone remembering four places is the step that goes wrong
prevention: allocate.py version --bump gains a --write that applies the number to all four literals itself and prints what it changed, so the number and its placement are one act. Until then: after any bump, grep -c the OLD version across the three files and expect 0, and run G35 before pushing rather than after. AND THE GENERAL SHAPE IS CLAUDE.md LAW 7's HABIT 1 WORKING AS INTENDED - a lane read a red it did not cause, said so, and named the owner; that is the only reason this was found in minutes rather than at merge

title: Two lanes took defect number 6199 under different module prefixes and G17 cannot see it, because it compares ID STRINGS and the rule is about the NUMBER
surface: 12-governance/10-defect-log.csv rows 3700-3701; 10-scripts/gates/g17_duplicate_ids.py; 10-scripts/file_defect.py
introduced_in: 2026-09-22 - lane P1-B took DEF-PAY-6199 and lane P0-DB took DEF-QAE-6199 within the hour, each allocating correctly against the world it could see
escape_reason: CLAUDE.md is explicit that there is ONE running number across the whole register - the register maximum plus one, so ids stay unique - and the module segment is a label on that number, not a namespace. G17 refuses a duplicate ID DEFINITION, so it compares DEF-PAY-6199 with DEF-QAE-6199, finds two different strings and passes. It reported exactly two duplicates on this branch and neither was this one. That is precisely the hazard CLAUDE.md already records one family along for CR numbers - the STRING is unique and the NUMBER is not, and a number is what a person says out loud - and the cure written there is G17 failing a duplicate NUMBER even when the suffixes differ. The same cure was never applied to the DEF family. allocate.py and file_defect.py both compute the maximum across every prefix, so they cannot ISSUE a collision from one world; what neither can do is stop two lanes in different worktrees computing the same right answer.
prevention: Teach G17 to compare the NUMBER for the DEF and OQ families as it already does for CR - strip the optional module segment before grouping. Until then a lane meeting a suspected collision greps the register for the bare number rather than the full id. This lane renumbered its own row to DEF-QAE-6200 because it was the LATER of the two (register row 3701 against 3700), which is DEF-053's convention, and did it as a byte-splice of one line so no other lane's row could move.

title: Three 'clean' type-checks were timeouts, so the branch carried three TypeScript errors for a whole session and every push reported green
surface: 07-frontend/src/features/payments/CountersTab.tsx + CounterDoors.tsx, and the lane's own tsc invocation
found_in: 2026-09-23, LANE P2-SCREENS, by running tsc with NO timeout wrapper and capturing its exit code
introduced_in: 35f86b374 (the required timeZone/dateFormat on CountersTabProps) and f77dca804 (size=small, where the kit's sizes are default|sm|row)
escape_reason: The lane ran 'timeout 560 tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json | head -30'. Under load this box needs longer than 560s, so timeout killed tsc BEFORE it printed anything - and the pipeline's exit code is head's, which is 0. The result was an EMPTY output file and a zero exit, which is indistinguishable from a clean pass and was read as one THREE TIMES. It is hard-won law 7's 'structurally incapable of failing' shape, and the sibling of the npx-tsc trap the react-tailwind-css-ui-generator skill already warns about: that one fetches a newer compiler and aborts on a config error, this one is killed before it speaks. Nothing downstream could catch it: vitest and vite build both strip types with esbuild rather than checking them, so 35 passing cases and two successful production builds were all green over a red type-check.
prevention: Never wrap tsc in 'timeout' and never pipe it to head. Redirect to a FILE and append the exit code in the same command - 'tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json > out.txt 2>&1; echo "TSC EXIT=$?" >> out.txt' - then refuse to call it green until the file literally contains 'TSC EXIT=0'. An empty output file with no exit line is a KILLED run, not a clean one. The general rule this is an instance of: a check whose output cannot distinguish pass from fail to a reader is worse than no check, because it is trusted.

title: BE-05 drops an undeclared f.<name> filter SILENTLY, so a narrowed question is answered with the whole list and the caller cannot tell
surface: 06-backend/core/pagination.py::parse_list_params
introduced_in: BE-05
escape_reason: It is not a bug in any one endpoint, so no endpoint's tests cover it, and it is DOCUMENTED behaviour - parse_list_params carries the comment 'undeclared filter names are ignored' and BR-SHL-010's fall-back-or-clamp semantics are deliberate for sort and dir, where falling back to a default is harmless. A filter is not like a sort. Falling back on a sort gives you the same ROWS in a different order; falling back on a filter gives you DIFFERENT ROWS, more of them, and a caller that asked to be narrowed reads row 0 as though it had been. DEF-PAY-6235 (lane P2-HEAD's row) is what that costs on one screen: GET /counters?f.mine=1&per=1 answered the supervisor's list of everyone's open tills, and the payments page head announced a colleague's drawer as 'Your counter' beside a button that takes money. Nothing went red - the read succeeded, both states rendered, and per=1 made the wrong row arrive faster.
prevention: Refused on GET /counters today by counters_api._refuse_an_unknown_filter, which is a local fix and says so: making parse_list_params refuse globally would change the answer of every list endpoint in the product on one screen's authority, and a client sending a stray f.* that has been quietly ignored for weeks would start 400-ing. THE QUESTION THIS ROW CARRIES: should an undeclared f.<name> refuse everywhere? Three shapes to weigh - (a) refuse, which is what this lane did locally and what makes a client bug visible at the moment it is written; (b) a strict_filters flag each endpoint opts into, which is safe and will be forgotten by exactly the endpoints that need it; (c) leave it and require every list's tests to assert the NARROWING rather than the shape, which is the check that would have caught this one. Whichever is chosen, the measurable thing first: count how many f.* names the front end sends today that no endpoint declares. If it is zero, (a) costs nothing.

title: Two suite reds nobody was reading: a P2.22 ledger assertion incapable of PASSING beside its mirror incapable of FAILING, and a close-count test red since billing published unissued_run_count on 2026-09-17

escape_reason: Both are reds that were being scrolled past. The P2.22 one is the sharper: JournalLine.ledger_account_id is a uuid.UUID and ledger.selectors.gl_account_id_for_designation returns a str, so 'assert debit.ledger_account_id == account_id' was FALSE for every value there has ever been - red from the moment ff1b3b3ee landed, never once green - and the very next line, 'assert credit.ledger_account_id != account_id', was TRUE for the same reason whatever account was credited, so a pair posted to the wrong side would have sailed through it. Both shapes law 7 names, on one money path, two lines apart. The identical fault sat in cr136_p2_counters_postgres_proof.py part D (DEF-PAY-6239), which says the comparison is the habit rather than the typo. The close-count one is a hold whose clock ran out: the test asserts billing has NOT published unissued_run_count, billing published it on 2026-09-17 in 8ca658102, and the test has been red ever since saying 'complete' == 'unknown'.
